One notable example is the Ekene Dili Chukwu Group, founded by the late transport mogul Augustine Ilodibe. The company, which operated a major fleet of luxury buses and haulage trucks, was a leading player in Nigeria’s transport industry. After Mr Ilodibe died in 2007, the business declined amid disputes among family members over his estate and the company’s management.

Another example is the Concord Group, founded by the late businessman and politician Moshood Abiola. The conglomerate included Concord Newspapers, Concord Airlines, Abiola Farms and Wonder Loaf Bakery. After Mr Abiola died in 1998, the businesses gradually declined, with the newspaper eventually ceasing publication and several other ventures disappearing.

The Henry Stephens Group, founded by businessman Henry Fajemirokun, also experienced a similar fate. The conglomerate had interests in engineering, banking, insurance, shipping and oil, but its fortunes declined after his death in 1978.

These examples illustrate the challenges of sustaining family businesses beyond their founders.

World.title: Methane Emissions: Ogun, FG intensify investigation in Ijebu-Ode, pledge lasting solution
World.content:
The Ogun State Government has intensified collaboration with the Federal Government to investigate and address recurring methane emission incidents in Ijebu-Ode and neighbouring communities, assuring residents that concrete measures are being taken to establish the source of the emissions and prevent future occurrences.

The intervention follows four reported incidents of gas emissions in Ijebu-Ode and its environs, which have generated persistent unpleasant odour and raised concerns among residents about possible environmental and health implications.

In a statement issued on Tuesday and signed by the Special Adviser on Media and Strategy to Governor Dapo Abiodun, Kayode Akinmade, the government disclosed that a joint team of experts from the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC), alongside development partners, had commenced investigations into the incidents.

The team, led by the Commission’s Deputy Director, Mr Omonedo Prosper, is currently examining emission patterns and possible sources of the gas, following preliminary briefings by state government officials on interventions already undertaken.

According to the statement, the NUPRC delegation expressed its readiness to work with the Ogun State Government and other relevant agencies to establish the cause of the emissions and develop a sustainable solution.

Akinmade said the state government was committed to making the findings of the investigation available promptly, implementing appropriate preventive measures and providing necessary health support and monitoring for affected communities.

He identified Ijebu-Ode, Ijebu East and Odogbolu, as well as other communities across Ogun East, as areas requiring attention as investigations and monitoring continue.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“We believe that collaboration with the Federal Government and research institutions is crucial. The Ogun State Government is resolute in its decision to implement the recommendations of the investigating team once investigations are concluded and to take concrete steps to ensure that the emissions do not recur,” he said.

The government stressed that the welfare, safety and well-being of residents remained its paramount responsibility, assuring communities that it would sustain its engagement with relevant federal agencies and technical experts until the matter was comprehensively addressed.

It would be recalled that following the incidents, the Head of the Department of Earth Sciences at Olabisi Onabanjo University, Professor Ikhane Phillips, explained that geochemical analysis would help determine the composition and source of the gas, while geophysical investigations would establish its possible underground origin and movement.

He noted that findings from ongoing site inspections and laboratory tests would provide the scientific basis for determining the appropriate interventions.

Similarly, the Commissioner for Environment, Mr Ola Oresanya, had disclosed that the state was working closely with the Federal Government to tackle the situation.

Oresanya also called for improved information sharing to address public concerns, while advising residents on precautionary measures during periods of unpleasant odour. He had also assured residents that the gas was not lethal.

Meanwhile, Ijebu Para’po Info Media has commended Governor Abiodun and the NUPRC for their intervention and efforts to find a lasting solution to the recurring emissions.

The group praised the state government for responding to the concerns of residents and maintaining engagement with relevant authorities, expressing optimism that the ongoing investigation would produce a permanent solution.

World.title: Nigerian lawmakers propose six-month jail term for doctors, nurses who delay emergency treatment
World.content:
The Senate on Wednesday passed for second reading a bill seeking to amend Nigeria’s National Health Act to prescribe a six-month jail term or an option of a fine of up to ₦300,000 for hospitals and healthcare workers who delay emergency medical treatment.

Senate President Godswill Akpabio announced the passage during plenary after a majority of senators supported it by voice vote.

After its passage, the bill was referred to the Senate Committee on Tertiary and Primary Health for further legislative scrutiny and a public hearing.

The proposed legislation is titled “A Bill for an Act to Amend the National Health Act, 2014 to Provide for Emergency Medical Treatment Standards and Referral Protocols in Healthcare Facilities and for Related Matters”.

The bill, sponsored by Abdulaziz Yar’adua (APC, Katsina Central), seeks to establish mandatory standards for hospitals and healthcare providers attending to patients requiring emergency medical attention.

The proposed amendment prescribed that hospitals would be required to commence treatment within 15 minutes of a patient’s arrival.

It also seeks to mandate hospitals, doctors, nurses and other healthcare providers to begin basic stabilisation measures, including oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids, pain relief and preliminary diagnostic procedures, within 30 minutes of arrival.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Leading the debate on the bill, Mr Yar’adua said that, where a licensed medical doctor is unavailable, a trained and certified nurse could conduct the initial assessment of an emergency patient and immediately commence treatment.

He said the bill also provides for immediate life-saving interventions, including cardiopulmonary resuscitation, airway management and bleeding control, once a life-threatening condition is identified.

The proposed legislation would prohibit hospitals from rejecting emergency patients, regardless of the circumstances, and require them to provide appropriate medical attention.

Other critical provisions

For patients requiring admission, the bill stipulates that a hospital bed should be assigned within two hours of arrival, provided bed space is available.

Where a healthcare facility lacks the capacity to admit an emergency patient, it would be required to commence resuscitation and stabilisation immediately and initiate the referral process within two hours of arrival or as soon as the patient is clinically assessed and considered stable for transfer, whichever comes first.

The bill further proposes that the transfer process be completed within three hours of arrival, except where external circumstances, including transportation difficulties, insecurity or natural conditions, prevent compliance.

To minimise delays during referrals, hospitals would also be required to commence ambulance dispatch or secure alternative patient transportation within 30 minutes of communicating a decision to refer a patient.

The proposed amendment, however, protects healthcare practitioners who document their inability to meet the prescribed requirements because of inadequate resources.

Such practitioners would be required to comply with the referral protocol and report the circumstances to hospital management or the appropriate authority.

Patients who died after alleged delays in emergency treatment

Nigeria has recorded several cases of patients who died after allegedly being denied or delayed emergency medical treatment at hospitals. Some of the most prominent cases involved victims of armed robbery and road accidents who reportedly encountered administrative barriers while seeking urgent medical attention.

In September 2009, Bayo Ohu, a journalist with The Guardian, was shot by armed men who invaded his Lagos home. He was reportedly denied treatment at a hospital because his relatives did not have a police report. He died while being taken to another hospital.

In November 2019, Moradeun Balogun, a 29-year-old podcast host, was stabbed by armed robbers in Lagos. She was reportedly denied treatment at a hospital because she did not have a police report. She was subsequently taken to another facility, where she died.

In 2021, Ebenezer Ayeni, an Ibadan-based music producer, was shot by armed robbers shortly before his wedding. He was reportedly taken to the University College Hospital and J-Rapha Hospital, both of which allegedly demanded a police report before treating him. He died about four hours after the shooting.

In October 2023, Greatness Olorunfemi was reportedly pushed out of a moving commercial vehicle by suspected “one-chance” criminals in Abuja. She was taken to Maitama District Hospital. Although, a panel set up by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesome Wike, later revealed that the victim was brought to the Maitama Hospital dead

In another case, an unidentified boy who was among victims of a road accident along the Bauchi-Jos Highway reportedly died after being denied treatment at Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University Teaching Hospital in Bauchi because of a lack of bed space. The hospital subsequently set up a committee to investigate the incident.

These incidents and several others have raised concerns about the enforcement of existing laws requiring healthcare providers to prioritise emergency medical care and the need for stronger accountability for hospitals and medical personnel.

The proposed amendment seeks to address such concerns by establishing mandatory timelines for emergency treatment, stabilisation and referral, while providing sanctions for healthcare providers who fail to comply.

World.title: Reps propose fines, licence withdrawal for hospitals that delay emergency treatment
World.content:
The House of Representatives has passed a bill for second reading that seeks to impose financial penalties, suspend licences, and shut down healthcare facilities that refuse or delay emergency medical treatment.

The proposed legislation also seeks to introduce criminal penalties for health workers who wilfully refuse to attend to emergency patients or abandon them.

Sponsored by Akin Rotimi (APC, Ekiti), the bill seeks to amend the National Health Act, 2014, to strengthen emergency medical services and establish enforceable standards for triage, stabilisation and referral across healthcare institutions.

The bill passed second reading during Wednesday’s plenary after lawmakers considered its general principles.

Presenting the bill, Mr Rotimi, the House spokesperson, said. However, ugh the National Health Act prohibits hospitals from refusing emergency treatment, “Nigerians continue to lose their lives or suffer preventable complications because of delays arising from administrative bottlenecks, demands for payment before treatment, unavailable hospital beds and poorly coordinated referrals.”

He argued that the existing legal provisions needed to be reinforced with clear operational standards and consequences for non-compliance.

According to Mr Rotimi, the proposed amendment provides for financial penalties, suspension of operating licences and possible closure or withdrawal of licences for healthcare establishments that refuse, delay or obstruct emergency medical treatment.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said it also provides for criminal sanctions and professional disciplinary proceedings against health workers who deliberately refuse to attend to emergency patients or abandon them.

The bill, he said, further proposes civil compensation against healthcare facilities where a violation of the emergency treatment provisions results in injury, disability or death.

However, it seeks to protect healthcare workers from liability where they act in good faith, properly document resource limitations and comply with established referral procedures.

Beyond sanctions, the proposed legislation introduces mandatory timelines for healthcare facilities attending to emergency patients.

It requires hospitals to commence triage within 15 minutes of a patient’s arrival and begin basic stabilisation within 30 minutes.

Life-saving interventions must commence immediately once a life-threatening condition is identified. Where a medical practitioner is unavailable, trained and certified nurses may conduct triage.

The bill also requires that patients needing admission be assigned an available hospital bed within two hours.

Where a facility has no available bed, it must commence stabilisation and initiate a referral within two hours of the patient’s arrival or immediately after clinical stabilisation.

It further requires hospitals to arrange transportation within 30 minutes of a referral decision and complete the transfer within three hours, except where circumstances beyond their control prevent this.

The proposed amendment also mandates healthcare workers involved in emergency medical services to undergo training and certification at intervals not exceeding 18 months.

It assigns the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria and the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria the responsibility of jointly developing and maintaining a standardised national emergency care curriculum.

Mr Rotimi said the provisions were intended to ensure the right to emergency treatment is reflected in actual healthcare delivery rather than remaining a declaration in law.

READ ALSO: Closing the gap between healthcare availability and access in Nigeria

“In a medical emergency, time is the difference between life and death,” he said.

He added that the bill would distinguish genuine resource limitations from negligence and deliberate abandonment while strengthening institutional accountability.

Debate

Contributing to the debate, Chinedu Ogah (APC, Ebonyi) supported the bill but called for provisions linking emergency medical treatment to health insurance coverage.

He said emergency patients should not be required to make deposits or wait for payment arrangements before receiving medical attention.

Mr Ogah suggested the bill should require emergency patients to be covered under the National Health Insurance Scheme to ensure financial constraints do not delay treatment.

“They should liaise with health insurance, so that all those emergency people must be insured by the National Health Insurance Scheme, so that every moment they have sucan h emergency, they will not wait for any deposit for them to be treated,” he said.

His contribution was seconded by Makki Yalleman (APC, Jigawa).

Following the debate, Benjamin Kalu, the Deputy Speaker, who presided over the plenary, referred the bill to the House Committee on Health Services for further legislative action.

World.title: Enugu Air begins Lagos–London operation in December – Official
World.content:
Enugu Air has secured regulatory approval to commence direct flights from Lagos to London Gatwick in December 2026, marking a major milestone in the airline’s international expansion.

The state-owned airline also announced that bookings for the new route are now open, with intending passengers able to make reservations through its online booking portal.

The airline disclosed this in a statement issued on Wednesday, describing the approval as a significant step towards strengthening air connectivity between Nigeria and the United Kingdom.

The development comes barely six weeks after Enugu Air operated its maiden international flight to Douala, Cameroon, on 23 September 2026.

According to the statement, the Lagos–London Gatwick service will be operated in partnership with Omni-Blu Aviation (OBA), which has been designated as the operating partner for the route.

“Enugu Air has received approval for its Lagos–London Gatwick route, with Omni-Blu Aviation (OBA) appointed as the designated operator under a strategic partnership.

“Bookings are now open, and flights will commence in December 2026.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The approval marks a major milestone in Enugu Air’s expansion, strengthening connectivity between Nigeria and the United Kingdom and opening new opportunities for passengers and trade.

“This milestone reflects the bold vision and transformative leadership of the Executive Governor of Enugu State, His Excellency, Dr Peter Ndubuisi Mbah, whose strategic aviation agenda is positioning Enugu as an emerging gateway for international connectivity, investment, tourism and economic growth,” the statement read.

Enugu Air was launched in July 2025 with an initial fleet of three Embraer aircraft, comprising the E170 and E190 series, as part of the Mbah administration’s integrated blueprint for a modern, multimodal transport ecosystem.

The initiative is also aimed at positioning Enugu as a major regional aviation hub in West and Central Africa.

Since its launch, the airline has expanded its fleet and route network, with the latest approval signalling a further push into international operations.

The commencement of the Lagos–London service is expected to broaden travel options for passengers, strengthen business and trade links, and enhance Nigeria’s air connectivity with the United Kingdom.

World.title: IOM moves to combat migration misinformation
World.content:
… Partners PAU on research, fact-checking, ethical journalism

By Sola Ogundipe

The International Organisation for Migration (IOM) and Pan-Atlantic University (PAU) have entered into a partnership to tackle misinformation, negative narratives and irresponsible media reporting on migration in Nigeria through research, journalism training and improved media education.

The partnership, formalised through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed by IOM and the university’s School of Media and Communication, seeks to strengthen public understanding of migration and equip journalists, students and communication professionals with the skills to report migration issues accurately, ethically and responsibly.

The initiative comes amid growing concerns over how migration is portrayed in public discourse, particularly the tendency to frame it largely around crises, irregular movement and negative experiences, often overlooking its human, economic and social dimensions.

Under the agreement, both institutions will develop academic content, organise training programmes for journalists and communication professionals, conduct joint research and create practical learning opportunities for students.

The collaboration will also explore digital storytelling, fact-checking, multimedia journalism and public awareness campaigns to counter misinformation and promote more balanced discussions on migration.

Speaking at the signing ceremony, IOM Nigeria Chief of Mission, Sharon Dimanche, said the partnership represented an investment in the people responsible for shaping public understanding of migration.

She observed that migration was frequently reduced to statistics, crises and negative headlines, with the human experiences behind it receiving inadequate attention.

“Migration is often reduced to numbers, crises or negative headlines. But behind every movement is a person, a family and a story. If we want people to understand migration better, we must invest in those who shape the conversation, particularly journalists, students, researchers and communicators. This partnership will help bring evidence, practical experience and human stories into classrooms, newsrooms and public discussions,” Dimanche said.

She stressed that improving public understanding required deliberate investment in journalists, students, researchers and other communicators who influence how migration is discussed.

According to her, the partnership would bring evidence, practical experience and human stories into classrooms, newsrooms and public conversations.

The Vice-Chancellor of Pan-Atlantic University, Professor Enase Okonedo, FCA, welcomed the agreement, describing the collaboration as an opportunity to connect academic research and teaching with the realities of migration in communities.

Okonedo said the partnership would give students, faculty members and media professionals opportunities to engage directly with migration experts while strengthening their knowledge and professional competencies.

“Migration affects economies, communities and individual lives in many different ways. Universities have an important role in helping society understand these issues through research, education and informed debate. Our partnership with IOM will create opportunities for students, faculty and media professionals to engage directly with migration experts and strengthen their knowledge and professional skills,” she said.

Also speaking, Dean of the School of Media and Communication, Dr Ikechukwu Obiaya, said the collaboration would promote public awareness, strengthen ethical journalism and equip media professionals and students to address migration-related issues more effectively.

He said that students would benefit from practical learning opportunities, while joint research initiatives would generate evidence-based findings to inform public discourse and migration policies.

“Migration affects economies, communities and individual lives in many different ways. Universities have an important role in helping society understand these issues through research, education and informed debate. Our partnership with IOM will create opportunities for students, faculty and media professionals to engage directly with migration experts and strengthen their knowledge and professional skills,” he noted.

The agreement builds on previous cooperation between IOM and the School of Media and Communication on migration communication and journalist capacity development, including initiatives associated with the Global Migration Media Academy, which promotes ethical and responsible reporting on migration.

Both institutions are also expected to explore joint lectures, research projects, mentorship programmes, workshops and public dialogues involving journalists, government agencies, civil society organisations, academics and migration practitioners.

The partnership comes as IOM marks 25 years of operations in Nigeria, while Pan-Atlantic University’s School of Media and Communication celebrates its 20th anniversary. Although the MoU does not involve financial commitments, specific activities will be implemented through jointly agreed work plans.

The collaboration is expected to strengthen the capacity of a new generation of journalists and communication professionals to interrogate migration issues beyond sensational headlines and contribute to more accurate, evidence-based public conversations.

World.title: HIV: Lagos survey reveals treatment gains, testing gap
World.content:
… Women record twice men’s prevalence as state targets wider coverage

By Chioma Obinna

Lagos State has recorded significant progress in HIV treatment, with 93.4 per cent of people living with the virus who know their status receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), a new survey has revealed.

However, only 58.3 per cent of people living with HIV know their status, highlighting a major testing gap that could undermine efforts to control the epidemic.

The 2025–2026 Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) Impact Survey also found that HIV prevalence among adults aged 15 to 64 was twice as high among women as men, at 1.6 per cent and 0.8 per cent, respectively.

The findings were presented at the dissemination of the Lagos State Summary Sheet of the survey at the Sheraton Hotel, Ikeja, on Wednesday.

The survey has prompted renewed calls for intensified HIV testing, improved access to treatment and sustainable funding to close existing gaps in the state’s response.

Speaking at the event, the Permanent Secretary, Lagos State Ministry of Health, Dr Dayo Lajide, described the survey as an important milestone in strengthening the state’s HIV response through credible evidence and informed decision-making.

She said the findings would help assess progress since the 2018 Nigeria HIV/AIDS Indicator and Impact Survey and support efforts towards achieving the UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets.

Lajide disclosed that “the 2025 HIV Health Sector Report estimated that 192,911 people were living with HIV in Lagos, while 129,977 were receiving antiretroviral therapy, representing 65.7 per cent treatment coverage and leaving more than 60,000 people outside treatment.”

She also highlighted gaps in services for mothers and children, noting that although prevention of mother-to-child transmission coverage increased from 45 per cent in 2018 to 57.6 per cent in 2025, early infant diagnosis and paediatric treatment remained areas of concern.

The Permanent Secretary called for targeted interventions to improve case identification, treatment linkage, retention in care and services for children exposed to HIV.

She reaffirmed the state government’s commitment to sustaining services through the procurement of rapid diagnostic kits and antiretroviral medicines, strengthening health systems and integrating HIV services into routine healthcare.

Lajide also stressed the need for domestic resource mobilisation and sustainable financing amid changes in the global healthcare funding landscape.

Presenting the survey findings, APIN/PHIS3 Survey Lead, Dr Ubong Okon, said the assessment examined HIV prevalence, testing, treatment access and viral load suppression.

Conducted between November 2025 and February 2026, the survey covered 205 enumeration areas and 6,450 households. Okon disclosed that 93.5 per cent of the 6,748 eligible households completed household interviews.

The findings showed that while 93.4 per cent of people living with HIV who knew their status were receiving treatment, 88.9 per cent of those on treatment had achieved viral load suppression.

Health Assistant Coordinator in the Office of the US Embassy’s Department of State, Abuja, Omoshalewa Oyelaran, identified awareness of HIV status as a major priority, stressing that people who do not know their status cannot be linked to treatment.

She said the survey provided Lagos with a clear and independent picture of the epidemic, showing who was living with HIV, receiving treatment and achieving viral suppression.

APIN Public Health Initiatives Chief Executive Officer, Dr Jay Osi Samuels, described the survey as a major achievement and called for more regular assessments to ensure that policymakers had timely information to guide interventions.

He also acknowledged the support of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (US CDC), commending Lagos State and other stakeholders for their cooperation.

US CDC Country Deputy Director, Dr Gbolahan Cole, said the United States Government had invested significantly in the survey, including training field personnel and strengthening laboratory capacity.

He reaffirmed the agency’s commitment to working with Lagos State and its partners to address the identified gaps and provide technical assistance.

Meanwhile, Lagos State AIDS Control Agency Chief Executive Officer, Dr Folakemi Animashaun, said the findings came at a critical time as the state moves towards greater domestic ownership of its HIV response.

She said the survey would guide planning, budgeting, accountability and funding priorities, stressing that its value depended on translating the findings into action.

The Network of People Living with HIV/AIDS in Nigeria, represented by its Strategy Manager, Inolode Emmanuel, urged stakeholders to keep community voices central to HIV interventions.

He described antiretroviral therapy as representing “hope, dignity, survival and the opportunity to live a healthy life.”

Director of Disease Control, Lagos State Ministry of Health, Dr Oladipupo Fisher, urged stakeholders to use the findings to strengthen interventions, reach people living with HIV who remain outside care and improve treatment outcomes.

The survey was supported by the United States Government in collaboration with federal and state health agencies, APIN/PHIS3, civil society organisations and community representatives. Stakeholders called for sustained investment and evidence-based action to advance efforts to end HIV as a public health threat by 2030.

World.title: FG tasks education academy with digital skills revolution
World.content:
…Jegede demands policy overhaul, AI integration, teacher training reform

By Joseph Erunke, Abuja

The Federal Government has designated the Nigerian Academy of Education (NAE) as the country’s apex national institution for digital literacy and leadership development, as part of efforts to align the education system with emerging technologies and future workforce demands.

However, the Academy has called for an urgent review of the National Policy on Education, a comprehensive overhaul of teacher education and professional development, and fundamental changes to classroom teaching and learning to achieve the objective.

The President of the Academy, Emeritus Professor Olugbemiro Jegede, disclosed the new national mandate at the opening of the NAE 2026 Annual Congress in Abuja, where he urged the government to move beyond piecemeal reforms and address structural weaknesses in the education sector.

The congress was attended by the Minister of Education, members of the National and State Assemblies, heads of educational parastatals and other stakeholders.

Under the new arrangement, the Academy is expected to spearhead the development of Nigeria’s national digital skills framework and provide intellectual leadership for policies aimed at preparing students and the future workforce for a technology-driven economy.

Its responsibilities will include promoting the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), emerging technologies, innovative teaching methods and evidence-based practices into education policies and classroom delivery.

Speaking at the event, Jegede warned that Nigeria could not build a competitive economy on an education system still dependent on outdated teaching methods and policies that no longer reflect contemporary realities.

“Nigeria stands at a volatile crossroads where obsolete educational paradigms collide with an unforgiving 21st-century reality. The era of comfortable, incremental reforms is over,” he declared.

Describing the Academy as the intellectual engine for Nigeria’s future-ready economy, Jegede said it would no longer restrict itself to issuing advisory recommendations while critical challenges confronting the education sector persisted.

“We are here to intentionally disrupt the archaic architectures holding our nation back,” he said.

The NAE president identified a comprehensive review of the National Policy on Education as one of the most urgent measures required to reposition the sector, arguing that changes in technology, the economy and society had made a reassessment imperative.

He also urged the Federal Government to enforce existing laws and regulations governing the composition of governing boards of educational institutions and parastatals, stressing the need for institutional accountability and compliance with established standards.

On teacher development, Jegede advocated a fundamental restructuring of teacher education and professional training to equip educators with the skills required to operate effectively in digital learning environments.

He said the transformation must extend beyond policy documents to actual classroom practices, calling for a comprehensive review of instructional methods to reflect contemporary educational demands.

The Academy president also advocated policies guaranteeing equitable access to digital technologies in schools across the country.

He warned against a situation in which students’ access to modern learning tools was determined by their geographical locations, stressing that learners in rural and underserved communities must not be excluded from the opportunities offered by emerging technologies.

According to him, achieving meaningful digital transformation would require coordinated action by the Federal Ministry of Education, state ministries of education, the legislature and other relevant institutions rather than isolated interventions by individual agencies.

Jegede further challenged members of the Academy, particularly newly inducted Fellows, to deploy their academic expertise in addressing the country’s educational challenges.

“The Academy has no room for sedentary scholars or armchair theoreticians. Nigeria requires your raw intellect and your immediate, unyielding involvement to reshape our pedagogical destiny,” he said.

He urged education experts to contribute actively to developing digital competencies, promoting emerging technologies and building an education system capable of producing graduates who can compete in the global labour market.

Jegede maintained that the Academy’s new mandate should be assessed not by the volume of policy recommendations it produces but by the measurable impact of its interventions on teaching, learning and national human-capital development.

The 2026 Annual Congress also featured the investiture of four distinguished academics as Fellows of the Academy.

Among those honoured was Professor Josiah Olusegun Ajiboye, the Academy’s First Vice-President, in recognition of his academic standing and contributions to education.

The congress also paid tribute to deceased members and relatives of Fellows, including Professor David Adamu Baikie, one of the Academy’s founding members, as well as the late Mrs Lassa and Mr Omotayo Olarinoye.

The Academy’s leadership reaffirmed its commitment to preserving the legacies of its departed members through continued dedication to academic excellence, educational advancement and national development.

With its new national responsibility, the NAE is expected to play a more prominent role in shaping Nigeria’s education sector, particularly as artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies increasingly influence employment requirements and economic growth.

Jegede said the ultimate measure of the initiative’s success would be the Academy’s ability to translate intellectual expertise and policy recommendations into practical reforms that prepare Nigerian learners for the demands of the future.

World.title: Tinubu congratulates Zenith Bank founder Jim Ovia on his 75th birthday
World.content:
Ovia

By Johnbosco Agbakwuru

ABUJA–PRESIDENT Bola Tinubu has congratulated Mr. Jim Ovia, the founder and Chairman of Zenith Bank Plc, on his 75th birthday.

President Tinubu commended Ovia’s remarkable contributions to Nigeria’s banking industry, economic development and private-sector growth, describing him as a visionary entrepreneur, accomplished banker and distinguished business leader.

“Mr. Ovia’s dedication, resilience and commitment to excellence have not only grown Zenith Bank into a banking behemoth but also helped the growth of the Nigerian financial services sector.

“His pioneering role in establishing Zenith Bank in the 90s and building it into one of Nigeria’s leading financial institutions, with significant presence across Africa, Europe and beyond is remarkable,” the President said.

President Tinubu affirmed that Ovia’s entrepreneurial journey reflects the importance of innovation, discipline, sound corporate governance and long-term investment in national development.

The President also laudsled his contributions to digital infrastructure, awareness and inclusion, education, youth empowerment, philanthropy and human capital development, particularly through initiatives that create opportunities for young Nigerians to achieve their potential.

As Mr. Ovia marks this milestone, President Tinubu wished him continued good health, strength and more years of productive service to Nigeria and humanity.

World.title: Ex Afreximbank President, Oramah urges Africa to turn global shocks into opportunities
World.content:
By Henry Ojelu & Deborah Oladeji

Former President of the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), Professor Benedict Oramah, has urged African countries to take advantage of changing global realities and technological advancements to accelerate economic transformation.

Oramah made the call while delivering the keynote address at the 20th AELEX Annual Lecture in Lagos, with the theme, “Beyond Survival: Global Shocks, the Information Age and Africa’s Opportunity to Leapfrog.”

He said Africa must move beyond reacting to global disruptions and strategically position itself to benefit from emerging economic and technological opportunities.

According to him, geopolitical tensions, deglobalisation and rising protectionism are reshaping the global economy, creating an opportunity for African countries to rethink their development strategies.

He identified dependence on foreign capital, currencies and raw material exports as major constraints to the continent’s growth, stressing the need for African countries to take greater control of their resources and financial systems.

“Capital is our greatest constraint. Capital that we own but do not control is not ours,” he said, noting that between $350 billion and $500 billion in African foreign exchange reserves were held outside the continent.

Oramah called for the strengthening of indigenous financial institutions, increased local currency financing and investment in industries capable of processing the continent’s natural resources.

He also advocated the expansion of the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) and effective implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to boost intra-African trade.

Citing Kenya’s mobile money revolution, he said technology could enable African countries to leapfrog traditional stages of development.

He stressed the need for investment in energy infrastructure, data centres and critical minerals processing to prevent the continent from remaining dependent on technologies developed elsewhere.

The Chairman of the occasion and Chairman of Ecobank Nigeria Limited, Mrs Bola Adesola, said effective leadership, strong institutions and adequate preparation were critical for businesses and governments to withstand global shocks.

She emphasised investment in technology, business continuity planning and resilient supply chains, urging institutions to prepare for disruptions rather than wait for crises.

In his welcome remarks, a founding partner of AELEX, Mr Fubara Anga, SAN, described the annual lecture as a platform for discussing national issues, influencing public policy and strengthening institutions.

He called for greater involvement of state and local governments in attracting investments and driving economic development, rather than leaving the responsibility solely to the Federal Government.

The question-and-answer session, moderated by Mr Femi Ojumu, examined issues including artificial intelligence, digital sovereignty and Nigeria’s energy infrastructure.

World.title: Kwara converts Omu-Aran General Hospital to teaching hospital
World.content:
By Demola Akinyemi, Ilorin

Kwara State Governor, AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, on Wednesday laid the foundation for the conversion of the General Hospital, Omu-Aran, into the Thomas Adewumi University Teaching Hospital under a public-private partnership arrangement aimed at expanding access to specialised healthcare in Kwara South.

The project is expected to strengthen medical education, improve healthcare manpower development and reduce the burden on existing tertiary health facilities in the state.

Speaking at the foundation-laying ceremony, the governor, who was represented by his deputy, Kayode Alabi, described the initiative as a milestone in the development of healthcare infrastructure in Kwara South.

“Today marks another milestone as we witness the establishment of the first Teaching Hospital in Kwara South. This remarkable achievement, conceived and actualised through a strategic partnership with the Kwara State Government through the Ministry of Health, will deeply promote medical education, improve human resources in health and contribute significantly to increasing access to quality healthcare delivery for our people,” he said.

AbdulRazaq said establishing a tertiary healthcare facility in the southern part of the state would decentralise specialised medical services and reduce pressure on centrally located hospitals, which residents often find difficult to access.

He expressed confidence that the facility would contribute to reducing preventable deaths and improving healthcare outcomes across communities.

The governor said the project reflected his administration’s commitment to partnerships with private stakeholders to accelerate development, adding that upgrading the existing facility would bring medical services closer to residents of Omu-Aran and neighbouring communities.

He commended the founder, management, staff and students of Thomas Adewumi University for their commitment to medical education and development, while urging residents of Omu-Aran to support the project.

In his remarks, the Founder and Chancellor of Thomas Adewumi University, Engr. Johnson Bamidele Adewumi, said the former General Hospital, established on February 1, 1973, by the administration of the late General David Bamigboye, offered an opportunity to expand specialised healthcare services in Kwara South.

He said the university adopted the teaching hospital project as part of its vision to train medical doctors and other allied health professionals.

Adewumi explained that rather than establish an entirely new facility, the university approached the state government with a proposal to transform the existing hospital through a strategic partnership.

He clarified that the arrangement did not involve the sale or transfer of ownership of the hospital.

“Under the approved framework, ownership of the hospital remains firmly vested in the Government of Kwara State, while Thomas Adewumi University undertakes the construction and development of necessary academic infrastructure. For the avoidance of all doubt, the hospital was neither bought nor put on sale,” he said.

The chancellor, however, appealed to the state government to provide the necessary financial support for the extensive upgrading of the hospital’s infrastructure and engagement of specialist consultants.

He noted that the financial and technical requirements of a tertiary teaching hospital were beyond the capacity of a private individual or the host rural community.

Adewumi said the project was designed to be completed within 18 months, adding that a team led by Professor Kuranga, a former Chief Medical Director of the University of Ilorin Teaching Hospital, and 17 other professors had been involved in developing the initiative.

The ceremony was attended by government officials, traditional rulers and academics, including the Olupo of Ajase-Ipo, Oba Ismail Yahya Alebiosu; the Olomu of Omu-Aran, Oba Raheem Adeoti; the Commissioner for Health, Dr Amina Ahmed El-Imam; and a former Vice-Chancellor of the University of Ilorin, Professor Shuaib Oba Abdulraheem.

Also present were the APC senatorial candidate for Kwara South, Prince Lekan Adewoye, and Oloriewe Raheem Adedoyin, among other dignitaries.

World.title: Nasarawa APC crisis: Govt calls for probe of rally disruption
World.content:
By Edwin Philip, Lafia

The Nasarawa State Government has called on security agencies to investigate an incident that reportedly disrupted activities surrounding Vice-President Kashim Shettima’s visit to the Emir of Lafia during Wednesday’s All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign rally.

The government made the call following reports of disturbances during the Vice-President’s visit to the traditional ruler and allegations of an incident involving Governor Abdullahi Sule at the rally held at Lafia Square.

The governor’s Personal Assistant on Social Media, Emmanuel Innocent Akwe, had raised concerns over the incident, alleging that the governor was pelted with objects suspected to be stones by some aggrieved party members.

In a statement, Akwe described the reported incident as unacceptable and called for respect for the office of the governor and the unity of the APC in the state.

The state government subsequently expressed concern over the reported disruption of the Vice-President’s visit to the Emir, urging security agencies to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The Secretary to the State Government, Labaran Magaji, who made the government’s position known in a statement, said Shettima had visited the traditional ruler as a mark of respect for the traditional institution.

He regretted that the visit was reportedly disrupted by actions he described as disrespectful to constituted authorities and the office of the Vice-President.

Magaji urged security agencies to conduct a thorough investigation, identify those responsible for any wrongdoing and ensure that anyone found culpable was dealt with in accordance with the law.

The development comes amid political disagreements within the state chapter of the APC following the party’s recent governorship primary.

However, the circumstances surrounding the reported disturbances and the identities of those responsible have yet to be independently established.

As of the time of filing this report, there had been no official clarification on the allegations surrounding the incidents.

World.title: IFC, Access Holdings partner to boost trade finance across Africa
World.content:
.partnership targets businesses, cross-border trade, access to global markets

By Udeme Akpan

The International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, and Access Holdings Plc have signed a partnership agreement to expand trade finance, support enterprise growth and improve African businesses’ access to regional and international markets.



The partnership is expected to strengthen Access Group’s capacity to finance businesses, facilitate cross-border trade and support sustainable economic growth across its markets.



The agreement, signed on the sidelines of the Africa Financial Industry Summit (AFIS) 2026 in Luanda, Angola, on November 4, 2026, also forms part of Access Holdings’ broader capital-raising programme aimed at attracting development finance institutions and other investors to support its growth.



The agreement was signed by Aigboje Aig-Imoukhuede, Chairman, Access Holdings; Ethiopis Tafara, IFC Regional Vice President for Africa; and Roosevelt Ogbonna, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Access Bank Plc.

Under the partnership, IFC’s investment is expected to reinforce the Group’s capital base, enabling it to sustain and expand financing for businesses and trade activities that drive economic growth across Africa.

Commenting on the transaction, Aig-Imoukhuede said the partnership reflected a shared commitment to strengthening African financial institutions and supporting the continent’s economic development.

He said: “Our partnership with IFC has always been anchored on a shared belief that strong African financial institutions are essential to Africa’s growth. This investment is a vote of confidence in the institution we have built and, in the direction, we are taking it.

“Having built scale across Africa, our task now is to turn that scale into value: for the businesses we finance, the trade we facilitate and the communities we serve.

“Strengthening Access Group’s capital base deepens its role as a bridge between Africa and global markets, enabling us to mobilise more trade finance and investment for African enterprises.”

He added that the transaction was an important step in the Group’s efforts to attract long-term investment to support disciplined and sustainable growth.

Also speaking, Tafara said expanding access to trade finance was critical to helping African businesses grow, enter new markets and create jobs.

He said: “Across the World Bank Group, we are working to mobilize private capital, strengthen financial markets and create the conditions for private sector-led growth.

“This partnership with Access Group will help channel more financing to businesses across the continent and translate Africa’s entrepreneurial potential into greater economic opportunity.”

For IFC, the partnership aligns with its strategy of mobilising private capital and working with financial institutions to improve access to finance, strengthen markets and create opportunities for businesses to expand and generate employment.

World.title: FMBN’s Non-interest Mortgage as Alternative to Solving Housing Deficit
World.content:
By Richard Imhoagene





According to data from the Housing Market Information Portal (HMIP) of the Federal Government’s National Housing Data Steering Committee, Nigeria has a staggering housing deficit of just under 15 million units. While this manifests in multidimensional circumstances, it exposes a housing situation that requires innovation beyond conventional construction and housing finance that supports housing for all Nigerians.

Nigeria’s housing challenge goes beyond the need to build more houses. It also involves addressing the existing challenges that make it difficult for ordinary Nigerians to live in decent homes. For many Nigerian households, the difficulty lies not only in finding a suitable property but also in accessing financing arrangements that align with their income, circumstances and preferences.

For some Nigerians, particularly those whose religious or ethical convictions discourage interest-based transactions, conventional mortgage financing presents an additional consideration. Even where they have the financial capacity to acquire a home, they may be reluctant to participate in arrangements structured around interest-bearing loans. These realities underscore the need for a more diverse housing finance market, one that recognises that a single financing model may not adequately serve the needs of a diverse population.

So when the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria (FMBN) introduced the Non-Interest Mortgage Product, formally known as the Non-Interest Lease-to-Own Housing Scheme, and based on the Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek (IMBT) model, on October 27, 2026, it sent a signal within the housing ecosystem that an agency of government was beginning to look towards inclusion and dynamism for bridging the huge housing deficit in the country.

Launched by the Minister of Housing and Urban Development, Muttaqha Darma, the product introduces an alternative arrangement through which eligible National Housing Fund (NHF) contributors can access housing and eventually acquire ownership. The introduction of this product raises an important question about inclusion in Nigeria’s mortgage market, especially whether providing alternatives to conventional interest-based financing brings more people into a market where participation has historically remained limited?

Addressing the Gap in Mortgage Market

Nigeria’s mortgage market has long faced structural challenges, including limited access to long-term financing, high property acquisition costs and the relatively low purchasing power of many households. Beyond these constraints, the structure of available mortgage products may not appeal to everyone.

The Non-Interest Mortgage Product is touted as a unique scheme meant to bridge the gap created by one-size-fits-all opportunities. It provides a financing arrangement that does not rely on the conventional interest-on-loan principle. Although the product is designed within the framework of non-interest finance, it is not restricted to any particular religious group. Any Nigerian who meets the applicable NHF eligibility requirements can potentially benefit.

Its significance, therefore, extends beyond religious considerations. It introduces greater choice into the mortgage market and recognises that expanding access to homeownership requires different financing structures capable of accommodating a wider range of prospective homeowners. However, the extent to which it will improve inclusion will ultimately depend on affordability, public understanding, the availability of suitable properties and the ability of eligible contributors to access the facility.

For the Bank’s Managing Director/Chief Executive, Shehu Usman Osidi, the initiative reflects the Bank’s commitment to making homeownership more accessible, inclusive and responsive to the diverse aspirations of NHF contributors. It also builds on the Bank’s recent efforts to develop additional pathways to homeownership, including the launch of the Diaspora NHF Mortgage Loan in August 2026.

Why is Non-interest Mortgage Different?

The distinction between FMBN’s new product, the Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek and a conventional mortgage lies primarily in the underlying contractual and financing arrangement. Under a conventional mortgage, a financial institution provides a loan to a borrower for the purchase of a property. The borrower repays the principal amount alongside interest over an agreed period, with the property serving as security for the loan.

The Non-Interest Lease-to-Own Scheme operates differently. Based on the Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek model, it combines a lease arrangement with the eventual transfer of ownership. Under this structure, the property is acquired and owned by the financial institution, which leases it to the customer for an agreed period. The customer makes rental payments for the use of the property, while the contractual arrangement provides for the eventual transfer of ownership after the agreed obligations have been fulfilled.

The underlying principle is Profit for Lease, as against Interest on Loan. Rather than advancing an interest-bearing loan for the customer to purchase a house, the arrangement is based on the leasing of an identified asset and the transfer of ownership at the end of the agreed period. This distinction is important because the non-interest character of the product is not established simply by changing the terminology used to describe payments. It is rooted in the structure of the transaction, the ownership arrangement and the contractual relationship between the parties.

The facility provides access to up to N50 million, with a lease period of up to 30 years, subject to the applicable terms and approval conditions. It also provides for early repayment without additional charges, while the beneficiary’s payment obligation is assessed against income to support affordability. The product incorporates applicable insurance arrangements to provide protection against specified risks, including death, critical illness and property damage.

As with any long-term housing commitment, prospective beneficiaries will need to understand the contractual obligations, payment structure, property ownership arrangements and conditions governing the eventual transfer of title. The introduction of this model does not, by itself, resolve the wider affordability challenges confronting the housing market in Nigeria. However, it broadens the range of financing options available and provides an opportunity to bring prospective homeowners who have different financing preferences into the formal mortgage system.

Beyond Financing Model: Question of Housing Delivery

The success of an alternative mortgage arrangement cannot be measured solely by its introduction or the number of people who express interest in it. Its real value will depend on how many Nigerians can use it to secure decent and affordable homes. This was re-echoed at the launch of the product by the Housing Minister who charged the Bank to anchor implementation on four principles of simplicity in application, speed in processing, transparency in transactions and scale of delivery across the country.

His message placed the emphasis firmly on results. “The test of this product is not today’s launch but how many Nigerians become homeowners through it,” he declared, urging FMBN to extend the immediate benefits beyond Kano to other parts of the country. The commissioning of the FMBN-Ijarah-01 Estate in Bichi, Kano State, alongside the handover of keys to the pilot project’s inaugural beneficiaries, provided an initial demonstration of the arrangement in practice.

The project illustrates the relationship between housing finance and actual housing supply. A financing product can only deliver meaningful benefits where there are suitable properties available at prices that prospective beneficiaries can afford.

This is particularly important in a country where the cost of land, building materials, infrastructure and property development continues to influence the price of completed homes. For the initiative to achieve wider reach, there will need to be a sustained supply of qualifying properties across different locations, supported by partnerships with credible developers and efficient project delivery arrangements.

There is also the question of accessibility. Information about the product, its contractual structure, eligibility requirements and application procedures must be communicated in clear and understandable terms. This will enable prospective beneficiaries to make informed decisions rather than simply viewing it as another mortgage product. Ultimately, the test will be whether the arrangement creates a practical and sustainable pathway to homeownership for Nigerians who need it.

Looking Beyond Homeownership

While expanding access to homeownership remains important, Nigeria’s housing challenge also requires attention to the needs of households that depend on rented accommodation. In major urban centres, rising rental costs and the substantial upfront payments demanded by landlords have made securing decent accommodation increasingly difficult for many low- and middle-income earners.

A typical two-bedroom apartment in a satellite town in the Federal Capital Terrotory costs between N2.5 million and N3.5 million. The situation is a similar one in Lagos and other major cities. And this is for areas several kilometers away from the major city centres. For a N3 bedroom apartment, annual rental obligations rise as high as N3.5 to N5 million. If we’re to go by the recommendation of annual housing expenditure not exceeding a third of household income, that would require households to earn as much as N8 to N15 million every year to afford such rents.

The reality is that many Nigerians have to make do with even much cheaper housing to cope, and rental payments remain a challenge. In response, the Federal Government through the FMBN is set to introduce the Rent Assistance Loan. Billed for launch in November 2026, it is designed to help eligible NHF contributors meet their rental obligations.

Under the proposed arrangement, approved rent payments will be made directly to landlords, with beneficiaries expected to repay the facility over a 10-month period, subject to the approved terms. Nigerians can access up to N2 million to support rental obligations.

Also in the pipeline is the Micro Home Improvement Loan intended to support eligible beneficiaries in undertaking improvements to their homes. Once introduced, these initiatives will further broaden FMBN’s housing finance offerings, extending support beyond home acquisition to other important aspects of housing affordability and improved living conditions.

A Broader Housing Finance Ecosystem

The introduction of alternative mortgage financing alongside plans for rental assistance and micro home improvement reflects a broader understanding of the different housing needs of Nigerians. For some households, the priority is acquiring a home through a financing arrangement that aligns with their preferences. For others, it is obtaining the financial support required to secure decent rental accommodation while they work towards greater financial stability.

The NHF Mortgage Loan continues to provide a conventional interest-based route to homeownership, offering eligible contributors access to up to N50 million at an interest rate of 6 per cent per annum, with a repayment period of up to 30 years, subject to applicable conditions. Other interventions, including the existing Rent-to-Own Scheme, Home Renovation Loan, Individual Construction Loan and Cooperative Housing Development Loan, address different aspects of housing acquisition, construction and improvement. The Diaspora NHF Mortgage Loan Scheme also extends mortgage participation to eligible Nigerians living abroad.

Together, these arrangements demonstrate why housing finance should not be approached from a single perspective. Homeownership, rental affordability, housing improvement and access to suitable financing are interconnected aspects of the broader housing challenge. However, the introduction of more products must be accompanied by effective implementation, adequate funding, efficient administration and continuous assessment of their impact. The number of products available is less important than the extent to which they address genuine housing needs.

For the Non-Interest Mortgage Product, the critical considerations will be whether it provides a credible alternative to interest-based financing, whether its payment obligations are affordable and whether it can reach Nigerians who have previously been reluctant to participate in conventional mortgage arrangements.

For emphasis, Nigeria’s housing challenge requires more than the construction of additional houses. It requires financing arrangements that recognise the diversity of the population, respond to different income realities and provide practical pathways to secure accommodation. The introduction of alternative mortgage financing is therefore, a step towards addressing these needs. Its real test will be whether it translates into greater inclusion, improved affordability and tangible homeownership opportunities for Nigerians.

•Richard Imhoagene, a housing analyst and social commentator, writes from Abuja

World.title: A Tale of Four Crucial Elections
World.content:
I left Nigeria two weeks ago and within these past 14 days, there have been four consequential elections across South America, Europe, Asia and North America. In Serbia on 25 October, the students who started a nationwide protest two years ago to demand accountability, drew up a list of candidates, mobilised the electorate and defeated President Aleksandar Vučić who has been in power for the last 12 years. Two days later (27 October) in Israel, the much-awaited parliamentary election produced a cliffhanger result that leaves Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu utterly frustrated since there may be no government without a deal with the Arab parties whose membership in the Knesset has almost doubled. Then in an unprecedented political turn-around in Brazil on 30 October, the 81-year-old incumbent President Lula da Silva secured a fourth term with a margin of 4.43 million votes despite trailing in the first round by 2.2 million votes. Finally, in the United States on Tuesday, Democrats gained five governorship seats and won both the Senate and House, firmly taking control of Congress with surprise victories in several Republican strongholds that include Ohio, Texas, South Carolina and Kansas. Remarkably, Kansas last elected a Democrat 94 years ago!

I am currently in the U.S. where pundits are still trying to come to terms with the political implications of the massive ‘Blue Tsunami’ of Tuesday night. Several gender and ethno-religious records were also broken by the Democrats such that House Minority Leader, Hakeem Jeffries, is poised to become the first Black Speaker in January. So overwhelming is the nature of the Democratic victory that President Donald Trump could not but concede to a defeat that many describe as a repudiation of his (foreign and domestic) policy choices and a referendum on his stewardship. Trump, of course, has attributed the results to the fact that he was not on the ballot saying with him, the Republicans “would have won in a landslide.” Not even his own deputy, Vice President J.D. Vance (who has attributed the loss largely to the war in Iran), takes his principal serious on that claim.

Serbia. Israel. Brazil. United States. There are lessons from these four countries that will serve us in Nigeria as we prepare for the 2027 general election. Let’s start with Brazil where no presidential candidate had ever come from behind to win a runoff poll since the country returned to direct elections in 1989. Instructively, Lula lost the first round with 45 percent to Senator Flavio Bolnosaro’s 47 percent, but he won the run-off with 51.79 percent of total votes. The defeated Bolsonaro has refused to concede, asking the courts to annul the result because voting was extended by two hours. He seems to be clutching at straws. Not only did Bolnosaro’s own party join the call for that extension at the time, but it has also been established that those two hours approved by the Supreme Court produced only about 34,000 ballots. Besides, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party has recognised the outcome of the election and accepted Lula’s victory. Bolsonaro has taken refuge in the U.S.

Most political pundits have credited Lula’s victory to the power of social media. One of his supporters, André Janones, a 42-year-old congressman, started and ran a WhatsApp group called ‘Lula’s Army’. From 60,000 followers after the first round, the aggressive mobilization that followed ballooned the membership to nearly 11 million. Lula himself was persuaded to get a smartphone (reportedly he never had a mobile phone of his own until the election), and he began taking selfies at rallies. In his victory speech, Lula praised Janones whom he described as “our general” who was “raising the morale of our troops every day.” But we must read that story correctly. The real campaign work was done offline. Supporters were asked to list friends and relatives they could persuade or get to the polls, with special attention to teenagers and people above 70, for whom voting is optional. Lula also had the advantage of incumbency while Bolsonaro scored an own goal. In the final television debate on 23 October, he called the president ‘nine fingers’, a taunt about the finger Lula lost in a factory accident as a young metalworker. Although Bolsonaro apologised on air, many undecided voters reportedly did not take it well.

In Serbia, following the collapse of the roof of a popular train station in November 2024, killing no fewer than 15 people, students took to the street, accusing the government of President Vucic of nepotism, corruption and negligence. Calls for a transparent investigation led to months of sit-ins, blockades and marches led by students, and then a demand for snap elections. When that demand was met, apparently because some powerful people misread the room, the students drew up a list of 250 candidates to contest against the ruling party. Those candidates include academics, civil society activists, and other professionals with no prior involvement in politics (and none is a student). With a tacit endorsement of the students, several leading opposition parties chose not to run and urged their supporters to back them. At the end, the candidates on what became known as the ‘Student List’ took about 53% of the vote, and Vučić conceded on the election night even before all the votes were in.

Perhaps nobody has captured what happened in Serbia as succinctly as Giorgio Fruscione, a Research Fellow at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI). “It is a historic achievement that highlights the value of democracy at a time when European streets are in turmoil, making the (Serbian) students a role model for the rest of the continent too,” says Fruscione. “I cannot think of anything similar anywhere in the world–a group of young people, unknown to most, with no party structures, no money and no leadership, managed effectively to bring down an autocrat who controlled all the media, the police and criminal networks, and had almost unlimited financial resources at his disposal. All this without a single act of violence, in a country whose reputation has often been associated with violence and political instability.”

Meanwhile, Israel is still reeling from the outcome of its election that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been struggling to discredit. The ruling bloc–made up of his Likud party, ultra-Orthodox and a far-right supremacist faction–won 53 seats while the opposition bloc, led by a former military general, Gadi Eisenkot, won 48. Ordinarily, the majority required to form government in the 120-seat parliament is 61 but both leaders have pledged not to deal with the 19 members from the Arab parties. President Isaac Herzog begins consultations this week and must name a candidate to form the government. Failure could send Israelis back to the polls. About one in five Israeli citizens is Arab. They voted in numbers never seen before, and the system counted those votes. The difficulty is that the men who require those seats do not want to be seen as needing them.

Overall, these are four countries with four different systems, and none of them is perfect. But we can learn from them. The first lesson is about the efficacy of a strong opposition. I spent the 2010/2011 academic session as a Fellow at the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs at Harvard researching why ruling parties so rarely lose elections. I found that in the two preceding decades, they won 96 percent of competitive presidential elections across the world, and the main reason was a divided opposition. Serbia presents a textbook case for that point: several parties stepped aside to back the ‘Students List’ and, in the process, rewrote the democratic history of their country.

In Nigeria, those who want to unseat the incumbent president in the coming 2027 general election cannot keep negotiating into January and expect to be taken seriously. Especially when presenting a united front doesn’t even guarantee success. In Brazil, most of the eliminated right-wing candidates rallied behind Bolsonaro after the first round which he won, and the main opposition candidate still lost at the end. But there is also a lesson for those in power in Nigeria. To imagine invincibility is to ignore the lessons of contemporary history. Vucic had the advantages of office in Serbia, and he was upended by students; Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority in Israel and Trump is now effectively a lame duck American president with Tuesday’s electoral clean sweep by the Democratic Party.

This brings me to another lesson. Serbian voter turn-out was nearly 69 percent. Young people, African Americans, Latinos exercised their franchise in large numbers across the U.S. on Tuesday. In Israel, Arab voters moved from about 53 percent to about 80 percent and upended the arithmetic of a nation. All these are in sharp contrast to what happens in Nigeria, where only about 27 percent of registered voters participated in 2023. Yet, an election can be lost by those who stay at home as surely as by those who are ‘rigged out’.

Then, the third lesson. Israel should remind us that voters can hand politicians a result nobody planned for. Under Section 134 of the Constitution, a presidential candidate needs the highest number of votes and at least 25 percent in at least 24 states. If nobody achieves that, there is a second election, something Nigeria has never had. But as we have seen in Brazil, Serbia and Israel, there is always a first time for everything. Another lesson, especially from the American election is that big money doesn’t always translate to electoral victories. Although both parties spent billions of dollars, the Republican candidates in highly competitive races had extraordinary support from wealthy donors, including from Elon Musk who reportedly dished out about $450 million! The point was made most eloquently by Ms Keisha Lance Bottoms. Addressing supporters after overcoming billionaire Rick Jackson to become Georgia’s first elected female governor and the first Black governor in the state’s history, Bottoms said: “In big and small ways, you’ve shown that no amount of money will ever, never ever, ever overcome the power of the people.”

Let me now make the point that goes to the heart of what I wrote last week. Serbian citizens who feared fraud were vigilant as observers without resorting to violence. All the threats from American politicians before Tuesday were about going to court. Section 60(3) of the Electoral Act 2026 now requires presiding officers to transmit polling unit results to the IReV portal, although the manual Form EC8A becomes the primary source where there is ‘communication failure’. Since tribunals must now receive IReV data in evidence, a party that is truly worried about rigging should be training agents for every polling unit and securing its copy of every result sheet. It should not be telling supporters to bring kerosene.

The final point: If there is anything that the elections in Serbia, Brazil, Israel and United States have taught us, it is that when the people are determined to make a change, nothing can stop them.

Belt and Road in the Age of AI

The 2026 edition of the Media Cooperation Forum on Belt and Road is currently being held in Fuzhou, Fujian Province of China with the theme, ‘Pursuing Common Understandings and Aspirations: A Decade of Belt and Road Media Cooperation’. The 4th Council Meeting of the Belt and Road News Network (BRNN) will also be convened at the sidelines to review the BRNN’s work report (2024-2026), promote the third Silk Road News Awards, and admit new Council members. Ordinarily, I should be in China attending both sessions as one of the 43 Council members. But because the invitation came after I had committed myself to this vacation, I had to politely explain my absence. Asked to send a video message, below is the text of my presentation for the 4th BRNN Council meeting.

================================================================

In April 2019, I sat in the conference hall of People’s Daily in Beijing as one of the founding members of Belt and Road News Network (BRNN) Council. At the time, the network had 182 member organisations. Today BRNN has attracted 323 media outlets from 117 countries worldwide. What that growth reveals most eloquently is that in a noisy and divided world, serious media organisations want to talk to one another. That perhaps explains why dialogue among our media still matters. When our newsrooms speak directly, we can report on our different societies with context and nuance. Above all, we can report accurately, and accuracy remains the only currency of our profession.

In the age of disinformation, that is no small thing. THISDAY newspapers in Nigeria where I work and our sister organisation, ARISE Television, have given us a direct line to colleagues across Asia, Europe, Latin America and the rest of Africa. These media outlets have also given us access to content and contacts that have deepened our coverage of a relationship that now touches almost every sector of the Nigerian economy.

Looking ahead, I have three expectations. One, we need more exchange in both directions, of journalists, stories and perspectives, so that African voices are heard in Beijing as clearly as Chinese voices are heard in Nigeria and the rest of Africa. Two, we need practical cooperation on the tools reshaping our industry, including the responsible use of artificial intelligence in newsrooms. Three, we need the confidence to tell complete stories, in terms of the difficulties as well as the successes. At the end of the day, credibility is what will make the Belt and Road story believable to sceptical audiences.

What is remarkable about the growing rise of China, especially in Africa, is that development can be measured in critical infrastructure like roads, railways and ports. Nigerians see this in the Lagos–Ibadan railway and the Lekki Deep Sea Port. Since 1st May this year, China has granted zero-tariff access to all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations, Nigeria included. At a time when many are raising barriers, that is a practical argument for openness, and the shared prosperity that openness makes possible.

This year marks the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and Africa. It is also the China–Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges. No exchange between peoples lasts longer than the one carried out through honest journalism. That remains our common responsibility. Thank you very much for listening as I look forward to joining you next year.

• You can follow me on my X handle, @Olusegunverdict and on www.olusegunadeniyi.com
