The final point: If there is anything that the elections in Serbia, Brazil, Israel and United States have taught us, it is that when the people are determined to make a change, nothing can stop them.

Belt and Road in the Age of AI

The 2026 edition of the Media Cooperation Forum on Belt and Road is currently being held in Fuzhou, Fujian Province of China with the theme, ‘Pursuing Common Understandings and Aspirations: A Decade of Belt and Road Media Cooperation’. The 4th Council Meeting of the Belt and Road News Network (BRNN) will also be convened at the sidelines to review the BRNN’s work report (2024-2026), promote the third Silk Road News Awards, and admit new Council members. Ordinarily, I should be in China attending both sessions as one of the 43 Council members. But because the invitation came after I had committed myself to this vacation, I had to politely explain my absence. Asked to send a video message, below is the text of my presentation for the 4th BRNN Council meeting.

================================================================

In April 2019, I sat in the conference hall of People’s Daily in Beijing as one of the founding members of Belt and Road News Network (BRNN) Council. At the time, the network had 182 member organisations. Today BRNN has attracted 323 media outlets from 117 countries worldwide. What that growth reveals most eloquently is that in a noisy and divided world, serious media organisations want to talk to one another. That perhaps explains why dialogue among our media still matters. When our newsrooms speak directly, we can report on our different societies with context and nuance. Above all, we can report accurately, and accuracy remains the only currency of our profession.

In the age of disinformation, that is no small thing. THISDAY newspapers in Nigeria where I work and our sister organisation, ARISE Television, have given us a direct line to colleagues across Asia, Europe, Latin America and the rest of Africa. These media outlets have also given us access to content and contacts that have deepened our coverage of a relationship that now touches almost every sector of the Nigerian economy.

Looking ahead, I have three expectations. One, we need more exchange in both directions, of journalists, stories and perspectives, so that African voices are heard in Beijing as clearly as Chinese voices are heard in Nigeria and the rest of Africa. Two, we need practical cooperation on the tools reshaping our industry, including the responsible use of artificial intelligence in newsrooms. Three, we need the confidence to tell complete stories, in terms of the difficulties as well as the successes. At the end of the day, credibility is what will make the Belt and Road story believable to sceptical audiences.

What is remarkable about the growing rise of China, especially in Africa, is that development can be measured in critical infrastructure like roads, railways and ports. Nigerians see this in the Lagos–Ibadan railway and the Lekki Deep Sea Port. Since 1st May this year, China has granted zero-tariff access to all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations, Nigeria included. At a time when many are raising barriers, that is a practical argument for openness, and the shared prosperity that openness makes possible.

This year marks the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and Africa. It is also the China–Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges. No exchange between peoples lasts longer than the one carried out through honest journalism. That remains our common responsibility. Thank you very much for listening as I look forward to joining you next year.

• You can follow me on my X handle, @Olusegunverdict and on www.olusegunadeniyi.com

World.title: A BOOST TO WORKERS’ WELFARE
World.content:
BENARD EDIVRI writes that Oborevwori’s 13th-month salary is a significant intervention in public service welfare

Leadership is ultimately measured by its impact on people. Beyond the roads constructed, bridges commissioned and public buildings completed, the enduring value of governance lies in the policies that improve people’s lives, recognise their sacrifices and create opportunities for a more secure future.

This is the human dimension of Governor Sheriff Oborevwori’s decision to sign the Thirteenth Month Salary Law, 2026, into law in Delta State. The initiative represents a significant intervention in public service welfare and reinforces the principle that development must be about people, not merely physical structures.

At the Executive Council Chambers of Government House, Asaba, where the governor signed the legislation alongside four other bills, Oborevwori described the initiative as part of his administration’s commitment to reforms under the MORE Agenda. He expressed optimism that the measures would strengthen public institutions, improve service delivery and promote economic development.

Yet, among the measures signed, the Thirteenth Month Salary Law carries a particularly direct message to the state’s workforce: the contributions of public servants matter, their welfare deserves attention, and their commitment to public service should be recognised.

The public service is the engine room of the government. Behind virtually every policy, programme and development project are thousands of workers whose daily responsibilities sustain the machinery of the state.

Teachers educate future generations. Healthcare professionals attend to the health needs of the people. Administrative personnel keep government institutions functioning, while technical officers, engineers and other professionals translate policy decisions into practical outcomes. Their motivation and wellbeing are therefore directly connected to the quality of governance.

Oborevwori’s decision to institutionalise a thirteenth-month salary benefit for eligible public servants reflects an appreciation of this relationship. The governor explained that the initiative was designed to boost workers’ morale, reward their contributions and improve productivity.

It is a recognition that public servants should not be considered merely as employees occupying government offices, but as indispensable partners in the development process.

In a period when households face competing financial responsibilities, an additional salary benefit can provide meaningful support. It can help workers meet family obligations, plan for important expenses and approach the end of the year with greater financial reassurance.

More importantly, it communicates something beyond money: that the government recognises the sacrifices of its workforce and is willing to translate that recognition into a tangible welfare intervention.

The significance of the Thirteenth Month Salary Law extends beyond individual beneficiaries. When workers receive additional income, the benefits can circulate through the wider economy. Families may have greater capacity to purchase goods, pay for services, support children’s education and meet household needs. Local businesses, retailers and service providers may also benefit from increased consumer spending.

This is the wider economic argument behind the initiative. The outgoing Delta Head of Service, Dr Mininim Oseji, recognised this dimension when he described the law as a boost to workers’ welfare and family wellbeing. He also observed that the policy had the potential to stimulate business activities and commended the governor for introducing it.

Oseji’s remarks are particularly significant because they highlight the connection between employee welfare and economic activity. A policy that improves the disposable income of workers can have implications for families, neighbourhood businesses and the wider commercial environment.

Of course, the extent of this impact will depend on implementation and the wider economic conditions. Nevertheless, the underlying principle is sound: investing in workers’ welfare can also contribute to economic confidence and social wellbeing.

One of the most important aspects of Oborevwori’s approach is his insistence that development goes beyond infrastructure to include policies capable of improving people’s lives.

This is an important distinction in the assessment of public leadership. Infrastructure remains essential to economic growth and social development, but it is not the only measure of progress. Citizens also need policies that improve their welfare, protect their dignity and respond to the everyday realities of their lives.

A government may build roads and bridges, but the people who work in its institutions must also be able to provide for their families. It may expand public services, but those services depend on motivated and committed personnel. It may pursue economic growth, but such growth must ultimately translate into improved living conditions.

The thirteenth-month salary initiative speaks directly to this people-centred understanding of development.

Compassionate leadership is not simply about making sympathetic statements. It is about recognising the needs of people and designing policies that respond to them. In this instance, the administration has chosen to give legislative backing to a welfare measure intended to reward public service and improve workers’ morale.

By signing the bill into law, Oborevwori has moved the initiative beyond a general expression of goodwill and placed it within a formal legal framework. The real value of the policy will, however, be determined by its implementation.

Eligible workers must receive the benefit in accordance with the provisions of the law, while the relevant government institutions must ensure that the necessary administrative and financial arrangements are in place.

Sustainability is equally important. A welfare initiative of this nature must be supported by responsible fiscal planning so that the government can honour its commitment without compromising other essential public services.

These considerations do not diminish the importance of the policy. Rather, they underscore the need to translate its promise into a dependable benefit for workers.

The governor’s commendation of the Delta State House of Assembly also highlights the importance of cooperation between the executive and legislature in advancing policies that respond to public needs. The participation of the Chief Judge, representatives of the judiciary, the Deputy Speaker, principal officers of the Assembly, the Attorney-General, the Secretary to the State Government, commissioners and other senior officials at the signing ceremony further reflected the institutional significance of the occasion.

Ultimately, workers will judge the initiative by the consistency with which it is delivered. Oborevwori’s welfare intervention must also be understood within the broader context of his administration’s MORE Agenda.

The ambition of any development programme should be to improve the quality of life of citizens through effective governance, economic opportunities, social investment and institutional performance.

The thirteenth-month salary benefit contributes to that objective by recognising the people who help the government deliver its responsibilities.

It also sends a message to the public service that productivity and welfare should go together. Workers are expected to demonstrate professionalism, commitment and efficiency, but the government equally has a responsibility to create conditions that encourage and sustain those qualities. This mutual responsibility is central to building an effective public service.

A motivated workforce can improve institutional performance, strengthen service delivery and help translate government policies into meaningful outcomes for citizens. In that sense, workers’ welfare is not simply an expense; it is an investment in the capacity of the government to serve its people.

The Thirteenth Month Salary Law offers an opportunity to redefine how development is discussed in Delta State. It reminds us that progress is not measured only in kilometres of roads, completed buildings or the scale of capital projects. It must also be measured in the security of families, the dignity of workers and the ability of public institutions to respond to human needs.

For Oborevwori, the challenge now is to ensure that the law delivers its intended benefits consistently and sustainably. If effectively implemented, it could become an important feature of the state’s public service welfare framework and a source of encouragement to workers who contribute daily to its development.

The broader lesson is that good governance requires both the construction of infrastructure and the strengthening of the human institutions that make development meaningful.

By placing workers’ welfare firmly within his administration’s policy agenda, Governor Oborevwori has demonstrated the importance of a leadership approach that recognises the people behind government performance.

The ultimate measure of this initiative will be the difference it makes in the lives of eligible public servants and their families. But its message is already clear: the government must not lose sight of the people it exists to serve.

That is the essence of compassionate leadership at play, a recognition that the most enduring legacy of governance is not simply what is built, but how people’s lives are improved.

Edivri writes from Asaba, Delta State

World.title: THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS AND IMPLICATIONS FOR NIGERIA
World.content:
The post-midterm relationship between Nigeria and the U.S. will be more institutional and demanding, contends FOLAWIYO KAREEM OLAJOKU

On Tuesday, November 3, 2026, American voters went to the polls in what has now become one of the most consequential midterm elections in modern American history. When the results began to emerge in the early hours of Wednesday morning, it was clear that something fundamental had shifted in the political landscape of the United States. Democrats had not merely won a narrow victory, they had swept into power in both chambers of Congress, reclaiming the House of Representatives with a decisive majority and flipping at least seven Senate seats to secure a 54-seat majority in the upper chamber. The scale of the victory was felt in places long considered unassailable Republican strongholds. In Texas, James Talarico became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat since 1988. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton broke a Democratic drought stretching back to 1932. In South Carolina, another seat long written off as safe for Republicans fell. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed made history as the nation’s first Muslim United States Senator. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa became the first Hispanic woman governor, and in Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman governor. Vice President JD Vance, speaking in the aftermath of the defeat, pointed to the war in Iran as the principal reason for the Republican collapse, but voters in exit polls told a much more domestic story. They spoke of the cost of living, of grocery prices that had not come down, of housing costs, of a sense that power in Washington had become too concentrated, and of a desire to restore balance and oversight to government. It was, in the classic American pattern, a rebuke to the sitting president, but the depth of the rebuke was extraordinary.

For Nigeria, this was not a distant American drama to be watched with detached curiosity. It was a turning point in its most important bilateral relationship outside the African continent. Nigeria and the United States have a relationship that is long, complex, and at times contradictory, shaped by oil, by migration, by security, by religion, by trade, and by the sheer weight of Nigeria’s demographic and economic importance. What happens in Washington does not stay in Washington. It reaches Abuja, it reaches Lagos, it reaches the battlefields of Borno and the creeks of the Niger Delta, it reaches the visa queues at the American embassy, and it reaches the trading floors where the naira is priced against the dollar. To understand what the midterms mean for Nigeria, it is necessary first to understand where the relationship stood just one year ago, because only then can the scale of the shift be fully appreciated.

In October 2025, the relationship between Nigeria and the United States was at one of its lowest points in decades. The Trump administration had designated Nigeria a Country of Particular Concern for religious freedom under the International Religious Freedom Act, a label reserved for states judged to tolerate systematic religious persecution. The designation was accompanied by strong public language from Washington about the plight of Nigerian Christians, and by threats of possible military action. In Abuja, there was shock, anger, and a deep sense of being misunderstood. The Nigerian government insisted, with considerable justification, that the violence in the country was not a simple religious war, but a complex tapestry of jihadist insurgency, banditry, farmer-herder conflict over land and water, criminal kidnapping networks, and the spillover of instability from the wider Sahel. To reduce it to a single narrative of Christian persecution was, in the view of many Nigerians, not only inaccurate, but dangerous, because it obscured the real drivers of violence and made them harder to solve.

What followed was a remarkable exercise in Nigerian diplomacy, one that deserves to be studied as a case study in crisis management. President Bola Tinubu did not respond with public confrontation or with angry rhetoric. Instead, he sent his most trusted hand into the room where the narrative was being written. National Security Adviser Nuhu Ribadu led a delegation to Washington, moving methodically through the White House Faith Office, the State Department, the National Security Council, the Department of War, and the corridors of Congress, the very institutions where the CPC designation had taken shape. His task was not to deny that Christians had suffered, because they had, but to reframe that suffering as one component of a shared threat rather than the whole of it. He spoke of Boko Haram and Islamic State, of Muslim victims as well as Christian victims, of the thousands of Nigerians of all faiths who had been killed, displaced, and traumatised. He presented data, he presented evidence, and he presented a plan. Within weeks, both governments had agreed to establish a Joint Working Group, co-chaired on the Nigerian side by Ribadu, bringing together defence, intelligence, foreign affairs, police and humanitarian officials under a single coordinating structure. The momentum continued into July 2026, when the newly confirmed Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs, Frank Garcia, made Nigeria the centrepiece of his first official Africa tour, holding extensive talks with Ribadu on security, justice-sector reform, digital transformation and regional stability.

The results of that diplomatic effort were concrete and, by any measure, significant. The United States deployed Special Operations Forces, including elite units, to train and equip Nigerian troops under what Trump termed the historic US–Nigeria 2026 Defence Cooperation Roadmap. Joint operations followed, including coordinated strikes against Islamic State elements in the northwest in December 2025, and a further coordinated attack on ISIS hideouts in the Lake Chad area in May 2026. A five-year US–Nigeria health cooperation agreement valued at approximately 5.1 billion dollars was concluded. And in July 2026, Trump wrote a letter to Tinubu that was made public by the Presidency, praising his decisive leadership, calling it a true honour to stand with Nigeria against terrorism, and describing the relationship as crucial. From formal rebuke to formal commendation, from the language of concern to the language of comradeship, in the space of nine months, Nigeria and the United States had travelled a remarkable distance. The midterms now interrupt that trajectory, not to end it, but to complicate it, and to test whether a relationship built in a moment of crisis can survive a change in the political weather in Washington.

The first and most immediate change that a Democratic Congress brings is the return of oversight and conditionality. A Republican Congress, particularly one aligned with a Republican president, had given Trump wide latitude on foreign policy, allowing him to conduct security cooperation with Nigeria largely on the basis of executive authority and personal rapport. A Democratic Congress will not do that. It will insist on its constitutional role. For Abuja, this is a double-edged sword. On the one hand, oversight may slow down security cooperation, it may introduce bureaucratic delays, and it may create moments of political embarrassment when difficult questions are asked in public. On the other hand, oversight may also institutionalise the relationship, moving it from a presidential understanding between Trump and Tinubu to a legislated, bipartisan framework that survives beyond 2028 and beyond the personalities who created it. A partnership that is debated, authorised, and funded by Congress is, in the long run, a more durable partnership than one that rests on a letter.

The second change concerns religious freedom, an issue that will now return to the centre of the relationship with renewed force. The CPC designation was never fully lifted in political terms, even as the diplomatic tone softened. Democratic members of Congress, particularly those with strong human rights constituencies and close ties to faith-based advocacy groups, are more likely to press Nigeria on religious freedom, on farmer-herder violence, and on the protection of minorities. They are more likely to demand reports, to invite witnesses, to hold hearings, and to link future assistance to demonstrable progress. Nigeria will need to do what it did successfully in late 2025, which is to tell its own story with data, not with defensiveness. The narrative that insecurity is driven by banditry, by resource competition, by arms trafficking, and by jihadism, and not by a state-sponsored religious war, must be sustained in Congress, not just in the White House. That will require a sustained presence in Washington, not a one-off delegation, and it will require the Nigerian government to be able to show, with credible evidence, what it is doing to protect all its citizens, of all faiths, in all parts of the country.

The third change concerns immigration and the diaspora, and for many ordinary Nigerians, this may be the most immediate and personal consequence of the midterms. The Trump administration instituted immigration policies that restricted travel to the United States by Nigerian nationals, among others, including for students, for businesspeople, and for family members seeking to visit relatives. Those policies have caused real pain, separating families, disrupting businesses, and making it harder for Nigerian students to access American universities. A Democratic Congress is likely to push back on travel bans, on visa restrictions, and on mass deportation policies that have disproportionately affected Nigerians. It is likely to demand greater transparency in visa adjudication, to challenge the use of sweeping security justifications for broad bans, and to advocate for pathways that recognise the contribution of the Nigerian diaspora to American society. For the more than five hundred thousand Nigerians living in the United States, a vital source of remittances, of investment, and of advocacy for Nigeria, this could be the most immediate relief from the midterms, a loosening of the pressure that has weighed on their daily lives for two years.

The fourth change, and perhaps the most consequential for Nigeria’s economy, concerns trade, tariffs, and the African Growth and Opportunity Act, known as AGOA. This is where the midterms could hurt or help most, depending on how Abuja responds. Under Trump’s April 2025 tariff action, Nigeria faced a fifteen percent tariff on exports to the United States, although petroleum products were exempt. After a February 2026 Supreme Court ruling invalidated those tariffs, the President imposed temporary tariffs under a different statute, leaving Nigeria with a ten percent tariff on some exports. AGOA itself expired on September 30, 2025, and Congress reauthorized it in February 2026 through the end of the year, making benefits retroactive. That reauthorization, however, expires in weeks, and the new Congress will have to decide whether to renew it, and for how long. A Democratic Congress is historically more supportive of AGOA and more sceptical of unilateral tariffs. That creates an opportunity, but also a danger. If Nigeria waits, if it assumes that a Democratic Congress will automatically renew AGOA out of goodwill, it may find itself caught in a crowded legislative calendar where Africa is not the priority. Nigeria has a narrow window, before the new Congress is sworn in on January 3, 2027, to lobby for a long-term, multi-year AGOA renewal, not another short-term extension that leaves exporters in uncertainty. If Abuja misses this window, Nigerian exporters in agriculture, in textiles, in light manufacturing, in the creative industries, will face renewed uncertainty, and the hard work of building non-oil exports to the United States will be undermined.

Despite the blue wave, however, there are three fundamentals that have not changed, and it is important for Nigeria not to overreact to the midterms. The first is that America still needs Nigeria. Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country, its largest democracy, its top oil producer, and the United States’ second-largest trade partner in sub-Saharan Africa. No United States strategy for West Africa, on terrorism, on critical minerals, on countering Russian and Chinese influence, on migration, on health security, works without Abuja. The United States knows this, and the Democratic Party knows this. The second fundamental is that Trump still controls foreign policy for two more years. Congress can investigate, it can fund, and it can block, but the President remains Commander-in-Chief. The Defence Cooperation Roadmap and the Joint Working Group are executive creations. They will continue, but now under congressional scrutiny. The third fundamental is that Nigeria’s own 2027 elections are now the test. Washington, under either party, will watch Nigeria’s own elections closely. How Nigeria conducts its 2027 polls, whether they are credible, transparent, peaceful, and broadly accepted, will determine whether the next Congress sees Nigeria as a democratic partner to invest in, or as a problem to manage. Nigeria cannot demand democracy promotion from Washington while failing to practise it at home.

What, then, must Abuja do now? The midterms reward preparation, not panic, and they reward a strategy that is patient, institutional, and forward-looking. The first task is to engage the new Congress early. The Ribadu model worked with the executive. It must now be replicated with the incoming leadership of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, with the new chairs, with the new ranking members, and with the freshmen who have just been elected and who will be forming their views on Nigeria for the first time. The second task is to lock in AGOA, and to make a bipartisan case for it. AGOA is not aid, it is American jobs and Nigerian jobs, it is American consumers getting affordable goods and Nigerian producers getting access to the world’s largest market. The third task is to institutionalise security cooperation, to move from letters and personal rapport to formal agreements, to reporting requirements, and to joint benchmarks that a Democratic Congress can defend to its voters. The fourth task, and perhaps the most important, is to lead on the narrative. Nigeria cannot allow its security story to be written for it in Washington again. Data on civilian protection, on inter-faith peacebuilding, on prosecutions for violence, on the work of the military and the police, must be presented proactively, consistently, and credibly. Nigeria must be its own best advocate, in Washington and in the world.

In conclusion, the pre-midterm relationship between Nigeria and the United States was warm but personal. It depended on Trump’s letter, on Ribadu’s shuttle diplomacy, on a moment of crisis that brought two governments together. The post-midterm relationship will be cooler, more institutional, and more demanding. Congress will ask harder questions. Assistance will come with conditions. Security cooperation will face oversight. Trade will be debated, not decreed. That is not a setback. It is a maturation. If Nigeria navigates it well, if it engages early, if it tells its story honestly, if it conducts its own elections credibly, the result could be a Nigeria–United States relationship that is no longer hostage to one election in Washington or to one personality in Abuja, but anchored in shared interests, in shared laws, and in shared democratic accountability. The midterms did not end the partnership. They tested whether it can survive democracy in both countries. That test starts now, and how Nigeria responds in the next ninety days will shape the relationship for the next decade.

Olajoku, Ph.D, writes from Abuja,

folajoku@gmail.com

THE LABOUR CONGRESS/TRADE UNION SQUABBLE

NLC and TUC leaders must rise above their differences to face the common challenges squarely, writes MONDAY PHILIPS EKPE

Some days ago, the President of Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC), Mr Joe Ajaero, told Nigerians that his Trade Union Congress (TUC) counterpart, Mr Festus Osifo, spent more time abroad than the country and argued that he was, therefore, not in a position to truly understand the socio-economic travails of his members. That punch was the culmination of a chain of unsteady events. On October 8, the NLC issued a two-week ultimatum to the federal government to resolve their pending agreements and restore prices of petroleum products to the 2024 levels when the last minimum wage negotiations were held.

Sadly, that deadline died without achieving any of its goals. Then, a meeting between the government and some labour leaders, led by the NLC president, was convened and presided over by the Minister of Labour and Employment, Dr Muhammad Maigari Dingyadi. The Joint National Public Service Negotiating Council (JNPSNC) and Joint Health Sector Union (JOHESU) reportedly participated also. Essentially, what the gathering accomplished was the government’s six months’ award of 70,000 naira to its workers to cushion the biting costs of transportation. Those present welcomed the assistance like half bread that’s better than none.

The TUC president whose absence there unsettled some industry watchers, however, promptly dismissed the offer as part of government’s “haphazard measures”, demanded immediate increase of workers’ remunerations and accused Ajaero of short-changing those he was leading. The rejection didn’t surprise many people, quite frankly. And soon afterwards, organisations like the Senior Staff Association of Statutory Corporations and Government-Owned Companies (SSASCGOC) Senior Staff Association of Universities, Teaching Hospitals, Research Institutes and Associated Institutions (SSAUTHRIAI) and the Nigerian Union of Allied Health Professionals (NUAHP) lined up behind Osifo’s stand. Their premises couldn’t be more cogent. As they put them, “with transportation, food, housing and other essentials becoming increasingly unaffordable, this intervention is no substitute for decent wages, fair remuneration or sustainable improvement in workers’ living standards.” It would take deliberate blindness or aversion to the facts to contest the validity of that argument. But then, how many employers can meet most of their staff’s needs? What can’t be denied, though, is the failure of successive governments to truthfully engage the workers in order to address their legitimate demands.

Ajaero may appear to have compromised the yearnings of the country’s workforce by accepting the insufficient cash subsidy speedily. But his explanation to labour reporters in Lagos the other day could win him sympathisers. His word: “Giving workers ₦70,000 as a transportation intervention for six months is not enough, although it provides some relief. For somebody earning ₦70,000, receiving another ₦70,000 is certainly meaningful. But what happens after six months? There are also other policies that must be considered, particularly transportation. We cannot accept a situation where workers receive ₦70,000 as temporary relief and, after six months, the government simply withdraws the intervention without providing an alternative.

“Nobody should assume that because the six-month period has expired, workers must return to their previous state of poverty. We have left Egypt; we cannot go back to Egypt. As far as the minimum wage negotiations are concerned, the new negotiations must recognise the existing wage structure and the improvements already achieved. You cannot begin negotiating from a position that ignores those gains.” See, some native intelligence won’t hurt. Ajaero may have applied wisdom in embracing this amount which, considering our poor government’s accountability, can soon be frittered away without trace. It then makes sense to take whatever they’re given and ask for more later! Only that the conditionalities for receiving, if any, mustn’t turn out to haunt or further enslave the beneficiaries now and in the future.

Those who think that the bickering between NLC and TUC is orchestrated by the government aren’t alarmist, even if they don’t possess hard proofs. Oftentimes, governments all over the world are the primary enemies of organised labour. For centuries, workers’ revolutions have taught political and business leaders to beware of workers who dare to unite in the pursuit of their common causes. Thankfully, Nigeria had recorded bold, noble and momentous strides by labour unions, many of which were beyond their own jurisdictions, despite the existing difficulties. They confronted colonists, stood against military tyrants, fought for the enthronement of democracy and aggressively canvassed human rights in concert with the mass media and civil society.

Those are some of the legacies handed down to the present labour leaderships – accomplishments they should seek to sustain and bequeath to their successors. True, each dispensation comes with its own peculiarities, so, there can’t be credible reasons to drop the ball now. These are clearly not the best times for the residents of Nigeria. The current cost of living is among the worst since the country was created. In the midst of this stark truth, Ajaero and Osifo must stick together – shoving aside all odds – and remain true to their primary task of safeguarding the dignity of labour.

For, in the words of Abraham Lincoln, “capital is only the fruit of labour, and could never have existed if labour had not first existed. Labour is the superior of capital, and deserves much the higher consideration.” Even in an age when artificial intelligence (AI) is feared to compete disproportionately with the worker, the human element can’t be ignored.

Pope Francis also articulates the supremacy and strategic role of the labourer thus: “There is no worse material poverty, I am keen to stress, than the poverty which prevents people from earning their bread and deprives them of the dignity of work. Youth unemployment, informality, and the lack of labor rights are not inevitable; they are the result of a previous social option, of an economic system that puts profit above man; if the profit is economic, to put it above humanity or above man, is the effect of a disposable culture that considers the human being in himself as a consumer good, which can be used and then discarded.”

Yes, public and private sector workers constitute only a fraction of the Nigerian populace but the magnitude of the responsibilities on their leaders shouldn’t be lost. In the absence of any worthwhile representation in the nation’s parliaments, the unions can be a strong force to extract or enforce good governance. The fast-approaching general polls make this point even more pertinent. Ajaero and Osifo can actually make great, enduring names for themselves by responsibly fighting for the interests of their members and, by extension, those of the rest Nigerians.

Dr Ekpe is a member of THISDAY Editorial Board

World.title: 10TH AFRICAN WOMEN CONFERENCE: A RENEWED CALL TO SERVICE
World.content:
The 10th Anniversary Edition of the Africa Women Conference (AWC) holding in Accra, Ghana is more than a milestone, is more than the celebration of ten remarkable editions, it is a tribute to a vision that has grown into a respected Pan-African platform for dialogue, collaboration and action.

The purpose of the conference is to bring together women leaders, policymakers, development partners, entrepreneurs, academics, civil society organisations, traditional institutions and young people to develop practical solutions for the advancement of African women and girls.

AWC has consistently provided a platform for their voices to be heard, their experiences to shape policy conversations, their enterprises to gain visibility and their leadership potential to be strengthened.

The establishment of the AWC Leadership Development Centre for Women and Girls created a platform for training, mentorship and the development of emerging female community leaders. AWC-Next has also expanded engagement with students, young professionals, youth leaders and girls at the grassroots, ensuring that the next generation is prepared to sustain and advance this important work.

Through partnership with DataCamp Donates USA, AWC secured 100 training licences for women and girls across Africa, selected from more than 3,500 applicants. Participants received structured training in artificial intelligence, data science, data analysis, Python, SQL, Excel, Power BI, machine learning and entrepreneurship.

Following rigorous performance assessments, 37 outstanding participants progressed to advanced specialisation and professional certification tracks. This initiative demonstrates how AWC is translating conference resolutions into practical interventions that remove financial barriers, build a sustainable pipeline of African female technology professionals and prepare women and girls to participate meaningfully in the future of work and the digital economy.

Past AWC editions have further demonstrated the value of collective action. The eighth edition in Zambia advanced important conversations on digital inclusion, financial access, agritech, entrepreneurship and women’s participation in the digital economy.

In direct response to the digital gender gap highlighted at that Conference, the AWC Women and Girls Digital Technology Hub—AI and Data Science Programme was established.

The ninth edition in Ghana strengthened collaboration around leadership, innovation and sustainable development. Delegates adopted resolutions supporting affirmative action, mentorship, STEM education, women-led enterprises, financial inclusion, cultural reform and greater representation for women in decision-making. The proposed Pan-African Women’s Film Initiative also emerged as a platform for documenting and amplifying the authentic stories of African women.

These achievements remind us that conferences must produce more than inspiring speeches and beautiful memories. They must generate partnerships, influence institutions, strengthen communities and improve the lives of women and girls.

This conviction inspired the theme of the 10th Anniversary Edition: “A Decade of Impact: From Commitments to Action—Advancing Justice, Economic Power and Leadership for African Women and Girls.”

The theme challenges us to examine the distance between the promises we have made and the actions we have taken. Africa has adopted several laws, policies and international commitments protecting the rights of women and girls.

Yet discriminatory practices, weak enforcement, gender-based violence and limited access to justice remain realities for many. Our task must now move beyond policy declarations to effective enforcement, accountability and measurable results.

Economic empowerment must equally go beyond small interventions that merely help women survive. African women must be positioned to own productive assets, access finance and technology, participate meaningfully in regional and international trade, build competitive enterprises and benefit from the opportunities presented by the African Continental Free Trade Area.

When women have access to capital, markets, digital tools and supportive policies, they create jobs, strengthen families and contribute significantly to national development.

We must also transform the institutions and social norms that continue to restrict women’s leadership. Women deserve equitable representation in political, corporate, academic, traditional and community decision-making. Representation must not be treated as a favour granted to women; it is essential to inclusive governance, social justice and sustainable development.

As women gather in Ghana 4-6 November 2026, every participant should approach this anniversary as a renewed call to service. Let us move from discussing inclusion to building inclusive institutions; from advocating economic empowerment to investing in women-led enterprises; and from calling for justice to demanding enforcement and accountability.

Our success will not be measured solely by the quality of our deliberations in Accra. It will be measured by what we do afterwards: the younger women we mentor, the girls whose education we support, the discriminatory practices we challenge, the women-owned businesses we patronise and invest in, and the policies we help translate into meaningful change.

Dr. Jumai Ahmadu, Convener, Africa Women Conference (AWC)

World.title: THE ALETO GAS PIPELINE EXPLOSION
World.content:
Regulators must enforce safety standards

The cause of the recent gas pipeline explosion at the Old Bori Road in Aleto community, Eleme Local Government Area of Rivers State, is still being investigated. The explosion involved a pipeline belonging to the Nigerian Gas Infrastructure Company Limited (NGIC), a subsidiary of the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC). That the explosion occurred only weeks after an earlier gas leak along the same pipeline corridor raises questions about whether the underlying weaknesses responsible for the previous incident were adequately investigated and addressed. While reports indicated that residents sustained injuries and homes and businesses were damaged, experts familiar with pipeline transportation of high-pressure gas blame it on aging infrastructure.

For Aleto, the authorities should establish the precise route and boundaries of the pipeline’s approved right-of-way as well as the legally applicable setback and any restrictions on buildings within the corridor. It is also important to find the actual distance between the pipeline and each affected building and whether any structures were erected within a prohibited area. Did the pipeline’s operator and the relevant regulators adequately monitor encroachment? Equally important is community participation. Did residents, farmers and young people living along the pipeline corridors receive safety education or encouraged to report suspicious activities, leaks, ground disturbances and other warning signs?

This growing danger is not confined to Eleme. In Bille community, Degema Local Government Area, residents have reportedly witnessed persistent gas bubbling from the ground, water bodies and residential wells, accompanied by fumes and cracks in parts of the community. Civil society organisations, including Social Action, Kebetkache Women Development and Resource Centre, Chikoko Movement, Civil Rights Action, MiiDeekor and Health of Mother Earth Foundation (HOMEF), have joined environmental advocates and community stakeholders in demanding urgent government intervention. The Ijaw Youth Council Eastern Zone Chairman, Datolu Sukubo, has accused the federal government and relevant companies of failing to respond adequately to the problem since October last year. He argued that operators should not evade responsibility simply because investigators have yet to establish a direct equipment failure or conventional pipeline leak.

Meanwhile, the detected gas leaks and the Eleme pipeline explosion have prompted renewed engagement between the authorities in Abuja and Port Harcourt. Governor Siminalayi Fubara has demanded a swift and comprehensive resolution, while pledging to upgrade Bille’s primary healthcare centre. The Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas), Ekperikpe Ekpo, has also maintained that the federal government is working towards a sustainable solution. But all these assurances must translate into measurable results. Gas seepage that threatens public health, water sources, fishing, farming and other livelihoods requires prompt investigation, transparent disclosure of findings and effective remediation.

Ultimately, hosting oil and gas pipelines should not condemn rural communities to perpetual anxiety. Companies must invest in infrastructure renewal, continuous monitoring, and emergency preparedness. Regulators must enforce safety standards independently while holding operators accountable for negligence. Government, in both the federal and the state, must also ensure that affected residents receive medical attention, environmental protection, compensation where appropriate and meaningful participation in decisions affecting their lives.

The Eleme explosion should serve as a turning point. A thorough, independent investigation must establish its cause, determine whether earlier warnings were adequately addressed and identify the officials or operators responsible for any failures. The findings should be made public, with clear deadlines for implementing corrective measures. Nigeria cannot continue to treat pipeline explosions and gas seepage as isolated emergencies. The recurring incidents in Eleme and Bille expose a wider challenge of infrastructure integrity, environmental governance and corporate responsibility. The real test for the authorities and operators is not how quickly they respond after disaster strikes, but how effectively they prevent the next one.

World.title: IEC reports encouraging voter turnout as 12 million cast their votes
World.content:
President Cyril Ramaphosa cast his vote at Hyde Park High School for the local government elections. Image: X/ANC

The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) says it is encouraged by the voter turnout at voting stations across the country, with more than 12 million people having cast their ballots by 17:00 on Wednesday, 4 November.

South Africans headed to the polls on Wednesday for the 2026 Local Government Elections, with voting stations open from 07:00 to 21:00.

IEC SAYS AROUND 12 MILLION VOTERS CAST THEIR BALLOTS

According to the IEC, preliminary figures indicated that approximately 12 million voters had cast their ballots by 17:00.



Gauteng recorded the highest number of voters at three million, followed by KwaZulu-Natal with 2.5 million, Western Cape with 1.5 million, Eastern Cape with 1.4 million and Limpopo with 1.1 million.

Other provincial figures included Mpumalanga with 854 901 voters, North West with 702 1337, Free State with 588 237 and Northern Cape with 299 381.

HOW THE VOTES WILL BE COUNTED

The IEC said counting would begin at each voting station shortly after voting closes.



The counting process will take place in the presence of party agents, independent candidate agents and accredited observers.

According to the Commission, the process will include the following steps:

Sealed ballot boxes will be opened, and ballot papers will be checked for the IEC’s security stamp.

Ballot papers will be sorted and counted separately for each electoral contest, including the proportional representation (PR) ballot, ward candidate ballot and, where applicable, the district council PR ballot.

The results for each contest will be reconciled against the ballot papers received, issued, unused, spoilt and counted at the voting station.

Results slips will be completed in duplicate, signed by the presiding officer and countersigned by party agents. They will then be displayed at the voting station once counting and tallying have been completed.

Party agents will be allowed to photograph the signed results slips.

The results will subsequently be scanned and captured at the local IEC office before undergoing verification and independent external auditing.

The IEC said its Results Operations Centres would allow political parties, independent candidates, observers and the media to monitor the capturing, verification and processing of results.



This is intended to strengthen transparency and ensure the integrity of the electoral process.

“Once counting, capturing and verification have been completed and outstanding queries resolved, the Electoral Commission will declare the final results and announce the allocation of seats in municipal councils within the prescribed seven-day period,” the Commission said.

World.title: Tumisho Masha under fire over pic of marked ballot paper
World.content:
Tumisho Masha is under fire fter posting a picture of his marked ballot paper at a voting station. Images via X

Actor Tumisho Masha is facing widespread backlash after he posted a picture of his marked ballot paper inside a voting station

His defiant act, a criminal offence, came after the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) urged the public to obey the rules ahead of Wednesday’s local government elections.

TUMISHO MASHA POSTS PIC OF MARKED BALLOT PAPER

On X, Tumisho Masha trended over his tweet, which he has since deleted, showing off his marked ballot paper.



The picture was taken at his local voting station, Lyndhurst Primary School, and revealed who the actor had voted for in the local government elections.

He captioned the tweet: “A mark has been made. ActionSA is the only party that knows how to fix Joburg”.

The veteran actor deleted the tweet, but not before it was screenshot by multiple other X users, including the account @CrimeWatch_RSA. 

The account posted the screenshot, warning Tumisho Masha that he had contravened the Electoral Act 73 of 1998.

“The matter will be further handled by the Gauteng SAPS”, the account added.

GAUTENG #LGE2026 | An actor, Tumisho Masha (@TumishoMasha), has contravened the Electoral Act 73 of 1998. The matter will be further handled by the Gauteng SAPS.



You are reminded that it is a criminal offence to photograph a marked ballot paper and/or share it. pic.twitter.com/Bq4fsulklw  November 4, 2026

Tumisho appeared to respond to the backlash with a tweet that read: “Everybody calm down. It’s really not what you think”.

Everybody calm down it’s really not what you think 😂😂😂 — Tumisho Masha (@TumishoMasha) November 4, 2026

WHAT DOES THE LAW SAY?

Under Regulation 38(1A) of the Election Regulations, 2004, under the Electoral Act 73 of 1998, making a photograph or other image of a ballot paper marked by a voter on election day or during special voting is prohibited.



Regulation 38(2) states that it is a criminal offence punishable by law.

A person convicted of contravening this regulation can face a fine or imprisonment of up to one year.

World.title: RIP | Elderly woman dies while waiting to vote in KZN
World.content:
An elderly woman died after collapsing while waiting to cast her vote in Durban on Wednesday, 4 November. Image: X

An elderly woman died after collapsing while waiting to cast her vote at a polling station in Durban on Wednesday, 4 November.

The woman, believed to be in her late 60s, collapsed at Shallcross Primary School during South Africa’s 2026 local government elections.

According to reports, she experienced a medical emergency while standing in the queue. Her family rushed her to a nearby hospital, where doctors declared her dead on arrival.



Ambulance allegedly failed to arrive

Election observer Pretty Jwarah said people at the voting station tried to assist the woman after she collapsed.

Jwarah said they gave her water and contacted her daughter before calling for an ambulance.

However, the ambulance allegedly failed to arrive, prompting the family to arrange private transport to hospital.

Jwarah later contacted the woman’s daughter, who confirmed her mother’s death.

The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) presiding officer at the voting station confirmed the incident.

LGE 2026 | An elderly woman has died after collapsing while waiting to vote at Shallcross Primary School, south of Durban. Community members say an ambulance was called, but it did not arrive. pic.twitter.com/9lD9h4r1C8  November 4, 2026

IEC seeks answers

IEC KwaZulu-Natal spokesperson Thabani Ngwira said the commission was gathering information to establish the circumstances surrounding the woman’s death.

Vedan expressed condolences to the family and said the right to vote should never come at the expense of human life and dignity.

The woman’s identity has not been released, while the cause of her death remains unconfirmed.

World.title: KZN police probing theft of ballot papers in KwaZulu-Natal
World.content:
Ballot boxes and election materials were stolen at a second voting station in KwaZulu-Natal. Image: Nokwanda Ncwane

The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) has confirmed that unused ballot papers and election materials were allegedly stolen at a voting station in KwaZulu-Natal during the 2026 Local Government Elections.

The incident reportedly happened overnight between Tuesday and Wednesday, 4 November, as South Africans headed to the polls.

BALLOT PAPERS AND ELECTION MATERIALS STOLEN IN KZN

The IEC said it received a report of the theft of unused ballot papers and a stamp at Mnyameni Secondary School in Ward 2, eThekwini.



“Unused ballots and election security materials, including the certified voters’ roll, were reported stolen at the voting station overnight.

“The Commission can confirm that the voting station had sufficient materials to continue operations, except for the voters’ roll, which needed to be reprinted for the voting station. By plan, we do issue a new security pack and ballot papers specifically for Election Day,” KZN Electoral Officer Ntombifuthi Masinga said.

POLICE INVESTIGATE THEFT OF VOTING MATERIALS

KwaZulu-Natal police spokesperson Colonel Robert Netshiunda confirmed that police had opened a burglary case after voting materials belonging to the IEC were reportedly stolen from a voting station in Hillcrest between Tuesday night and Wednesday morning.

[WATCH] Police spokesperson Col. Robert Netshiunda says investigations are underway following the theft of unused ballot papers at Mnyameni Zenex Secondary School, Durban. He adds that a police officer was removed from election operations after arriving in a vehicle displaying a… pic.twitter.com/XjshkQWKNt — Newzroom Afrika (@Newzroom405) November 4, 2026

Netshiunda said it was reported that the IEC’s presiding officer had gone to the school, which was being used as a voting station, on Tuesday evening and placed sensitive materials, including ink, the voters’ roll and ballot papers, inside an unlocked guardhouse.

“The presiding officer reportedly locked the school gate and left. According to information, there was a group of about ten people who could see what the official was doing inside the guardhouse. The school does not have a security guard overnight.



“When the presiding officer arrived at the school on Wednesday morning, she noticed that the gate of the school was open and there were people standing outside the school gate. When she proceeded to the guardhouse, she found that ballot papers and other IEC materials had been stolen. The matter was then reported to the police,” Netshiunda explained.

Netshiunda said police investigations would also seek to establish why ballot papers were transported to a voting station the night before the elections without a police escort.

“Part of police’s responsibilities during the elections is to escort presiding officers with sensitive materials from warehouses to voting stations and back without fail, and the movement of sensitive material is done on the day of the elections,” he added.

World.title: Love eating late at night? Scientists have news to share
World.content:
Love eating late at night? Your late night snacking may reveal more than you think. Image: Ron Lach via Pexels

We have all been there, feeling peckish long after dinner. Whether it’s a packet of chips in front of the television, a chocolate bar after dinner or a raid on the fridge before bed, plenty of people enjoy a late-night snack.

But scientists investigating this everyday habit have found something about eating late at night that could make you think twice before reaching for your next bite.

What researchers discovered about eating late at night

Researchers at Oregon Health & Science University in the United States analysed data from almost 200 000 people to see whether eating late at night was linked to liver disease.



The study drew on three long-running research projects: the Nurses’ Health Study, the Nurses’ Health Study II and the Health Professionals Follow-up Study.

The researchers examined participants’ reported eating habits and health outcomes over a median follow-up period of 16 years.

They found that people who reported eating late at night had a higher risk of two liver conditions: metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), commonly known as fatty liver disease, and cirrhosis, which involves serious scarring of the liver.



Their findings, published in Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology, showed an association between late-night eating and a 20% to 30% higher risk of liver disease compared with not reporting this eating habit.

The researchers defined late-night eating broadly as eating after dinner or after bedtime. The study did not establish a specific cut-off time that applies to everyone.

Eating late at night: Why the timing of meals could matter

The timing of meals may matter because the body operates according to a natural 24-hour cycle known as the circadian rhythm.



This internal clock helps regulate sleep, hormones and metabolism. The liver also follows these rhythms, which influence how the body processes nutrients.

Dr Andrew McHill, an associate professor and sleep and circadian physiologist at Oregon Health & Science University, said previous research had found that eating during the biological night could reduce the body’s ability to metabolise food efficiently.

Disruptions to the body’s normal rhythms have also been linked to metabolic problems, including obesity and diabetes.



Researchers are now investigating whether meal timing could also influence liver health, potentially offering another way to address health risks without necessarily changing what people eat.

Should you stop snacking before bed?

The findings do not mean that everyone who eats an evening snack will develop liver problems.

Fatty liver disease can range in severity, and only a small proportion of people with the condition develop serious complications such as cirrhosis.



Lead researcher Dr Robert Wilechansky, a liver specialist at Oregon Health & Science University, suggested that limiting calorie intake in the hours before bedtime might be beneficial.

But there is still more work to do before researchers can establish whether changing meal times actually improves liver health.

One limitation is that the study relied on participants reporting eating habits and medical diagnoses. Although the researchers accounted for several other factors, an observational study cannot establish cause and effect.



The participants were also drawn from three specific research cohorts in the United States of America, so the findings may not apply equally to every population.

Researchers are now recruiting participants for further clinical research to investigate whether eating earlier can improve measures of liver health in people with existing fatty liver disease.

For now, the study adds to growing evidence that the timing of everyday habits may matter for long-term health.



Do you also love picking up a snack late at night?

World.title: Zimbabwe investigates luxury vehicles as Bellarmine Mugabe faces fresh arrest
World.content:
Chatunga Mugabe arrested as Zimbabwe probes two luxury cars over import permit violations. Images: X@Zimblogger

Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of late former Zimbabwean president Robert Mugabe, has been arrested alongside four other men following an alleged assault on a Zimbabwe Anti-Corruption Commission (ZACC) investigator during an operation targeting two luxury vehicles suspected of being illegally kept in the country.

The 29-year-old was arrested on Tuesday evening at Brompton Guest Lodge in Newlands, Harare, where investigators were following up on information about a Lamborghini and a Mercedes-Benz GLE 53 registered in South Africa.

According to ZACC spokesperson Simiso Mlevu, preliminary investigations suggested that the vehicles entered Zimbabwe under temporary import permits issued by the Zimbabwe Revenue Authority (ZIMRA).



However, investigators suspected that the vehicles had remained in the country beyond their permitted periods.

Mlevu said the Lamborghini entered Zimbabwe in June and was recorded as having exited on 12 July.

The Mercedes-Benz reportedly entered the country on the same day and was recorded as having left for South Africa on 10 October.

Despite the recorded departures, ZACC investigators found both vehicles at the Harare lodge on Tuesday.

An official was allegedly assaulted during the operation, prompting the commission to report the incident to the police.

National police spokesperson Commissioner Paul Nyathi confirmed the arrest of Chatunga and four other suspects: Munashe Mubawu, 43, Terrence Johannes Chinyemba, 42, Fredson Peter, 33, and Solomon Pamire, 34.



The five face assault charges and were expected to appear in court on Thursday.

Their alleged individual roles in the suspected vehicle smuggling case have not been established.

What Zimbabwe’s temporary import permit rules say

ZIMRA allows qualifying visitors to bring foreign-registered private vehicles into Zimbabwe under Temporary Import Permits (TIPs).

However, the permits come with strict conditions governing how long vehicles can remain in the country.

According to ZIMRA, vehicles must generally be exported when the permit holder first leaves Zimbabwe, within three months of importation, or within any shorter period specified by the authority.

Extensions may be granted under certain circumstances, but vehicles cannot simply remain in the country indefinitely.

ZIMRA has also warned that vehicles breaching temporary importation conditions may be seized.

In October 2026, the authority introduced enhanced controls requiring additional documentation and verification for certain applications, with permits ordinarily limited to 30 days.

Chatunga’s previous encounters with police

The latest arrest adds to Chatunga’s previous encounters with law enforcement in Zimbabwe and South Africa.

He was previously arrested in South Africa following a shooting incident at his Johannesburg residence in which his gardener was wounded.

He was subsequently deported to Zimbabwe after admitting to being in the country illegally.

He has also faced allegations involving cannabis possession and an incident at a police checkpoint in Bubi, near Beitbridge.

World.title: 'Bread and butter' issues dominate SA elections
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - South Africa voted on Wednesday in local government elections dominated by anger over failures in water and power supply that are expected to result in a further slide in support for the ANC.

Control of the major cities is at stake in the vote for 257 councils that will gauge the political mood ahead of the next national elections in 2029.

Moses Mashaba, a 27-year-old street vendor from Johannesburg's Soweto township, said he voted because "things have been horrible".

"Sometimes we don't have water or electricity. There is also a high unemployment rate, which has been frustrating," he told AFP.

Polling stations began closing at 9pm after a 14-hour day, but authorities said anyone still in a queue would still be able to cast their ballot.

Counting would start at polling stations soon after the last votes had been cast, with final results due by Sunday, the election authority said.

Of 29.2 million registered voters, 12 million had cast their ballots on Wednesday by 5pm, it said in its turnout figure.

Some 2.6 million people were allowed to vote early on Monday and Tuesday but only 1.4 million did so.

World.title: From ballot boxes to council seats: What happens before IEC declares election results
World.content:
MIDRAND - Voting stations for the 2026 local government elections closed at 9 pm on Wednesday.

But the work of the Electoral Commission (IEC) continues.

Once every eligible voter has cast their vote, the focus moves to counting, reconciling and verifying votes before the country can know who will take seats in the 257 municipal councils.

Briefing the media on Wednesday night, IEC Chief Electoral Officer Sy Mamabolo outlined the nitty-gritty.

READ | Gauteng tops voter turnout as 12 million South Africans cast ballots by 5pm

Once polls are closed, ballot papers will then be counted at the voting stations in the presence of party agents, independent agents and accredited observers.

“Sealed ballot boxes will be opened, and ballot papers are checked for the official security stamp of the Commission. Ballots are then sorted out and counted separately for each ballot type, namely whether it's a PR ballot, vote ballot and, where applicable the voting district PR ballot.”

Once the counting has been completed, officials will then move to reconcile results of each contest against the ballot papers received, issued, and those that remain unused at each station.

“That process must reconcile every ballot that was received by the station. Result slips are completed in duplicate, signed by the Presiding Officer and countersigned by party agents before being displayed at the station as soon as counting is complete."

Before the IEC can declare the election results, they are then subsequently scanned and captured at the local office of the Commission and subjected to verification and independent external auditing.

The results operation centres, provide political parties, independent candidates, observers and the media with an opportunity to monitor the capturing, verification and processing of results.

World.title: World leaders hope for reset after US midterms
World.content:
PARIS - World leaders voiced hopes for a reset with the United States on Wednesday after voters delivered a huge midterm election defeat to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.

The Democrats seized control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, giving them the power to block legislation and hold up Trump's appointments.

Germany

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he hoped to see new initiatives to end the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.

"With their majority in both chambers of Congress, the Democratic Party will likely seek to shift the political course in the United States," Wadephul said.

Through cooperation between the United States and Europe, "there may be a new opportunity to launch a fresh initiative" to resolve conflicts, he said.

Spain

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said Trump's defeat showed that the global far-right was on the wane.

"It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will soon happen in Spain," the socialist leader said, with elections looming later this month.

The far-right wave is "no longer growing, it is unravelling," he added.

Russia

Russia hopes Trump will continue his "peacemaking efforts" after the midterm elections, the Kremlin said.

"President Trump continues to exercise his powers. We sincerely hope that he will also continue his peacemaking efforts," spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.

South Africa

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the result could thaw strained ties between Pretoria and Washington.

"We're hoping that on a bilateral basis, there will be a coming together of minds where we will find a proper path forward on geopolitics as well as on trade matters and investment matters," he said.

He added that he hoped the result would "introduce a new era in world relations".

EU

The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas voiced hope the new US Congress would support Ukraine and ramp up pressure on Russia.

"I hope that the new Congress... will continue supporting Ukraine and also putting more pressure on Russia," she said, adding that Europe and the United States "are much stronger together" in pushing Moscow to end its war.

UK

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the result was an opportunity for the world to "unite" around resolving cost-of-living issues.

"President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living," Burnham said.
