World.title: Africa: How Many More COPs Before Climate Promises Become Action?
World.content:
A woman wades through floodwaters in Bor, Jonglei State, South Sudan, where communities continue to live with the effects of flooding from previous years as the country prepares for further climate-related shocks.

Every year before COP, the same question surfaces: what is the one thing Africa needs from this summit?

Ahead of COP31, the answer emerging from a World Resources Institute Africa webinar was clear: Africa must move beyond asking what it can receive from global climate negotiations and focus on what it can bring. With geopolitical tensions, energy disruptions and climate shocks exposing vulnerabilities across African economies, speakers argued that the continent must use the summit to advance practical solutions that strengthen energy security, protect food systems and mobilise climate finance.

A reinvented agency



Olufunso Somorin, Regional Principal Officer for Climate Change and Green Growth at the African Development Bank, said these challenges were interconnected, warning that simultaneous disruptions to energy, food and economic systems could undermine the continent's development gains. He described them as a triangle of reality - when one is hit, the others strain, and when all three are hit, the development gains of recent years are at risk.

"COP of today, it is now a trade forum. It is now a marketplace."

He said that Africa needed to rethink its approach to global climate negotiations and strengthen its position as a partner in shaping climate solutions rather than simply seeking assistance. His answer was what he called a "reinvented agency". Africa, he said, must move "away from this idea of Africa that needs to be helped, to an Africa that needs to be partnered with."

He also questioned the pace of the process itself, asking that after 30 COPs, how many more does it take to get things done?

That means understanding what COP has become. "COP of today, it is now a trade forum. It is now a marketplace. And what you get out of a marketplace is largely based on who you are and what you bring to the marketplace," he said.

Strengthening energy security

Energy security was one of the key issues at COP31, with the prevailing situation of geopolitical tensions and disruptions to the global energy supply underpinning the risks of being dependent on external energy sources. Africa has significant renewable energy potential. However, the challenge remains translating these resources into reliable and affordable electricity that can support economic growth, businesses, and industrial development.

Yasmin Abdulwassie, Senior Manager for Climate in Africa at the Children's Investment Fund Foundation, said high financing costs and limited public budgets remained major obstacles to scaling up renewable energy investments. "The challenge is really translating that potential into affordable, reliable energy that can be replicated and scaled," she said.

She said philanthropy can help by funding project preparation, policy reform and investment pipelines, so that transition pathways are country-led. She pointed to South Africa's Just Energy Transition Partnership. The initiative, she said, initially announced with $8.5 billion, had grown to more than $14 billion, proof that investors back credible country platforms.

She also highlighted Senegal's Renewable Energy Investment Facility as another emerging example of efforts to attract investment and support the country's energy transition. "So that type of catalytic role that philanthropy plays is not just about unlocking finance, but helping countries turn lasting financing possibilities for economic reform," said Abdulwassie.

Somorin said that achieving universal energy access would require stronger partnerships that connect national ambitions with clear financing strategies. He cited Mission 300, which aims to connect 300 million people in sub-Saharan Africa to electricity by 2030, as an example of how shared targets and country-specific strategies can accelerate progress.

He said 37 African countries had developed national energy compacts outlining their strategies for expanding electricity access, helping attract investment from development finance institutions, the World Bank, the African Development Bank and philanthropic organisations. He said the initiative demonstrated the importance of having a collective goal while agreeing on practical steps to achieve it.

"It is a new way of defining partnership where you have a collective goal, but you also have a shared discussion on the how. How do we get there? What do we need to do differently?" he said.

Beyond energy security, COP31 is urged to give greater attention to adaptation, particularly ensuring that climate finance reaches countries and communities most vulnerable to climate change.

Abdulwassie said that the climate summit should move adaptation commitments toward "real, measurable outcomes," particularly in food systems, water and livelihood infrastructure. She set out three priorities. The first is a credible financing pathway. Countries have committed to tripling adaptation finance by 2035, but Abdulwassie said the detail is missing. "How are we going to do it? How will progress be measured?" she asked, adding that these questions need answers at COP31 and at every milestone after it.

The second is better indicators, and here she pointed to the Belém-Addis vision, a two-year process that runs toward COP32 in Ethiopia. Current metrics, she said, tend to count activities, such as how many farmers completed climate-smart agriculture training. She argued the measure should be whether a farmer's livelihood "stays intact or improves despite climate shocks," and that credible results of that kind are what attract further financing.

The third is matching national adaptation plans with investment plans. She cited a Malawi initiative, backed by philanthropy and led by the African Climate Foundation, in which more than 20 of the country's priority adaptation proposals have been matched with potential investors. The aim, she said, is to give adaptation the same investable pipelines that mitigation projects increasingly have.

Closing the adaptation finance gap

The challenge of mobilising climate finance for adaptation was also highlighted by Somorin, who said African countries needed to rethink how adaptation projects are financed and how their economic value is presented to investors.

"Adaptation is very complex," Somorin said, and the sector has made it harder by lumping everything together as "climate action." He said that adaptation remains more difficult to finance than mitigation because projects often lack the clear financial returns that attract private investors.

Put all climate projects in one finance basket, he said, and about nine in ten that emerge would be mitigation projects. They are simply easier to finance and attract capital more readily. Africa also faces a structural handicap. In every other region, he said, private capital drives climate action. Africa is the only place where public money leads.

His first proposed fix is to stop treating the two as separate. "You use mitigation finance to drive adaptation goals," he said. He gave an example of a solar-powered irrigation scheme in a semi-arid region that cuts emissions through clean energy, but it also lets farmers grow and earn all year round, which is an adaptation result. The more deliberately adaptation is built into mitigation projects, he said, the more capital will reach it.

"I argue that you use mitigation finance to drive adaptation goals," he said.

Somorin also called for a change in how investors assess adaptation projects, arguing that their wider economic benefits should be recognised alongside their immediate financial returns.

He said financiers needed to understand the distinction between financial viability and economic viability, particularly where investments generate long-term benefits that may not immediately translate into revenue. Somorin said the task is to help financiers see that the economic value is real and can be monetized, either now or later, as new markets emerge to turn it into financial returns.

Africa has documented 11 financial instruments for mitigation projects but, at best, three for adaptation. Expanding these financing options, he said, would let more resources flow and would bring non-traditional investors into the adaptation space.

Philanthropy can help unlock larger investments

While development finance institutions have a role in mobilising investment for climate action, Abdulwassie said philanthropic capital could help address some of the structural barriers preventing African countries from accessing climate finance. "Philanthropy alone, we know, cannot close that gap," she said. However, she identified three areas where it could have a catalytic impact: strengthening national institutions, developing country-led investment platforms, and building stronger partnerships across the climate finance ecosystem.

The first is institutional capacity. Where African institutions don't exist, or need strengthening, she said, philanthropic money is best spent building them. That leads to country ownership and brings "the local voice, the local agenda" to the table, alongside partners such as the African Development Bank. She pointed again to South Africa's Just Energy Transition Partnership, where philanthropic partners and multilaterals helped the government negotiate what international financing would look like. She also made a pointed aside: more grants should go directly to countries to help scale such efforts.

The second is building investment platforms with countries rather than for them. Philanthropy can provide technical expertise, convene partners and help design financing mechanisms and instruments. The models must be contextual, she said, because every country's energy pathway, food system and growth path is different.

The third is strengthening the wider ecosystem of African climate leadership. She cited philanthropic support for the first two Africa Climate Summits, the resulting Nairobi and Addis Ababa declarations, and efforts to give African countries a collective voice through the African Union during South Africa's G20 presidency.

The stakes, she said, are high: climate finance flowing into Africa is less than 2% of what is needed, nowhere near the continent's needs. Without African leadership in these rooms, she argued, the finance ambitions cannot be met.

"Bringing in that collective voice because I believe that ensures that African leadership is there to shape African priorities," she said.

Turning country platforms into action

Somorin said his experience working with country platforms at the African Development Bank had shown that strong national leadership was essential to their success.

He outlined three factors that can help these platforms move beyond coordination. First, governments need clearly defined climate goals and realistic objectives that reflect their national capabilities, political circumstances, and development priorities.

"Nothing substitutes for strong leadership," he said. He named the difference it makes by comparing Rwanda with Niger. Clear, well-structured country goals matter, he said, but so does honesty about capability. Countries that are still asking partners to help train their people, when they should be implementing, are not ready to move. Goals also have to fit a country's political and socioeconomic realities. He said, "You cannot ignore" even when they seem unrelated to climate.

Second, countries must understand the strengths of their development partners, including multilateral institutions, philanthropic organisations and NGOs, and bring them together around clearly allocated responsibilities.

Third, governments must demonstrate their own commitment by contributing resources to the initiatives they want partners to support. Somorin said that countries which tell partners they need support for 80% of a project because they will supply 20% make faster progress than those that put in nothing and ask for everything. A government that commits a set share of its budget over five years, and assigns people to learn and deliver, finds it much easier to leverage what others bring.

Building towards an African COP32

Ethiopia is set to host COP32 in 2027. Abdulwassie said African countries should begin preparing now to ensure the summit delivers beyond political commitments. She said that COP32 should not be viewed as an Ethiopian event alone, but as an opportunity for African countries to unite around shared development priorities and strengthen the continent's influence in global climate discussions.

"COP32 is not just an Ethiopian COP, but an African COP," she said.

Abdulwassie outlined three priorities for the road to COP32. First, African leaders must work together to agree on key priorities. She pointed to the African Union summit in February and the pre-COP period as chances to agree on priorities that can outlast political cycles, including the action agenda and the initiatives each presidency will announce.

Second, Africa should use the run-up to COP32 to showcase successful climate initiatives already underway, demonstrate their results and identify which approaches can be adapted or scaled up in other countries.

Third, she called for greater recognition of local voices, particularly those of young people and communities already driving climate action. She said communities' ambitions and practices need to reach leaders and be translated into action. "How do we make sure the voice of youth in particular ... is translated into action?" she asked. She warned that decisions made today would shape the world inherited by future generations.

Close 

Development partners, she said, should engage Africa not in terms of handouts but as true partners, in a relationship where Africans have resources to trade and engage with, at COP32 and beyond.

To make COP31 a success for Africa, Abdulwassie pointed to stronger continental unity, partnerships and visibility in global climate discussions.

She said African countries needed to speak with a stronger collective voice while building momentum around energy, food security and water resilience. She also stressed the importance of having more Africans present at the summit to share their ambitions, experiences and progress.

Somorin said Africa's voice and leadership must be central to global climate discussions, particularly given the continent's limited contribution to climate change and its disproportionate exposure to its impacts. The voice, agency and significance of that continent, he argued, can never be ignored, but the starting point is Africa asserting its own agency, because the global climate equation is incomplete without Africa's development and resilience.

He urged African countries to move away from the perception of a continent waiting to be helped.

"Africa should be recognised not only for its vulnerability but also for its potential to contribute to global solutions," said Somorin. "If there's any region that could play a significant role in the global solution, it is Africa."

Protecting Africa's industrialisation ambitions

Soha Benchekroun, a climate resilience and industrial development policy researcher and adviser, argued that climate negotiations must give greater consideration to Africa's right to industrialise and move up global value chains.

The aim for COP31, and for the "African COP" in Ethiopia a year later, said Benchekroun, is to make sure climate action "does not undermine our industrialization trajectories." Most African countries are only starting to climb global value chains and build manufacturing and processing capacity at home. Many have moved to restrict raw material exports and promote local processing, a trend she called positive.

The threat, she said, comes from unilateral trade measures adopted in the name of climate policy by industrialized countries: carbon border adjustments, carbon pricing and related regulations. She said the negotiated rules should seek to limit the harm of these measures to African and other developing economies. The timing is pressing, she noted, with more carbon border mechanisms on the way, including the UK's, due to start in January 2027.

"Justice and a good outcome is first about doing no harm to our African development and industrial development pathways," she said.

Benchekroun also said that the just transition debate has focused on wider energy access while giving the right to development, and industrial development in particular, only marginal attention. "We do not expect COPs to sort out our energy infrastructure challenges, nor to promote our own industrialization," she said, "but at least a good start would be to not hinder them." What lifts a continent out of poverty, she said, is infrastructure, industrial development, and local value addition, paired with ways to turn them into benefits for society.

World.title: South Africa: Voters Demand Water, Electricity and Dignity As Ramaphosa Heads to Polls
World.content:
South Africans in queuing to vote in the 2026 Local Government Elections.

Voters at Hyde Park High School in Johannesburg want the local government elections to bring better services, safer communities and leaders who listen.

Gloria Chabalala brought her daughter to the voting station to teach her about a democratic right her grandparents only enjoyed later in life.

Johannesburg voters want more than election promises. They want water, electricity, housing and safer communities.

As South Africans cast their ballots in the 2026 local government elections, voters at Hyde Park High School say they are hoping for leaders who will put their needs first.

The voting station is also where President Cyril Ramaphosa and First Lady Dr Tshepo Motsepe are expected to cast their ballots.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

For residents, however, the election is about choosing leaders who can improve their daily lives.

Among those who arrived to vote was Johannesburg resident Melisa Mandy, who praised the smooth voting process and the help she received from election officials.

"The IEC is very helpful, telling us exactly where to go. It's quite an efficient and fast process," she said.

Mandy, who was born and raised in Johannesburg, said she had watched the city change over the years.

She hopes the election results will bring positive changes to the city she calls home.

"It's a special occasion today. I think it's a turning point in the country. Everyone needs to participate," she said.

For another voter, Gloria Chabalala, election day was also a chance to teach her young daughter about South Africa's democracy.

She brought her daughter to the voting station so she could see what it means to take part in an election.

Her daughter still has about 10 years to go before she is old enough to vote, but Gloria wants her to understand the importance of having a say in who leads the country.

She remembered her late father, who died in 2005.

Although he lived into his 70s, he only had the opportunity to vote a few times during his lifetime.

His experience is a reminder to Gloria that the right to vote was not always available to all South Africans.

"I was telling my daughter how important it is for her to vote because her grandparents only got to vote much later in life. It's important that they understand the importance of us being here and this right that we have," she said.

Gloria said her daughter already knows about some of South Africa's political parties and is beginning to understand the choices voters make.

But beyond teaching her daughter about democracy, Gloria wants the elections to bring real change.

Close 

She believes South Africans deserve leaders who will tackle the problems affecting their communities.

"We all deserve dignity. We all deserve water, we all deserve electricity. We all deserve housing. We don't need crime," she said.

For Gloria, these are basic needs that every community should have.

She hopes those elected will serve all residents and make decisions that put people's needs ahead of their own interests.

While Mandy hopes to see Johannesburg change for the better, Gloria wants her daughter to grow up understanding the value of voting and the responsibility that comes with choosing leaders.

Both voters see the elections as an opportunity for change, but their hopes go beyond what happens at the ballot box.

As Ramaphosa and Motsepe prepare to vote at Hyde Park High School, residents are making their own choices about who should lead their communities.

For Gloria, the real test will come after the votes have been counted.

She wants leaders who will turn election promises into working services and make sure communities have the water, electricity, housing and safety they deserve.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 4, 2026
World.content:
UN to Withdraw Peacekeeping Mission from Western Sahara

The United Nations has started preparations to withdraw its peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara. This follows Russia and the United States vetoing each other's proposals to extend the 35-year deployment. The UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) was established in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and support a settlement between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front. The latest disagreement in the Security Council followed a US proposal to renew the mission's mandate while placing Morocco's autonomy plan at the centre of efforts to resolve the dispute. Russia rejected the proposal, arguing that it favoured Morocco's position and could prejudge questions of sovereignty. The US subsequently vetoed Russia's alternative proposal. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has expressed concern about the possibility of renewed fighting and urged both parties to exercise restraint. He also reiterated the need to respect the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination. Morocco controls most of the territory, while the Polisario Front continues to push for an independent state.

HRW Urges Ethiopia to Lift Suspension of Independent Newspaper

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Human Rights Watch has called on the Ethiopian government to immediately reverse its decision to suspend the licences of The Reporter, one of the country's oldest independent media outlets and its last privately owned Amharic newspaper. The Ethiopian Media Authority announced that the publication's print and online operations would be suspended indefinitely, accusing it of repeatedly violating media laws and publishing content that undermines national interests, including foreign investment, tourism and diplomacy. Human Rights Watch said that the decision reflects an escalating crackdown on independent journalism and civic freedoms in the country. Since 2025, authorities have reportedly shut down several media outlets, deported foreign correspondents and targeted local journalists through arrests, office raids and other forms of intimidation. The organisation said the government has also increased pressure on The Reporter, including the arrest of some of its journalists. Its director for the Horn of Africa, Laetitia Bader, said that the government should lift the suspension, while Ethiopia's international partners should pressure authorities to end attacks on independent media.

Service Failures, Water Crisis, and Coalitions Set to Shape South African Municipal Elections

Service delivery failures, water shortages, electricity disruptions and rising living costs are among the key issues influencing South African voters as the country heads to municipal elections. Residents in communities like Tembisa have vented their anger at sewage in the streets, inconsistent electricity and poor local infrastructure, with some wondering if voting will make any real change. Water supply and quality have become particularly important issues with a number of areas facing prolonged shortages and aging infrastructure unable to meet demand. Water rights organisation WaterCAN said that almost 70% of the country's wastewater treatment works are in a critical state, contributing to pollution in rivers and streams. The elections are also expected to test the African National Congress's declining support, with polling suggesting the party could lose further ground and more municipalities could be governed through coalitions. Immigration has been a major theme in the campaign messages as parties look to capitalize on public concerns about illegal immigration and border management. Meanwhile, the Independent Electoral Commission is investigating more than 700 complaints relating to election misinformation, including false claims about asylum seekers being mobilised to vote. Analysts said that turnout will be crucial in determining the outcome, particularly as municipal elections have historically recorded lower participation than national polls.

Libyan Religious Body Issues Ruling Prohibiting Sale and Use of Nike Products

Libya's highest religious authority, Dar al-Ifta, has issued a religious ruling prohibiting Muslims from buying, selling, or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo. The Tripoli-based institution argues that the American sportswear company's name is derived from the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo is inspired by her wings. It says wearing clothing displaying the logo amounts to promoting symbols associated with the worship of multiple gods, which it considers contrary to Islamic teachings. The religious committee has also accused Nike of supporting Israel and reiterated calls for a boycott of companies it considers supportive of the country during the war in Gaza. The ruling was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani, but does not amount to an official government ban and carries no specified legal penalties. The institution has previously issued similar rulings against jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury brand Van Cleef & Arpels. The latest decision has sparked mixed reactions on social media, with some welcoming it while others have questioned its relevance amid Libya's wider political and economic challenges.

At Least 27 Civilians Killed in Burkina Faso Attacks

Human Rights Watch said that at least 27 civilians were killed in two attacks by Al-Qaeda-linked armed group Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) in Burkina Faso's northern Yatenga province in September. The first attack took place on September 1, when more than 60 fighters stormed an artisanal gold mining site near Soubo village, killing 24 civilians, injuring at least 20 others and destroying hundreds of shelters, motorcycles and mining equipment. Witnesses said the attackers opened fire on people who were sleeping or working at the site, while some victims were shot as they attempted to escape. Four days later, an explosive device detonated on a road near Mera village, killing three people travelling on a motorcycle, including a five-year-old child and a 65-year-old woman. Human Rights Watch said that the attacks appear to constitute war crimes and has called on Burkina Faso's authorities to strengthen protection for vulnerable communities, investigate the killings and prosecute those responsible. The organisation also raised concerns about the use of improvised explosive devices, which pose a serious threat to civilians. It says the attacks come amid a wider pattern of violence by Islamist armed groups and serious abuses against civilians by government forces and allied militias.

Close 

Kenya Registers Thousands of Ethiopian Refugees Fleeing Clashes

Kenyan authorities, working with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the Kenya Red Cross Society, have begun registering Ethiopian refugees fleeing renewed clashes in the border town of Moyale. More than 50,000 people have reportedly crossed into Kenya since fighting intensified in late October, prompting growing concern over the humanitarian situation along the border. The registration exercise began around October 31 at temporary reception centres in Marsabit County, including Harhosa and OMC camps. Officials are issuing identification wristbands to newly arrived refugees before conducting household profiling to establish their needs and coordinate humanitarian assistance. Many displaced people are currently sheltering in temporary camps, schools and churches, while others are staying with relatives and host communities. Humanitarian agencies say urgent assistance is needed, particularly food, clean water, emergency shelter, sanitation, healthcare and protection for women and children. The UNHCR, International Organization for Migration, UNICEF and other partners are working with Kenyan authorities to coordinate the response. They have appealed for approximately 8.9 million dollars to provide assistance over three months. The latest influx follows renewed clashes in Moyale, where longstanding territorial and administrative disputes between Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regional states have escalated into violence, resulting in civilian casualties, injuries and the destruction of homes and businesses. Kenyan authorities have also increased security along the border following reports of stray bullets landing in areas on the Kenyan side.

World.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopian-American Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia, Faces Up to 22 Years in U.S. Prison
World.content:
Addis Abeba — Abraham Teklu Lemma, a naturalized U.S. citizen of Ethiopian descent and former U.S. government IT contractor, pleaded guilty on November 3 to conspiring to transmit highly classified national defense information to Ethiopian government officials, potentially exposing him to nearly 22 years in prison.

Abraham, 53 or 54, of Silver Spring, Maryland, admitted conspiring from 2021 until his arrest in August 2023 to collect and transmit classified U.S. government materials to Ethiopian officials in political, military and intelligence roles, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

The information, which included documents, handwritten notes, photographs, maps and satellite imagery, was primarily related to the armed conflict in Ethiopia and classified up to Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI).

"[He] exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government," U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro said, describing the conduct as a betrayal of his oath and a threat to national security.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said Lemma "betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree," using his IT access to remove classified national defense information from secure facilities and transmit it to Ethiopian officials.

Prosecutors said Abraham hoped the information would help Ethiopian officials "to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict."

According to the Justice Department, Abraham worked as an IT administrator and contractor at the U.S. Department of State, Department of Justice and National Reconnaissance Office, holding Top Secret/SCI security clearance.

He allegedly concealed his activities by hand-copying classified information into notes that he carried out of secure facilities, while also removing electronic materials from classified systems. He used encrypted messaging applications to transmit the information.

In one exchange on December 18, 2021, Abraham told a conspirator, "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia." Later that day, after sharing additional information, he wrote, "Please send Dro[nes]."

The materials were linked to the armed conflict and paramilitary groups opposing the Ethiopian government, prosecutors said.

Abraham was arrested in August 2023 after a criminal complaint unsealed the following month accused him of gathering and delivering national defense information to aid a foreign government, conspiracy and willful retention of classified information.

Court documents from the case described his access to and copying of dozens of intelligence reports, including at least 85 during one period, many concerning Ethiopia. Investigators alleged he removed classification markings, copied materials onto CDs and DVDs, and transmitted them through encrypted applications to an individual connected to Ethiopia's intelligence service.

He initially pleaded not guilty.

Under the plea agreement, which remains subject to court acceptance, he faces a recommended sentencing range of 120 to 262 months in prison. Sentencing is scheduled for April 14, 2027, before Senior Judge John D. Bates.

The case was investigated by the FBI's Washington Field Office, with prosecutors from the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia and the Justice Department's National Security Division.

Close 

Abraham's activities overlapped with the devastating war in the Tigray region, which erupted in November 2020, six years ago this month. The two-year war brought together Ethiopian federal forces, Eritrean troops and Amhara forces against the Tigray forces.

The war later spread to the Amhara and Afar regions, resulting in widespread casualties and displacement. It was marked by crimes against humanity, war crimes and forced deportations in Tigray, as well as war crimes in Amhara and Afar, before formally ending with the November 2022 Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. However, implementation challenges and residual tensions persisted after the deal.

U.S. prosecutors said Lemma's alleged efforts were intended to support Ethiopian officials in targeting opposing paramilitary fighters during and after the conflict.

World.title: Burkina Faso: Islamist Armed Group Targets Civilians
World.content:
Deadly Attack on Mining Site; Apparent Use of Banned Explosive Devices in Northern Province

An Al-Qaeda-linked armed group killed at least 27 civilians in two attacks in Burkina Faso's northern Yatenga province in September 2026.

The group's relentless, unlawful attacks put civilians across Burkina Faso at grave risk. The laws of war prohibit attacking civilians, and those who order, commit, or assist serious violations of the laws of war with criminal intent may be prosecuted for war crimes.

Burkina Faso authorities should urgently strengthen protection for threatened communities, investigate abuses, and fairly prosecute those responsible.

(Nairobi) - An Al-Qaeda-linked armed group killed at least 27 civilians in two attacks in Burkina Faso's northern Yatenga province in September 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. These attacks violated international humanitarian law and are apparent war crimes.



On September 1, the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, or JNIM) attacked a gold mining site in Soubo, Ouahigouya district, killing 24 civilians, injuring at least 20 others, and burning property. On September 5, three civilians on a motorcycle, including a child, were killed by an explosive weapon on a dirt track near Mera village, also in Ouahigouya district. Local residents believe JNIM forces had planted an improvised explosive device (IED).

"The JNIM armed group's relentless, unlawful attacks put civilians across Burkina Faso at grave risk," said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. "The authorities should urgently strengthen protection for threatened communities, investigate abuses, and fairly prosecute those responsible."

In September and October, Human Rights Watch remotely interviewed 15 people, including 4 witnesses to the Soubo attack and 3 to the Mera attack, as well as human rights defenders and journalists. Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated four videos posted online showing the aftermath of the Soubo attack and analyzed satellite imagery and fire detection data to corroborate witness accounts.

On September 1 at about 1 a.m., over 60 JNIM fighters riding motorbikes stormed an artisanal gold mining site about 1.5 kilometers northwest of Soubo village. They fired on civilians sleeping and working there, and at those trying to flee.

"I've seen dozens of injured people, many by bullets, others because they fell while fleeing and fractured their legs or arms," a 45-year-old man said. He said that those with gunshot wounds were treated at the regional university hospital in Ouahigouya. Witnesses said the attack lasted about two hours. Fearing further attacks, residents stayed away from the site for two to three days.

During the attack, JNIM fighters destroyed hundreds of temporary structures such as sheds and huts, as well as motorcycles and mining tools.

JNIM's Sharia Committee, in a September 30 response (English, Arabic) to Human Rights Watch, acknowledged that JNIM forces attacked Soubo, but stated that the victims were members of the government-allied militias, known as Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie, or VDP) and "not civilians." However, witnesses told Human Rights Watch that soldiers and VDPs were neither present during the attack nor stationed at the site, although they occasionally patrolled the surrounding area.

Mining sites are lucrative revenue sources for JNIM in Burkina Faso. The armed group leverages mining economies to generate revenue through "taxation" and extortion, recruit new fighters, secure essential supplies, and expand territorial control.

Witnesses said that they believed JNIM, whose fighters include many ethnic Fulani, attacked the site in retaliation for the military's targeting of Fulani people since 2022. Fulani communities, they said, had also worked at the gold mining site but had been killed and otherwise abused by the military and VDPs who viewed them as JNIM collaborators. A 45-year-old man said that while hiding in a pit to avoid getting shot, he heard a fighter say: "You chased us away, but you won't exploit this place."

At about 9:30 a.m. on September 5, an explosive weapon detonated as people rode a motorcycle along a dirt track about three kilometers from Mera village on the route to Soubo and Sissamba. It killed the 40-year-old driver and his two passengers, a 65-year-old woman and a 5-year-old boy. Mera is near the Soubo mining site, in an area where JNIM fighters frequently carry out attacks.

Witnesses said they saw no JNIM fighters nearby at the time of the explosion but had seen at least four fighters traveling along the track on two motorbikes the previous evening.

A motorbike rider, 40, said, "I saw a motorcycle in front of me with three people on it, and suddenly there was an explosion.... Dust flew around like a whirlwind. I heard a loud bang that threw me off [the bike]. The explosion shook the ground."

Human Rights Watch could not independently verify the type of explosive weapon used or how it was detonated. However, JNIM has repeatedly carried out attacks in Burkina Faso using IEDs. A 2025 report by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, a global coalition of nongovernmental organizations including Human Rights Watch dedicated to eradicating landmines and cluster munitions, noted JNIM's use of IEDs in Burkina Faso. In 2024, Burkina Faso was among the countries with the highest rate of casualties--more than 200--due to landmines and explosive remnants of war globally.

All parties to Burkina Faso's armed conflict are bound by Common Article 3 to the 1949 Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law. The laws of war prohibit attacking civilians, looting, and destroying civilian property. Individuals who order, commit, or assist serious violations of the laws of war with criminal intent may be prosecuted for war crimes. The Burkinabè government has an obligation to investigate and appropriately prosecute alleged war crimes committed within its territory.

"JNIM forces should immediately cease unlawful attacks against civilians and appropriately punish responsible commanders," Allegrozzi said. "Burkina Faso's authorities should urgently improve demining efforts and increase assistance to victims of IED attacks."

Since the start of its insurgency in Burkina Faso in 2017, JNIM has repeatedly attacked civilians and forcibly displaced tens of thousands of people. Burkina Faso's armed forces and VDPs have also committed serious abuses against civilians, especially Fulani, during operations against Islamist armed groups. In a report released in April 2026, Human Rights Watch documented that the Burkinabè and allied militia have targeted Fulani communities because of their alleged support for Islamist armed groups, resulting in the ethnic cleansing of entire communities.

The nongovernmental group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data reported that JNIM carried out 125 attacks across Burkina Faso from January to August, resulting in the killing of 188 civilians, at least 16 of them in IED attacks.

Explosive devices can be designed or fabricated to be detonated by a person's presence, proximity, or contact. Such victim-activated devices function as antipersonnel mines and are prohibited internationally, regardless of whether assembled in a factory or improvised from locally available materials. They can also be made to detonate on command by various simple means or by a simple timer. Victim-activated IEDs are inherently indiscriminate weapons and are banned under the Mine Ban Treaty, which Burkina Faso ratified in 1998.

Soubo, Yatenga Province, September 1

Witnesses said they identified the attackers by their clothes, including headscarves and a white flag with black writing, characteristic of JNIM.

"They carried weapons and wore turbans," said a 40-year-old artisanal miner and farmer. "They shouted Allah Akbar and shot at people at random." JNIM is known to operate in the area and carry out attacks against government security forces and civilians.

"The assailants began shooting everywhere and then went shed-by-shed," a 37-year-old restaurant owner said. "I lay down in my restaurant and they found me.... They shot point-blank at two of my customers who fell in front of me." She said that when JNIM fighters set her restaurant on fire, she had to get up to avoid being burned. One fighter wanted to kill her, but another told him to let her go because she was a woman. "They told me: 'Tell your husbands not to come here anymore. These places belong to us."'

When residents who had fled the site of the attack returned, they found the victims' bodies still on the ground or inside the mining pits. "I went back to the site three days later and saw the huge damage, a site covered in ashes," said a 40-year-old artisanal miner. "I saw at least 20 bodies. The bodies were swollen and gave off a foul smell. I helped pick up the bodies and carry them for burial." Residents said the bodies were buried in the cemeteries of the nearby villages of Soubo, Pirgo, and Sissamba.

In June, Burkina Faso's territorial administration minister had issued a decree suspending artisanal mining activities in Ouahigouya district from July 1 to September 30, to protect miners "from the high risk of landslides during the rainy season." However, residents said, about a thousand people--mostly artisanal miners, but also shopkeepers, owners of small restaurants, and children--were at the site at the time of the attack. They said people had continued working despite the authorities' suspension order, since officials never visited the site to enforce the suspension or check whether activities had ceased.

Close 

"The terrorists burned a lot of property, huts under which there were small restaurants, motorcycles, small straw houses, mills, water pumps, and other equipment," the 40-year-old artisanal miner said. "The fire spread from one hut to another. My barrel and my shed were also burned."

Human Rights Watch analyzed NASA satellite data and found evidence of numerous fires at the Soubo mining site on September 1 at 1:11 a.m. local time, corroborating witnesses' accounts.

Human Rights Watch also verified and geolocated four videos posted to TikTok on September 2 and 4, showing the destruction at the mining site. However, the videos only show a small part of the destruction visible in the satellite imagery. In imagery recorded on October 10, hundreds of structures are destroyed or no longer visible with burn scars on and around partially damaged structures, while others are completely destroyed. Satellite imagery recorded prior to the attack, on August 26, shows that the site contained at least 800 structures, consistent with witness accounts that at least 1,000 people were at the site.

Human Rights Watch reviewed a list provided by residents with the names of 24 victims, all civilians, including three women, ages 31, 36, and 37, and 21 men, ages 27 to 45.

Mera, September 5, Yatenga province

A farmer, 43, working in a field with other men near the road said he rushed to the scene after hearing the explosion. "When we arrived, we found a large hole at least one meter deep," he said. "A few pieces of the woman's remains were not far from the hole - the woman had no body left. The man had been propelled far from the hole, near the bushes, as well as the child who had lost his lower limbs."

"The blast knocked the wind out of me, dust filled my throat, and I couldn't see anything," a 37-year-old man said. "The debris went very high before falling everywhere. I smelled a sharp, irritating odor, like sulfur." He said that he and other people "took plastic tarps, collected the bodies and body parts, and carried out the burial the same day just after 2 p.m. in Yaoua village."

Witnesses said that after the explosion, soldiers arrived at the scene. The farmer said, "The military stepped in after the explosion to secure the area, searched for other IEDs and defused three of them, so we could safely take the bodies and bury them."

World.title: Kenya: Govt Eyes HPV Vaccination for Boys Amid Low Second-Dose Uptake Among Girls
World.content:
Nairobi — The government is considering extending the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programme to boys as Kenya steps up efforts to prevent cervical cancer and other HPV-related diseases.

Medical Services Principal Secretary Ouma Oluga said vaccinating boys could become an important part of the country's long-term disease prevention strategy, although the current programme remains focused on girls.

His remarks come amid concerns over low completion rates for the HPV vaccine among girls, with the latest Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey showing that only 20 per cent have received the recommended second dose.

The survey found that 59 per cent of girls had received at least one dose of the HPV vaccine, an increase from 30 per cent recorded in the 2022 survey.



However, the significant drop between first-dose and second-dose coverage raises concerns about Kenya's ability to ensure that more girls complete the recommended vaccination schedule.

Oluga acknowledged that more efforts are needed to strengthen HPV vaccination and expand protection against the virus among young people.

He said the government could consider extending the programme to boys in the future, describing it as an important area for further attention.

"Maybe in the future, we will also consider vaccinating boys," Oluga said.

The PS also highlighted the burden of cervical cancer in Kenya, saying the disease affects approximately 7,000 women every year.

Cervical cancer is largely caused by persistent infection with high-risk types of HPV, a common virus primarily transmitted through sexual contact.

HPV vaccination before exposure to the virus offers the strongest protection against infection and related diseases.

While HPV vaccination programmes have traditionally prioritised girls because of the vaccine's role in preventing cervical cancer, vaccinating boys can also help reduce transmission and protect them against other HPV-related conditions, including certain cancers.

The latest survey figures suggest that Kenya has made progress in increasing access to the first HPV vaccine dose, with coverage rising from 30 per cent in 2022 to 59 per cent.

However, the fact that only 20 per cent of girls have received the second dose points to persistent challenges in follow-up, public awareness and access to vaccination services.

Close 

Expanding the programme to boys would require additional planning and resources, with the government yet to announce a timeline for the proposed intervention.

Oluga's remarks therefore signal a possible future policy direction rather than an immediate change to the national HPV vaccination programme.

WHOOPI GOLDBERG WARNS DEMOCRATS TO 'TAKE CARE OF BUSINESS' AFTER MIDTERM WINS

"You got the House, you got the Senate. So, come January, I want to see an actual agenda. What's your plan to lower housing costs? Are you going to build more affordable housing? What about healthcare? Are you going to fight to lower premiums, protect Medicaid? Are you going to stop Americans from going broke because they got sick? What about wages?" he asked.

PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP

World.title: New Jersey pre-K aide faces 61 charges, accused of filming himself sexually assaulting students at school
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A former New Jersey elementary school aide who worked with pre-K students for roughly four years is facing dozens of criminal charges, including aggravated sexual assault and manufacturing child sexual abuse material, after investigators discovered numerous images and videos of students on his electronic devices, prosecutors said.

Shaun M. Stebbins, 44, worked at Woodbine Elementary School in Cape May County from February 2022 until his arrest in neighboring Atlantic County on March 29, according to the Cape May County Prosecutor's Office.

The investigation expanded into Cape May County after authorities in Atlantic County and Somers Point notified prosecutors in April that a separate sexual assault investigation involving Stebbins at his home had uncovered suspected crimes in the neighboring county.

FORMER NEW JERSEY MIDDLE SCHOOL TEACHER INDICTED ON NEW CHARGES, INCLUDING MANUFACTURING CHILD ABUSE MATERIAL

A search of Stebbins' devices allegedly revealed numerous images and videos of Woodbine Elementary School students, prosecutors said. Authorities did not disclose how many students were involved or provide details about when the material was recorded.

According to court documents, Stebbins filmed and performed sex acts on children in a school bathroom and during nap time, ABC7 reported.

Cape May County prosecutors announced 61 charges against Stebbins on Oct. 30, including 29 counts of manufacturing child pornography, five counts of aggravated sexual assault, 13 counts of sexual assault by sexual contact and 14 counts of endangering the welfare of a child.

The manufacturing and aggravated sexual assault charges are first-degree offenses that can carry prison sentences of 10 to 20 years under New Jersey law.

The remaining charges are second-degree offenses, typically punishable by five to 10 years in prison.

SCHOOL EMPLOYEE ACCUSED OF SECRETLY FILMING 12 GIRLS IN CHANGING ROOM FACES NEW CHARGES

Cape May County Prosecutor Jeffrey H. Sutherland said his office continues to investigate the case.

"Children are among our most vulnerable population, and we have a responsibility to protect their safety and well-being. Anyone who harms a child will be held accountable through our justice system."

Stebbins remains in the Atlantic County Correctional Facility pending court proceedings.

The Woodbine School District, the Cape May County Prosecutor's Office and the Atlantic County Prosecutor's Office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

World.title: West Hollywood unanimously passes ordinance granting protections for polyamorous relationships
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

West Hollywood, California, unanimously passed a city ordinance Monday that would allow citizens in "multipartner domestic relationships" to receive protections under city law.

"It is hereby declared as the public policy of the City of West Hollywood that it is necessary to recognize and protect the right and opportunity of all persons to have multi-partner domestic relationships formally recognized and respected, and to be free from discrimination on account of their partnership in a multi-partner domestic relationship," the ordinance read.

"Diverse relationship structures, including relationship structures involving more than two adults engaged in a loving, committed, and consensual relationship, are becoming increasingly common."

PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH FACES INTERNAL REVOLT AFTER PROPOSING CLERGY MUST BE IN MONOGAMOUS RELATIONSHIPS

The West Hollywood City Council voted 5-0 to allow people within a relationship involving three or more people to sign a statement with the city clerk. The declaration would grant qualifying partners certain rights, including hospital and jail visitation rights.

However, the ordinance would not officially recognize polyamorous relationships as a "marriage" or a registered domestic partnership in violation of state or federal law. Still, West Hollywood is one of only a handful of local governments that have enacted some form of protection for multipartner relationships.

Fox News Digital reached out to the City of West Hollywood's communications department for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

POLYAMOROUS ‘THROUPLE’ FIRES BACK AT CRITICS OF THEIR RELATIONSHIP: ‘WE COME FROM DIFFERENT SCHOOLS OF THOUGHT’

In a comments to Fox News Digital, University of Virginia professor and Institute for Family Studies senior fellow Brad Wilcox lamented the passing of this ordinance for potentially normalizing polyamory and paving the way for polygamy.

"The dangers of legally recognizing polyamorous relationships are twofold," he said. "First, it normalizes households where children live with adults who are not related to them by birth or adoption, an arrangement the research consistently links to higher risks for kids.

"Second, it paves the way for polygamy, which the scholarly literature shows fuels gender inequality and hurts child well-being, because wives and children end up competing for a man’s attention and resources.

"So, what seems like a progressive move here in West Hollywood can lead to some illiberal destinations that are bad for women and children."

MASSACHUSETTS CITY RECOGNIZES POLYAMOROUS RELATIONSHIPS IN NEW DOMESTIC PARTNERSHIP ORDINANCE

West Hollywood first passed an anti-discrimination ordinance to protect polyamorous relationships in March. This latest ordinance will go into effect 30 days after it was adopted.

World.title: Top-ranked Miami faces nightmare injury concern as star receiver Malachi Toney set to undergo ankle surgery
World.content:
Miami's highly anticipated showdown against Notre Dame on Saturday night had another layer added to the storylines on Wednesday, as the health of Heisman Trophy contender Malachi Toney will now linger over the next month.

The No. 1 Hurricanes were already underdogs heading into the matchup in South Bend, but now head coach Mario Cristobal will be without his top playmaker on offense besides quarterback Darian Mensah.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

During practice on Wednesday, Malachi Toney suffered an injury to his ankle that forced the wide receiver to leave practice and head straight to a local facility to be evaluated for what could be a massive hit to the Hurricanes' national title hopes.

CFP RANKINGS: NOTRE DAME FACES SUDDEN DEATH, SEC FEELING GOOD, AND BIG TEN CLOSE TO HITTING THE PANIC BUTTON

While there was some optimism earlier in the afternoon that this could end up being an injury that doesn’t keep Toney off the field on Saturday night, there was obviously growing concern later on in the day that this could potentially keep Malachi off the field for an extended period of time.

"Malachi Toney sustained an injury during Wednesday’s practice and is currently undergoing further evaluation by the team’s medical staff," Miami said in a statement earlier on Wednesday. "We will share additional updates as appropriate."

Now, the star wide receiver will undergo surgery on his ankle, after an MRI and X-ray were done on Wednesday evening, as CBS Sports first reported.

Toney suffered a high-ankle sprain, according to sources, and will undergo the infamous "TightRope" surgery that Miami is hoping will have the star wide receiver return for the College Football Playoff in four to six weeks.

But, this is obviously a "hopeful" mindset by Miami football officials.

Multiple gambling establishments had already bumped Notre Dame from 5-point favorites to 6.5-point favorites by Wednesday evening.

All eyes on Miami, as Heisman Trophy candidate could play major factor in CFP rankings

The health of Malachi Toney will be one of the most talked about subjects over the next month, given the initial CFP rankings that were released on Tuesday night.

Following the win last weekend against North Carolina, the Miami wide receiver has now accounted for 1,027 yards receiving, with 13 touchdowns on 73 receptions.

What does this Hurricanes offense look like without its star wide receiver? We're about to find out, given the unfortunate news that he will be undergoing surgery.

Just like any other player at this time, Toney was dealing with the type on bumps and bruises you would expect eight games into the season.

If the Hurricanes were to lose on Saturday night without Malachi on the field, the subsequent three weeks would be interesting to watch unfold from a rankings standpoint.

We've already seen Ohio State be punished for not having Julian Sayin at quarterback, coming off the loss to USC.

OHIO STATE'S NATIONAL TITLE HOPES ARE RIGHTFULLY FADING AFTER USC DELIVERS REALITY CHECK IN SHOCKING UPSET

What would the committee have to say when it comes to Miami not having a Heisman Trophy candidate on the field if the injury were to keep Toney out for at least a few weeks?

These are all questions that will be answered one way or another in the coming weeks.

Notre Dame faces what could be a must-win game in the CFP committee’s eyes

On the other side, this is setting up to be a pivotal game for Notre Dame after being ranked 11th in the first CFP poll of 2026.

There is no sugarcoating the fact that the Fighting Irish do not have a signature win this season, and their strength of schedule leaves much to be desired. BYU is the only ranked team they have played that appears in the College Football Playoff top 25.

"But when you look at Notre Dame’s schedule and the wins that they have, vs. the teams that are ahead of them, they don’t have that signature win right now. They lost in their only Top-25 matchup at BYU. The next best win as on a neutral site against Wisconsin," CFP chairman Hunter Yurachek noted.

"They’ve a great opportunity in front of them this weekend at home vs. Miami to get that signature win that I think they need to move up in the rankings. But the committee is very impressed by them. They wouldn’t be 11th if we were not."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Following the game against No. 1 Miami, the remaining schedule for Notre Dame will see them play Boston College, SMU and Syracuse, with the Mustangs currently having the only winning record out of the three.

Just when you thought Notre Dame's college football playoff standings would be the main storyline heading into Saturday’s showdown, we are now paying attention to see how Miami responds without its Heisman Trophy candidate.

World.title: Grocery store cyberattacks are ‘psychological warfare’ that could strike US, former FBI agent warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Former FBI Special Agent Nicole Parker warned that the next attack on Americans’ sense of security could come through the grocery aisle after suspected hackers have turned up supermarket freezer temperatures in Europe and fueled fears that everyday necessities could become weapons of "psychological warfare."

Parker warned that cyberattacks targeting the systems people rely on for food and other essentials could also strike the United States.

"Every human being has to eat," Parker told Fox News Digital. "This is the grocery store."

HACKERS COULD ALREADY BE INSIDE AMERICAN UTILITIES, CYBER EXPERTS WARN OF 'TROJAN HORSE' THREAT

Her warning comes as the Army Criminal Investigation Division’s Cyber Field Office works with the Defense Commissary Agency and the Defense Criminal Investigative Service to determine what caused refrigeration failures at military commissaries in August, an Army CID spokesperson confirmed to Fox News Digital.

Investigators are also working with French law enforcement as they examine whether the U.S. failures could be linked to refrigeration outages in Europe. A cyberattack has not been established as the cause of the military commissary malfunctions.

MAJOR US GROCERY CHAINS HIT BY CYBERSECURITY INCIDENT

At least six commissaries, grocery stores on military bases serving military personnel, experienced refrigeration problems in late August.

"ALL frozen food has spoiled," Fort Huachuca in Arizona said in an Aug. 26 Facebook post.

FOREIGN HACKERS BREACH TWO MORE US WATER UTILITIES, THREATEN SAFETY OF COLORADO RESIDENTS

Other affected locations included F.E. Warren Air Force Base in Wyoming, Naval Station Newport in Rhode Island, Columbus Air Force Base in Mississippi and Travis Air Force Base and Fort Irwin in California. Fort Irwin limited commissary sales to dry goods after its malfunction.

In at least one case, refrigeration units were set to higher temperatures overnight rather than simply shutting off, Reuters reported.

HOW FOREIGN HACKERS COULD 'CRUMBLE' AMERICA BY TARGETING ONE ESSENTIAL UTILITY

Separately, refrigeration systems at European supermarkets were disrupted Monday, forcing some retailers to discard food. Reuters reported that affected businesses included stores in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg, with temperatures in some systems reaching 122 degrees Fahrenheit.

Parker said the incidents underscore a threat she has long discussed with former FBI colleagues: cyberattacks targeting critical infrastructure.

AMERICA'S NEXT WAR COULD REACH US SOIL, TOP ARMY GENERAL WARNS

"What we're seeing right now is in Europe and other places, but it can very well happen on our soil," she said.

She described the danger as "asymmetrical warfare" in which an attacker can disrupt daily life without firing a missile or sending troops onto a battlefield.

AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY

"No one in law enforcement underestimates the harm that could be caused by a cyberattack against our country or against our allies," Parker said.

The identity of those behind the European incidents remained unknown, Reuters reported Wednesday. Parker also cautioned against drawing conclusions about who was responsible.

UKRAINE SAYS AIR ALERT SYSTEM HACKED AFTER FALSE RADIATION WARNING IN KYIV

"Again, we don't know who did this," she said.

For Parker, the potential damage goes beyond spoiled food. Targeting a basic necessity can also shake the public’s sense of security.

IF HACKERS CRIPPLE AMERICA'S WATER, THE CONSEQUENCES COULD BE CATASTROPHIC

"This asymmetrical warfare has a very strong psychological impact, but we're Americans. We will not falter ever," she said.

Parker said the response must extend beyond investigators tracking down hackers. Elected officials and local leaders responsible for keeping communities running need training and plans to help residents if essential services are disrupted.

"We're in a place now where it's not just enough for law enforcement to be prepared," she said.

City managers, mayors and city council members must understand potential threats and how they would take care of their communities, Parker said. She stressed the need to identify vulnerabilities and stop attacks before they happen.

Parker urged families to keep basic supplies on hand and have a plan in case a cyberattack disrupts essential services.

"I think if you are prepared, you do not have to fear," Parker said.

She encouraged Americans to keep food, water and needed medicine on hand, gather important documents in a designated location and talk about how family members would communicate during a power outage. She also suggested having a battery-operated AM radio.

"I'm not saying that, you know, you need to go buy everything off of the shelves," Parker said.

Instead, she urged people to think about practical preparations as they go about their routines.

For Parker, who lives in Florida, the approach is familiar.

"We're used to hurricanes," she said. "The preparation would be very much the same."

Fox News Digital's Bonny Chu contributed to this report.

World.title: Tony Butala, voice behind 'The Way You Look Tonight' and The Lettermen co-founder, dead at 87
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Lettermen co-founder, Tony Butala, died Sunday, Nov. 1, at the age of 87.

Tracy Clark, the band's media coordinator, confirmed his death to The Associated Press with a statement, saying, "We have lost an integral member of The Lettermen family."

"It is with profound sadness that we announce the recent passing of Tony Butala, founding member of the international recording artists ‘The Lettermen,’ and recipient of a Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame," the statement read.

"Our most heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with his children, grandchildren, siblings, the love of his life, the entire Lettermen organization and all who knew and loved him."

JOHN ANDERSON, COUNTRY MUSIC HALL OF FAMER, DEAD AT 71

A cause of death was not disclosed, and there will be no public viewing. Details about celebrations of life in both Wisconsin and California will be announced at a later date.

He co-founded The Lettermen in the late 1950s with Jim Pike and Bob Engemann, and the group released its first hit, a rendition of Fred Astaire's "The Way You Look Tonight," in 1961, which earned the trio a Grammy nomination.

The band recorded 20 hits that reached the Billboard Hot 100 chart and earned four Grammy Award nominations.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Butala remained a member of the group for over 60 years, releasing hits such as "Goin' Out of My Head/Can't Take My Eyes off You," "Everything Is Good About You," "Come Back Silly Girl," "Theme from a Summer Place" and "Hurt So Bad."

He retired from performing with the band in 2019, the same year Pike died at the age of 82 from complications related to Parkinson's Disease. Engemann died in 2013.

A year after retiring, Butala attended the ceremony honoring the band with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. After his retirement, the band continued on with new faces, and the current lineup includes Donovan Tea, Bobby Poynton and Rob Gulack.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Tony never met a stranger," the official band statement continued. "His life was a living example of talent, perseverance, and refinement. But, above all, his true joy was entertaining and sharing his music with audiences worldwide."

Butala began his professional singing career as a child, performing on KDKA Radio in Pittsburgh at the age of 8 and moving to Los Angeles with his mother at 10 to further his career.

Once in Los Angeles, Butala joined the Mitchell Boys Choir, and it appeared in classic films like "White Christmas," "Peter Pan," "War of the Worlds" and "On Moonlight Bay."

A Washington state sheriff's deputy has died and another remains on life support after they were ambushed while responding to a domestic violence call that turned deadly, authorities said Wednesday.

Spokane County Sheriff's Office deputies responded to a home Tuesday after a woman ran to a neighbor's house reporting that her brother had shot her, FOX 13 Seattle reported.

Responding officers learned the suspect had an active felony arrest warrant and had access to multiple guns and additional victims could be inside the home.

NYPD OFFICER SHOT, GUNMAN KILLED AFTER ARMED BARRICADED STANDOFF IN BROOKLYN: POLICE

The Spokane County Sheriff's Office deployed a SWAT team to assist at the home. As SWAT officers approached the house, a gunman opened fire from inside.

PHILADELPHIA POLICE OFFICER KILLED, PARTNER SHOT 12 TIMES IN AMBUSH; SUSPECT FOUND HIDING IN TREE

PHILLY OFFICER MURDERED IN LINE OF DUTY PROMOTED TO SERGEANT AS POLICE FROM AROUND US ATTEND HIS FUNERAL

World.title: DSA accused of ‘elevating’ antisemitic, pro-terror rhetoric after Hasan Piker hosts election stream
World.content:

The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) chose controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker to host its official election night livestream, drawing a blunt response from Anti-Defamation League (ADL) CEO Jonathan Greenblatt, who accused the group of elevating rhetoric supportive of terrorism and antisemitism.

"Of all the people the DSA could have chosen to host its official election night livestream, it chose Hasan Piker, someone who proudly expresses support for terrorist organizations and traffics in antisemitism," Greenblatt wrote in a post on X.

"Let that sink in. The DSA isn't distancing itself from this kind of rhetoric. It's elevating it."

The DSA saw several of its endorsed or supported candidates win on Tuesday night, including Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Melat Kiros in Colorado, Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Claire Valdez in New York and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York.

HASAN PIKER DECLARES 'WOKE IS BACK,' FANTASIZES ABOUT PUTTING DONALD TRUMP IN PRISON

In his post, Greenblatt included a link to an ADL article with statements by Piker that the organization criticized, including comments the ADL said have "alluded to classic antisemitic tropes and conspiracy theories."

The article contains some of Piker's more infamous remarks, such as when he referred to Orthodox Jews as "inbred" and his classification of Zionism as "an exterminationist ideology built around ethnoreligious supremacist values."

Piker did not hold back in his response to Greenblatt, writing, "Suck it Jonathan, your best friend Elon burned 450 million to lose races all over the country tonight you bald piece of s---!!!"

The ADL did not immediately respond to Piker’s remarks about Greenblatt.

On Tuesday, Piker described the election as a "blue-clear apocalypse" after Democrats won major gains in the House and Senate. Pike livestreamed for more than 13 hours, offering his signature political commentary as votes were tallied.

"Trumpism is dying, and I could not feel any better," Piker told his audience. "Just imagine a world where Donald Trump is in f---ing prison."

He also gloated over Republicans' defeat, saying, "This is perhaps the worst possible scenario for the Republican Party. I think their odious agenda, their corruption, the destabilizing impact that they’ve had, the endless warfare and its consequences on the American economy, are finally coming back to bite them."

RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY

Ahead of the midterm elections, Piker drew attention in political circles as he interviewed and even campaigned with DSA-backed and DSA-aligned candidates. Piker came to national prominence after he campaigned with Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

While his race was not explicitly DSA-backed, the organization said El-Sayed "supports DSA priorities like Medicare-for-all."

El-Sayed's decision to appear with Piker drew criticism. The candidate appeared to distance himself from the streamer, holding no additional campaign events with him toward the end of the election cycle. This came after critics accused Piker of suggesting that Jewish Americans' support for Israel could lead to antisemitic violence against them.

DEMOCRATS CONDEMNING HASAN PIKER AS BACKLASH SPREADS THROUGH PARTY

"People don't f--- with Israel any longer. And if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they're singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone will come around and take action not against Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker said during a Twitch stream in August.

While El-Sayed did not outright condemn the comments, he responded to Piker, saying, "I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past.

"My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters. Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk."

World.title: Former ‘Diddy’ prosecutor to lead investigation into alleged Cornell sexual assault
World.content:
New York Attorney General Letitia James announced Wednesday that a former federal prosecutor who oversaw the criminal case against Sean “Diddy” Combs will lead the investigation into an alleged 2024 sexual assault at a Cornell University fraternity house.

Former federal prosecutor Jacqueline Kelly, a Cornell graduate, was also the first chief of the civil rights unit in the criminal division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York. Kelly is now a partner at Boies Schiller Flexner, a firm that represented women who accused Jeffrey Epstein of sexual abuse.

James, who was re-elected as the state’s top law enforcement official Tuesday, said in a statement that Kelly “is a seasoned prosecutor who has overseen numerous cases from investigation through trial.”

“With her criminal legal expertise, commitment to public service, and judicial experience, I am confident that she will lead a fair and comprehensive investigation,” James added.

In a statement, Kelly thanked James for the opportunity to lead the review that was ordered Oct. 1 by Gov. Kathy Hochul after the governor raised concerns that the local district attorney who originally considered charges did not do a proper assessment.

“All New Yorkers deserve a fair and thorough inquiry into the facts of this case,” Kelly said in a statement. “I look forward to lending my years of experience as a federal prosecutor to the Office of the Attorney General as we examine all available evidence.”

A former Cornell student filed a lawsuit under the pseudonym Jane Doe in September, accusing seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity of plying her with drugs and sexually assaulting her after what was initially a consensual threesome at the chapter’s house on Oct. 19 and 20, 2024.

The woman, who later dropped out of school, reported the incident to the university and to campus police in November 2024. Records reviewed by NBC News show that the Cornell University Police Department interviewed several witnesses and obtained other evidence.
