"The President had a 35% favorable rating and voters disliked his gas prices, chaos, tariffs, abusing allies and hugging Putin," Bacon said in one of a series of critical posts on X.

"The President’s global tariffs were brutal to the GOP in the Midwest," Bacon wrote. "We should have never defended them."

World.title: Senior Democratic congressman says party 'going to put an end' to Trump's tariffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A senior Democrat says his party will work to end U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs on allies, including Canada, when it takes control of Congress next year.

"We want to have free and fair trade with Canada like the rest of the world. So that's going to be very much on our agenda," Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrat on the House judiciary committee, told CBC News Wednesday on Capitol Hill.

His comments came hours after American voters handed a seismic win to Democrats in Tuesday night's midterm elections, giving them control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

It's raising questions north of the border about what this could mean for lifting tariffs on Canadian industries.

WATCH | Raskin on Trump's tariffs: Senior Democrat wants new Congress to move 'very quickly' on tariffs | Duration closed caption 2:05 Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin tells the CBC's Erin Collins that he hopes Democrats will try to remove tariffs on Canada 'within the first 100 days' after the party gains control of Congress in January.

"That's one of the reasons we won Congress back — because we're going to put an end to these tariffs," Raskin said.

"Congress controls taxes and tariffs under the Constitution. Congress regulates commerce internationally and domestically. And so we're gonna do everything in our power to make it very clear that we have not imposed 50 per cent tariffs on our democratic allies and friends in Canada."

Raskin was re-elected to a sixth term on Tuesday night and is in line to chair the powerful judiciary committee.

He said he hopes to see movement on the Canada trade file "within the first 100 days" of Democrats taking power in the new year.

"We want to tell our democratic allies around the world, especially our best friends like Canada, that the forces of democracy and freedom have won in this Congress, and we are going to [be] moving very quickly to restore normal ties," he said.

LeBlanc says strategy unchanged

Canada's point man on the Canada-U.S. trade file said earlier on Wednesday that the federal government's strategy isn't changing in the short term.

While the results are widely seen as a strong repudiation of Trump and his economic policies, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc wouldn't weigh in ahead of a caucus meeting on Wednesday morning in Ottawa.

"It's not particularly constructive for Canadians to interpret results in a foreign country's election," he said. "Our job is to focus on what we can control, and that's to work with the people that Americans have elected."

LeBlanc noted the trade talks are conducted with Trump and his cabinet.

"They remain in office today. And those are the people with whom we'll be having those conversations," he said.

Canada has been seeking a trade deal with the U.S. in hopes of lowering steep tariffs on Canadian goods, including targeted sectors like autos, steel, aluminum and softwood.

WATCH | 'Our focus hasn't changed,' LeBlanc says: 'Our focus hasn't changed,' LeBlanc says as Democrats take U.S. Congress | Duration closed caption 1:14 Dominic LeBlanc, Canada-U.S. trade minister, congratulated the politicians elected in the U.S midterms but stressed that the Liberal government remains focused on strengthening the economy and diversifying trade relationships — adding that the Trump administration remains in place.

One of the big questions for the Canadian side is how the infamously volatile U.S. president reacts to the midterm shellacking and whether it gives Prime Minister Mark Carney's government more leverage.

Trump was already signalling some movement on the trade file, telling Fox News on Tuesday morning he was close to a deal.

Carney didn't go quite as far but told reporters that afternoon that the White House has shifted its stance on some of what he called Canada's "red lines," including language requirements and Canada's ability to strike trade deals with other countries.

WATCH | Carney on the state of U.S. trade talks: 'We've made progress' with U.S. on trade talks, Carney says | Duration closed caption 1:36 Following a conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump over the weekend, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday that the U.S. has 'clearly shifted' on Canada's 'red lines' around sovereignty, language and trade deals. 'They're asking less and they're offering more,' Carney said.

"They're asking less and they're offering more," the prime minister said, adding the two leaders will meet in China later this month.

He said there is still work to be done before a deal is inked. Autos are expected to be a key sticking point, as they were in August before talks collapsed — triggering new tariffs on both sides.

Trump still has his veto powers

A blue Congress doesn't necessarily mean it's clear sailing for Canada. The new crop of representatives and senators won't be sworn in until January, and even after that Trump will still be able to lean on his executive authority.

After the results came Trump posted an image of a red MAGA-style hat with the word "VETO," although he also told Politico "I don't want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything."

Vermont Sen. Peter Welch is urging his party to concentrate on "bread and butter" affordability issues, including passing legislation ending tariffs.

Welch, along with fellow Democrat New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, introduced a bill in September that would repeal the Trump administration's 50 per cent tariffs and import bans on Canadian goods

"We can't force the president to sign the legislation we put on his desk, but we can pass it in good faith. And then if he signs it, great. America wins," Welch told CBC's Power & Politics.

"If he vetoes it, then America knows. So we've got to be purposeful, do things that really matter for everybody, not just Democrats."

Vermont Sen. Peter Welch is pushing for legislation to end the trade war with Canada. (J. Scott Applewhite/Associated Press)

David Cohen, former U.S. Ambassador to Canada, cautioned that despite some of the remarks coming out of the blue camp, it remains unclear what a landslide win will actually mean for trade.

"You need the White House and the administration — the executive branch of government — to be able to make meaningful change in trade policy," he told host David Cochrane.

"I just worry that people will get their hopes up that there is a way, for example, for Canada to get an overall deal with the United States that do not have some level of tariffs in them. That just may not be possible."

LeBlanc said the potential actions of the next U.S. Congress make for an "interesting discussion," but that's "not going to change the work that we have to do in the next two weeks."

"The American Congress will act in the interests of the American Congress. Our work will be focused on what we can do here at home," he said.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said it's on Carney and his government to leverage the results to land a tariff-free trade deal with the U.S. administration.

"Americans hate these tariffs," he said. "Let's leverage that goodwill to pressure the administration and Congress to remove all the tariffs, lower the cost of living for Americans but also boost jobs and business for long-struggling Canadians."

NDP Leader Avi Lewis pointed out not all Democrats are against tariffs.

"We do see certain elements within the Democratic Party that have supported the tariffs or have been silent on that," he said.

"If the prime minister were to channel the progressive Carney that we saw in the last election campaign, it would be a great time to build relationships with those Democrats and start laying the seeds for a lasting trade deal that really reduces those tariffs."

World.title: Russian hacker group claims to have posted B.C. school district information on dark web
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A shadowy Russian ransomware group has posted screenshots on the dark web from what appears to be a database stolen from the Burnaby School District.

The group — which calls itself Qilin — claims to offer downloads of information allegedly taken during a massive data breach school officials have said included medical information, detailed learning assessments, and personal information about both staff and students.

Qilin is renowned as a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) provider that offers tools and infrastructure to hackers anywhere in the world in exchange for a percentage of proceeds demanded from victims.

While CBC News has not downloaded the contents of the files themselves, the screenshot samples posted on the Qilin website contain school district letterhead and human resource categories attached to what appear to be bulky files of data.

'Harassment Investigations' and 'Discipline'

The September attack on the Burnaby School District raised alarms with parents and students who contacted CBC News concerned that children's data may be in the hands of cybercriminals bent on exploiting deeply personal information for profit.

Working with CBC's visual investigations team, CBC News located the database shortly after the school district warned parents in an email Tuesday that "the threat actor claims to have published files and information from this incident on the dark web."

Hackers breached computer systems belonging to the Burnaby School District in September. The information they stole has been posted to the dark web. (CBC News)

The files appear on Qilin's dark web site in what is effectively a multi-page listing of sets of data stolen from various agencies, companies and individuals worldwide.

According to the screenshots posted online, the files contain a terabyte worth of data and have allegedly been seen nearly 4,000 times since they were first posted publicly on Oct. 15.

Screenshots of the files include folders labelled "Harassment Investigations," "Discipline," "Payroll" and "Mental health and Wellness."

CBC News has not viewed the contents of the folders.

In a statement to CBC News, the Burnaby School District said it has shared " reliable information with staff and families as it becomes available."

"We have engaged an external expert to help confirm whether data from the Burnaby School District has in fact been posted on the dark web and, if so, the nature and extent of any affected information," the statement said.

Widespread concern

According to the school district, hackers gained access to the district's systems on Sept. 21. The perpetrators appear to have started posting information online almost immediately.

CBC News received numerous emails about the incident after district superintendent Karim Hachlaf wrote to families on Oct. 14 confirming that "files taken containing personal information were copied and stolen by the criminal parties responsible for the attack."

CBC's visual investigations team took this screenshot of the dark web site where data stolen from the Burnaby School District in September appears to have been posted. The site belongs to Qilin, a Russia-linked group that provides hackers with online tools in exchange for a cut of ransomware profits. (CBC News)

Hachlaf's note claimed "most of the information maintained by the district about students, parents and guardians remains secure" but noted that "some bus touring information, student intervention records and other student assessments" had been affected "in a limited and smaller number of cases."

The warning sparked widespread concern.

"Help, our school has compromised our children's identity," one parent wrote to CBC News in an email that contained a copy of Hachlaf's note.

"I am a current Grade 12 student in the Burnaby Schools District who's been affected," wrote one student.

"Currently students and families have received virtually no clear communication."

Crippling attacks on institutions

In recent years, Qilin has been tied to a series of crippling high-profile ransomware attacks — most notably a 2024 cyberattack on Britain's National Health Service that saw major London hospitals cancel operations and blood transfusions.

Just last month, Japanese authorities handed over a Russian national accused of being involved with Qilin in connection with a European ransomware attack to German authorities.

The files contain medical information, detailed learning assessments and personal information about both staff and students. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Ransomware attacks on health-care services and school districts have risen around North America, with schools in the U.S and Canada being targeted.

More than 60 million students and nine million teachers in both countries were impacted by a data breach of educational software provider PowerSchool.

The Associated Press found files describing sexual assaults, private hospitalizations and parental abuse among troves of data dumped online by a ransomware group that demanded $1 million in exchange for 300,000 files stolen from a school district in Minneapolis.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security describes Qilin's business model as one in which "a core group of developers will sell or lease their ransomware variant to other threat actors, called affiliates; the core developers will support affiliates' deployment of their ransomware in exchange for upfront payment, subscription fees, a cut of profits, or all three."

According to a threat profile prepared by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in 2024, Qilin has been operating since 2022, likely originating from Russia. The threat profile claims Qilin was observed "recruiting affiliates on a hacking forum" in 2023.

"Qilin is known to target organizations in various countries and industries, including education, healthcare and critical services, with geographical regions targeted including Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States, among others. The group's targeting appears to be opportunistic rather than targeted," the threat profile reads.

"Victims are directed to communicate with the attackers via dark web portals or encrypted messaging services, ensuring the attackers' anonymity and complicating law enforcement efforts to track interactions. Payments are demanded in cryptocurrencies … However, even after payment, there is no guarantee that victims will receive the decryption tools required to recover their data."

Seeking 'information they can use'

Chester Wisniewski, chief information security officer and director of Vancouver-based computer security firm Sophos, told CBC News that attacks on schools are particularly common at the start of the school year in September and October.

"They're vulnerable because they're serving a large portion of the public, and them being offline or unable to open the schools provides an enormous amount of public pressure to do something," Wisniewski said.

"Usually they're after payroll information, they're after medical and personal information they can use. They're trying to upset the staff and the parents of the students in the case of a school, to get them to apply pressure on the school to pay an extortion demand."

To that end, Wisniewski said the thieves "don't care about your kids' grades, but they might care about their disabilities, or their learning problems, or their behaviour problems, or sensitive information about the finances of the staff members that work in the school."

Wisniewski said the Burnaby School District is working with another firm to strengthen security. He added that the public should refrain from blaming the victim.

Despite the fears of parents, Wisniewski said past attacks on other school districts have rarely resulted in individual harm.

"The odds of something happening to your child's information despite it being published on the dark web where criminals hang out — it's a pretty low risk," he said.

"But it's certainly something to be concerned about and take protective actions."

World.title: Alberta's governing UCP endorses proposed riding boundary changes as NDP reiterates concerns
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta's governing United Conservatives have officially endorsed changes to provincial riding boundaries that the Opposition NDP says it believes are “rigged” to help the UCP win the next election.

Premier Danielle Smith's UCP caucus, in a vote split along party lines, voted Wednesday to endorse the proposed riding changes and put the new boundaries into a bill to be debated in the house.

Justice Minister Mickey Amery has said he expects legislation to pass by the end of the year ahead of the scheduled election in October 2027.

The riding report came from a panel with a majority of members selected by the UCP.

The NDP alleges the report dilutes urban ridings in Lethbridge and Calgary by merging them with adjacent rural areas to favour the UCP in a process known as gerrymandering.

Gerrymandering, which is common in the United States, sees electoral districts drawn up not for reasons of shared geography and priorities but by voting patterns in order to assist one political party.

Speaking during a debate of the proposals Wednesday, Amery defended the rural-urban hybrid ridings that have become the focus of debate, saying they already exist in Alberta.

"Hybrid ridings also do something else: they bring together communities that share services, employment, infrastructure and economic interests, regardless of whether a municipal boundary happens to run between them," said Amery.

With 2024 legislation, Smith's government removed the requirement that electoral boundaries respect municipal boundaries as a guiding principle.

The NDP has charged that the latest process to redraw the report was illegitimate from the start, and pleaded until the last minute for the UCP to instead revert to the map recommended by an independent public commission.

Nenshi said Wednesday that he believes the changes are designed to help vulnerable UCP ministers keep their seats.

"It strikes a knife into the heart of Alberta's democracy," he said.

The latest redrawing has been a controversial and complicated affair since the premier rejected the main recommendations of a public boundaries commission early this year. The commission came back with a split report.

Bucking political norms, Smith's government voted down the commission's majority position in the legislature and restarted the process with a new advisory panel.

Traditionally, Alberta's chief justice helps find a current or retired judge to chair and oversee the work. But earlier this year, the acting Alberta chief justice declined to participate, calling the new process "irregular."

The panel, chaired by retired Alberta justice Brian O'Ferrall, was given direction based on some recommendations from the previous commission's chair, including expanding the number of ridings to 91 from 87 to preserve two rural ridings that were to be dissolved.

Smith has said urban representation, amid population growth in cities, shouldn't come at the expense of rural Alberta.

But Nenshi told the house Wednesday the panel went well beyond those marching orders without justification and without considering public feedback.

WATCH | Panel proposes new electoral maps for Alberta: Alberta panel proposes new electoral maps | Duration closed caption 2:37 A new report from an independent body recommends several changes to Alberta's electoral boundaries, ranging from restoring rural ridings to redrawing some ridings in Calgary and Lethbridge. CBC's Michelle Bellefontaine explains.

The proposals would split the southern city of Lethbridge into four ridings from its current two. It would have one strictly urban riding while the other three would see some neighbourhoods linked to sprawling adjacent rural areas.

It also includes additional hybrid ridings for the west side of Calgary.

In question period earlier Wednesday, Smith called Nenshi's allegations "ridiculous," and said if anyone gerrymandered the maps to benefit the UCP, "they failed miserably."

She said under the proposed maps, if the UCP were to win the popular vote by the same margins as it did in the 2023 election, the NDP would gain three seats and the UCP would gain one.

"[Nenshi's] trying to set it up so that people will doubt the integrity of elections," she said.

World.title: Beach weather in November? In Canada? These photos prove it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Even at the best of times, it's hard to imagine swimming outdoors in November — no matter where you live in Canada. But 2026 is changing that conventional wisdom.

Parts of Quebec and Ontario have been experiencing potentially record-setting summer-like temperatures this week, with highs over 20 C.

Normal highs in major cities this time of year are around 10 C.

In Montreal on Wednesday, it was 22 C, but felt like 24 C. Good enough for a trip to the beach.

Verdun Beach in Montreal attracted swimmers and sunbathers on Wednesday as temperatures reached 22 C. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

According to the Weather Network, the weather anomaly is due to a strong, high-pressure ridge off the U.S. East Coast and a warm front associated with a Colorado low — a low-pressure area caused by the Rocky Mountains that tends to track northeastward. Those systems combined are pushing warmer air into parts of Canada.

Toronto has also been warmer than normal.

With a high around 21 C in Toronto Wednesday, some people took to a hammock to enjoy the sunshine. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

Wearing shorts in Toronto in November? Why not? This man took advantage of the warmth as he walked his dogs Tuesday. (Alex Lupul/CBC)

WATCH | So what's behind these warm temps?: What’s behind the warm November weather in London? | Duration 1:54 The first week of November in London, Ont. has seen temperatures as high as 21 degrees, according to Environment Canada. It’s welcome news for some Londoners who want to make the most of the warmth before the snow hits, but what’s behind the unseasonably high temperatures?

El Ni ñ o effect

This year's strong El Ni ñ o is probably part of the story, too.

Bill Merryfield, a research scientist at Environment and Climate Change Canada, says El Ni ñ o usually affects Canada toward the end of the year, causing unusually mild fall and winter temperatures.

"This year's event is truly exceptional because this warming has already exceeded three degrees, which is well above that of any previous event and is expected to go even higher before the usual peak of El Ni ñ o in November or December," he said, referring to Pacific Ocean temperatures tied to the weather phenomenon.

Two people take a break on Parliament Hill during an unseasonably warm Nov. 4. (Dan Taekema/CBC)

It was a warm day under the fall foliage at Toronto's High Park. (Alex Lupul/CBC)

A cyclist in Toronto took advantage of the delayed start of cooler temps, too. (Alex Lupul/CBC)

People had the same idea in western Quebec, too.

World.title: Former NASA chief economist named new head of Canadian Space Agency
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alexander MacDonald was named the new president of the Canadian Space Agency late Wednesday evening.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly made the announcement in Ottawa during a tribute event to the late Marc Garneau, the first Canadian to travel to space.

MacDonald served as NASA's first chief economist, according to a government news release. In that role, he helped establish the "Moon to Mars" strategy, which includes the recent Artemis II mission that saw Canadian Jeremy Hansen travel around the moon earlier this year.

"As incredible as this year has been, I am even more excited about what the future holds for Canadians in space," MacDonald told the Ottawa crowd at Thursday's event.

"Space has never been more important for the strength and future of Canada, and never before has the world looked to Canada more for global leadership in the space domain."

MacDonald takes over from Campbell

MacDonald is taking over from outgoing president Lisa Campbell, who had been in the role since 2020. His appointment comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney's government looks to expand Canada's space capabilities.

Earlier this month, Joly also appointed Hansen as a special advisor to the government on developing a new space strategy.

The federal government listed space-based platforms for surveillance as a key priority in its new defence industrial strategy released in February. The Carney government is also looking to expand co-operation with European countries in space as part of the proposed partnership with the European Union.

World.title: Jimmy Kimmel roasts Trump in late night monologue amid 'blue tsunami' midterms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Late night host Jimmy Kimmel had some choice words for U.S. President Donald Trump last night as a “blue tsunami” stormed the country during the U.S. midterm elections.

Kimmel, host of ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel Live!, dragged the president through the verbal mud in his monologue Tuesday night, in a clip that has since racked up more than eight million views as of Wednesday afternoon.

“Trump was reportedly angry and cursing as the results came in,” he said. “Word from inside the White House is he’s already run out of dipping sauce containers to throw at the television set.”

He added, “the blue wave made landfall, and now the Red Wedding begins,” referencing a famous massacre in the HBO show Game of Thrones.

No major late-night shows aired live during the election results, but Kimmel’s show was taped later in the night than usual, around 7 p.m. in Los Angeles, so that Kimmel could react to the early results.

And react he did.

“After all the talk about Nicki Minaj’s ass, John Husted’s ass, the only ass on Trump’s mind tonight is the one that just got handed to him,” Kimmel said, referencing Trump’s perplexing comments in recent weeks fixating on the gluteal physique of colleagues.

Jimmy Kimmel poses with the award for outstanding host for a game show for Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? during the Emmys in 2026, in Los Angeles. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

“Democrats have officially taken the House, thanks to President Trump. Blob Vila flipped another house.”

The night saw Democrats retake the House and the Senate, winning several key races and flipping seats long held by Republicans.

Although the full results aren’t in yet, the Democrats have already gained seven seats in the Senate, 25 seats in the House, and five seats among governors, according to The Associated Press, making for a historic midterms for the U.S.

Leading up to the midterms, Trump frequently urged his supporters to “pretend I am on the ballot” in a bid to rally his base.

He struck a different tone on the phone to Fox News as the results came in, claiming that the sitting president always loses the midterms, and taking no responsibility for the Republican defeat.

“I shouldn’t feel guilty, because virtually … no matter how good the president is, you lose. I don’t know why. Nobody’s explained that,” he said.

WATCH | What will Democrats do now?: Democrats seize control of U.S. House, Senate. What will they actually do? | Duration closed caption 22:42 The Democrats flipped several key seats in the U.S. midterm elections, and will take control of both the House and the Senate in January. What will they do with their new-found power?

He has blamed losses on lackluster candidates, even though Trump himself had endorsed or selected many candidates who suffered historic losses in areas long thought to be safe Republican seats. Trump hand-picked Darline Graham to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham as Senator in South Carolina, but she lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in an upset. Trump also endorsed Ken Paxton for Senator in Texas, only for James Talarico to make history as the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Texas in nearly 40 years.

“I have to believe he saw some of this coming, because this morning he was bragging about his approval rating in another country,” Kimmel said in his monologue, before playing a clip of Trump on Fox News talking about how he has a 99 per cent approval rating in Israel and joking that he’d move to Israel to become prime minister “if people ever get tired of me in the U.S.”

“That might be the best idea he’s ever had,” Kimmel said.

U.S. President Donald Trump walks from the podium after speaking at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on Monday in Washington. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

He slammed Trump for focusing on transgender people, “reflecting pools, racism against whites, Tylenol and Canada,” instead of priorities that align with “what Americans are worried about,” such as war, healthcare, climate change and inflation.

The Republicans’ historic losses come after an estimated $183 million US was poured into anti-trans attack ads attempting to criticize Democrats for supporting transgender people, according to The Associated Press.

Trump has repeatedly called for Kimmel to be fired by ABC in response to being the target of Kimmel's comedy.

World.title: National chief didn't mean to 'hurt anybody' with remarks on Métis identity
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The national chief who came under fire for her comments on Métis identity last week says she didn't want to "hurt anybody" but maintains there's a widespread issue of people falsely claiming to be Indigenous across Canada.

When asked about the idea of abolishing the Indian Act on Oct. 26, Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said there's "a big group" of Métis people who "probably have First Nations roots" in Canada.

First Nations need control over who can claim membership, as the federal government has had too much say for too long, the national chief said.

"There's a lot of confused people out there who are claiming to be Indigenous, a lot of pretendians, and then a whole group of everybody else who says, 'I'm Métis,'" she said.

"Can you trace yourself back to a First Nation?"

Métis leaders condemned the remarks, including Manitoba Métis Federation President David Chartrand , who called them "racist," as the Métis are included in Section 35 of Canada's Constitution, which recognizes and affirms Aboriginal rights.

CBC News asked Woodhouse Nepinak on Tuesday about Chartrand's response and whether she felt she misspoke.

"This is bigger than a Manitoba issue," she said. "This is a Canada-wide issue, and I think there is pretendianism, and there [are] box-checkers in educational institutions, in governments, in government contracting, in business development."

The national chief said Canada created the issue and must "rectify the wrongs" caused by the Indian Act, which dictates who is classified as a status Indian, as well as Bill S-2 — proposed federal legislation that would end the second-generation cutoff for Indian status eligibility.

Decried as " legislative extinction " and " definitional genocide ,” the second-generation cutoff blocks children from acquiring Indian status when two consecutive generations of parents have a partner who is non-status.

"Deal with all of those issues first, on lands and the issues of membership with First Nations, before trying to dovetail into other groups of people in this country," Woodhouse Nepinak said.

The national chief said she did not intend to cause harm with her comments last week.

"It's the truth that there's a big problem in this country with identity and identity issues, with certain groups of people," she said.

"You should be able to trace yourself back to First Nations people…. I'll leave that there."

Indian Act discussion 'sideswiped' other issues

The national chief's initial remarks came as First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers met to discuss Indigenous rights for the first time in two decades. During that meeting, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew called for the Indian Act to be abolished.

On Tuesday, Woodhouse Nepinak also disputed claims by Kinew and Prime Minister Mark Carney that the idea to change or abolish the Indian Act was raised and supported by some chiefs in the room.

"No one" else brought up abolishing the Indian Act during the landmark meeting, the national chief said.

The chiefs involved had spent weeks preparing for the meeting and were focused more on the major projects legislation they say threatens their rights, but those conversations "went to the wayside" when Kinew and Carney made their remarks, she said.

"Those conversations can't be sideswiped just on one bombshell," Woodhouse Nepinak told reporters during a media scrum in Ottawa on Tuesday.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Democrats retake control of the US Congress in a heavy blow to Trump
World.content:
Democrats retake control of the US Congress in a heavy blow to Trump

4th Wednesday, November 2026 - 09:09 UTC Full article

CBS News projected a Democratic majority in the House shortly after 10 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday; with dozens of seats still to be decided, Democrats had passed the 218 needed

The Democratic Party on Tuesday regained control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate in the midterm elections, winning in Republican strongholds such as Texas, Ohio and Kansas in a heavy blow to President Donald Trump, who will govern for the remaining two years of his term with Congress in opposition hands.

CBS News projected a Democratic majority in the House shortly after 10 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday; with dozens of seats still to be decided, Democrats had passed the 218 needed. In the Senate, they secured a majority with victory in Iowa and hold at least 53 of the 100 seats, with results in Alaska and Mississippi still pending. According to El País, it is only the seventh time the party in power has lost both chambers in a midterm election.

Democrats won Senate seats in states where they had not done so for decades. In Texas, James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton; in Ohio, Sherrod Brown regained the seat from Jon Husted; in Kansas, Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton became the state’s first Democratic senator in almost a century. They also won in Iowa, with Josh Turek; in Maine, where Troy Jackson defeated Republican Susan Collins, a senator since 1997; in North Carolina, with Roy Cooper; and in South Carolina, with Annie Andrews. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, will be the first Muslim senator in US history. Republicans held seats in Florida, Idaho and Montana.

In governor’s races, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott in Texas and will be the first Hispanic woman to lead the state; Xavier Becerra will be California’s first Hispanic governor since 1875; and Deb Haaland, in New Mexico, the first Native American woman to govern a state. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds will be the state’s first Black governor.

Trump told Fox News he was “a little surprised” and that the Democrats “did a good job”, attributing part of the defeat to the Iran war and higher fuel prices. He told The New York Times he would accept the results and hoped to reach agreements with the opposition. On his social network, however, he wrote: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”, and posted an image of his cap bearing the word “VETO”, a reference to his threat to veto the new Congress’s laws.

With majorities in both chambers, Democrats will be able to block the White House’s legislative agenda and open investigations into the first half of the term. Former president Barack Obama said voters had sent “a clear message” in favour of “a politics that brings people together rather than divides them”. China said it was ready to “keep working” with Washington, and the Kremlin said it expected Trump to maintain his foreign policy. Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said “Americans have said no to war”.

Polls had identified the cost of living, corruption and the Iran war as voters’ main concerns, and turnout was at record levels for a midterm election.

World.title: Paraguay takes over Ueno Bank, with 3 million customers, and freezes its deposits
World.content:
Paraguay takes over Ueno Bank, with 3 million customers, and freezes its deposits

4th Wednesday, November 2026 - 08:27 UTC Full article

“We proceeded to close the entity; therefore, neither the app, nor the cards, nor any service of the entity is active,” said a member of the Central Bank’s board. Photo: EFE/ Juan Pablo Pino

Paraguay’s Central Bank on Tuesday took over Ueno Bank, one of the country’s largest banks, after its solvency ratio fell below 50% of the legal minimum, and froze all its assets and liabilities, including the savings of some 3 million customers and more than US$800 million in public funds. The bank immediately suspended all its services.

“We proceeded to close the entity; therefore, neither the app, nor the cards, nor any service of the entity is active from today,” said Liana Caballero, a member of the Central Bank’s board, which took the decision unanimously. According to its own figures, Ueno’s customers are equivalent to 60% of the country’s adult population, and it manages public funds including about US$380 million from the Social Security Institute, which runs pensions and public healthcare.

The Deposit Guarantee Fund covers savings of up to 75 minimum wages, about 228 million guaraníes or roughly US$38,200 per person. Those with larger balances will have to wait for the Superintendency of Banks’ final accounting. “The priority will always be small savers,” said Central Bank President Carlos Carvallo, who described the situation as “an isolated, one-off event” and said the financial system “remains sound and healthy”.

According to Carvallo, the takeover followed months of investigation that revealed loans to companies linked to the bank’s owners. On October 18, the Association of Banks of Paraguay had asked the Central Bank to report on the solvency of institutions that benefited from facilities in merger processes and warned about a bank’s credit exposure, which it did not identify, to companies in its own group. Days earlier, senators from the ruling party and the opposition had called on President Santiago Peña to dismiss the Central Bank’s leadership, which Peña backed.

Carvallo, who ran Ueno Bank before Peña appointed him to head the Central Bank in 2023, said he had signed his resignation, although he will remain in office until the bank’s resolution is complete. According to the Paraguayan press, several of the bank’s executives were detained, including its president, Miguel Vázquez.

The crisis had immediate political fallout. Vice President Pedro Alliana “paused” his bid for the ruling Colorado Party’s presidential nomination in order to “put the house in order”. The opposition Authentic Radical Liberal Party said it would push for impeachment proceedings against Peña and Alliana. “They plundered the pensioners’ money and this cannot be left like this,” said its presidential hopeful Ricardo Estigarribia, according to the newspaper ABC Color. In 2024, the Social Security Institute’s purchase of about US$32 million in Ueno bonds caused controversy; Peña, who called the reports a “media campaign”, was a shareholder in Ueno Holding, not the bank, and sold those shares in April 2025.

World.title: Trump accepts midterm defeat but says Republicans would have won “in a landslide” had he been on the ballot
World.content:
Trump accepts midterm defeat but says Republicans would have won “in a landslide” had he been on the ballot

4th Wednesday, November 2026 - 08:16 UTC Full article

“We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out,” he said

US President Donald Trump said he accepts the results of the midterm elections, in which Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress, and signalled willingness to negotiate with the opposition, but blamed the Republican defeat on his absence from the ballot and threatened to veto the new Congress’s legislation.

“I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” Trump told The New York Times. “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.” In a call to Fox News he admitted being “a little surprised” — “I thought we’d do better; we had tremendous rallies” — and acknowledged that Democrats “did a good job”. He told Politico he spoke with Democratic leaders at around 11 p.m. on Tuesday and would rather strike deals than spend his final two years vetoing legislation; according to NBC News, he said several newly elected Democrats had called him, though he did not name them. He cited immigration as a possible area of cooperation, according to CNBC.

His tone on social media was very different. Before polls closed on the West Coast, he wrote on his Truth Social platform: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”, despite having spent weeks urging supporters to vote “as if I were on the ballot”. An hour after his conversation with Democrats, he posted an image of a red cap bearing the word “VETO”, a reference to his threat to block the new Congress’s legislation. “It’s one of the strongest powers a president has,” he told Fox News. “They send me crazy proposals and I veto them. After a couple of months of vetoes, they ask: ‘How can we get this done?’ And we work together.”

Trump also said he would “become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost”, and claimed without evidence that Fox News “bears responsibility for these losses” by giving airtime to the opposition. He criticised Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott, defeated by Democrat Gina Hinojosa, for turning “moderate”, and said he had no regrets about endorsing candidates such as Darline Graham in South Carolina and Ken Paxton in Texas, both of whom lost their Senate races.

The defeat confirms the fear Trump himself voiced in January before his party’s lawmakers, when he warned that if they lost the midterms, Democrats would find “a reason” to impeach him for a third time. According to the Associated Press, impeachment of the president or members of his Cabinet “is not off the table”. With control of both chambers, Democrats will also be able to block his legislative agenda and open investigations.

Democratic leaders celebrated the result. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called it a “generational remake of the Senate map”, and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said “the American people are crying out for transformational change”.

His acceptance of the result contrasts with his refusal to concede defeat to Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election, which he still does not acknowledge. Trump will leave the White House in January 2029 and cannot run again, so the defeat also opens the race to succeed him in the Republican Party.

World.title: Markets react to the US midterms: the dollar falls and gold rises
World.content:
Markets react to the US midterms: the dollar falls and gold rises

4th Wednesday, November 2026 - 08:00 UTC Full article

The dollar index, which measures its value against a basket of currencies, remained in negative territory near 101.50

The US dollar weakened against major currencies on Wednesday morning and gold rose more than 2% to above US$4,000 an ounce as markets assessed the Democratic victory in the midterm elections, which will give the opposition control of both chambers of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency.

The dollar index, which measures its value against a basket of currencies, remained in negative territory near 101.50, and the yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note fell below 4.95%, according to financial analysis platform FXStreet. Wall Street index futures were mixed. The dollar’s biggest fall was against the Swiss franc, at 0.4%. The euro briefly rose above US$1.1250, its highest in two weeks, before easing to 1.1230, and sterling extended its winning streak to a sixth day above US$1.3450, ahead of an expected Bank of England rate rise on Thursday.

Analysts at Germany’s Commerzbank warned that “US equities, and in particular the tech-heavy Nasdaq, are likely to come under pressure today”, and that because the dollar’s recent strength had benefited from equity-related capital inflows, “dollar weakness could consolidate somewhat further in the coming hours”. In the longer term, they said a more constructive political debate in the United States, “admittedly a very remote possibility”, could reduce the political risk premium priced into the dollar.

Trump told The Wall Street Journal that the Iran war was “partially to blame” for the Republican defeat and that he has no plans for personnel changes in his administration.

World.title: Spain’s transport minister resigns after the train crash that killed at least 69 people
World.content:
Spain’s transport minister resigns after the train crash that killed at least 69 people

4th Wednesday, November 2026 - 07:44 UTC Full article

Spain’s Transport Minister Óscar Puente resigned on Tuesday, six days after a collision between two high-speed trains near the town of Urda, in Toledo province, that killed at least 69 people. Puente also said he was withdrawing his name from the Socialist Party’s lists for the snap general election on November 29.

“A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year,” he told Congress at the end of a lengthy session in which he presented new rail safety measures and faced opposition criticism. He was also referring to the crash at Adamuz, in Córdoba, on the same line, which killed 46 people in January. Puente said his decision was driven by “political dignity”. Days earlier he had said he did not intend to step down.

The People’s Party and Vox, as well as some of the government’s allies, had called for his resignation, accusing him of blaming human error for the crash to avoid responsibility for a high-speed rail system whose credibility Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez admitted was “broken”. Sánchez praised Puente, who “faced up to the situation, provided answers and solutions, and then stepped aside. Out of dignity. Of his own accord. Out of respect for the victims.”

The crash happened on the morning of October 28 on the Madrid-Seville line, when a Renfe AVE train carrying 397 passengers ran into the back of an Iryo train with 147 passengers on board, which had stopped after a failure in the computerised signalling system. Recordings of conversations between the control centre and the drivers, published by the Spanish press, show the controller authorised the AVE to continue “at normal speed” even though the Iryo train was still stationary about 25 kilometres ahead. In another recording, the Iryo driver warns the control centre that he cannot restart the train. It was Spain’s worst rail disaster since the Santiago de Compostela crash in 2013.

The resignation comes at a key moment in the political calendar, less than four weeks before the general election. According to the BBC, many analysts see the crash as a heavy blow to the prospects of the Socialist government, which polls already placed behind the People’s Party.

World.title: Cristina Kirchner meets Lula’s digital strategist in a bid to replicate his comeback in Argentina
World.content:
Cristina Kirchner meets Lula’s digital strategist in a bid to replicate his comeback in Argentina

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 20:16 UTC Full article

Kirchner, who is serving a final six-year sentence for corruption under house arrest and is barred for life from public office

Former Argentine president Cristina Kirchner on Monday received Brazilian lawmaker André Janones, creator of the WhatsApp channel that helped Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva win re-election, in Buenos Aires, as the Peronist opposition looks to Brazil for keys to defeating Javier Milei in the 2027 presidential election.

Janones, a federal deputy for the state of Minas Gerais, runs “Lula’s Army”, a WhatsApp channel with more than 10.4 million followers to whom he sends daily instructions to share and amplify content on social media, a strategy credited with part of Lula’s comeback against Flávio Bolsonaro on October 25. On the day of the Brazilian election, the Peronists launched their own “Peronism’s Army”, which had passed 80,000 followers after Janones’ visit.

Kirchner, who is serving a final six-year sentence for corruption under house arrest and is barred for life from public office, posed with Janones in a photo he shared on social media with the message: “Beside Cristina Kirchner to tell the world that yes, we can defeat the far right.” Lula’s channel was told to share the post, which drew more than 60,000 interactions within an hour. Janones also met Sergio Massa, the Peronists’ last presidential candidate, but not Buenos Aires province governor Axel Kicillof.

The visit came amid an internal Peronist struggle over the 2027 presidential candidacy, in which Kicillof, backed by several governors and mayors, faces the Kirchner and Massa camp. The former president, who hopes to overturn her conviction before international courts, said in an interview with The Washington Post published on Monday that she could run again: “When I recover my political rights, why not?”

Janones, re-elected as a deputy in October, has ruled out a ministerial post in Lula’s new government and returns to Brazil on Tuesday. His team denied he plans to work on the campaign of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez ahead of the November 29 general election.

World.title: The Pope arrives in an Argentina where bishops are among Milei’s firmest critics
World.content:
The Pope arrives in an Argentina where bishops are among Milei’s firmest critics

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 09:29 UTC Full article

Leo XIV has placed social justice at the heart of his pontificate, while Milei has called it “an aberration”

Pope Leo XIV will arrive in Buenos Aires on Sunday on a visit that Javier Milei’s government presents as strictly pastoral, but which takes place amid tension with Argentina’s Catholic hierarchy, one of the most critical voices against the president’s austerity policies. The pontiff will begin a tour in Uruguay on Friday that will continue in Argentina from November 8 to 11 and end in Peru.

“The Pope belongs to all Argentines, not to a political party or a political colour,” presidential chief of staff Karina Milei, who led negotiations with the Church and the Vatican, has repeatedly said. The secretary of worship, Agustín Caulo, insisted it is “an apostolic tour” and that “this should not be politicised”. Authorities expect some 7 million people to follow the Pope in Buenos Aires, Claypole, Luján and Córdoba, in what Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva described as “the largest operation in our history”.

The underlying differences are well known. Leo XIV has placed social justice at the heart of his pontificate, while Milei has called it “an aberration”. A study by sociologist Sol Prieto of the National Scientific and Technical Research Council (Conicet) of documents published by the Argentine Bishops’ Conference between January 2024 and September 2026 found that 42 of the 44 referring to public policy, or 95%, take “a critical position”, on issues such as the social situation, the environment, institutional quality, the lowering of the age of criminal responsibility and a decree curbing migrants’ rights.

Ten days ago, when Milei questioned the idea that many people cannot make ends meet, the president of the Bishops’ Conference, Marcelo Colombo, replied: “That people cannot make ends meet is a fact of reality, not something that needs to be proven.” The Archbishop of Buenos Aires, Jorge García Cuerva, said the Pope “will find a wounded Argentina”. “There is no affinity, but a very strong aversion between most Argentine bishops and Milei’s government,” said researcher Fortunato Mallimaci, who identifies opposition to abortion as one of the few points of agreement.

According to El País, the government sought to limit mass gatherings but the Vatican’s position prevailed, and the Pope will celebrate open-air Masses. Two events are particularly uncomfortable for the government, according to the newspaper: the meeting with trade unionists, business leaders and social movements at the Catholic University of Argentina and the visit to the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione, a home for people with disabilities, one of the sectors hardest hit by spending cuts. The place of Vice President Victoria Villarruel, estranged from Milei, at official events also remains undecided.

World.title: Ayuso honours Kast in Madrid on the eve of the Ibero-American Summit: “We defend the same things”
World.content:
Ayuso honours Kast in Madrid on the eve of the Ibero-American Summit: “We defend the same things”

3rd Tuesday, November 2026 - 09:18 UTC Full article

Kast, on his first European tour since taking office in March, replied that Madrid “is one of the most open, free and prosperous regions in Europe” and stressed security, the focus of his government

The president of the Madrid regional government, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, on Monday awarded the region’s International Medal to Chilean President José Antonio Kast, who is in the Spanish capital for the 30th Ibero-American Summit of Heads of State and Government. “On both sides of the Atlantic we defend the same things,” Ayuso said at the ceremony.

“We are free nations and we defend our governments and liberal democracies and the rule of law, which will not yield to authoritarianism,” said the People’s Party leader, who contrasted Chile with Cuba, Nicaragua and Venezuela. Ayuso praised Chile as “an example of what a nation can achieve when it trusts its citizens” and highlighted Kast’s “commitment to freedom, security, prosperity and the defence of institutions”. “We do not want citizens dependent on power; we want them to be masters of their own lives,” she added.

Kast, on his first European tour since taking office in March, replied that Madrid “is one of the most open, free and prosperous regions in Europe” and stressed security, the focus of his government. “It is the first duty of the state. And when the state fails in that duty, the most vulnerable pay. Without security there is no order, without order there is no peace and without peace there is no freedom.”

The Community of Madrid’s International Medal, created in 2017 and purely honorary, is awarded on the regional president’s personal initiative. Previous recipients include Argentine President Javier Milei and Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa; Venezuelan opposition leaders Juan Guaidó and Edmundo González; Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky; Pope Leo XIV; and the United States, for the 250th anniversary of its independence. Manuela Bergerot, spokeswoman for Más Madrid in the regional assembly, accused Ayuso of turning the award into “the membership card of her far-right international”. A group of demonstrators protested outside the regional government headquarters.

Kast began the day with a private meeting with Vox leader Santiago Abascal, with whom he has close ties, and plans to meet Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez during the summit, which brings together the countries of Latin America with Spain, Portugal and Andorra.

World.title: US $40M Pilgrim’s Pride plant will open Thursday in Gómez Palacio, Durango
World.content:
Pilgrim’s Pride Corporation, the multinational chicken producer, will launch on Thursday its US $40 million El Porvenir plant in Gómez Palacio, Durango, which is expected to create over 300 jobs.

The project is part of Pilgrim’s broader plans to invest $1.3 billion in Mexico between 2026 and 2030 under the Sheinbaum government’s Plan México economic strategy, which is expected to increase production by more than 373,000 metric tonnes and generate over 4,000 direct and 16,000 indirect jobs.

The investment will be divided among several states, with $200 million allocated to Durango and Coahuila in the northern border zone, $150 million to Querétaro, San Luis Potosí and Hidalgo in El Bajío and the center, and $950 million to the southeastern states of Veracruz, Campeche and Yucatán.

Durango’s Foreign Investment Attraction Unit head, Arturo Ortiz Galán, said that the new production line will support local suppliers and the region’s poultry businesses, helping to reinforce Durango’s position as an industrial and agri-food hub. The plant will also expand Pilgrim’s value-added product range by producing cooked chicken.

Ortiz Galán said the expansion was made possible through collaboration with the federal government, which has provided investment incentives.

“Thanks to the good relationship that [Durango] Governor [Esteban] Villegas has with President Sheinbaum, I have been able to easily initiate discussions and secure support from all the relevant ministries,” Galán said. “It’s very positive that there’s a plan to digitalize all processes and create a one-stop shop for investments.”

It delivers food to approximately 30 million Mexicans, employs around 12,600 people across Mexico, and provides 50,000 indirect jobs through its partner farmers, logistics providers and supply chain.

In January, President Sheinbaum praised the Mexican business environment for attracting high investment from Pilgrim’s.

“This investment they are making… is because they have been successful and because they know that investing in Mexico is safe and allows them to continue growing,” Sheinbaum said during a morning press conference.

With reports from Milenio and Mexico Industry

World.title: As Ibero-American Summit gets underway in Madrid, foreign ministers cite ‘excellent’ Spain-Mexico relations
World.content:
Mexico-Spain relations are in “excellent” shape, Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco said Wednesday after a meeting with his Spanish counterpart in Madrid.

In a social media post, Velasco said that he and Spanish Foreign Affairs Minister José Manuel Albares spoke with “our usual closeness and trust” about the “excellent” state of relations between Mexico and Spain, a leading source of foreign investment in Mexico.

“We highlighted the good rapport between President [Claudia] Sheinbaum and Prime Minister [Pedro] Sánchez, which drives a constructive, results-oriented agenda,” he wrote.

“Mexico and Spain will continue to strengthen this fraternal friendship and the dialogue that unites us,” Velasco said.

His meeting with Albares took place on the first day of the Ibero-American Summit, a gathering of leaders and officials from Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries. Velasco is representing Sheinbaum at the event.

After meeting with the Mexican foreign minister, Albares also described Mexico-Spain relations in positive terms.

“Spain and Mexico have strengthened our political, economic and cultural relations over the past year year for the benefit of our sister nations,” he wrote on social media.

There is no doubt that Mexico-Spain relations have improved during Sheinbaum’s presidency after they deteriorated considerably during Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s six-year term in office.

In 2019, López Obrador requested an apology from Spain for human rights violations during the Conquest of Mexico, while in 2022 he advocated a “pause” in bilateral relations while asserting that Mexico had been “looted” for years due to “economic-political promiscuity in the leadership of the governments of Mexico and Spain.”
