AMLO’s 2019 request for an apology was “vigorously” rejected by the Spanish government, but in March of this year, King Felipe VI of Spain acknowledged that during the Spanish conquest and colonization of the Americas, “there were significant abuses” and “moral and ethical controversies.” As Mexico News Daily reported at the time, his remarks constituted an unprecedented statement on the matter for a king of Spain.

In April, Sheinbaum met with Prime Minister Sánchez at the “In Defense of Democracy” summit in Barcelona.

Sheinbaum had also called for an apology for abuses committed by Spain during the Conquest and the fall of Tenochtitlán, but in Barcelona, she acknowledged that there had been “a rapprochement from both the Spanish … [prime minister] and the king himself.”

The Ibero-American Summit

In a statement released on Tuesday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (SRE) noted that Sheinbaum had designated Velasco to lead the Mexican delegation at the 30th Ibero-American Summit in Madrid on Nov. 4 and 5.

“The Mexican delegation’s presence will be key to continuing to advance cooperation in areas of interest to Mexico, such as the environment and climate change, human mobility, disaster risk reduction, education, gender equality, and science and technology,” the SRE said.

“At the meeting, the host country will report on its results over the past two years in charge of the Pro Tempore Secretariat of the Summit and will hand the presidency over to Honduras for the 2026-2028 period,” the ministry said.

“The first Summit was held in Mexico, in Guadalajara, in 1991. Since then, it has been an important forum for dialogue and cooperation between the two regions,” the SRE said, referring to Latin America and Europe.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mexican-Americans among historic winners in Tuesday’s US elections
World.content:
Mexican American candidates captured the governorships of Texas and California, and at least three Latino Democrats flipped Republican congressional seats in Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections.

Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, will become the state’s first Latina governor ever, and Texas’ first Democratic governor since Ann Richards from 1991 to 1995.

Her victory helped end a Democratic drought in Texas statewide elections dating to 1994.

In the California governor’s race, Democrat Xavier Becerra — whose mother was born in Jalisco and whose father was born in Sacramento but raised in Mexico — had a 64% to 36% lead over Republican Steve Hilton, a former Fox News host, in preliminary returns.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum welcomed their victories Wednesday morning.

“We are very pleased that Mexican Americans have this recognition,” she said in her daily press conference.

Becerra, who previously served as California attorney general and U.S. health and human services secretary under President Joe Biden, became the first Latino elected governor of California.

A previous Latino governor of California, Romualdo Pacheco, was not elected to the post but served nine months in 1875 after the seated governor left to join the Senate. Pacheco was the lieutenant governor at the time.

Hinojosa grew up in the border city of Brownsville, Texas, where her parents began their careers as legal aid lawyers representing farmworkers. Her mother, Crisanta Guerra Lozano, was born in the city of San Luis Potosí, and her father, Gilberto Hinojosa, chaired the Texas Democratic Party from 2012 to 2025.

She recalled crossing into Mexico regularly with her family for breakfast and shopping as a girl.

In South Texas, Tejano singer Bobby Pulido — winner of Latin Grammys for best Tejano album in 2022 and 2025 — defeated incumbent Republican Rep. Mónica De La Cruz in the 15th Congressional District, flipping a seat in a district President Donald Trump carried by 18 percentage points in 2024.

Pulido said last month he lacked U.S. health insurance and had traveled to Mexico for medical care.

The conservative Democrat campaigned on border security and support for government-funded health care and safety net programs, according to the New York Times. His outreach included free performances at quinceañeras and other local celebrations.

His victory marked a reversal in a district viewed as a test of Latino voters’ political loyalties after Trump’s gains two years earlier.

“Hispanics, they’re not so partisan,” Pulido said by way of an explanation. “It’s very much, ‘Are you gonna go fight for me?’ That’s what matters.”

Added Javier Palomarez, president and CEO of the United States Hispanic Business Council: “We are a community that doesn’t vote party. It votes person.”

Democrat Katy Padilla Stout was projected to win Texas’ 23rd Congressional District against Brandon Herrera, a gun-focused YouTube personality, according to CBS News, flipping another Republican seat.

The sprawling border district stretches from San Antonio to El Paso. Its previous Republican representative, Tony Gonzales, resigned in April. Trump carried the current district by 14 points.

In Nebraska, Democrat Denise Powell defeated Republican Brinker Harding to become the state’s first Latina elected to federal office and the first woman to represent its 2nd Congressional District.

Powell, who co-founded a group helping local women run for office, also became the district’s first Democratic winner in a decade. She flipped the seat held by retiring Republican Rep. Don Bacon.

In another notable Texas victory, Democrat and longtime sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia defeated Trump-backed Republican Carlos de La Cruz in a San Antonio-area district redrawn by Republicans to favor their party. As redrawn, the majority-Hispanic district would have backed Trump by more than 10 percentage points in 2024.

With reports from El Financiero, Quadratín San Luis Potosí, CBC, Hindustan Times, Fast Company and Nebraska Examiner

World.title: El Jalapeño: Chipotle mystified after Mexican diners treat fast-casual burrito bowl as lunch instead of cultural offense
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

SAN PEDRO GARZA GARCÍA, Nuevo León — Executive leadership at Chipotle Mexican Grill confirmed Tuesday that they are currently re-evaluating their entire global strategy after local diners surprisingly failed to fiercely oppose their version of Mexican-inspired cuisine.

After the U.S. fast-casual chain opened its first Mexican location in the affluent municipality of San Pedro Garza García earlier this year, corporate analysts fully expected a wave of diplomatic friction, or at least a sternly worded statement from local culinary boards. Instead, customer volume has remained consistently high, forcing corporate strategists to confront the unsettling possibility that people simply enjoy a large, convenient bowl of rice, beans and meat without converting their meal break into a cultural referendum.

“We prepared extensive crisis-management protocols for the inevitable national backlash against charging 180 pesos for a scoop of guacamole,” said Chipotle Director of Global Brand Strategy Mark Henderson, speaking via video conference from the packed dining area of the company’s Nuevo León restaurant. “Our market research explicitly warned us that bringing an Americanized version of Mexican food into actual Mexico was the culinary equivalent of selling canned air to a mountain town. We were braced for total outrage, but people keep coming back and asking for extra salsa.”

According to company officials, early performance metrics far exceeded initial corporate expectations, which had originally budgeted for three weeks of novelty-driven foot traffic followed by a swift, dignified retreat from the market. Company leadership now plans to open four additional locations in Nuevo León before expanding into Mexico City, where executives are reportedly preparing an entirely new set of contingency plans in case diners there also treat lunch as just lunch.

Internal memos revealed that brand researchers initially attributed the sustained high sales to a clerical error, suspecting that local patrons were under the mistaken impression that Chipotle was an upscale American salad bar.

At press time, Chipotle board members were reportedly holding an emergency summit to discuss whether the chain could safely introduce hard-shell tacos without triggering a public outcry.

World.title: Mexico’s economy nearing ‘strong’ according to the latest MND Economy Index™
World.content:
Listen to this article

THE MND ECONOMY INDEX™

Providing broad insight into the Mexican economy

MND Intelligence · Sixth edition

Welcome to the sixth edition of the MND Economy Index™, part of the MND Intelligence™ suite of data products from Mexico News Daily.

The MND Economy Index™ is a 10-pillar, 19-indicator composite index that compiles a broad range of economic data into a single score between 0 and 100, giving Mexico News Daily readers a clear, accessible picture of how the Mexican economy is performing across multiple dimensions.

In the inaugural MND Economy Index™ article, published in late May, we not only analyzed the index score — 63.4 out of 100 — but also explained what the index is, why we developed it and how it works. Click here to read (or re-read) those explanations.

In this edition of the MND Economy Index™ — which uses economic data primarily from the month of August — the index score is 74.5, an increase of 1.4 points compared to the previous score.

The score for August is the highest since we began publishing the MND Economy Index™, reflecting improvements in various parts of Mexico’s economy.

Before we look more closely at the latest index result, here is a short guide to what the overall index score means.

85–100: Exceptional — the economy performing at a high level across nearly all indicators.

— the economy performing at a high level across nearly all indicators. 75–84: Strong — strong broad-based performance with only minor areas of concern.

— strong broad-based performance with only minor areas of concern. 60–74: Above neutral — meaningful strengths, but with notable room for improvement.

— meaningful strengths, but with notable room for improvement. 50–59: Mixed — passing marks overall, more indicators above benchmark than below.

— passing marks overall, more indicators above benchmark than below. Below 50: Broad underperformance — more indicators below benchmark than above.

Mexico’s economy on the verge of a ‘strong’ assessment

As noted above, the latest MND Economy Index™ score is 74.5, an increase of 1.4 percentage points compared to the previous score. The latest score is just 0.5 percentage points below the score required for a “strong” assessment for Mexico’s economy.

Below you will see the score for each of the ten pillars that make up the index, expressed out of 10 to reflect each pillar’s exact contribution to the final composite score.

Pillars are color-coded using a traffic light system: green (a score above 7.5) indicates strong performance; yellow (5.0–7.5) signals decent performance but with room for improvement; and red (below 5.0) flags a pillar that is falling short of its benchmark. Where a pillar score has improved compared to the previous month, an upward arrow appears alongside its corresponding traffic light; a downward arrow indicates a deterioration; and a pause symbol denotes no change.

As you’ll see below, scores for four of the ten MND Economy Index™ pillars increased in August compared to the previous month. Scores for five pillars declined, while the score for one was unchanged.

Collectively, the increases were more significant than the decreases, allowing the index score to rise.

🟢 ⬇️ INFLATION (9.54)

The score for this pillar fell to 9.54 in August from 9.68 in July. Despite the decline, the inflation pillar retained its position as the top contributor to the overall MND Economy Index™ score.

Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate increased to 3.26% in August, ending a four-month streak of declines. The increase caused a slight decrease in the score for the current inflation component of the pillar as the headline rate moved away from the Bank of Mexico’s 3% target.

The score for the pillar component that considers the 12-month forward inflation forecast was unchanged as the Bank of Mexico’s outlook for the third quarter of 2027 is applicable to both July and August. The central bank is predicting a headline inflation rate of 3.2% in the third quarter of next year.

🟢 ⬆️ MONETARY POLICY (9.46)

The score for this pillar increased to 9.46 from 9.32 in July.

The Bank of Mexico’s benchmark interest rate remained at 6.50% in August after the central bank’s board voted to keep it at that level at a monetary policy meeting on Aug. 6. Therefore, there was no change in the interest rate component of the pillar score.

The increase in the pillar score was due to a decline in Mexico’s real interest rate in August — i.e., the Bank of Mexico’s benchmark interest rate minus the annual headline inflation rate.

The real interest rate in August was 3.24%, a reading 0.54 points above the 2.7% neutral midpoint.

The real interest rate in July, at 3.38%, was further away from the neutral midpoint than the reading in August.

🟢 ⬆️ MANUFACTURING SECTOR HEALTH (8.53)

The score for this pillar increased in August, rising to 8.53 from 7.9 in July.

The exports component of the pillar remained at the maximum score due to a 40.4% annual increase in export revenue in August, well above the 16.7% threshold needed for a perfect ten. Official data shows that over 94% of Mexico’s export revenue in August came from the shipment abroad of manufactured goods.

The increase in the overall pillar score was due to 4.1% year-over-year growth in manufacturing output in August. The year-over-year gain represented a significant improvement from the 1.6% increase in July.

🟢 ⬆️ ECONOMIC GROWTH (8)

The score for this pillar increased to 8 in August from 7.6 in July.

The increase was due to a higher annual economic growth rate in August. The annual growth rate in August was 3.5%, according to final data published by INEGI on Oct. 23. Year-over-year growth in July was slightly lower at 3.3%.

At her morning press conference on Oct. 26, President Sheinbaum said that growth of 3.5% in August was “very good news.”

She noted that construction, including housing and public infrastructure projects, was helping to drive growth. Sheinbaum also noted that the production of electronics in Mexico was providing momentum to the economy.

🟢 ⬆️ SOVEREIGN RISK (7.72)

The score for this pillar increased to 7.72 in August from 7.41 in July.

The score for the sovereign credit ratings component of the pillar remained unchanged in August, as there were no month-over-month changes to the Mexico ratings of Moody’s (Baa3/stable); S&P (BBB/negative); and Fitch (BBB-/stable).

The increase in the overall pillar score was due to a narrowing in Mexico’s 5-year credit default swap spread. The credit default swap spread was 77.89 basis points at the end of August, down from 87.19 basis points at the end of July. The narrower spread reflected a decrease in the market-implied cost of insuring against a Mexican sovereign default.

🟡 ⬇️ CURRENCY STABILITY (6.73)

The score for this pillar declined slightly to 6.73 in August from 6.79 in July.

The standard deviation of daily exchange rate movements decreased to 0.25% in August from 0.40% in July, leading to an increase in the score for that component of the pillar.

The decrease in the pillar score in July was due to a lower spot rate score. The score for that component declined because the peso strengthened against the US dollar in August to trade at 16.99 to the greenback at the end of the month, an appreciation of 1.9% compared to the end of July.

The exchange rate was thus more distant from the index’s 19.00 USD:MXN baseline, which is based on the 2025 average rate. This pillar penalizes significant deviation from the 19.00 USD:MXN baseline in either direction, recognizing that a peso that has strengthened too far from this benchmark can erode export competitiveness and reduce the purchasing power of remittances, just as a weakening peso raises import costs.

The spot rate component of the currency stability score will increase in the next MND Economy Index™ as the peso depreciated 6% in September to trade at 18.08 to the dollar at the end of that month.

🟡 ⬇️ INVESTMENT CLIMATE (6.46)

The score for this pillar decreased to 6.46 in August from 6.58 in July.

The decrease was due to lower annual growth on the S&P/BMV FIBRAS Total Return Index, which tracks the performance of Mexico’s listed real estate investment trusts. The index grew 24.9% annually to the end of August, down from a 27.4% year-over-year increase at the end of July.

The score for the foreign direct investment component of the pillar remained steady as the latest available data is still that published by the Economy Ministry in late August. That data shows that foreign direct investment in Mexico increased 2.1% annually in the first six months of 2026 to reach a record-high $34.96 billion. Annual FDI growth of 25% is required for a perfect score in that component of the investment climate pillar.

🟡 ⏸️ PRODUCTIVITY (6.4)

The score for this pillar remained steady at 6.4 in August after increasing to that level in July from 3.8 in June.

Data published by the national statistics agency INEGI on Sept. 10 showed that the IGPLE — INEGI’s quarterly productivity measure — increased 1.7% annually in the second quarter of 2026. That level of productivity growth was significantly stronger than the +0.1% reading in the first quarter of 2026.

INEGI will publish productivity data for the third quarter of 2026 in early December.

🟡 ⬇️ LABOR AND EMPLOYMENT (6.11)

The score for this pillar decreased to 6.11 in August from 6.18 in July. Scores for two of the pillar’s three components stayed the same while one declined.

The number of people in formal sector jobs rose 1.5% in the 12 months to the end of August, on par with the annual growth rate at the end of July.

Nominal wages were up 6.7% year-on-year at the end of August, the same increase recorded at the end of July.

Year-over-year growth in Mexico’s informality rate was 0.2 points at the end of August, up from an annual increase of 0.1 points at the end of July. In August, 55% of all Mexican workers worked in the informal economy. Lowering the informality rate is a major challenge for the Mexican government.

🟡 ⬇️ EXTERNAL INCOME (5.51)

The score for this pillar increased in August, rising to 5.51 from 5.26 in July. A year-over-year reduction in remittances in August — just the second decline this year — was a drag on the pillar score, but a strong increase in international tourism revenue more than offset it.

Incoming remittances declined 3.6% year-on-year to US $5.45 billion in August, the first decline of any month since January.

Thus, the score for the remittances component of the pillar fell sharply, although not so far as to warrant a score of zero, as that would require a year-over-year decline of 16.67%.

The pillar score increased in August as international tourism revenue grew compared to the same month of last year, whereas it declined in July. International tourist spending increased 7% year over year in August to reach $2.4 billion.

The MND Economy Index™ trend

In the graph below you can see how the MND Economy Index™ score has changed over time.

We have now calculated a total of ten index scores in the period between March 2025 and August 2026. The difference between the lowest score (56.9 in March 2025 — predating the publication of the first MND Economy Index™ article) and the highest (74.5 in August 2026) is 17.6 points.

The much higher score in this edition of the MND Economy Index™ indicates that Mexico’s economy is performing much better now than it was early in President Sheinbaum’s six-year term.

The improvement in the index score this year has been significant, increasing more than 10 points between March and August.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice is ‘67% complete,’ Sheinbaum reports: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🕊️ Government presents progress under Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice: The mañanera focused on advances made over the past year under the plan, which the government devised after the assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo on Nov. 1, 2025. President Sheinbaum said the presentation would cover areas other than security.

The mañanera focused on advances made over the past year under the plan, which the government devised after the assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo on Nov. 1, 2025. President Sheinbaum said the presentation would cover areas other than security. 📊 Sheinbaum says Plan Michoacán is 67% complete: The president said 1,680 of more than 2,500 “actions” under the plan have been completed.

The president said 1,680 of more than 2,500 “actions” under the plan have been completed. 💰 Planned investment more than doubles to 118 billion pesos: Sheinbaum said 118 billion pesos (US $6.3 billion) is slated for Plan Michoacán between 2025 and 2030, up from the 57 billion pesos originally announced. She said 72.43 billion pesos, or 61% of the total, has already been spent.

Sheinbaum said 118 billion pesos (US $6.3 billion) is slated for Plan Michoacán between 2025 and 2030, up from the 57 billion pesos originally announced. She said 72.43 billion pesos, or 61% of the total, has already been spent. 🎪 115 “Well-being Fairs” held across all 113 Michoacán municipalities: Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said residents completed more than 1.1 million administrative procedures at the fairs over the past year, including ones that facilitated access to welfare programs.

Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said residents completed more than 1.1 million administrative procedures at the fairs over the past year, including ones that facilitated access to welfare programs. 🛣️ 41 billion pesos invested in Michoacán highways: Infrastructure Minister Jesús Esteva said the government is upgrading 411 kilometers of highway, with the government and private sector investing more than 41 billion pesos (US $2.2 billion) in six projects.

Infrastructure Minister Jesús Esteva said the government is upgrading 411 kilometers of highway, with the government and private sector investing more than 41 billion pesos (US $2.2 billion) in six projects. 🏭 Work on Bajío Industrial Park to start this month: Deputy Economy Minister Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez said 9.3 billion pesos (US $498.5 million) will be invested in the park in Zinapécuaro, which will primarily cater to the agroindustrial and automotive sectors.

Deputy Economy Minister Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez said 9.3 billion pesos (US $498.5 million) will be invested in the park in Zinapécuaro, which will primarily cater to the agroindustrial and automotive sectors. 🎓 795,000 Michoacán students receive government scholarships: Education Minister Mario Delgado said primary, middle school, high school and university students all receive monetary assistance, funded with an investment of 5.7 billion pesos (around US $306 million).

Why today’s mañanera matters

A presentation on the progress made under “Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice” over the past year was the central focus of President Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference.

The government devised the plan in response to the assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo on Nov. 1, 2025, and general insecurity in Michoacán.

At the start of her Wednesday mañanera, the president noted that today’s presentation would focus on progress in areas other than security. She said that an update on the security situation in Michoacán would be presented at her press conference next Tuesday.

Data presented at Sheinbaum’s Oct. 13 mañanera showed that homicides in Michoacán declined 40.3% in the first nine months of 2026 compared to the same period of last year.

The president was accompanied on Wednesday by various high-ranking officials, each of whom spoke briefly about Plan Michoacán initiatives.

Today’s mañanera allowed the government to both highlight progress on the plan and explain how funds have been spent. Sheinbaum characterizes her weekday press conferences as exercises in transparency, a principle she says is central to her administration.

115 ‘Well-being Fairs’ held in Michoacán

Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez reported that 115 “Ferías del Bienestar,” or “Well-being Fairs,” were held across all 113 municipalities of Michoacán over the past year.

She said that officials helped Michoacán residents complete more than 1.1 million trámites (administrative procedures) at the fairs, including ones that facilitated their access to government welfare programs.

Rodríguez also noted that Michoacán residents exchanged 673 firearms for cash over the past year under the Sí al Desarme, Sí a la Paz (Yes to Disarmament, Yes to Peace) program. Those exchanges, she said, will save lives.

Key advances under Plan Michoacán

Officials presented key advances under Plan Michoacán across a range of areas. Not all of the investment they outlined is directly linked to Plan Michoacán funding. Summarized below are the presentations made by 10 officials.

Deputy Economy Minister Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez reported that work will start this month on the Bajío Industrial Park in the municipality of Zinapécuaro. He said 9.3 billion pesos (US $498.5 million) will be invested in the project. The industrial park will primarily cater to the agroindustrial and automotive sectors.

Agriculture Minister Columba López reported that more than 177,000 residents of Michoacán are working in the government’s reforestation/employment program called Sembrando Vida (Sowing Life). She said the government is investing almost 2.2 billion pesos (US $117.9 million) in the program in Michoacán this year.

María Luisa Albores, director of the Mexican Food Security agency (Segalmex), reported that the government has purchased more than 63,000 tonnes of corn directly from some 2,400 small-scale farmers in Michoacán.

Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena reported that the government is investing 168.2 million pesos (US $9 million) in “sustainable forestry” projects in Michoacán.

Energy Minister Luz Elena González reported that more than 1,200 electricity projects have been completed in Michoacán, increasing electricity coverage to 99.99% of homes in the state. She said that 508 million pesos (US $27.2 million) were invested in the projects.

Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez reported that more than 2.46 million tourists visited Michoacán between January and August. She said tourist numbers increased 10.1% compared to the same period of last year. She said that tourism-related spending injected more than US $186 million into the Michoacán economy between January and August.

Infrastructure, Communications and Transport Minister Jesús Esteva reported that the government is upgrading 411 kilometers of highway in Michoacán. He said that the government and the private sector are investing more than 41 billion pesos (US $2.2 billion) in six highway projects in the state.

Welfare Minister Leticia Ramírez reported that the government is spending more than 30.4 billion pesos (US $1.6 billion) on welfare and social programs in Michoacán in 2026. She said that more than 1 million Michoacán residents benefit from the programs, which include pension schemes, educational scholarships and the distribution of fertilizer to farmers.

Education Minister Mario Delgado reported that over 795,000 students in Michoacán receive government scholarships. He said that primary school, middle school, high school and university students all receive monetary assistance. He said that the scholarships are funded with an investment of 5.7 billion pesos (around US $306 million).

IMSS Bienestar director Alejandro Svarch reported that a new hospital focused on the treatment of addictions had opened in Apatzingán. He also reported that a mental health center had opened in Huetamo. The combined investment in the two projects was 76.1 million pesos (US $3.6 million).

118 billion pesos in investment planned for Plan Michoacán by 2030

Presenting Plan Michoacán on Nov. 9, 2025, Sheinbaum described it as a “comprehensive strategy” and told reporters that it was based on 12 central tenets and included “more than 100 actions.”

Her presentation on Wednesday showed that there are, in fact, more than 2,500 Plan Michoacán “actions,” 1,680 of which have been “completed.” Sheinbaum said that represented progress of 67%.

She also said that 118 billion pesos (US $6.3 billion) is slated to be invested in Plan Michoacán between 2025 and 2030, the final year of her six-year term. That amount is more than double the 57-billion-peso investment that was originally announced.

Sheinbaum said that 72.43 billion pesos has already been spent on the plan. That amount represents 61% of the projected total.

Sheinbaum said that Plan Michoacán involves “very intense work” that is coordinated by the Interior Ministry. She also said that all of the federal government ministries have a “permanent presence” in Michoacán, one of 23 Mexican states governed by the Morena party.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Tourists, traffic and turtles, oh my!
World.content:
Let me be the first to officially welcome you to tourist season in Puerto Vallarta! It’s the time of year when local entertainment ramps up, traffic jams up, and the checkout lines at Costco pile up.

But we may get a little help with traffic this season with the opening of the new Amado Nervo Bridge. It’s not just car traffic, but sea turtle traffic, too. Puerto Vallarta is in the thick of hatching season, when the newborn tortuguitas stumble their way from their nests to the sea by the hundreds, and you can help them on their journey.

And everyone is hoping for a more tranquil winter than last, when, on Feb. 22, members of the Jalisco New Generation cartel blocked traffic and burned cars and OXXO stores in the downtown area. The aftereffects of which have changed perceptions of safety here and abroad.

Read on to learn about how the city is working to restore tourist confidence and attract new visitors, the opening of a new commuter bridge, and sea turtle season.

Vallarta works to restore tourist confidence

Puerto Vallarta is working to revive tourism and attract new visitors amidst a backdrop of increased public perception of insecurity. According to the National Urban Public Safety survey, Vallartenses’ perception of insecurity has more than doubled since last year, rising from 24.7% in September 2025 to 53.6% in September 2026. While significantly up since this time last year, locals’ perception of insecurity has actually decreased since June, when it peaked at 65.4%.

The survey measures public perception of insecurity and doesn’t reflect actual crime rates. Puerto Vallarta remains one of the safer places to travel compared to other tourist destinations, and experiences less theft and violent crime than most U.S. cities of the same size. Also, the U.S. State Department, known for being expeditious about issuing travel warnings, has no current restrictions on travel to Vallarta.

But perception is everything, so the Vallarta tourism industry is working hard to win back traveler confidence and attract new visitors. This fall, representatives from the Puerto Vallarta Tourism Trust toured western states, hosting seminars for high-performing travel advisors in Arizona, Colorado and Utah, and welcomed tourism representatives from the U.S., Canada and other parts of Mexico to Vallarta. They even traveled to Poland, which will have direct weekly flights to Vallarta starting in December.

Despite February’s unrest, Puerto Vallarta remains one of the top destinations for vacationers in the world and is among the Top 10 global destinations for the Thanksgiving holiday, according to a recent survey by Allianz Partners. And if the traffic and Costco lines are any indication, we’ll have a healthy tourist season this year.

Amado Nervo Bridge opening

Here’s hoping a new commuter bridge between Banderas Bay and Puerto Vallarta will ease traffic on the busy Highway 200. The new Amado Nervo Bridge officially opened to cars on Oct. 28th. The bridge is located east of the main tourist corridor, connecting the towns of San Vicente and Ixtapa and surrounding communities, all of which previously had to use the 200 to get from one municipality to the next.

Local transportation officials estimate the bridge will cut as much as 40 minutes from the commute and ease congestion on Highway 200, especially between Mezcales and the Puerto Vallarta airport. The bridge is two kilometers long with three lanes in each direction and a bike lane. It’s a bit out of the way of the normal tourist route, but will hopefully direct more local traffic eastward and make traveling along the 200 smoother.

Turtles take to the sea

Hundreds of thousands of baby sea turtles are making their journey to the sea along Puerto Vallarta’s beaches. November is one of the best months to see them during the height of hatching season.

In Vallarta, a collaborative network of local community groups, grassroots non-profits, university researchers, government agencies, and beachfront resorts runs sea turtle camps along the coast. These camps protect eggs and ensure as many hatchlings as possible reach the sea. When mother turtles come ashore at night to dig nests and lay their eggs, the next morning conservationists remove them and place the eggs into manmade nests at the camps. This helps protect the eggs from predators and poachers. Not all nests are moved; camps only have capacity to protect so many. But still, they manage to save and release more than 150,000 baby turtles each year.

Turtle camps can be found at various spots along the coast of Banderas Bay, including the south end of Varadero beach in front of the Vidanta resort, Playa Holi in front of La Isla Mall, and Boca de Tomates turtle camp north of Bocanegra in the Marina. (Boca de Tomates took a beating with recent storms and could use support to rebuild.)

Camps often invite the public to witness and help with baby turtle releases. There are few things more precious and inspiring in nature than watching a baby sea turtle stumble its way into the surf. Crowds cheer and gasp as the little guys earnestly follow their instincts into the water, only to be washed back onto the sand time and time again until they finally make it out. I highly recommend you try to see a release when you visit.

Debbie Slobe is a writer and communications strategist based in Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco. She blogs at Mexpatmama.com and is a senior program director at Resource Media. Find her on Instagram and Facebook.

World.title: 38th Morelia Music Festival kicks off next week, highlighting artists from Asia
World.content:
The historic city of Morelia, Michoacán, is gearing up to host the 38th edition of the “Miguel Bernal Jiménez” Music Festival, which will take place from Nov. 13 to 22.

Featuring Asia as a guest region, the festival will feature representatives from China, Japan, India, Thailand, South Korea and Indonesia, in addition to the participation of artists and musical groups from 13 countries.

“It’s a must-see show,” head of the event Verónica Bernal told news outlet Crónica in an interview.

The festival will take place in different locations across the city, including cultural and religious landmarks like the Morelia Cultural Center, the Clavijero Cultural Center, the Roses Conservatory, the Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe and more.

The opening concert will feature the National Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Ludwig Carrasco, with violinist Yesong Sophie Lee as soloist. The performance will take place on Nov. 13 at 8 p.m. at the Teatro Morelos, one of the event’s primary venues.

The inaugural program includes music by Tan Dun, winner of an Academy Award and a Grammy for the soundtrack to the 2000 film “Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon”, in addition to the performance of El Chueco, a famous 20th-century ballet composed by the Mexican composer Miguel Bernal Jiménez, whose legacy gives this festival its name.

#musitecamx #ballet #guillermokeysarenas #miguelbernaljimenez #compositormexicano ♬ original sound – Fonoteca Nacional de México @fonotecanacional 𝙀𝙡 𝙘𝙝𝙪𝙚𝙘𝙤 es un ballet que utiliza elementos populares y religiosos para contar la historia de un niño paralítico que le teme al mundo exterior y que, tras soñar que supera sus miedos, despierta para disfrutar las procesiones que desfilan frente a la puerta de su casa. El argumento es del bailarín y coreógrafo Guillermo Keys-Arenas, que encargó la música al compositor Miguel Bernal Jiménez, y la obra se estrenó en el Teatro de Bellas Artes en 1951. Sin embargo, con el tiempo la música se independizó de la puesta en escena y es considerada por algunos la mejor partitura del compositor. Bernal Jiménez falleció el 26 de julio de 1956 pero su legado sigue vivo a través de su música, que la Fonoteca Nacional difunde a través de Musiteca.mx. Encuentra la grabación competa en el link denuestra biografía. Fotografía: Caracterización de el Chueco. Guillermo Keys-Arenas, Heterofonía, núm. 114-115, enero-diciembre de 1996, p. 87. México, INBA, Cenidim #FonotecaNacional

Miguel Bernal Jiménez (1910–1956) was an organist, researcher and teacher, originally from Morelia. He was a prominent figure in 20th-century Mexican sacred music and a pioneer in the research of music from the era of New Spain.

According to Festival Director Bernal, other events will also feature works by the composer.

Among the most anticipated performances is Carnaval Barroco by the French ensemble Le Poème Harmonique, which combines music, theater, dance and acrobatics. The show will be part of the celebrations marking 200 years of diplomatic relations between Mexico and France.

Additionally, violinist Lidia Baich and pianist Donka Angatscheva will commemorate the 125th anniversary of the resumption of diplomatic relations between Mexico and Austria.

Bernal said that nearly half of the activities will be free of charge, with a program that includes masterclasses, children’s performances and the traditional floral carpets of Patamban. Tickets can be purchased at a discount (through Nov. 6) here.

With reports from Excélsior and Mi Morelia

World.content:
PERU · SECURITY

Published Wednesday, 4 November, 10:00 p.m. ET · Source: Peru’s Justice Ministry, prison service INPE and the government’s Unified Command

What happened Peru moved 30 high-danger inmates out of its Trujillo prison on Wednesday, 4 November, days after a riot killed three.

Why The government wants to break the grip of three gangs the ministry ties to extortion.

Not known The full list of prisons that received the 30 men has not been confirmed.

Next The 60-day prison emergency, extended from 5 November, keeps police and soldiers on duty until early January.

Peru has pulled 30 of its most feared prisoners out of a Trujillo jail where three inmates died in a riot on Sunday. Officials say the men are suspected members of three gangs that run extortion rackets, meaning they demand money under threat.

Peru’s Justice Ministry and INPE, the National Penitentiary Institute that runs the country’s prisons, announced the transfer on Wednesday, 4 November. The ministry says it aims to restore order and stop criminal groups operating from inside the jails.

Three Gangs Are Targeted in the Transfer

The transferred men are suspected members of Los Pulpos, La Jauría and Chicago Bulls, according to the Justice Ministry. These groups operate mainly in Trujillo, the capital of the northern region of La Libertad, where, the ministry says, they run extortion and illegal mining.

The operation was run by the Unified Command, the government’s joint security body, with INPE’s special operations group (GOES). Officials also searched prison blocks and seized mobile phones and other banned items that inmates use to coordinate crime.

The full list of prisons that received the 30 men has not been confirmed in the official accounts we reviewed. That matters, because the choice of destination decides how far the gangs’ reach is actually cut.

A Sunday Riot Forced the Government’s Hand

The trigger was a fight between inmates at the El Milagro prison in Trujillo on Sunday, 1 November. Three prisoners died and eight were injured.

President Keiko Fujimori responded on Monday, 2 November, by announcing a reorganisation of inmates across the whole prison system. She said every prisoner would be reclassified by danger, with the worst offenders moved to tougher jails.

Wednesday’s transfer follows that announcement. Extortion, in which gangs demand payments from shops and families under threat of death, is now the top worry for many Peruvians.

This Fits a Wider Crackdown

The riot struck a prison that was already under a state of emergency. Our report on the 60-day extension of the emergency at five prisons notes that the original order dates from early September.

That decree cites 156% overcrowding. The National Police keep order inside, with the armed forces supporting them.

The jails are also a political promise. Fujimori has made prison control the centre of her security policy, and we have reported her plan for two Bukele-style prisons, modelled on the mega-jails of El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele.

What It Means for US Readers

The likeliest winners are Peruvian shops and small firms squeezed by extortion payments, if cutting phone links really weakens the gangs. The likeliest losers are the transferred leaders, who lose their local networks.

US travellers face no direct change, because the emergency covers prison perimeters and a 200-metre (about 650-foot) strip around them, not tourist areas. They should still check the State Department’s Peru advisory before visiting Trujillo, and US firms with northern operations may see extortion risk shift as the gangs adapt.

What Would Confirm or Break the Plan

The emergency runs 60 days from Thursday, 5 November, so it lasts into early January. A new decree would be needed to continue it, and the National Police must report to the Interior Minister within five working days of its end.

Watch for three signals: whether extortion complaints in Trujillo fall, whether violence flares inside or outside prisons in retaliation, and whether the government publishes its full inmate classification list. A second riot before the emergency ends in early January would suggest the gangs still have reach inside the jails, while a drop below the 156% overcrowding level would show the plan is working.

What Is Not Known

It is not known why the Sunday fight started or which groups the dead belonged to. The government has not said how long the 30 men will stay where they were sent, and no figure on extortion cases in Trujillo was found.

For wider context, see our Trujillo city profile and the Peru hub.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Peru move 30 inmates out of Trujillo prison?

The government says the move restores order and stops gangs running crime from inside jail. It followed a riot on Sunday, 1 November, that killed three inmates.

Which gangs are the transferred inmates linked to?

The Justice Ministry links them to Los Pulpos, La Jauría and Chicago Bulls. It says the groups mainly operate in Trujillo.

World.title: Mexican Councilman Shot Dead After Threats
World.content:
Key Facts Who. Gabriel Rivas Ríos, a Cuernavaca councilman for Mexico’s ruling Morena party, was shot dead on 4 November 2026.

Attack. Gunmen on a motorcycle fired at him in his car in Cuernavaca, in Morelos state.

Probe. State prosecutors opened an investigation; the attackers fled and no arrests have been reported.

Time. As of 5 November 2026, 02:00 GMT.

Gabriel Rivas Ríos, a city councilman in Cuernavaca, was shot dead on the afternoon of Wednesday 4 November 2026. Gunmen on a motorcycle opened fire as he sat in a blue compact car in the Ejidos de Acapantzingo neighbourhood.

Cuernavaca, a city about 80 km (50 miles) south of Mexico City, is popular with foreign residents and weekend visitors. The killing also adds to a pattern of attacks on local politicians in Mexico.

Rivas Ríos represented Morena, Mexico’s ruling party, which former president Andrés Manuel López Obrador founded. He was also a longtime social activist, known locally as “the people’s councilman”.

Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What We Know

The shooting took place in front of a business called Miche Lui’s. Armed men on a motorcycle fired several shots at Rivas Ríos while he sat in his car.

He died of his wounds. The state Prosecutor’s Office of Morelos, known in Spanish as the Fiscalía General del Estado de Morelos, opened an investigation.

The attackers fled on the motorcycle. Security forces pursued them to Humboldt Street in downtown Cuernavaca, and no arrests had been reported at the time of publication.

Rivas Ríos had publicly reported death threats before the attack. That precedent is expected to be among the main lines of investigation.

A public complaint about threats gives investigators a written record to examine. This is why his earlier complaints are expected to guide the inquiry.

Morelos Governor Margarita González Saravia called him “my friend and fellow movement member”. She said: “In Morelos there is no room for impunity; we will act so that justice is done.”

She also told the state Peace and Security Construction Board (Mesa de Construcción de Paz y Seguridad) to coordinate its work. The state Prosecutor’s Office continues to lead the criminal investigation.

Archive photo: a street in Tepoztlán, Morelos state.

Who Was Gabriel Rivas Ríos

Rivas Ríos was a founding member of Morena in Morelos. Earlier in his career, he served as a state deputy for the PRD, the Party of the Democratic Revolution, in the 1990s.

He was a frequent critic of the city administration. He criticised it over water service, electricity costs and urban upkeep.

On 30 October, he led a march against a planned real estate project called Altoverde on environmentally sensitive land. We have no information linking that march to the attack.

In Plain English A regidor is an elected member of a Mexican city council. Regidores vote on local policy and keep watch over municipal services. Morena is Mexico’s ruling party at national level. Its name stands for the Movement of National Regeneration. The PRD, or Party of the Democratic Revolution, is an older party that Rivas Ríos once served.

What Is Not Known

The motive is not known. The attackers have not been identified.

It is unclear what protection Rivas Ríos had at the time of the attack. Authorities have not detailed any protection.

It is also unknown whether the threats came from named people. Investigators are expected to examine his earlier complaints closely.

No suspect has been announced, and no arrests had been reported by early Thursday. Any claim about who ordered the shooting would be speculation at this stage.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

Prosecutors in Morelos are investigating, and further facts may emerge in the coming days. Travellers planning a trip to Morelos should check the US State Department’s travel advisory for the state.

Many foreign residents and weekend visitors travel to Cuernavaca from the capital. News of a shooting in a city neighbourhood is worth noting for anyone planning a stay there.

Our earlier Morelos travel safety guide for American visitors explains how to plan a trip to the state. Our recent report on pay for Cuernavaca’s police officers gives more local context.

More coverage of the country is on our Mexico hub. For US investors and residents with ties to Mexico, the case is a reminder of the risks that local politicians face.

Rivas Ríos spent years in public life and local activism. Investigators now face the task of establishing who fired the shots and why.

We will follow the case as prosecutors release information. His family, colleagues and supporters have our condolences.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Gabriel Rivas Ríos?

He was a Cuernavaca city councilman for Morena and a longtime social activist. He was a founding member of Morena in Morelos and earlier a state deputy for the PRD.

What happened in Cuernavaca?

Armed men on a motorcycle shot him as he sat in a blue car in the Ejidos de Acapantzingo neighbourhood on 4 November 2026. He died of his wounds.

Has anyone been arrested?

No arrests had been reported at the time of publication. Security forces chased the attackers to Humboldt Street in downtown Cuernavaca, and the motive is not known.

Should visitors avoid Cuernavaca?

Prosecutors are still investigating, so the picture may change. Check the US State Department’s advisory for Morelos before travelling.

Sources Morelos State Prosecutor’s Office (Fiscalía General del Estado de Morelos); statements by Morelos Governor Margarita González Saravia.

World.title: US Delays Bondholder Seizure of Citgo
World.content:
The US Treasury building in Washington, whose sanctions office listed Gustavo Petro in October 2025 (Photo: G. Edward Johnson, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Published Wednesday, Nov. 4, 9:30 p.m. ET (10:30 p.m. Caracas) · Source: US Treasury Department (OFAC)

Washington has once again bought time for Citgo, Venezuela’s US refining business. On Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, the US Treasury delayed until Dec. 18 the day bondholders could start claiming shares of Citgo, the Houston-based refiner owned by Venezuela’s state oil company.

The move matters because Citgo is the prize in a long fight over Venezuela’s unpaid debts, which our venezuela us tensions guide places inside a wider US-Venezuela relationship. It also comes with a signal: Treasury says it would welcome a negotiated settlement.

Key Facts What happened: The US Treasury pushed to Dec. 18, 2026 the date creditors of Venezuela’s oil company may claim Citgo shares.

Who decided: OFAC, the Treasury office that enforces sanctions, issued General License 5AA, a blanket permit, on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026.

The opening: Treasury signals a favorable licensing policy toward any agreement to restructure or refinance the bond.

What happens next: The shield runs to Friday, Dec. 18, 2026, when OFAC must extend it again or let it lapse.

This story is part of our coverage of the venezuela us tensions. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Colombia Backs Venezuela Gas Pipeline Repair

In plain English Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), the state oil company, owes money on a bond secured by shares of Citgo. Bondholders hold a claim on those shares, but US sanctions block them from enforcing it until Treasury allows it, and Treasury keeps pushing the date back.

Why the Citgo Deadline Moved Again

OFAC, the Office of Foreign Assets Control, runs US sanctions. Its General License 5AA says the authorization for holders of the PDVSA 2020 bond, which pays an 8.5% coupon, now takes effect on Dec. 18, 2026.

Until then, transactions tied to selling or transferring Citgo shares for this bond stay prohibited unless OFAC specifically approves them. It pushes back the date set by General License 5Z, issued on Sept. 16, 2026, which was due to take effect on Nov. 5.

A Pattern Running Since 2018

Executive Order 13835, signed by President Donald Trump on May 21, 2018, requires US persons to get authorization before dealing in equity of companies the Venezuelan government owns. OFAC issued General License 5 on July 19, 2018 to let bondholders reach their collateral.

It replaced that license on Oct. 24, 2019 with a version that delayed the effective date, and has extended the delay several times since. Each extension postponed the moment bondholders could act, never cancelled their claim.

The Quiet Opening for a Deal

OFAC also updated its FAQ 595, the official question-and-answer page on this bond. It says that if parties reach agreement on proposals to restructure or refinance the payments owed to bondholders, additional licensing requirements may apply.

The same text says OFAC would encourage parties to apply for a specific license and would have a favorable licensing policy toward such an agreement. The wording applies only to an agreement between the parties, and they would still need to apply.

What It Means for US Readers

For US investors and funds holding PDVSA debt, the clock now points to mid-December rather than this week. Holders of the bond gain time to negotiate, while anyone hoping for a fast Citgo sale to recover money loses ground.

Citgo keeps operating under its current ownership for now. Watch for another OFAC notice before Dec. 18 and for any application for a specific license, which would reveal that real restructuring talks have started.

What Is Not Known

OFAC has not said what it wants from a restructuring, and no creditor, Venezuelan official or Citgo executive has commented on the new date. We do not know whether talks are under way or who would lead them. OFAC’s notice also does not mention the separate court-supervised sale of Citgo’s parent in Delaware to Amber Energy, an affiliate of the investment firm Elliott.

It is also unclear what Treasury will do when Dec. 18 arrives. OFAC has pushed the date back repeatedly, but nothing in the notice promises another extension.

What did OFAC do on Nov. 4, 2026?

It issued General License 5AA, which delays until Dec. 18, 2026 the authorization for PDVSA 2020 bondholders to enforce their claim on Citgo shares. The earlier date, set by license 5Z, was Nov. 5.

Can the bond be restructured?

OFAC says it would have a favorable licensing policy toward a restructuring or refinancing deal. Parties would need to apply for a specific license.

World.title: Brazil Power Giant Earns US$204M in Third Quarter
World.content:
BRAZIL ENERGY · EARNINGS

Published Wednesday, 4 November, 8:46 p.m. ET · Source: Axia Energia results announcement

Key Facts Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

The number Axia Energia earned R$1.11 billion (about US$204 million) in the third quarter of 2026.

The swing A year earlier it lost R$5.45 billion (about US$1.0 billion) on paper.

The signal Adjusted regulatory EBITDA, an operating profit gauge, rose 8.4% to R$6.9 billion (about US$1.3 billion).

What next Its earnings call is on Thursday 5 November; CEO Ivan Monteiro stays until April 2027.

Axia Energia, the Brazilian power group once called Eletrobras, swung back to profit in the third quarter. Most of the swing comes from last year’s accounting loss, though a regulatory operating measure rose too, and the result fell short of analyst forecasts.

Brazil’s largest power group went from a deep hole to a clear profit in a single year. Axia Energia reported net income of R$1.11 billion (about US$204 million) for July to September 2026, in results released after the São Paulo market closed on Wednesday 4 November.

A year earlier the company, the formerly state-controlled Eletrobras before its rebranding, booked a loss of R$5.45 billion (about US$1.0 billion). Power bills touch every corner of Brazil’s economy, so the health of the biggest generator matters well beyond its shareholders.

WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Why a Loss Became a Profit

Last year’s loss was an accounting result more than a collapse in earning power. In the third quarter of 2025 Axia lost R$5.45 billion but still earned an adjusted R$2.17 billion (about US$397 million), a measure that strips out one-off items.

One of those items was an update to what the company owes Brazilian transmission firms, which cut profit by R$303 million (about US$55 million). The full list of one-off items for the latest quarter was not available to us at the time of writing.

All conversions in this article use about 5.46 reais per US dollar, the market rate on 4 November. Reported net income also eased from R$1.19 billion (about US$218 million) in the second quarter.

Is the Business Getting Stronger?

The picture is mixed. EBITDA, short for earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, is a rough gauge of operating cash profit, and the company’s adjusted regulatory version rose 8.4% to R$6.9 billion (about US$1.3 billion).

Net revenue came to about R$10 billion (about US$1.8 billion), less than 1% above last year. Profit rose mainly because last year’s accounting loss was not repeated, not because the company sold much more power.

Other measures were weaker. Adjusted profit, which strips out one-off items, was R$1.76 billion (about US$322 million), down 19.1% from R$2.17 billion a year earlier but up from R$1.61 billion (about US$295 million) in the second quarter.

On the company’s international accounting basis, adjusted EBITDA fell 23% to R$4.53 billion (about US$830 million). Net debt stood at R$47.57 billion (about US$8.7 billion), or 2.0 times regulatory EBITDA.

Over the first half of 2026 the company earned R$3.8 billion (about US$700 million). Adding this quarter, our own arithmetic puts the nine-month total near R$4.9 billion (about US$900 million).

Our report on the first quarter shows how the year began.

What It Means for US Readers

Investors who judge Axia by operating profit come out ahead, since that regulatory measure improved. Those who read the headline as new growth lose out, because the profit swing mostly reflects a weak comparison year and revenue barely moved.

Axia shares trade on São Paulo’s B3 exchange under the ticker AXIA3. They rose roughly 2% on Wednesday, before the results came out, so the market has yet to price them.

Interest rates remain the backdrop for any Brazilian utility. Our Selic guide explains the benchmark rate set by Copom, the central bank’s rate committee, and the next date to watch is the release of the minutes of its latest meeting on Tuesday 10 November at 6:00 a.m. ET.

What Is Not Known

Analysts polled by LSEG, a financial data firm, expected net income of R$1.5 billion (about US$275 million) and EBITDA near R$7 billion (about US$1.3 billion), so the result fell short. We have not seen Axia’s full list of one-off items for the quarter, and the market’s verdict will show in Thursday’s trading.

The company holds its results call on Thursday 5 November. Chief executive Ivan Monteiro, a former head of the oil company Petrobras, stays until April 2027 while a succession process runs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Axia Energia make a profit in the third quarter of 2026?

Yes. It reported net income of R$1.11 billion (about US$204 million) for July to September, against a loss of R$5.45 billion (about US$1.0 billion) a year earlier.

How did Axia’s operations perform?

Adjusted regulatory EBITDA, an operating profit gauge, rose 8.4% to R$6.9 billion (about US$1.3 billion). Net revenue was about R$10 billion (about US$1.8 billion), little changed from last year.

Sources: Axia Energia, results centre and third-quarter 2026 announcement (4 November 2026); Axia Energia, third-quarter 2025 results announcement; Axia Energia, material fact on the CEO succession process (May 2026); market data for the exchange rate.

BOTSWANA · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Botswana, in southern Africa, is among the world’s biggest diamond producers by value.

The forecast Government now expects the economy to grow 3.8% in 2026, up from 3.1%.

The reason Stronger diamond output in the first half of 2026 drove the upgrade.

The US link Botswana’s minerals minister says US natural diamond sales are up 5% to 6% this year.

Botswana has raised its 2026 growth forecast to 3.8% from 3.1%, because its diamond mines are producing more after a two-year slump. Minerals and Energy Minister Bogolo Kenewendo said this week that US demand for natural diamonds is turning up again.

For US readers, the upgrade matters because the United States is the biggest market for natural diamonds, so American shoppers help decide how rich Botswana is. Our overview of who runs Botswana’s economy explains how closely the state and the diamond trade are tied.

What Happened

The Ministry of Finance has lifted its growth forecast for 2026 from 3.1% to 3.8%. The main reason is stronger diamond production in the first half of the year.

Kenewendo described a recovery in the mining sector after about two years of decline. She said sales of natural diamonds in the United States have grown about 5% to 6% this year, with double-digit growth in July.

She contrasted that with the two years before, when growth was about negative 3.3%. She called herself cautiously optimistic about the industry.

Why Diamonds Drive the Economy

Diamonds are the backbone of Botswana’s exports and government income. Most of the stones come from Debswana, a joint venture between the government and De Beers, the world’s best-known diamond company.

When demand falls, mines cut output and the government has less money to spend. When demand recovers, the effect runs through jobs, tax receipts and the currency, which is why one sector can move the whole growth figure.

The Risks Still Facing Natural Diamonds

Competition from lab-grown stones, uncertainty in the global economy and US tariff pressure remain headwinds for natural diamonds. Kenewendo said producers, including Botswana and De Beers, are working on marketing to win back buyers.

She added that interest in natural diamonds is improving in India and the Far East as well. That would reduce Botswana’s reliance on one buyer if it holds.

The government has also set up a new state exploration company. It is to search for minerals beyond diamonds, including critical minerals, the metals used in batteries and electronics.

What Else the Central Bank Did

The Bank of Botswana, the country’s central bank, kept its main interest rate at 5.5% on Thursday 29 October 2026. We covered that decision in our report on why Botswana held its rate.

A steady rate and a faster-growing economy can sit together, but borrowers will feel the higher rate set earlier this year. Our earlier report on Debswana’s output plans shows how the mines expect to supply the market.

What It Means for You

If you buy natural diamonds or hold shares in companies tied to them, a firmer US market is good news for the supply chain. It does not guarantee higher prices, because lab-grown stones keep pressing on the low end.

Investors in Botswana’s debt get a stronger growth story, although the full breakdown of the forecast is not yet public. Travellers and safari visitors need not change plans, since the news concerns the mines and the budget rather than tourism.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how much of the 3.8% comes from mining and how much from other sectors. The government has not said whether the July jump in US sales has continued since.

The forecast also depends on tariffs and on the pace of lab-grown competition, which remain risks for natural stones. A full breakdown of the revised forecast is still to come.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is Botswana’s New Growth Forecast for 2026?

The government now expects the economy to grow 3.8% in 2026, up from 3.1%. The Ministry of Finance cites stronger diamond production in the first half.

Why Do Diamonds Matter So Much to Botswana?

Diamonds are the main source of the country’s exports and state income. When global demand recovers, mines produce more and the whole economy benefits.

Are US Diamond Sales Recovering?

The Minerals and Energy Minister said US natural diamond sales are up about 5% to 6% this year, with double-digit growth in July. She called herself only cautiously optimistic.

What Are the Main Risks for Botswana’s Diamond Industry?

Lab-grown diamonds, global economic uncertainty and US tariff pressure remain headwinds. Producers are using marketing campaigns to defend demand for natural stones.

NAMIBIA · ENERGY

Key Facts The company Dangote Industries, led by Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote, runs Africa’s biggest refinery.

What happened Dangote began building a fuel hub near Walvis Bay, Namibia’s main port, on Wednesday 4 November 2026.

The price tag The project, including a regional pipeline, is put at about US$2.5 billion.

The size The tanks would hold about 600 million litres, eight times Namibia’s state fuel store.

The clock Dangote says the work will take 18 to 20 months.

Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote began building a fuel storage hub at Walvis Bay, Namibia’s main port, on Wednesday 4 November 2026. The project is put at about US$2.5 billion and includes a planned pipeline of about 1,700 kilometres (1,050 miles) to bring fuel to landlocked countries.

For US readers, the move shows how Africa’s biggest refinery now wants to control fuel supply far beyond Nigeria. It also puts a new fuel route on the south-west coast of Africa, where shipping and oil are of growing interest to investors.

What Happened at Walvis Bay

Dangote Industries, the group led by Aliko Dangote, launched the project at a ceremony outside Walvis Bay on Wednesday, with Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah present. The site lies in Erongo, the desert coastal region around the port.

The tanks will hold diesel and petrol for sale across southern Africa. Dangote said he wants to invest heavily in the region.

Separately, Dangote raised his target for investment in African industry from US$50 billion to US$60 billion by 2030. The new target is 20% above the old one.

What Will Be Built

The tank farm would hold about 600 million litres of fuel, of which 360 million litres would be diesel and the rest petrol. That is about eight times the 75 million litres held by the National Oil Storage Facility, run by Namcor, Namibia’s state oil company.

A pipeline of about 1,700 kilometres is planned to carry fuel inland towards Botswana and South Africa, and possibly to other countries. The company has also described a wider network with links to Zimbabwe, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo, but the route and the building schedule for the pipeline have not been fixed.

Dangote told reporters that the project should be finished in 18 to 20 months. Another account says it will take 18 months at most.

Why Landlocked Countries Matter

Botswana, Zambia and Zimbabwe have no coast, so their fuel arrives by road or rail over long distances. Dangote said he wants to invest heavily so that most landlocked countries can buy petroleum products at a cheaper price.

A large store at Walvis Bay would let tankers unload in bulk and let trucks or a pipeline carry the fuel inland. The same logic lies behind Dangote’s refinery in Nigeria, which is reported to process about 650,000 to 700,000 barrels of crude a day.

What It Means for You

Investors in US-listed funds with African exposure should see this as a sign of how fast Dangote’s group is expanding, not as a finished business. Our report on the Dangote refinery share offer explains how the parent refinery is being financed.

Energy and shipping firms should watch whether the pipeline gets a final route. That route decides which countries gain cheaper fuel.

What Is Not Known

It is not known when the pipeline will be built or who will pay for it beyond the Dangote group. Reports differ on the pipeline length and on the countries it will reach, and on the storage volume in barrels.

It is not known how much cheaper fuel will become at the pump. Namcor’s future role and the effect on its own storage business are also unclear.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Did Dangote Launch in Namibia?

Dangote Industries began building a fuel storage hub at Walvis Bay on Wednesday 4 November 2026. The project, with a planned pipeline, is put at about US$2.5 billion.

How Big Is the Fuel Hub?

The tanks would hold about 600 million litres, including 360 million litres of diesel. That is eight times the capacity of Namibia’s 75 million-litre state fuel store.

When Will the Hub Be Ready?

Dangote told reporters the project should take 18 to 20 months. The pipeline has no fixed schedule yet.

Which Countries Could Get Fuel by Pipeline?

A pipeline of about 1,700 kilometres is planned towards Botswana and South Africa, and possibly further. The final route has not been published.

01 The session in one read

Grain markets spent Wednesday, 4 November 2026, in two moods. Soybeans sank for a third day in a row, while corn and wheat made small gains.

The split matters because soybeans are the crop most exposed to Brazil and China, the two poles of world trade. Corn and wheat were mostly catching their breath after long slides.

Corn and wheat bounces look like pauses after steep falls rather than turns. The variable to watch is how fast Brazilian planting and Chinese buying progress through November.

03 Why it moved

The first and heaviest cause is Brazilian supply. Conab forecasts 181.6 million tonnes of soybeans from 49.3 million hectares, with area up 1.4%, and exports of about 118 million tonnes. Confidence: medium-high.

The second cause is China, the world’s biggest soybean buyer, which leans heavily on Brazilian beans. Its buying pace is the swing factor for prices. Confidence: medium.

The usual drivers were mixed. The dollar index eased 0.37% to 101.49, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell 5 basis points to 4.90%, which normally supports commodities. Oil’s fund USO fell 8.07% and the S&P 500 rose 1.58%, so broad markets were not fleeing risk. That suggests grain-specific supply, not macro stress, drove soybeans. Confidence: medium.

04 The trend behind it

Soybeans peaked on 10 September and have since lost 9.1% from that high. They are still 17.8% above the 12-month low reached on 13 January, so this is a pullback inside a higher range rather than a collapse.

Corn is 14.2% below its 1 September high and 5.6% above its 29 June low. Wheat is 21.5% below its 28 August high, the sharpest retreat of the three; the year-ago low in the data is a distortion of the fund’s history, so ignore the 428.6% figure.

Our own history adds perspective. After earlier falls as large as soybeans’ recent one, the fund was higher 20 sessions later in 16 of 29 cases, a median gain of 0.6% and a worst loss of 7.8%. For corn it was higher in 13 of 30 cases, median loss 0.7%; for wheat 7 of 20, median loss 1.8%. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil gains in volume but not necessarily in price. A larger crop and exports of about 118 million tonnes help farmers, traders and ports, yet softer prices squeeze margins for growers who buy fertiliser and machinery in dollars.

Argentina, the other great exporter, faces the same pressure from lower prices, though we could not verify fresh Argentine crop data. Importers such as Mexico and Chile, which buy corn and wheat, benefit from cheaper feed and flour.

06 The names to watch

SOYB, CORN and WEAT are exchange-traded funds that track soybean, corn and wheat futures, so they are proxies and not the crops’ own prices. Soybeans are the one to follow for Brazil and China.

Corn matters for livestock feed and ethanol, and wheat for bread prices. Wheat has the biggest drawdown, so any rebound there would be the clearest sign of bargain-hunting.

07 What would end it

For soybeans, the nearest support is the 21.71 low from 13 January, while resistance sits at the 28.14 high from 10 September. Corn’s markers are 16.47 and 20.29, and wheat’s is the 28.00 high.

Weather problems in Brazil’s planting, a surge in Chinese buying of American beans or a US-China tariff change would turn the picture. Without them, the drift lower is more likely to continue than reverse, though the base rates show it is close to a coin toss.

08 What to watch

Brazil planting: Pace of sowing in Mato Grosso and other states, since delays would tighten supply.

Pace of sowing in Mato Grosso and other states, since delays would tighten supply. China purchases: Whether Beijing keeps booking Brazilian beans or returns to US cargoes.

Whether Beijing keeps booking Brazilian beans or returns to US cargoes. US-China trade: Any change in China’s tariffs on American soybeans.

Any change in China’s tariffs on American soybeans. Support levels: Soybeans at 21.71, corn at 16.47, and wheat’s retreat from 28.00.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did soybeans fall?

Large Brazilian supply forecasts and China’s early buying of Brazilian beans weighed on prices, while the dollar and yields offered little pressure.

Do these funds show spot prices?

No. SOYB, CORN and WEAT track futures and are proxies for the crops.

Who benefits from cheaper grain?

Importers and livestock feeders benefit, while exporters and farmers face thinner margins.

Will prices keep falling?

Our history shows roughly even odds after similar falls, so it is not a reliable forecast.

World.title: Oil Fund Falls 8.07% as Petrobras Slides 6.97% | Oil, Nov 4
World.content:
Refinery towers beyond a lake in Barrancabermeja, an oil city in Colombia. The photo is a file picture and does not show any event linked to the bill. Photo: yesid ferney patiño / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0)

Key Facts Oil dropped sharply: the US crude fund USO, which tracks WTI, the US oil benchmark, fell -8.07% to US$145.41 on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, as traders bet on an end to the Iran war.

the US crude fund USO, which tracks WTI, the US oil benchmark, fell -8.07% to US$145.41 on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, as traders bet on an end to the Iran war. The cause was political: Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for the Republican losses, and markets read that as pressure to settle.

Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for the Republican losses, and markets read that as pressure to settle. Still far from calm: USO sits 14.2% below its 23 October peak of 169.53, yet 119.8% above its December 2025 low of 66.17.

USO sits 14.2% below its 23 October peak of 169.53, yet 119.8% above its December 2025 low of 66.17. Petrobras took the biggest hit: its New York shares fell -6.97% to US$19.61, a third straight loss and 25.0% below the 23 October high.

its New York shares fell -6.97% to US$19.61, a third straight loss and 25.0% below the 23 October high. Argentina and Colombia followed: YPF fell -7.14% and Ecopetrol -3.75%, Ecopetrol’s lowest close in at least three months.

YPF fell -7.14% and Ecopetrol -3.75%, Ecopetrol’s lowest close in at least three months. Wider markets cheered: the S&P 500 rose 1.58% and the VIX fear gauge fell 20.26%, so this was a rotation out of oil, not a panic.

the S&P 500 rose 1.58% and the VIX fear gauge fell 20.26%, so this was a rotation out of oil, not a panic. Prediction markets: Polymarket puts a 79.5% chance on WTI crude touching US$85 a barrel in November and 58.0% on US$95 (US$1.13 million traded, 7:42 p.m. ET, 4 November).

Today’s Focus Oil had a bad Wednesday, and the reason was politics rather than barrels. After Tuesday’s US midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for his party’s losses, and traders concluded Washington now wants the conflict over. The fund that tracks US crude, USO, fell -8.07%, and Brent, the international benchmark, fell sharply too. Latin America’s oil companies felt it at once: Petrobras, YPF and Ecopetrol all closed lower. Their fall is a reminder that these firms earn more when crude is dear, and that a war premium once priced in must now be taken out. A cheaper-oil world helps importers and drivers, but it squeezes the budgets and share prices of Brazil, Argentina, Colombia and Mexico, which sell crude.

01 The session in one read

Oil fell on a political signal, not a supply glut. Tuesday’s midterms went badly for the White House, and Vice President Vance pointed at the Iran war as the cause.

Traders heard a message: Washington has a reason to end the fighting. They sold crude on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, and the oil-tracking USO fund closed down -8.07% at US$145.41.

Assessment — War premium deflating, not a collapse MEDIUM The weight of evidence says traders are removing the risk premium that the Iran conflict added to oil, not rejecting the whole price structure. The fund remains 119.8% above its December 2025 low, so a large cushion of war-driven gains is still there to be lost; the variable to watch is whether Washington and Tehran turn the market’s hope of a settlement into an actual agreement.

02 The board

The sell-off was sharpest where oil matters most. Petrobras closed at US$19.61, down -6.97%, YPF at US$41.61, down -7.14%, and Ecopetrol at US$15.92, down -3.75%.

The shares fell more than the fund, which is typical: producers’ profits move harder than the oil price because their costs stay fixed.
