03 Why it moved

Cause one, and the heaviest: peace hopes after the midterms. Brent was already easing as traders priced a US-Iran settlement, and the political signal from the midterms turned a drift into a rout. Confidence: medium-high.

Cause two: fewer fears about the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which a large share of the world’s oil ships. Peace hopes lower the odds of any disruption there. Confidence: medium.

Some signals pointed the other way. US commercial crude stocks fell to 409.8 million barrels in the week to 30 October and distillate stocks fell 3.6 million to 99.3 million, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), the government’s statistics arm. Neither stopped the slide, which shows how dominant the Iran story is.

The usual cross-asset drivers agree with a risk-on day rather than an oil-specific shock. The dollar index eased 0.37% to 101.49, the 10-year US Treasury yield fell 5 basis points to 4.90%, and the S&P 500 rose 1.58% to 7,689. Gold’s fund GLD gained 3.68% to US$372.49, so investors still bought protection while selling oil.

04 The trend behind it

Oil is still in a long uptrend with a sharp recent reversal. USO is up 13.9% over 60 sessions and 1.04% over 20, but down 12.70% over five sessions and 14.2% below its 23 October peak of 169.53.

Petrobras is the clearest casualty: down 18.26% over 20 sessions and 25.0% below its 23 October high of 26.16, with three losing days in a row. It remains 69.9% above its January low of 11.54, so this is a retreat inside a large rally.

Our read is a new phase: the market has moved from pricing escalation to pricing resolution.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil is the most exposed. Petrobras is Brazil’s state-controlled oil giant, so lower prices cut into the cash that funds dividends and the state’s take.

Argentina’s YPF is the other big loser on the day. Vaca Muerta, the shale formation in Patagonia, is the country’s growth engine, and cheaper oil makes new investment harder to attract.

Colombia’s Ecopetrol closed at its lowest in at least three months and is 12.8% below its 15 September high of 18.26. Mexico’s Pemex, a state company, gains nothing from the fall, since lower prices cut government revenue.

Producers such as Guyana and Venezuela are weaker bets at lower prices. For travellers and importers, cheaper fuel is the one clear winner.

06 The names to watch

Petrobras is the first to watch. In our own price history since 2007, 42 earlier cases fell as far over 20 sessions, and in 25 of them (60%) the shares were higher 20 sessions later, with a median gain of 2.8%. The worst case was a further 50.5% loss, and history is not a forecast.

Ecopetrol offers a coin-flip by comparison. Across 115 earlier similar falls since 2008, it was higher 20 sessions later in 58 cases (50%), with a median of 0.2%.

YPF has no comparable record here, and trades as the highest-beta name in the group.

07 What would end it

The fall stops if peace talks stall. Any renewed attack, or a breakdown in US-Iran contacts, would bring the war premium straight back.

On the chart, watch 150 for USO as the first resistance and 169.53, the 23 October peak, as the ceiling. Support is the round 140 level, then the 12-month low of 66.17, which is far away. For Petrobras, 26.16 is the ceiling and 11.54 the floor.

The next dated check is the weekly US stockpile report from the Energy Information Administration, due Wednesday, November 11, 2026. The honest answer to whether this stops is that it stops when the war ends or flares again.

08 What to watch

US-Iran talks: Any announcement on a settlement, or its collapse, is the single biggest swing factor for oil.

Any announcement on a settlement, or its collapse, is the single biggest swing factor for oil. USO at 150 and 140: A rebound through 150 would show the sell-off was overdone; a break below 140 would signal deeper unwinding.

A rebound through 150 would show the sell-off was overdone; a break below 140 would signal deeper unwinding. Petrobras dividends: Lower oil prices test the payouts that make the shares attractive to foreign investors.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a prediction market where users bet real money, shows a 79.5% chance that WTI crude oil dips to US$85 a barrel at some point in November, 50.5% for US$80, 58.0% for a spike to US$95 and 34.5% for US$100, with about US$1.13 million traded. Prices were read at 7:42 p.m. ET on 4 November 2026. These are bets, not forecasts.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did oil fall on Wednesday, November 4, 2026?

Traders bet the Iran war is heading towards a settlement after the White House tied Tuesday’s midterm losses to the conflict.

Does a lower oil price help Latin America?

Importers and consumers gain, but exporters such as Brazil, Argentina, Colombia and Mexico lose revenue and share value.

Is USO the price of oil?

No. USO is a fund that tracks US crude futures, so its price differs from the barrel price.

Will the fall continue?

It depends on the Iran talks; history shows Petrobras rose in 60% of similar cases, but that is not a forecast.

World.title: Call Center Cuts Costa Rica Job Pledge Over Asian Competition
World.content:
A US-owned customer service company operating under Costa Rica’s free trade zone program has cut its minimum employment commitment by more than half. It told the government it can no longer compete on cost with call centers in India and the Philippines. TTEC Customer Management Costa Rica, which began operating here in 2007 as Teletech Customer Care Management, received approval from the Ministry of Foreign Trade (Comex) to lower its required workforce from 111 employees to 45.The original commitment dates from executive agreement 067-2007.

In its request, the company said it faces growing competitive pressure in international markets, chiefly from firms in India and the Philippines. It said operating costs and salary structures there are far lower than in Costa Rica. The company described that gap as a significant structural disadvantage. It said the disadvantage had weakened its ability to keep international contracts and attract new clients.

TTEC carried out a partial reduction of its staff before seeking the change. It has not disclosed how many people it currently employs in the country. Companies in the free trade zone regime receive tax and customs incentives in exchange for minimum investment and employment commitments. Those commitments are written into executive agreements and can be modified at the company’s request.

TTEC is far from the only company to ask for that change. Executive agreements published in La Gaceta show that at least 38 free zone companies have lowered their employment targets since 2023. Their combined commitments fell from about 38,450 jobs to about 19,864. The largest adjustment came from Amazon, which halved its commitment from 16,450 positions to 8,225 in January. Align Technology lowered its minimum from 4,992 to 2,500 under an agreement published in May. Align said artificial intelligence and automation had raised output per worker.

Service firms make up most of the companies that have reduced their targets. They include IT consultancies, technical support providers, back-office centers, call centers and data processors. The reasons the companies gave vary. Several, like TTEC, pointed to lower labor costs in Asia. Others cited automation and artificial intelligence, or a shortage of specialized talent.

A smaller group blamed the strong colón, which raises costs for companies that earn in dollars but pay salaries and local bills in colones. One of them, Sistemas Globales, estimated that its operating costs had risen by 23.6%. TTEC did not cite the exchange rate in its request. The pullback is now showing up in the overall numbers. Direct employment in free zone companies fell from 197,101 to 195,410 jobs through August, a 0.9% drop, according to Central Bank data published in its monetary policy report.

Central Bank president Róger Madrigal attributed the decline mainly to fewer jobs in administrative support, professional and technical services, and information and communications. A lower commitment does not always translate into an equal number of layoffs. Some companies are revising targets set at peak hiring rather than cutting existing staff, as Align said in its request.

Even so, the trend points to mounting pressure on service jobs in a regime that directly employs nearly 200,000 people. Those jobs have been among the steadiest sources of formal private-sector employment.

World.title: El Niño Leaves Gulf of Nicoya Fishermen With Catches Too Small to Pay for Fuel
World.content:
Fishermen in the Gulf of Nicoya say the unusually warm water El Niño has pushed against Costa Rica’s Pacific coast has left their nets close to empty, with many boats now returning from a day at sea with less fish than it takes to pay for the fuel. Giselle Campos, who fishes and gathers shellfish in Costa de Pájaros, Puntarenas, said her family now spends five hours on the water and may come back with two fish and 300 grams (about 10 ounces) of shrimp.

The same trips used to bring in 10 to 40 kilograms (22 to 88 pounds) of shrimp and 70 to 100 kilograms (155 to 220 pounds) of fish, she said. Accounts from Costa de Pájaros, Isla Venado and neighboring communities describe sharp drops in shrimp, snapper, snook and corvina, the catches that have long sustained small-scale fishing in the gulf.

They come less than two weeks after the National Emergency Commission (CNE) placed the waters off the entire Pacific coast under a red alert for El Niño, the first time the agency has extended an emergency alert to the sea. CNE President Alejandro Picado said at the time that the maritime alert was a response to the damage warming seas were doing to fishing and to the families who depend on it.

The alert zone covers 12 nautical miles, about 22 kilometers (14 miles), from the shoreline of Guanacaste and Puntarenas, including the gulfs of Nicoya and Papagayo. Picado said no end date had been set. According to the CNE, sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific have run above normal for the past five months, reaching the highest values recorded since 1950. Along Costa Rica’s Pacific coast, readings are 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal, the commission said.

Andrés Beita Jiménez, a marine biologist and science coordinator at the MarViva Foundation in Costa Rica, explained that in a normal year, winds crossing from the Caribbean through low-lying areas such as Guanacaste push the Pacific’s surface water offshore. That movement draws cold, nutrient-rich water up from the depths toward the coast, where sunlight turns those nutrients into plankton that feed the rest of the food chain.

El Niño weakens those winds, Beita said. Warm surface water stays put, more warm water flows in from across the Pacific, oxygen levels drop and the nutrient-rich upwelling stalls. He described the current event as one of the strongest on record, with warming reaching deeper layers of the ocean as well as the surface.

Beita stressed that the fish have not died off. Species that can move are heading to deeper or cooler water where they are not normally found, he said, which forces fishermen to travel farther and fish deeper to reach them. Less mobile life such as mollusks and corals cannot escape the heat and may suffer stress or bleaching.

That extra distance is where the numbers stop working. Ezequiel Álvarez, a 64-year-old fisherman in Costa de Pájaros who was born on Isla Caballo, said a catch of around seven kilograms (15 pounds) now barely covers the gasoline for boats that burn 15 to 19 liters (four to five gallons) per trip in two-stroke engines. He described the last 10 months as very hard.

Álvarez still goes out, but only on the most favorable tides, and he can afford to because he also uses his boat for tours of the gulf. Many of his neighbors have no such cushion, he said.

On Isla Venado, Yolanda Bolívar, 54, estimated that fewer than 30% of the island’s fishermen are still working. Catches have been falling for three years, she said, but the gulf used to recover somewhat after each seasonal fishing ban, which this year ran from May 1 to July 31. This time it did not.

Fishermen now risk spending fuel for two or three days, or even a week, and coming home with nothing, Bolívar said, so many have stopped going out. Sardines are what keep some families going, sold as bait to boats chasing mahi-mahi farther offshore. Others on the island have moved into tourism and transport, ferrying visitors between islands, building cabins or, as her own family has done, selling meals and produce from a home garden to neighbors and visiting tourists.

Campos said younger people from Costa de Pájaros, Manzanillo, Chomes and Punta Morales have found work on the Barranca–Limonal highway widening, but she worries about what they will do once the project ends in an area with few jobs. Older fishermen have little choice but to keep going out with hand lines and nets.

She said the monthly assistance payment from the social welfare agency IMAS, 145,000 colones (about $320), does not stretch far for households of seven or eight people. El Niño has struck a fishery that was already under heavy strain. Campos also blamed overfishing and illegal fishing for the losses.

A 2022 marine and coastal atlas of the Gulf of Nicoya produced by MarViva found that fishermen were already reporting declines from overfishing and from some species moving to cooler water. It also documented illegal gear such as explosives, shrimp drags, purse seines and undersized mesh, along with pollution carried into the gulf by the Tárcoles and Tempisque rivers.

How deep this year’s drop runs is still unmeasured. The Costa Rican Institute of Fisheries and Aquaculture (Incopesca) has published national catch statistics only through 2024 and has said its 2025 and 2026 figures are still being processed. The institute has not yet detailed any assistance plan for fishermen affected by El Niño.

Relief is unlikely to come quickly. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) has said conditions typical of a very strong El Niño could continue through the November-to-January period, part of an event forecasters have long expected to stretch into early 2027.

World.title: Corcovado’s Sirena Station Is Back to 366 Visitors a Day. Who Decided?
World.content:
Corcovado National Park has spent the past five months caught in a tug of war that has left many in the Osa Peninsula’s conservation community asking the same question: who is actually deciding how many people the park can handle?

The dispute centers on the Sirena Biological Station, the heart of Corcovado and its most visited sector. Technical reports compiled in June concluded that the station’s wastewater treatment plant had been discharging sewage since at least 2024 into the Camaronal creek, a tributary of the Sirena River, inside a protected area created in 1975.

The problem was not new to authorities. The Health Ministry had ordered a remedial plan as early as 2024, with a deadline of Dec. 31, 2025. A ministry inspection in October 2025 found wastewater discharges into the creek and no operating records or quality controls at the plant, and a follow-up inspection in March 2026 found the orders still unmet.

In late June, the acting director of the Osa Conservation Area, Juan José Jiménez Espinoza, cut Sirena’s daily limit to 150 visitors through September, 100 on day visits and 50 staying overnight. His resolution kept the same cap for November and December but limited it to day visits until overnight stays could be cleared.

Jiménez cited not only the sewage problem but an August 2025 Constitutional Chamber ruling that struck down a 2023 increase in park visitation because it had no technical or scientific justification. The court had given the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC) one month to issue new rules that clearly set out how visitor limits are calculated.

That deadline had long passed. The reaction in the southern zone was swift. Tourism groups, guides and transport operators protested the cut, arguing it lacked a technical basis and was hurting families who depend on the park.

On July 1, the same day residents and tourism business owners blocked roads in Uvita demanding more capacity and Jiménez’s removal, Environment Minister Mónica Navarro transferred him to head a department at SINAC’s national headquarters. Navarro acknowledged the move came after the capacity cut but said his services were more useful in another area of the ministry and that the decision responded to institutional needs.

On July 8, his replacement, Ólger Méndez Fallas, raised the limit to 225 visitors a day, even though the new resolution itself acknowledged that the treatment plant was still out of service. That decision rested on a report from the national water utility, AyA, stating that separate sanitary systems at the station continued to function for certain uses, and on a block of restrooms at the station entrance that operates independently of the plant.

Then, in a resolution that took effect Sept. 17, SINAC raised the limit again, to 366 people a day. The total breaks down into 230 day visitors, 105 overnight guests, 16 places for the Carate-Corcovado community development association that holds the use permit at the station and 15 for park administration.

That is 63 percent above the July figure and more than three times the 100 visitors a day long considered Sirena’s technical limit. SINAC describes the figure as a restoration of the station’s capacity rather than an increase. The Environment Ministry says the change followed compliance with the Health Ministry’s orders and the rehabilitation of the treatment plant, carried out with local communities and volunteer groups who contributed labor, logistics and money.

Yet the September resolution did not make clear whether the plant was operating. Instead, it framed the decision as a way to guarantee the continuity of socioeconomic activities that depend directly on the park. The same document disclosed that the Osa Conservation Area had asked the Constitutional Chamber for an extension to comply with the August 2025 ruling, more than a year after the court issued it.

That sequence is what conservationists find hard to square. The official who acted on a court order and a documented pollution problem was moved out. Capacity was then raised twice, to more than triple the station’s historical limit, while the agency asked the court for more time on the very ruling that requires a scientific basis for those numbers.

Some in the conservation community believe the real beneficiaries are small cruise ships. Their concern is how the tickets get used. Park entry must be reserved in advance, and critics on the peninsula say cruise operators can buy large blocks of the expanded capacity for passengers who arrive by tender, spend a few hours in the park and return to the ship for the night.

When those blocks are gone, they argue, independent travelers who book a lodge in Drake Bay or Puerto Jiménez, hire a local guide and boat captain and eat in local restaurants find fewer places left. In that view, a higher limit does not necessarily bring more money to Osa communities, and could bring less.

There is a precedent behind the suspicion. The legal challenge that led to the 2025 ruling, filed by then-lawmaker Ariel Robles, argued that the 2023 increase included 100 daily places at the San Pedrillo station for the exclusive use of cruise ships. Guides and residents have also complained that boat access has turned many Corcovado visits into same-day trips, which they say leaves less money in towns such as Puerto Jiménez.

Day visitors now take 230 of Sirena’s 366 places, and the increase arrives just before high season, when small expedition ships call along the Osa coast. SINAC has not said cruise traffic played any role in the September decision, and the published breakdown for Sirena includes no separate cruise allotment.

Supporters of higher limits make an argument that carries real weight on the peninsula. Corcovado anchors the economies of Puerto Jiménez, Drake Bay, Sierpe and surrounding communities, and a sudden cut during the busy months hits guides, boat operators and small lodges that have few alternatives.

Critics counter that visitor numbers at Sirena have been building for years while other stations such as Los Patos, La Leona and El Tigre went without investment, and that the infrastructure never kept pace. In June, SINAC asked the Rural Development Institute (Inder) for about 2.63 billion colones (roughly $5.8 million) to overhaul the station and set aside 50 million colones (about $110,000) for immediate work.

Sirena, El Tigre and Los Patos closed to tourists during October for regular maintenance and the heaviest rains. When it cut capacity in June, the Environment Ministry set Dec. 1 as its target for Sirena to run normally with a working treatment plant. With high season about to begin, the central question remains open: whether 366 visitors a day is a figure backed by science or by pressure. For now, the answer rests with the Constitutional Chamber.

World.title: El Refugio Costa Ballena: Making a Difference for Animals and the Community
World.content:
From rescuing animals in need to providing affordable spay/neuter surgeries and supporting community members’ loving pets, one local nonprofit is changing the lives of thousands of animals across the region.

In communities throughout the southern Pacific coast region, countless dogs and cats need help. Some have been abandoned and left to survive on their own. Others have loving families who simply cannot afford the food or veterinary care their pets need. Since 2017, El Refugio Costa Ballena has been working to change that reality, each and every day.

Located in Uvita, El Refugio Costa Ballena was founded with a straightforward but important mission: to help the dogs and cats in the community. Today, it is the only physical animal shelter in the area, providing a place of safety for animals in need.

Rescue, Rehabilitation, and Second Chances

At the heart of El Refugio’s mission is the rescue and rehabilitation of dogs and cats in need. To date, the shelter has rescued more than 1,200 animals, giving them an opportunity for care, recovery, and a better future.

Take Furia, a recent rescue. She was found on the streets in terrible condition – she has ehrlichia, chronic bacterial and fungal dermatitis, and her eyes are infected. She weighs only 12kg but should be double that. Now, she is receiving daily medical care and proper nutrition. In time, she’ll be ready for a home of her own.

Rescue is only the beginning. Once animals are ready for their next chapter, the rescue works to find them loving homes where they can become cherished members of a family. So far this year over 110 dogs and cats have been adopted through the organization, representing countless opportunities for new beginnings for both animals and the people who welcome them home.

Helping animals means addressing more than immediate emergencies.

Prevention and Community Assistance

El Refugio Costa Ballena provides free and low-cost castracion services to help control the population of unwanted dogs and cats. To date, the organization has provided more than 7,700 spay/neuter surgeries. These procedures are an important part of addressing animal overpopulation for the long term. By making sterilization more accessible, El Refugio helps reduce the number of unwanted animals and the suffering that often results when communities lack the resources to care for them.

The commitment also extends to pets who already have loving homes. Through its community assistance program, El Refugio Costa Ballena has provided food and medical care for thousands of dogs and cats whose families cannot afford these necessities. For families facing financial hardship, help with pet food or veterinary expenses can make an enormous difference. This combination of rescue, adoption, prevention, and community assistance reflects an important understanding: improving animal welfare requires not only caring for animals in crisis, but also helping prevent the crisis from happening in the first place.

A Community Effort That Needs Everyone

While El Refugio has made a substantial difference since its founding, the need for animal welfare services continues. The work of caring for vulnerable animals also requires the involvement of the wider community. There are many ways residents and visitors can help. Donate to provide essential support for the rescue’s work, including animal care, food, medical treatment, and spay/neuter programs.

Volunteer your time and energy to the organization’s mission. People who want to make a hands-on difference can reach out to learn what assistance is needed.

Foster an animal to provide a temporary home and create space and opportunities for other animals who need care.

Adoption offers one of the most direct ways to change an animal’s life. By welcoming a rescue dog or cat into the family, adopters provide a home and make it possible for the shelter to continue helping others.

Learn more about how to adopt, foster, volunteer, and donate, by visiting the website www.elrefugiocostaballena.com

Every Animal Deserves a Chance

The challenge of animal welfare is too great for any one organization to address alone. Every donation, every volunteer hour, every foster home, and every adoption can contribute to a better future for the dogs and cats of Costa Rica.

Helping animals starts with a community that cares. Together, we can give more animals the chance to live healthier, safer, and happier lives.

World.title: Weak Dollar Cuts Costa Rica Medical Tourism Revenue by Up to 15%
World.content:
Costa Rica’s private hospitals, clinics and medical offices are treating about as many foreign patients as they have in recent years, but they are taking in 10% to 15% less for that work because of the dollar’s slide against the colón, according to the Costa Rican Chamber of Health. Rodolfo Garbanzo, president of the chamber, said the drop is already visible in the financial statements of companies that serve medical tourists, as it is in every industry paid in dollars.

He said patient volume has changed little in recent years. The squeeze comes from a currency mismatch. Providers bill almost all of their services to foreign patients in U.S. dollars, while salaries, social security contributions, rent and suppliers are paid in colones. Every dollar a patient pays now converts into fewer colones to cover those costs.

The dollar closed at 452.62 colones on Tuesday in the Central Bank’s Monex foreign exchange market. That is more than 50 colones below its level on the same date last year and more than 200 colones below mid-2022, when it traded near 700. At a difference of 50 colones, a $10,000 treatment package converts into roughly 500,000 fewer colones than it would have a year ago, a loss of about 10% before a single local cost has risen. The colón’s strength reflects a record supply of dollars in the local market.

Central Bank figures cited by the chamber put medical tourism in Costa Rica at about $465 million in foreign currency a year, from 70,455 medical tourists spending an average of $6,600 each. Using those figures as a baseline, the chamber estimates the activity has generated about $9.3 billion and 1.4 million patient visits over the past 20 years.

The chamber said the exchange rate has not hurt Costa Rica’s reputation as a provider of medical services, even as the country grows steadily more expensive for visitors. Massimo Manzi, the chamber’s executive director, said the currency is without question a challenge for the country and its companies. He noted that about 94% of the sector’s patients come from the United States and Canada, and that in the United States health care costs remain very high while insurance coverage is employers’ second-largest expense after payroll.

That pressure, he said, continues to push more medical tourists toward Costa Rica. Roberto Herrera, the chamber’s first vice president, said part of the country’s regular tourist traffic also depends on private health care. He said a significant number of older travelers vacation in Costa Rica because they know that if something happens to them they can be treated locally rather than evacuated, since private care is available across the country.

The same exchange rate pressure runs through the wider tourism industry. An analysis by the Center for Tourism Studies, based on Central Bank balance of payments data, found that tourism brought in a record amount of foreign currency in the second quarter of 2026, yet the total converted to about 601 billion colones, 7.7% less than the roughly 651 billion colones of the same quarter a year earlier.

The center based that comparison on average quarterly rates of about 455 colones per dollar this year and about 505 a year before. Households living on dollar income face the same arithmetic, as the dollar’s fall below 450 colones has cut what a fixed pension or salary buys locally.

The chamber released its revenue estimate as it marked its 10th anniversary. Alongside it, the group cited a sector study counting more than 80,000 jobs tied to health and social services, pharmaceutical sales and medical manufacturing, along with about 1,457 private pharmacies, 555,000 memberships in prepaid medical plans and 599,000 private health insurance policies.

Costa Rica gave the activity a legal framework in 2023 with Law 10.320, which set rules to promote and regulate health tourism services and gave the chamber a seat on the interinstitutional commission that oversees it. The country is also pursuing wellness tourism in Nicoya as a related draw for high-spending visitors.

For now, the chamber describes the damage as a matter of margins rather than demand. The patients are still arriving. Each one is simply worth less once the dollars reach the bank.

World.title: Rare Sighting of Tapir Family in Costa Rica Highlights Importance of Forest Conservation
World.content:
A rare wildlife encounter in northern Costa Rica has captured the attention of conservationists after a family of three endangered tapirs was filmed walking together through patches of forest in Pital de San Carlos. The sighting is particularly unusual because the animals were traveling as a family group in broad daylight, offering a glimpse of one of Central America’s largest and most elusive mammals.

The encounter took place on October 23 during a field visit by specialists from the Foundation for the Development of the Central Volcanic Mountain Range (FUNDECOR). The organization’s environmental services team recorded a male, a female and a young tapir moving through the landscape, an observation that conservationists say highlights the importance of maintaining connections between forest habitats.

The footage was made public this week, drawing attention to a species that plays an important role in Costa Rica’s ecosystems but is rarely observed in family groups.

Dylana Álvarez Masís, a forest management specialist with FUNDECOR, described the encounter as highly unusual, particularly because the three animals were seen together outside dense forest cover. Known locally as dantas, Baird’s tapirs (Tapirus bairdii) are the largest native land mammals in Central America. Despite their size, they are often difficult to spot in the wild because they generally move through dense vegetation and tend to avoid human activity.

The animals have large, rounded bodies, short legs and distinctive elongated snouts that help them gather leaves, fruit and other vegetation. Adults can weigh several hundred pounds, making them considerably larger than most other mammals found in Costa Rica’s forests.

Tapirs are generally solitary animals, although mothers remain with their young for an extended period. Their reproductive cycle is also unusually slow. Pregnancy lasts approximately 13 months, and calves typically stay close to their mothers for at least a year. These characteristics make the sighting in San Carlos particularly interesting. Observing a male, female and young animal together provides an uncommon opportunity to document their behavior in a natural setting.

Beyond their appearance, tapirs perform an essential ecological function. They are sometimes called the gardeners of the forest because they eat fruit and disperse seeds over considerable distances as they move through their habitats. Some seeds pass through the animals’ digestive systems and are deposited in different parts of the forest, helping native trees and plants establish themselves in new areas.

Their movement through dense vegetation can also create small openings that allow sunlight to reach the forest floor, contributing to natural regeneration. For this reason, protecting tapirs can also help protect the wider ecosystems that depend on healthy forests.

However, the species faces significant threats throughout Central America. Baird’s tapir is classified as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), with habitat destruction, forest fragmentation and hunting among the main factors contributing to its declining population.

In Costa Rica, tapirs can still be found in protected areas such as Corcovado National Park and other large forest ecosystems. But their survival also depends on what happens outside national parks, particularly in regions where agricultural land, roads and human settlements divide natural habitats.

The Pital de San Carlos sighting illustrates why these connections matter. The animals were observed moving between separate patches of forest rather than remaining within one continuous wooded area. Conservation specialists refer to the ability of animals to move between these habitats as ecological connectivity. Maintaining these connections allows wildlife to find food, reach suitable breeding areas and move between populations.

When forests become isolated, animals may have difficulty moving safely between them. Roads, fences, agricultural expansion and other forms of development can create barriers, increasing the risk of wildlife becoming trapped in smaller areas of suitable habitat. FUNDECOR says observations such as the one recorded in Pital demonstrate the importance of strengthening conservation programs that maintain functioning connections between forests.

The organization works with landowners and communities on sustainable forest management and environmental services programs designed to protect natural resources while supporting local economic activities. Costa Rica’s Payment for Environmental Services program is one mechanism used to encourage landowners to maintain forest cover rather than clearing land for other purposes.

These efforts can be especially important in agricultural regions, where patches of privately owned forest sometimes provide the only connections between larger protected ecosystems. The presence of the young tapir also gives researchers an opportunity to learn more about how the species uses the landscape. However, a single sighting cannot establish that the local tapir population is increasing or that the animals face fewer threats than before.

Determining whether a population is recovering requires repeated observations and scientific monitoring over time. Camera traps, field surveys and other monitoring tools have become increasingly important for studying Costa Rica’s elusive wildlife, allowing scientists to identify where animals are moving and which habitats remain connected.

For residents and visitors, encounters with tapirs are a reminder of the remarkable wildlife that continues to inhabit Costa Rica’s northern region, even in places where forests are surrounded by farms and human settlements. The animals are generally shy, and anyone fortunate enough to encounter one in the wild should maintain a safe distance and avoid approaching or feeding it.

For conservationists, the unusual footage from Pital is more than an interesting wildlife moment. It shows why maintaining forest connections remains essential for protecting endangered species whose survival depends on having enough space to move, feed and reproduce.

And for three tapirs quietly making their way through the forests of San Carlos, those connections may help determine whether future generations can continue traveling through the same landscape.

World.title: Guards Find Sharpened Spoons as Costa Rica’s Megaprison Tops 600 Inmates
World.content:
Costa Rica’s new maximum-security prison held more than 600 inmates by Tuesday, eight days after the first transfers. Guards there have already found weapons made from eating utensils, and the government says inmates who make them will lose them. The Ministry of Justice and Peace confirmed the population on Tuesday. The High Containment Center for Organized Crime (CACCO), in San Rafael de Alajuela, received its first 123 inmates on Oct. 26.

According to the ministry, the people now held there include inmates linked to organized crime, homicide and femicide cases, as well as the killings of Public Force and Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) officers. During an inspection on Saturday, Oct. 31, the Penitentiary Police found sharpened plastic spoons and a homemade blade made of glass in one of the dormitories.

Justice and Peace Minister Gabriel Aguilar Vargas said inmates who turn utensils into weapons will have those utensils confiscated. He also said foam mattresses that inmates destroy will not be replaced, and that guards will keep inspecting dormitories, corridors and walkways. It is not the first disciplinary case at the facility. Aguilar reported an incident on Oct. 26, the first day of transfers, without identifying the inmate involved.

Under the prison’s rules, inmates who commit infractions can be moved to isolation cells within their module. Prison authorities can order isolation for up to 48 hours, and any longer period requires a judge’s approval, Aguilar said. The CACCO is designed for 5,100 inmates in five modules of 1,020 each. Each module has 17 cells of about 90 square meters (970 square feet), holding up to 60 people apiece.

At just over 600 inmates, the prison is at about 12% of that capacity. The government put its construction cost at 16.774 billion colones. At the inauguration in mid-October, Aguilar told the country’s crime bosses that the party was over. The government has promised uniforms, constant electronic monitoring, blocked illicit phone calls and no inmate leaders, and it has sharply limited conjugal visits.

The country’s highest-profile prisoners will not be moved there. Aguilar said on Oct. 27 that inmates with economic power and the ability to recruit others could quickly build new criminal structures in shared cells. They will stay in individual maximum-security cells at the La Reforma prison complex.

The prison has drawn support from Washington, where the US Embassy praised the new facility in October. It opens as violent deaths remain high. OIJ data show 706 homicides so far this year, compared with 745 at the same point in 2025, a drop of 5.2%. The first 48 hours of November brought 10 killings, compared with seven in the same period last year. Limón province has recorded the most homicides in 2026, with 185, and firearms were used in 567 of the year’s killings, according to the OIJ.

World.title: Honduran Migrant Caravan Heads to US Amid Midterm Elections
World.content:
Dozens of people left northern Honduras yesterday in a caravan bound for the United States, hoping the congressional elections will weaken U.S. President Donald Trump, who has maintained a crackdown on irregular migration. The Hondurans set out on foot from San Pedro Sula, many carrying backpacks or pulling rolling bags, on the same day as the pivotal elections in which Republicans and Democrats are vying for control of Congress.

“Trump is on his way out in these elections. That’s why we’re taking the risk. Here in Honduras, we have nothing left,” Jimena Morazán, 47, who is traveling with five family members, said. In Honduras, 61% of the country’s 11.2 million people live in poverty, and the homicide rate stands at 24 per 100,000 residents, three times the global average, according to official figures.

This is the third caravan of dozens of migrants to leave Honduras since September. Salvadorans, Guatemalans, Nicaraguans and Mexicans joined the previous groups along the route toward the southern U.S. border. Salvadorans also plan to leave the capital, San Salvador, on Wednesday aboard two buses to join the Hondurans at the Guatemala-Mexico border.

“We found out on social media that a caravan was leaving, and I decided to go with my family,” explained Jesús Carías, 30. Accompanied by his wife and three young children, he acknowledged that the journey would be “complicated.” “We’re putting ourselves in God’s hands and will see what they decide over there,” added Carías, who will be making his fourth attempt to enter the United States.

“While they’re going through the election process, we’ll be on our way. We have faith that we’ll arrive while they’re busy with that,” Beverly Medina, 39, who is traveling with her three-year-old daughter, said.

The Trump administration warned Thursday that it would revoke the visas of people organizing these caravans, which are largely coordinated through TikTok and WhatsApp. The U.S. Embassy in Tegucigalpa said on X that the caravans “have no chance of entering” U.S. territory.

Trump has made combating irregular immigration a central pillar of his domestic policy, conducting raids across the country and enforcing a policy of zero admissions at the southern border. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced last week that it had revoked the immigration status of 2.2 million foreign nationals since January 2025, in addition to restricting work permits.

World.title: Two Belize City men fined $505 each after admitting plans to steal copper wire
World.content:
Two Belize City men fined $505 each after admitting plans to steal copper wire

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two Belize City construction workers were fined $505 each after pleading guilty to going equipped to commit theft when police caught them with tools they admitted were intended to be used to steal copper wire.

Edward Montes, 46, a construction worker and electrician, and Kenrick Gonzales, a construction worker, both of Police Street, appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate in Court #2 on Wednesday.

According to police, the men were spotted hiding on the compound of the former Renco Battery business on October 30, 2026, while officers were conducting mobile patrols.

When questioned about their presence on the property, one of the men reportedly remained silent. Officers subsequently discovered pliers, electrical tape and power cable in the area.

Police say Montes admitted, “I came to get the copper out of the power line.”

Both men pleaded guilty to going equipped and were fined $505 each.

However, Montes faces an additional charge of resisting lawful arrest after allegedly pushing a police officer and struggling with officers as they attempted to detain him.

Montes pleaded not guilty to that charge and was granted bail of $300. His next court appearance is scheduled for January 29, 2027, when disclosure is expected to be provided.

The resisting arrest allegation remains before the court.

World.title: Shawn Garbutt, Celestino Zetina accused of armed home invasion at Belize City tacos vendor’s home
World.content:
Shawn Garbutt, Celestino Zetina accused of armed home invasion at Belize City tacos vendor’s home

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two men accused of carrying out an armed home invasion at a Belize City taco vendor’s residence, during which more than $2,500 worth of jewelry was stolen, made their first court appearance together this week.

Shawn Garbutt, 18, and Celestino Anwar Zetina, 24, appeared before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, November 2, following their separate arraignments in September and October.

Both men are charged with aggravated burglary in connection with the September home invasion at the Castle Street residence of tacos vendor.

According to police, the woman was leaving her home around 5:50 a.m. when two masked men, allegedly armed with firearms, confronted her. One reportedly grabbed her hand and forced her back inside the house while demanding money.

The intruders allegedly stole a jewelry box containing several gold chains, rings and other jewelry valued at approximately $2,525 before fleeing the area.

Police investigations led to the arrest of Garbutt, who was first charged and remanded in September. Zetina was subsequently charged on October 9.

Both men previously pleaded not guilty and remain on remand at the Belize Central Prison, as bail was not granted at the Magistrate’s Court because of the alleged use of firearms.

Their case was adjourned until December 2, 2026.

The allegations against both men remain unproven.

World.title: 18-year-old pleads guilty to threatening to burn down 39-year-old girlfriend’s home with her five children inside
World.content:
18-year-old pleads guilty to threatening to burn down 39-year-old girlfriend’s home with her five children inside

By Breaking Belize News Staff: An 18-year-old Belize City man has been remanded to prison after pleading guilty to threatening to burn down his 39-year-old girlfriend’s home with her and her five children inside.

Jaden Busano appeared before a magistrate in Court #5 on Wednesday, where he pleaded guilty to a charge of threat of death against his girlfriend, a cook and mother of five.

The charge stems from an incident on October 5, 2026, when Busano allegedly threatened the woman, telling her, “I wah burn down this house with all ah uno in it.”

In court, Busano admitted making the threat but claimed he was under the influence of alcohol and experiencing considerable stress. He also disputed claims that the woman was his former girlfriend, insisting they were still in an intimate relationship and that he considered himself a stepfather to her five children.

According to the police report, the woman had ended their relationship over allegations of infidelity, but Busano reportedly continued harassing her in an attempt to reconcile.

The woman also alleged that Busano had previously attempted to set fire to her home. She reported that on October 6, a relative alerted her to a fire in her backyard, where clothing, bags and a mattress had reportedly been set ablaze. The flames allegedly spread to the house before neighbours helped extinguish them.

Police say Busano subsequently admitted to the incident during an interview conducted in the presence of a Justice of the Peace.

Busano was previously listed as wanted by police on October 8 in connection with an investigation.

The magistrate accepted his guilty plea but deferred sentencing until Friday, November 6, 2026. Busano was remanded to the Belize Central Prison in the interim.

World.title: Transport CEO says National Bus Company created to provide better service
World.content:
Transport CEO says National Bus Company created to provide better service

By Zoila Palma: Transport CEO Chester Williams explains that National Bus Company was created to upgrade and enhance commuters experience.

“For far to long our Belizean people, particularly the commuters have been subjected to inferior public transportation. The buses owned and operated by most of the bus operators are dilapidated, constantly breaking down, passengers getting wet during rainy weather and are mechanically unreliable.

Due to this, the government of Belize through the Ministry of Transportation moved to establish the National Bus Company. This company was created after numerous consultations with the bus operators, other stakeholders and international organizations. After careful consideration a number of the operators came together which gave birth to the NBC. The Government of Belize joined the operators as the majority shareholder in NBC making it a public, private partnership,” Williams explained.

Williams further said that NBC was not created to run the other operators out of business.

“It was created with the view of provide adequate, reliable, affordable and comfortable transportation service to our commuting public. In order to fulfill its mandate the government and people of Taiwan will be giving a grant of 24 new electric buses and solar charging stations to the Government of Belize. These modern buses are the first step in modernizing the Belize Public Transportation System. It is the firm belief of this government that our commuting public deserve a transportation system that do not strip them of their human dignity,” he added.

The Transport CEO says that opportunities were given to bus operators to fix the transportation system but the government decided to step in partnering with some operators to improving the system.

He added that for more than 20 years, the system was broken and it further deteriorated with no hope until this plan came about.

“This new transportation system will not only benefit our commuters it will benefit us as a country. We will now be on par with our brothers and sisters in the region.

Let us push aside the obstructionist and move full speed ahead in created a modern, reliable, affordable and comfortable transportation system for our people, one that we can all be proud of and one that we all will feel comfortable riding one day,” he urged.

World.title: Leon Gomez detained under State of Emergency moments after receiving bail on drug charge
World.content:
Leon Gomez detained under State of Emergency moments after receiving bail on drug charge

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 35-year-old Belize City barber who was granted bail on a drug trafficking charge was detained by police under the ongoing State of Emergency (SOE) moments after his arraignment at the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday.

Leon Alexander Gomez, of Oleander Street, appeared unrepresented before a magistrate in Court #5, where he pleaded not guilty to possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply in connection with 4.57 grams of crack cocaine.

With no objection from the prosecution, Gomez was granted bail of $1,000 plus one surety of the same amount or two sureties of $500 each. His case was adjourned until December 30, 2026.

However, before Gomez could post bail, officers from the Criminal Investigation Branch arrived at the courthouse on Coney Drive and detained him under the State of Emergency. He was subsequently escorted to the Queen Street Police Station for processing ahead of his detention at the Belize Central Prison.

The development comes amid an intensified police crackdown following the declaration of a State of Emergency in 19 areas across Belize City, Ladyville, Cotton Tree and Unitedville.

Police previously disclosed that approximately 60 individuals had been identified for possible detention under the emergency measures, which took effect on November 1 following a deadly escalation in gang-related violence.

Gomez’s detention under the SOE is separate from the drug charge for which he was granted bail. He has not been convicted of that offence.

World.title: Lennox Gentle, accused killer of Kiffer McKenzie, asks court for case facts and food during third appearance
World.content:
Lennox Gentle, accused killer of Kiffer McKenzie, asks court for case facts and food during third appearance

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Lennox Linsford Gentle, 24, who is accused of the brazen daylight murder of Kiffer Alexander McKenzie in downtown Belize City, made his third appearance before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court this week, requesting a summary of the prosecution’s case and permission to obtain food after reportedly missing breakfast at prison.

Gentle, who remains unrepresented, appeared in Court #5, where he requested a copy of the summary of facts surrounding the murder charge. The presiding magistrate granted his request.

The prosecutor informed the court that the case file was not yet ready, prompting another adjournment to December 8, 2026, when disclosure is expected to be provided. Gentle was further remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Before leaving the courtroom, Gentle also requested permission to obtain food, explaining that the prison bus had arrived late and inmates were rushed to court without being given an opportunity to eat breakfast.

Gentle was arraigned on August 5, 2026, in connection with the June 13 murder of McKenzie, who was shot while seated inside his blue Jeep near the intersection of Albert and Orange streets with his two children.

Police say a gunman wearing a helmet approached McKenzie’s vehicle and opened fire before escaping on a motorcycle. Despite being wounded, McKenzie managed to drive along Albert Street before crashing into a parked vehicle near Tropicana. He was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Investigators reportedly relied on surveillance footage, information obtained through the Police Department’s Fusion Center and a statement from a female Special Constable to identify Gentle as the alleged shooter.

McKenzie was the son of the late George “Junie Balls” McKenzie.

Gentle remains in custody awaiting further proceedings.

World.title: Sergeant Albert Coc earns Bachelor of Laws degree from University of West Indies
World.content:
Sergeant Albert Coc earns Bachelor of Laws degree from University of West Indies

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Belize Police Department extends congratulations to Sergeant No. 764 Albert Coc on successfully obtaining a Bachelor of Laws (LLB) degree with Upper Second Class Honours from the University of the West Indies, Cave Hill Campus.

Sergeant Coc, who has served the Department for several years as a Police Prosecutor, is now pursuing his final two years of legal studies at the Norman Manley Law School.

“His achievement is a testament to his dedication, perseverance, and commitment to professional development. The Department is proud of his accomplishment and wishes him continued success as he advances in his legal career,” the BPD said.

The BPD says that it is confident that Coc’s knowledge and expertise will contribute meaningfully to the continued development of the Belize Police Department and, by extension, Belize.

World.title: Minister of Education and BNTU discuss strengthening collaboration
World.content:
Minister of Education and BNTU discuss strengthening collaboration

By Zoila Palma: Today, Education Minister Francis Fonseca reaffirmed the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology’s commitment to strengthening its partnership with the Belize National Teachers’ Union (BNTU) during a meeting with Nadia Caliz, President, and members of the BNTU Executive.

Discussions focused on matters of concern raised by the Union, the importance of maintaining a strong working relationship, and opportunities to enhance collaboration in support of Belize’s educators.

Minister Fonseca reiterated his commitment to continued dialogue and partnership in advancing the interests and well-being of teachers across the country.

The Minister was accompanied by Dian Castillo-Maheia, Chief Executive Officer; Yolanda Gongora, Chief Education Officer; Dr. Cecilia Ramirez-Smith and Terri Wesby Longford, Deputy Chief Education Officers; Ricardo Gideon, Director of PPRE.

World.title: Jamaica Baptist Union slams Gov’t’s abstention on Cuba embargo vote
World.content:
HAVANA, Cuba — People collect potable water from a public supply point in Havana on October 6, 2026. The US energy blockade on the communist-run island since last January has caused water supplies to falter, affecting nearly 29 per cent of Cuba’s 9.4 million inhabitants, according to official figures, with the situation worsening significantly since its start. (Photo: AFP)

KINGSTON, Jamaica – The Jamaica Baptist Union (JBU) is urging the country not to swap what is right for what is convenient in the wake of Jamaica’s abstention during the October 28 vote, which called for an end to the United States’ 66-year-old economic, commercial and financial embargo on Cuba.

“A vote that goes against the united will of the people’s representatives opens a gap between what Jamaica says and what Jamaica does. That gap weakens public trust. It also blurs the integrity of our foreign policy,” the JBU shared in a statement on Monday.

It noted that the government’s reasoning behind the abstention merits a closer look. It stressed that for more than 30 years, Jamaica spoke with one clear voice at the UN on this question.

“To abstain now is to break with that record,” the JBU said.

The union noted it was not questioning the Government’s right to set foreign policy and took seriously the information minister’s word that the country acted under no outside pressure.

It also acknowledged Foreign Minister Kamina Johnson Smith’s confirmation that Jamaica still opposes unilateral coercive measures that breach the UN Charter and her statement that the vote has not yet effected real change.

“Still, the Government’s reasoning needs a closer look. As Christians, we have to ask a plain question. Is a moral principle wrong just because it has not yet brought quick political results?” the union queried.

It noted that if the embargo is wrong, and the Government says it is, then voting against it is the least our conscience asks of us.

“A resolution does not stop being true because the powerful ignore it. The world did not stop condemning apartheid because it took decades for those condemnations to work. Moral witness is not measured by how fast it succeeds. It is measured by whether it is faithful. When a people’s suffering gets worse, that is a reason to speak more firmly, not to go quiet,” the union said.

Highlighting the suffering affecting Cubans including strangled access to food, medicine, energy and the means to grow, the JBU said it is no longer just a quarrel between governments rather a matter of human rights.

“To abstain on a vote about measures like these because we are tired of the debate or want to try a new tactic is to put convenience ahead of justice,” it added.

The union said it was also troubled by what the abstention says about who we are, noting the deep and beneficial relationship between Jamaica and Cuba.

“For half a century Cuba has trained our doctors, sent medical brigades to our clinics and built schools on our soil,” it said.

“Our Parliament recently passed a unanimous resolution on Cuba. It voiced deep concern about the hardship facing the Cuban people, and it backed reform in Cuba and dialogue between Cuba and the US to ease economic restrictions. The minister may be right that the motion did not call for the embargo to be lifted, and that it does not legally bind the executive. But a nation’s witness suffers when its Parliament says one thing and its vote at the UN says another,” it added.

The union noted that the effect on the region matters too, highlighting that Caricom split on this vote. Describing it as a worrying crack in regional solidarity.

“The small island states of the Caribbean have never drawn their strength from economic muscle. Our strength has come from moral clarity and from speaking with one voice. When we go quiet on the world stage, we weaken the shield that international law gives to every small nation,” it said.

Stressing that it does not give its blessing to any political system or ideology and acknowledging that Cuba faces its own problems, the union, however, rejected the idea that punishing a whole people is a fair way to force political change.

“Silence in the face of this kind of hardship is not neutrality. It is consent,” the union stated.

World.title: JLP wants Phillips, Brown Burke sanctioned after ‘violent conduct’ in Parliament
World.content:
JLP General Secretary Senator Charles Sinclair

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The governing Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) is calling for the People’s National Party’s Mikael Phillips and Dr Angela Brown Burke to be sanctioned for what it described as crude, unbecoming and violent conduct in the House of Representatives on Tuesday.

In a statement on Wednesday, the JLP claimed Phillips aggressively charged in the direction of Kingston Western Member of Parliament Desmond McKenzie after McKenzie told him not to disrespect House Speaker Juliet Holness.

The statement further claimed that Phillips shouted at Holness and called her wicked, prompting McKenzie to tell him to do better and to consider whether he would wish for his mother to be spoken to in such a disrespectful fashion.

It added that Phillips attempted to physically attack McKenzie and has since admitted uttering expletives in Parliament.

The statement also accused Phillips of making a false claim about what McKenzie said to him.

JLP Deputy General Secretary Charles Sinclair says “Phillips’ so-called apology is not good enough and the North West Manchester MP should face strong sanctions for his violent conduct, which was caught on videotape.”

Sinclair added that Phillips also owes Holness, McKenzie, the Parliament and the people of Jamaica an unequivocal apology which is not riddled with excuses and false statements.

He pointed to videos emerging online of the altercation, noting that is shows the PNP Chairman and St Andrew South West Member of Parliament Angela Brown Burke imposing herself in the parliamentary aisle, in violation of parliamentary convention as the speaker departed the chamber.

Sinclair described as startling Burke’s alleged physical assault of Holness while shouting “coward”, saying it represents a new low for the Jamaican Parliament.

According to Sinclair, Brown Burke should be strongly sanctioned for her inappropriate, crude and violent conduct.

He said this is not the first time Brown Burke has shown utter disrespect to the speaker, but the physical contact represents a dangerous escalation.

Sinclair says the JLP stands with Holness and called on all well-thinking Jamaicans to denounce the behaviour of the PNP representatives in Parliament, adding that the consistently unbecoming conduct is clearly condoned by the party leadership.

World.title: Phillips regrets House outburst, says Mckenzie insulted his deceased mother
World.content:
Manchester North Western Member of Parliament (MP) Mikael Phillips

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Manchester North Western Member of Parliament (MP) Mikael Phillips has apologised for his use of an expletive during Tuesday’s confrontation at Gordon House, while accusing Government MP Desmond McKenzie of making an offensive remark about his deceased mother.

Phillips, in a statement Wednesday, said he regretted his response to the exchange but insisted that accounts of the incident circulated by Deputy Leader of Government Business Robert Nesta Morgan were “inaccurate and misleading”.

According to Phillips, he was standing with two other Opposition MPs discussing the circumstances surrounding the premature adjournment of the House of Representatives when the speaker exited the chamber.

He alleged that shortly after the speaker left, McKenzie, the MP for Kingston Western, verbally attacked him.

“As soon as the speaker left, the Member of Parliament for Kingston Western, Desmond McKenzie, verbally attacked me, making an offensive reference to my deceased mother. He then repeated the offence,” Phillips explained.

The Opposition MP acknowledged that he became angry and responded with an expletive, describing his reaction as inappropriate.

“My reaction was inappropriate, and I regret that I allowed myself to respond in that manner. I sincerely apologise to the Jamaican people,” he said.

However, he rejected Morgan’s claim that he pushed Opposition Leader Mark Golding during the confrontation, maintaining that Golding was not involved in the incident.

READ: Opposition, not Gov’t, responsible for ‘unparliamentary behaviour’ in House — Morgan

Phillips also said that although two Government MPs intervened, he did not physically touch either of them.

Questioning Morgan’s account, Phillips argued that the deputy leader of government business was not in the immediate vicinity when the incident occurred.

“It is deeply irresponsible for a Member of Parliament, particularly one entrusted with a leadership role in the House, to circulate an account that is so fundamentally at odds with what actually occurred. Mr Morgan should withdraw his false and malicious claims immediately,” Phillips said.

The Manchester North Western MP also linked the confrontation to growing tensions in Parliament, accusing the Government of repeatedly seeking to curtail debate and restrict the Opposition’s participation in parliamentary proceedings.

He argued that efforts to limit members’ opportunities to speak and debate have contributed to an increasingly strained atmosphere in the House and undermined parliamentary order.

“The right of elected representatives to speak, question and debate is fundamental to our parliamentary democracy. When those rights are repeatedly frustrated, it undermines the proper functioning of Parliament and contributes to an atmosphere of unnecessary tension,” he said.

Phillips maintained that Parliament should remain a place where differing views can be expressed freely and respectfully, while acknowledging that all MPs have a responsibility to uphold order and decorum.

He called for restraint from both sides of the House and urged the Government to respect the rights of elected representatives to perform their parliamentary duties without unnecessary obstruction.

World.title: ‘We will not be bullied’: Golding clarifies events leading to parliamentary uproar
World.content:
PNP President Mark Golding Photo: Karl Mclarty

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Opposition Leader Mark Golding has provided an account of the events that led to Tuesday’s parliamentary uproar, explaining that the Opposition’s protest was triggered by what he described as the Government’s abuse of parliamentary procedures to shut down debate on a censure motion concerning Jamaica’s position on Cuba.

Golding said the confrontation followed the Government’s decision to bring the debate to an early close without allowing the Opposition an opportunity to contribute to the motion it had tabled.

Opposition Member of Parliament (MP) Anthony Hylton opened the debate before Leader of Government Business Floyd Green responded. However, Golding said Speaker Juliet Holness subsequently allowed the Government to move to end the debate without giving him or other Opposition members an opportunity to speak.

“Anthony Hylton MP opened the debate on our censure motion in regard to the Government’s deception in the House the week before on the matter of Cuba. Minister Floyd Green then responded in the censure motion debate. The speaker, however, allowed a blatant abuse of power by the Government, letting them move a motion to bring an early close to that debate without letting me or anyone else on our side speak on our own motion,” Golding said in a video posted to his social media on Wednesday.

He questioned the fairness of the decision, noting that Opposition members were also prevented from challenging the move after their microphones were switched off.

“Mek that make sense? We weren’t allowed to speak on the motion that we had brought. Then we were prevented by the speaker from questioning that decision to bring it to an early close as she shut off our mics. We have a right to speak and we all stood up in protest,” he said.

Golding also explained the circumstances surrounding his exchange with the speaker, saying he had to raise his voice to be heard because his microphone was off and there was considerable noise in the chamber.

“So I raised my voice to make the point to the speaker that she has a duty under the standing orders to take into account the interests of the minority in this situation. I had to speak loudly to be heard because the speaker wouldn’t turn on my mic and there was a lot of noise in the room. I didn’t say anything rude or use any inappropriate language in making that point,” he said.

He said Opposition members maintained their protest rather than allow the sitting to continue without being given an opportunity to speak, prompting the speaker to adjourn the House.

“We will not be bullied,” Golding said.

Tensions escalated further after the formal proceedings had ended, with a confrontation between Manchester North Western MP Mikael Phillips and Government MP Desmond McKenzie, which was captured on video.

In condemning the conduct of Opposition MPs, Deputy Leader of Government Business Robert Nesta Morgan said McKenzie intervened to urge Phillips to show respect towards the speaker, prompting Phillips to respond with a series of expletives before advancing aggressively towards him. Morgan said Phillips had to be restrained by several members of the House.

READ: WATCH: House in turmoil over Cuba censure motion

In an additional release, the Opposition sought to outline its objections to the handling of the censure motion, accusing the Government of manipulating the House’s Standing Orders to avoid accountability over Jamaica’s abstention from a United Nations resolution calling for an end to the United States embargo against Cuba.

The Opposition said it had expected the motion, tabled by Hylton on Tuesday, to be debated at the next sitting, as Standing Orders prohibit debate on a motion on the same day it is tabled.

However, it said Green moved to suspend the Standing Orders and proceed immediately to which Opposition MP Phillip Paulwell objected, citing the procedural breach and the absence of the prime minister during debate on a censure motion against the Government.

According to the Opposition, the speaker ruled that the Standing Orders, including the notice requirement, be suspended, allowing Hylton to open the debate, followed by Green.

The Opposition said that when its members prepared to contribute, Green moved to close the debate without further contributions. It objected, citing Standing Order 38(2), which bars the early closure of a debate where doing so would oppress the minority.

Golding then called for a division, which the speaker acknowledged, but no vote was taken amid the disorder in the chamber. The sitting was subsequently adjourned, leaving the censure motion unfinished.

Golding said the Government could not be allowed to use parliamentary procedures to prevent scrutiny of an issue of national importance.

“The censure motion stands, and every Opposition voice must be given the opportunity to be heard,” he said.

Hylton also accused the Government of seeking to avoid accountability, saying: “The Government misled the House on Cuba. It then tried to bury the consequences. We will not rest until accountability is delivered.”

The Opposition maintained that the dispute goes beyond parliamentary procedure, arguing that it concerns democratic accountability and the public’s right to know about decisions affecting Jamaica’s international standing and reputation.

It further contended that the Government’s handling of the Cuba vote had damaged Brand Jamaica and reiterated its demand that the censure debate resume at the next sitting, with all members allowed to contribute.

World.title: Opposition, not Gov’t, responsible for ‘unparliamentary behaviour’ in House — Morgan
World.content:
Deputy Leader of Government Business Robert Nesta Morgan.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Deputy Leader of Government Business Robert Nesta Morgan has condemned the conduct of Opposition Members of Parliament (MPs) during Tuesday’s sitting of the House of Representatives, singling out Manchester North Western MP Mikael Phillips over an expletive-laden confrontation with Government MP Desmond McKenzie.

The incident occurred shortly after the House was adjourned following heated exchanges during debate on a motion seeking to censure the Government over Jamaica’s decision to abstain from a United Nations resolution calling for an end to the United States embargo on Cuba.

According to Morgan, tensions escalated after Phillips verbally confronted House Speaker Juliet Holness. Morgan said McKenzie intervened and urged Phillips to show respect towards the speaker, prompting Phillips to respond with a series of expletives before moving aggressively towards McKenzie.

Morgan said Phillips had to be restrained by several members of the House.

He also referenced video footage of the incident, which he said showed Phillips making apparent physical contact with Opposition Leader Mark Golding as he moved towards McKenzie.

READ: WATCH: House in turmoil over Cuba censure motion

In a statement on Wednesday, condemning the conduct of Opposition members, Morgan criticised comments allegedly made towards the speaker during the sitting.

“We wish to decry the unparliamentary behaviour of several members of the Opposition, both during the sitting of the House, as we were carrying out the nation’s business, and after. Particularly the leader of the Opposition, who made unparliamentary comments to the speaker, Angela Brown Burke, who also made unparliamentary comments off mic, but especially Mikael Phillips, who moved aggressively towards Member of Parliament from West Kingston, Desmond McKenzie, and had to be restrained by several members of the House based on his behaviour.

“We are representatives of the people. Our duty is to go to Parliament and conduct the business of the country and the people of Jamaica in a respectful and professional manner,” Morgan said.

He said the Government would not condone the conduct displayed by Opposition members, arguing that it reflected poorly on Parliament and set a negative example for the public.

“Our side, that is the Government side, will not tolerate, condone or support the type of behaviour that we saw today [Tuesday] in Parliament from the Opposition. It sets a bad example to everyone who is observing what is happening in the House,” Morgan said.

“We do not want it to be said that all parliamentarians or the Parliament is behaving in this manner. The distinction must be made that the behaviour was of the Opposition and not the Government side. A behaviour that we condemn, a behaviour that we reject and a behaviour that we will constantly speak and act against,” he added.

The confrontation followed an increasingly contentious sitting of the House, during which Opposition members protested after Leader of Government Business Floyd Green called for debate on the censure motion to be brought to an end.

The motion, brought by Opposition MP Anthony Hylton, challenged the Government’s decision to abstain from the October 28 United Nations General Assembly resolution on the US embargo against Cuba. The abstention marked the first time Jamaica had not supported the resolution since it was introduced in 1992.

World.title: Hard truths
World.content:
TUFTON... we must obtain more value from the investments we have already made (Photo: JIS)

THE latest review of Jamaica’s public health sector presents a mixed bag of progress and troubling setbacks, with improvements in infrastructure and staffing overshadowed by soaring medicine costs, weaknesses in primary health care, and persistently high maternal and neonatal deaths.

Most alarming is the finding that complications from non-communicable diseases (NCDs) account for nearly four in every five deaths in Jamaica, while too many patients are turning up at hospitals with conditions already at an advanced stage.

The findings are contained in the Jamaica Health Public Expenditure Review, prepared by the World Bank at the request of the Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ) and the Ministry of Health and Wellness, covering the years 2016 to 2022.

Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton, who presented aspects of the report, along with the Government’s response, to Parliament on Tuesday, did not shy away from the findings, describing the review as “candid” and declaring that the Government accepts its conclusions.

“The review asks how much Jamaica spends on health, how well that money is spent, and what results it buys for our people,” Tufton explained.

He noted that the review measures Jamaica’s progress against the World Bank’s 2017 review, and compares the island’s performance with countries of similar demographic profiles.

He told Parliament that NCDs cause close to 80 per cent of deaths, maternal and neonatal mortality remain too high, and Jamaica’s per capita health expenditure is still below that of comparable countries, including Brazil, Grenada, Guyana, St Lucia, Dominica, Suriname, and Colombia.

Too much of the country’s health care spending, he acknowledged, is also being channelled into expensive late-stage hospital care, while medicine costs have risen rapidly.

“We need more nurses and more doctors in our health centres. And our service level agreements with the regional health authorities are not yet used to their full potential to hold the system accountable,” Tufton acknowledged.

According to the minister, “None of these findings comes as a surprise to the ministry. They validate the internal assessment that the ministry itself undertook, which led to the development of Vision for Health 2030, our 10-year strategic plan.

“That assessment told us that a health system built for acute and infectious disease must be reoriented towards prevention, primary healthcare and the management of chronic illness; that our workforce must grow and be deployed where it is needed most; that our facilities need sustained investment and maintenance; and that we need stronger governance and accountability for results,” said Tufton.

He posited that, working independently, the bank has reached the same conclusions.

“That tells us that we have diagnosed the problem correctly and that we are on the right road,” he said before reminding of the steps the ministry has taken over the past 10 years to address each of the bank’s findings.

“The ministry has not waited. Over the past decade we have acted on each of these fronts,” said Tufton.

On the matter of prevention, he reminded of the ‘Jamaica Moves’ programme launched in 2017 to tackle physical inactivity, poor diet, and the risk factors for NCDs. He also reminded of the ‘Know Your Numbers’ campaign, which encourages Jamaicans to have annual health checks and understand what he values mean for their health status.

On primary care, Tufton said the health and wellness ministry adopted the Primary Health Care Policy and, through the Health Systems Strengthening Programme, with support from the Inter-American Development Bank and the European Union, was upgrading health centres into comprehensive facilities. These include the Greater Portmore Health Centre, and redeveloping Spanish Town Hospital.
