World.title: TFR down, need relook at popn control laws like 2-child norm for polls: SC
World.content:
Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Observing that laws aimed at controlling population growth in the country had lost their significance because of a fall in the total fertility rate (TFR) from 3 to 1.9, below the replacement level of 2.1, Supreme Court Wednesday said the foundation of such laws had "crumbled", they had become "counter-productive" and their validity, which was upheld by it two decades ago, needed to be re-examined in the present situation.The court then decided to review its 2003 verdict for disqualifying individuals with more than two children from contesting elections to panchayati raj institutions.A bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said the earlier perception that population had a negative impact on development did not hold anymore, and not keeping the law abreast of changing times would have consequences far beyond the specific precedent or the law in question."Even though India's population is not yet declining, the TFR falling below the replacement rate will soon result in a demographic transition towards an older population with a declining share of the working-age population. Laws aimed at limiting population growth have now lost significance. If we fail to take note of such demographic changes, India will face serious consequences...," it said. Disqualification provisions on the basis of more than two children for local body polls have been in effect in various states. The court passed the order while examining the validity of a Maharashtra law which was challenged by a woman sarpanch. The court allowed her to hold the post despite the disqualification provision and referred the issue to a larger bench.

World.title: SC: Can't become third chamber of Parliament
World.content:
'Can't interfere in norms for SC/ST seats in house'

NEW DELHI: Refusing to blur the constitutional 'Lakshman Rekha' that separates the three organs of governance,

Wednesday said it cannot usurp legislature's exclusive powers to interfere in the criteria for reserving an assembly or parliamentary constituency for Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes.

"We cannot become the third chamber of Parliament," a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said while refusing to entertain a petition seeking quashing of a notification reserving Kadipur assembly constituency in UP for SCs.

The CJI-led bench said identification of constituencies to reserve them for SCs or STs was the sole prerogative of the legislature and the court could not interfere in it, and suggested the petitioner could resort to protests to make elected representatives take corrective measures.



The bench, which has been dealing with a large number of petitions on CJP protests, said in a lighter vein, "It is a good season for protest, dharna and 'naare baji'. You can also raise your voice (in protest) and tell the elected representatives that time is ripe for revising the criteria of reserving constituencies for the SC community and adopt the principle of rotational reservation. By approaching the constitutional court, you have dialled a wrong number.





"

Appearing for a petitioner, senior advocate Gagan Gupta questioned the manner in which constituencies were geographically identified and reserved for SCs and asked whether "Section 9(1)(c) of the Delimitation Act, 2002, can constitutionally operate in a manner which permits the same territorial constituencies to remain reserved for SCs over successive electoral cycles without any mechanism for periodic rotation".

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The bench said, "Delimitation is a legislative exercise and the guidelines for carrying out that exercise cannot be tweaked by the courts. Can the judiciary mandate the Delimitation Commission to adopt rotational reservation policy while demarcating constituencies for SCs?"

The SC agreed with Allahabad HC, which had said that since Articles 330 and 332 provide for reserving constituencies for SCs and STs, no general candidate could claim that his right to contest from constituencies reserved for SCs and STs was violated.

World.title: Prez can be prosecuted after leaving office but not ECs, says petitioner
World.content:
The Supreme Court has tagged two petitions challenging Section 16 of Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, with a pending plea raising a similar issue.

The provision bars courts from entertaining or continuing civil or criminal proceedings against serving or former CECs and election commissioners for acts done or purported to be done in discharge of official duties.

A bench told lawyers for Manoj Jha and Arun Agrawal that the cases would be tagged with the pending matter.

Jha's plea argues that Section 16 gives officials wider protection than President, MPs, and SC and HC judges, covering civil and criminal proceedings during tenure and for life, without exceptions for corruption, mala fides or crime.



It says President may be prosecuted after leaving office, while a former election commissioner arguably cannot.

"A member of Parliament who takes a bribe to vote can be tried but an EC who takes a bribe while "purporting" to act in office arguably cannot. A sitting judge of this court can be prosecuted with sanction yet a retired election commissioner cannot be prosecuted with or without it. The Constitution places no functionary above the law, however Section 16 of the CEC does," the plea said.

Agrawal's plea said the wording "is or was" creates lifelong immunity, while "purporting to act" could cover conduct outside lawful authority. It said the provision contained no good-faith condition and could bar prosecution for corruption, forgery and other serious offences.

World.content: The gunfight at Taodaijang village in Noney involved militants of Zeliangrong United Front-Jenchui (ZUF-J) and Zeliangrong United Front-Kamson (ZUF-K), the latter backed by NSCN-IM. Two of the dead belonged to ZUF-J, a signatory to the cessation of operations (CoO) agreement with Centre since 2022, and the third to ZUF-K.The trigger for the clash was purportedly a statement from ZUF-K on Nov 1, accusing ZUF-J of betraying the Naga by hobnobbing with security forces.In Kangpokpi district, Committee on Tribal Unity, Sadar Hills, extended its shutdown by 48 hours, until 5 pm on Nov 6, after accusing the govt of failing to identify who abducted and killed two Kuki-Zo tribesmen last week.The fresh turmoil comes a day after chief minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh directed security agencies to identify "active" armed groups, excluding those engaged in peace talks with the state govt.

on the Kedartal trekking route in Uttarkashi district, with rescue teams recovering two more bodies on Wednesday, taking the toll to four, report Gaurav Talwar & Ashish Mishra. World.title: Private sector participation in nuclear energy: AERB will provide enabling environment without compromising safety, says Chairperson
World.content:
A.K. Balasubrahmanian, Chairperson, Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB), has sought to allay concerns regarding the entry of private players into the country’s sensitive nuclear energy sector, asserting that there will be no compromise on safety aspects. The sector, he said, is being opened up at the right time, given the emerging power requirement of the country.

As a regulator, the AERB will provide an “enabling environment” for private players, but at the same time, the board will not dilute the regulatory and safety requirements, Mr. Balasubrahmanian told The Hindu on the sidelines of a two-day symposium on the emerging frontiers in nuclear science and technology organised here this week by the Atomic Energy Retirees’ Association.

World.title: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed claims victory in Michigan Senate battle
World.content:
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed said early on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) that he had won a US Senate seat in Michigan over former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, which would make him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.

“Michigan, we did it!” Mr. El-Sayed said in a speech at his election headquarters in Detroit.

“I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.”

U.S. midterm elections 2026 LIVE updates

Mr. El-Sayed won despite a last-minute hiccup in his campaign when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, came out in support of Rogers at the 11th hour.

The Michigan doctor rallied voters on leftist campaign promises, including universal health care, to hold a key U.S. Senate seat for Democrats, taking over from the retiring Gary Peters.

Republicans ran a scorched-earth campaign to paint Democrats as communists and branded Mr. El-Sayed a terrorist who would endanger Americans.

But the straight-talking 42-year-old El-Sayed pledged to help cash-strapped voters navigate America’s thorny health care system.

“You deserve to be able to see a doctor without getting a huge bill,” he told Michiganders on the eve of the vote, vowing to upend America’s divisive multi-billion-dollar for-profit medical system.

During the race, Mr. El-Sayed drew huge campaign crowds across the state, even in deeply conservative Republican areas.

Mr. El-Sayed also vowed to get “money out of politics” and address the harsh economic woes that have voters yearning for a political newcomer to shake up the status quo.

The election makes Mr. El-Sayed the first Democratic doctor in the Senate since 1969.

Tech billionaire Elon Musk joked on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) about Republicans' defeat in U.S. midterm elections after spending hundreds of millions of dollars to help the party.

World.title: U.S. Midterm election Democrats win five governor races as Hinojosa, Bottoms, Haaland make history
World.content:
Democrats are on track for big gains in governor races, notching victories in Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Georgia and Wisconsin, according to U.S. media projections, with a number of other races still too early to call as of early Wednesday (November 4, 2026).

Three candidates made history. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the country’s first Black woman elected governor. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa became the first Latina governor in the state’s history, unseating a well-financed Republican incumbent in a historically conservative state. And in New Mexico, Democrat Deb Haaland became the country’s first female Native American governor.

A total of three dozen governor races were on the ballot in the elections, with President Donald Trump’s unpopularity and the cost of living at the top of voters’ minds, alongside local concerns ranging from water rights and data centres to cancer rates.

If Democrats can manage a net gain of at least two seats, they will lead a majority of states for the first time since 2010.

Here are eight key governor races.

Gina Hinojosa becomes state’s first Latina governor in Texas

Ms. Hinojosa, a Texas state representative, defeated Texas Governor Greg Abbott to become the first Democrat to be elected governor since 1990. She also became the first Latina governor in the state’s history.

Ms. Hinojosa emerged as an unexpected competitor to one of the best-known and best-funded Republican governors in the country. Mr. Abbott outspent her nearly 8-1, according to The Texas Tribune.

Democrats initially wrote off the Texas governor’s race and struggled to find a candidate willing to run against Mr. Abbott.

Keisha Lance Bottoms becomes first Black woman elected governor in U.S.

Ms. Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, beat Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire healthcare executive, in the race to succeed Republican Governor Brian Kemp. In doing so, she became the first Black woman elected governor in the U.S. and the first Democrat elected governor of Georgia in more than a quarter century.

Both parties viewed the gubernatorial race as an early test of voter sentiment in a state that will likely be a key presidential battleground in 2028.

Mr. Jackson, who spent more than $100 million of his own money on the race, generally aligned himself with Mr. Trump’s agenda, while Ms. Bottoms sought to mobilise the diverse Democratic coalition that helped Joe Biden win the state in 2020.

Ms. Bottoms rose to national prominence in 2020 as she guided Georgia’s largest city through protests, civil unrest and the COVID-19 pandemic. Her base is in the Atlanta metro area, whose rapid growth has reshaped Georgia politics.

Amy Acton defeats Vivek Ramaswamy after a contentious campaign in Ohio

Democrat Amy Acton, a physician, defeated Republican entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy after a race that drew national attention over an explosive attack ad featuring Ms. Acton’s estranged mother. In a video run by the Ramaswamy campaign, Donna Arthur disputed Ms. Acton’s account of a childhood marked by homelessness and sexual abuse and urged Ohioans not to vote for her.

Ms. Acton, a former director of the Ohio Department of Health who led the state’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic, has said she was sexually abused by her stepfather. The stepfather, who died in 2004, fled the state after he was charged with raping his stepdaughter and never stood trial.

The state’s reputation as a perennial swing state faded after 2016, when Mr. Trump won it with strong support from working-class voters, who helped to turn it into a reliably Republican state. Democrats have won just one of the state’s last nine gubernatorial elections.

Rob Sand wins first open governor’s race since 2006 in Iowa

State Auditor Rob Sand, the only Iowa Democrat currently holding statewide elected office, beat Republican businessman Zach Lahn in the state’s first open governor’s race since 2006. Incumbent Republican Governor Kim Reynolds did not seek re-election.

The state’s incidence of cancer, at the second-highest rate in the country behind Kentucky, emerged as a major campaign topic alongside kitchen-table issues such as the cost of living. Interest was fuelled by worries that exposure to nitrates, pesticides and other environmental contaminants may be contributing to the high cancer rate.

The race also focused on education and government accountability. Mr. Sand campaigned as an independent watchdog critical of Republican fiscal management and the state’s private-school voucher programme. Mr. Lahn embraced lower taxes, school choice and a more conservative approach to social issues.

David Crowley defeats Trump-endorsed Tom Tiffany in Wisconsin

A central question in Wisconsin’s gubernatorial race has been whether voters, who backed Mr. Trump in 2024 and Mr. Biden in 2020, want a governor aligned with the Republican president. Republican Tom Tiffany, a three-term U.S. representative endorsed by Mr. Trump, has played down that connection. But his Democratic opponent, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, won the race after seeking to link Mr. Tiffany to Mr. Trump’s agenda.

In Congress, Mr. Tiffany has supported conservative causes such as gun rights and lower taxes, and co-sponsored federal legislation that would have banned most abortions after about six weeks of pregnancy. Mr. Crowley campaigned on support for abortion rights. Wisconsin bans abortion after 20 weeks and requires a 24-hour waiting period as well as parental consent for minors.

Democrat Aaron Ford trumps Joe Lombardo in tight race

Democrat Aaron Ford won the election as Governor of Nevada, defeating Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo.

Mr. Ford, the attorney general, defeated the incumbent Mr. Lombardo in what was considered one of the country’s most competitive governor’s races.

Mr. Ford ran with the backing of the Democratic congressional delegation, California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice-President Kamala Harris.

All eyes on Arizona as race yet to be called in drought-hit state

Water has become a key campaign issue in drought-hit Arizona, where Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs is seeking re-election against Republican U.S. Representative Andy Biggs. Other top issues are the cost of living and immigration, with Ms. Hobbs seeking to position herself as tougher on border security than many national Democrats.

Mr. Biggs is a former head of the right-wing U.S. House Freedom Caucus, which has pushed for deep cuts in federal spending. Abortion rights have featured prominently in the race, with Ms. Hobbs a supporter while Mr. Biggs has a long record as an opponent. Arizona voters approved a constitutional amendment protecting abortion rights in 2024.

Democrat Jocelyn Benson and Republican John James battle for Michigan

Michigan’s race was one of the most competitive gubernatorial contests, pitting Democrat Jocelyn Benson, the state’s top election official, against Republican U.S. Representative John James. The candidates were battling to succeed term-limited Democratic Governor Gretchen Whitmer, making it one of 19 open-seat races this cycle.

Michigan is a closely divided swing state that Mr. Trump won in 2016 and 2024, while Mr. Biden carried it in 2020. Neither party has elected back-to-back governors in the state since the 1960s.

World.title: U.S. VP Vance says Iran war was the reason Republicans lost midterms
World.content:
U.S. Vice-President JD Vance said on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) that the Iran war was the reason Republicans lost the midterm elections, as he sought to distance himself from the conflict ahead of a possible 2028 White House run.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Mr. Vance said in a lengthy post on X, apparently referring to President Donald Trump’s remarks that the war was “part of it” but remained justified.

“Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” Mr. Vance added.

Mr. Vance had reportedly been sceptical about the war, which Mr. Trump launched in February.

World.title: U.S. midterm elections 2026 LIVE: Republican U.S. House Speaker to step down; Zelenskyy hopes Democrat gains will bring more help for Ukraine
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in an interview on Wednesday (November 4, 2026), said he hoped gains by Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections would generate more help for Ukraine in its war with Russia. His remarks came after Democrats seized control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress in a sweeping rejection of U.S. President Trump’s party and his policies. “I am also grateful to the Republicans, but the Democrats speak very clearly about supporting Ukraine and providing assistance to Ukraine,” he said in comments provided in German by ZDF before the interview was broadcast.

Also read: U.S. Midterm Election night agenda: When polls close and when to expect results

U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson will step down as Republican leader following his party’s crushing midterm election defeat, his spokesperson confirmed. Mr. Johnson, the highest-ranking Republican in the United States after President Donald Trump and Vice-President J.D. Vance, is second in the line of presidential succession.

Also read: U.S. midterm elections: An economy under pressure, political shift and the road ahead

Mr. Trump backed Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) as questions swirl about his future following the midterms rout. Asked whether he was considering replacing Hegseth, whom he has described as a champion of the war, Mr. Trump told reporters: “No, I think he’s doing a very good job.” The vote reflected deep anger over living costs, tariffs and Mr. Trump’s war against Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular President.

(With inputs from agencies)

World.title: DRI seizes 7.85 kg of hashish smuggled from U.S. to Mumbai in mirror frame; one arrested
World.content:
The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) has seized 7.85 kg of hashish concealed inside the wooden frame of a bathroom mirror shipped from New York to Mumbai through an international courier service. One person was arrested on November 2 in connection with the seizure, officials said.

Acting on specific intelligence, officers of the DRI’s Mumbai Zonal Unit intercepted a suspicious consignment at the International Courier Terminal in Mumbai. The parcel, declared as a framed bathroom wall mirror, was examined for suspected drug concealment.

During the inspection, officers dismantled the wooden frame and recovered eight concealed packets containing 169 smaller packets of a blackish, resinous substance. Preliminary testing using a Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) field testing kit returned a positive result for hashish. The recovered substance had a total gross weight of 7.85 kg.

Following the seizure, DRI officials traced the consignee of the parcel and arrested the person on November 2 under the provisions of the NDPS Act, 1985. The agency has not disclosed the identity of the arrested person.

Officials said further investigation is under way to identify others involved in the smuggling operation and establish possible links to domestic and international drug trafficking networks.

World.title: Vance tries to distance himself from Iran war after Republican Party’s deep losses in midterm elections
World.content:
J.D. Vance publicly broke from President Donald Trump's defence of the Iran war on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) after the Republican Party's deep losses in the midterm elections, attempting to distance himself from voters' clear rebuke of the President as the Vice President faces questions about his own political ambitions.

Mr. Vance, who has said he would decide after the election whether to run for President in 2028, issued a lengthy social media post blaming the unpopular conflict with Iran for the GOP's (Grand Old Party) drubbing. Mr. Vance said, "If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”

But arguing that the war was worth it is what Mr. Trump repeatedly did on the campaign trail and continued to do in interviews as election results came in. Mr. Trump told The New York Times late Tuesday that the decision to go to war this year was “very wise" and told Politico it was “an absolutely correct one.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) about the Vice President's post.

The Republican, who had long advocated for restraint in U.S. military intervention overseas, was lukewarm in his defence of the conflict after Mr. Trump launched it and even became the face of an unsuccessful attempt to end the fighting.

About six in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to the AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 1,00,000 voters in the United States. Most of those voters dissatisfied with the Iran war backed the Democratic candidate in their U.S. House race, but the survey suggested the Iran war was not the leading issue for most voters.

Only about one-third of voters said the war in Iran was “crucial” to their vote for Congress, well below the roughly half who said that about the cost of living or government corruption.

Nearly all voters who backed the Democratic candidate in their U.S. House race said going to war with Iran was the “wrong decision,” while roughly eight in 10 voters who backed the Republican candidate said it was the “right decision.”

A former Marine who served in Iraq, Mr. Vance had been critical of that conflict and said after becoming Vice President that a Trump administration would not send troops into the “open-ended conflicts” of the past.

After Mr. Trump launched the war with Iran this past spring, Mr. Vance was noticeably quiet in speaking about it, a conspicuous change for a politician known for being a pugnacious defender of the President.

This summer, he tried to argue the conflict was worth it, telling conservative podcast host Megyn Kelly in an interview that, “If we transformed the Middle East, this is fundamentally worth it."

But after Democrats swept control of both the House and the Senate on Tuesday (November 3, 2026), defeating GOP candidates even in deep-red areas that Mr. Trump carried by wide margins two years ago, Mr. Vance said in his post that “the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone."

He said Republican voters cast their ballots for Democrats because of the war, the cost of living, America not being prioritised and the U.S. relationship with Israel — a dynamic where he's also sounded a different note than Mr. Trump.

Unlike the President, Mr. Vance declined to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection and this summer publicly chastised members of Israel’s government for opposing Mr. Trump’s efforts to resolve the war with Iran.

Mr. Vance, who has been a staunch defender of the administration's immigration policies, also appeared to be seeking some distance from the immigration crackdown that drew a backlash.

“I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement — by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance,” he wrote.

But he said he rejected any politicians who might propose amnesty for people living in the country illegally.

World.title: Riyadh rolls over $3bn as prospects of $10bn US facility wane
World.content:
• Aurangzeb says proposed US facility is not essential, would provide additional support if secured

• Further Eurobond, Panda bond and rupee-linked dollar-settled issuances planned

• Govt targets $4bn reduction in external debt

ISLAMABAD: Pakistan has secured a $3 billion rollover from Saudi Arabia, as prospects of a proposed $10bn US backstop facility appear to have waned, it emerged on Wednesday.

Speaking to journalists at Parliament House, Finance Minister Muhammad Auran­gzeb confirmed that Riyadh had extended the $3bn financing it provided in April this year to bridge a gap arising from $3.5bn in repayments to the United Arab Emirates.

“It has been extended and for a reasonable period. You don’t need to worry as to for how long given the kind of strategic relationship we have,” he said when asked about the facility, which matured on Oct 31 under its three-month term.

He said he had a very good meeting with his Saudi counterpart, Mohammed Al-Jadaan, during the recent World Bank-IMF meetings in Bangkok. Saudi Arabia had already extended its $5bn facility until 2028.

Asked whether Pakistan had also sought additional support, the minister categorically denied it, saying this was not needed as foreign exchange reserves covered more than three months of imports and would be strengthened to provide a four-month import cover by the end of the year through capital markets.

Responding to another question about the prospects of the $10bn Exchange Stabilisation Support Facility (ESSF) requested from the US in July this year, he sought to lower expectations that he himself had raised over the past several months. “What we asked for back in July and were looking at was the market access. We have got the market access,” he said, referring to the $3bn bond Pakistan issued in September against orders worth $6bn.

“If that (ESSF) materialises, fantastic, it will be a liquidity support facility. Otherwise, we have plans for further Eurobond issuance, Panda bond issuance and rupee-linked dollar-settled bond,” the minister said.

He added that he had held meetings with 70-80 institutional investors in Bangkok, who had a very clear view of Pakistan, and that offers were available for five-year and 10-year maturities, “because clearly we are looking beyond the [IMF] programme”.

He said the government was looking at the US from a broader perspective, as the US Export-Import Bank and Development Finance Corporation (DFC) needed to support their investors and exporters in Pakistan. “That is real financing and real credit,” he said, adding that the ESSF request was for a liquidity support facility to help the sovereign. “If possible, fine; if not, we are going to move forward, with or without it.”

The finance minister also reported that the IMF Executive Board meeting to approve a disbursement of $1.2bn to Pakistan would be held in December.

External debt

Earlier, he told the Senate Standing Committee on Finance that Pakistan was targeting a reduction of $4bn in external debt during the current fiscal year and $3.5bn next year, compared with $4.5bn in the last fiscal year.

He said the government was seeking to replace expensive short-term borrowing with longer-maturity financing through bonds and private placements to reduce refinancing risks. He said external debt had been rising by $5-6bn annually, from $45bn in 2014-15 to around $100bn, but had increased by only $1bn annually over the past two years.

“Our objective is not to increase external debt. All the transactions like Eurobond, Panda bond or private placements have been replacement bonds to replace expensive with cheaper facilities,” he said, adding that fiscal discipline had helped contain the fiscal and current account deficits and, despite oil and wheat import bills, the current account deficit would be no more than 1pc this year.

“This is hard-earned stability that helped create buffers to meet our requirements despite floods and war in the region, and foreign exchange reserves crossed $21.5bn, which is the best-ever level of reserves in our history,” he said, adding that Pakistan could not afford to lose this basic hygiene.

Finance Secretary Imdadullah Bosal told the committee, which was presided over by Senator Saleem Mandviwalla, that public debt had declined to 68.6pc of GDP by the end of June 2026, from 75.1pc in fiscal year 2022-23. Year-on-year growth in public debt had slowed to 7.7pc in the last fiscal year, the lowest in 20 years, he said.

The secretary said domestic debt amounted to Rs58.8 trillion by the end of August 2026, down from Rs68.4tr at the end of June, while foreign debt remained stable at $98.2bn.

He reported net financing requirements of $11bn after rollovers and refinancing, of which $5bn had already been repaid in the first four months of the current fiscal year. The remaining $6bn was payable over the next seven months.

The committee took strong exception to the difficulties faced by parliamentarians in obtaining foreign exchange for personal travel, saying the humiliation they faced at the hands of banks and the central bank was unacceptable.

Mr Mandviwalla directed the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) to review existing procedures, including clearance requirements relating to politically exposed persons (PEPs) and the mandatory personal appearance of parliamentarians before exchange companies, despite their submission of valid passports, tickets and visas.

The committee also expressed serious displeasure over the SBP’s response, dated Oct 30, 2026, to a letter sent by the committee secretary on its behalf to the SBP governor. It observed that the matter had been addressed by a deputy director-level officer instead of an appropriately senior authority.

The chairman termed the requirement for personal appearance humiliating and called for an immediate review of the existing procedures, warning that the committee would take serious notice if the matter remained unresolved.

Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

World.title: 'United opposition' gathers at Fazl's Islamabad residence, vows stronger alliance
World.content:
Opposition leaders on Wednesday gathered at the residence of Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman in Islamabad and agreed to strengthen their alliance and parliamentary coordination.

After a meeting during which they discussed several matters, including the emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, JUI-F and TTAP decided to form committees to resolve mutual differences and take forward consultations on a multi-party conference (MPC).

National Assembly (NA) and Senate opposition leaders, Mahmood Khan Achakzai and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, respectively, attended the meeting. MNA Asad Qaiser, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja, NA Chief Whip Amir Dogar and Senator Noorul Haq Qadri were present from PTI.

Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) — headed by Achakzai — termed it a meeting of a “united opposition”.

An earlier statement by JUI-F said the gathering was to discuss “the situation of emergency and governor’s rule” in KP, as well as plans for an MPC.

In its statement, TTAP said the meeting was also “discussing unity and solidarity among opposition parties, the supremacy of the Constitution and law, the protection of democratic rights, a joint strategy to address the current political situation, and a future course of action”.

On Aug 20, following a meeting between Fazl and Achakzai, the alliance and JUI-F had announced plans to form a “united opposition”.

Speaking to the media after the meeting, Achakzai said the delegation had called on Fazl with the objective of building an alliance to strengthen Parliament.

He condemned what he described as a character assassination campaign against the JUI-F chief and declared that the opposition stood firmly with him.

He added that the possibility of convening an MPC was also discussed during the meeting.

In his remarks, Fazl also said the opposition would work to strengthen its presence in Parliament and protect the interests of every part of the country.

Referring to the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (Fata), he said his party had opposed the 2018 merger, adding that the issue was now being linked to a struggle over resources.

He also expressed concern over what he alleged were attempts to bring Gwadar, the coastal belt and Sindh’s islands under federal control.

The JUI-F chief said the opposition had already represented the people’s concerns regarding the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, stressing that it was speaking about the public mandate and national interests.

The leaders agreed to continue consultations and establish a committee to address differences among opposition parties.

Senator Abbas alleged that the governor’s rule had been illegally imposed in KP and accused the authorities of targeting those who raised their voices for the country’s welfare.

On its part, the Centre maintains that the security situation in the province and the PTI-led provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the counterterrorism fight “compelled” it to take the measures on Oct 11.

Addressing reporters, the Senate opposition leader lamented that the sanctity of homes and the privacy of citizens were being violated as authorities detained people from their residences.

He warned of decreasing public confidence in the country’s institutions, claiming Pakistan had reached one of the worst periods in its history.

TTAP said its spokesperson Akhundzada Hussain Ahmad Yousafzai, PTI founder Imran Khan’s legal counsel Khalid Yousaf Chaudhry, and Agha Nasir Shirazi also attended the meeting.

The JUI-F team included its vice-president and KP chapter president Senator Maulana Attaur Rehman, senators Kamran Murtaza and Maulana Attaul Haq Darwish, alongside party members Akram Khan Durrani, Aslam Ghauri, Maulana Salahuddin Ayubi, Hafiz Hamdullah and Zahid Durrani.

PTI alarmed over Imran’s ‘high blood pressure’

Meanwhile, PTI’s Raja raised concerns about Imran’s health, saying his blood pressure was not under control. He thanked Fazl for supporting the PTI and alleged that the JUI-F chief was being “punished” for standing with the party.

Imran — in prison since Aug 5, 2023 in multiple cases — had complained of uncontrolled and fluctuating blood pressure along with palpitations, headache and restlessness in early August, according to annexures attached to a jail report submitted to the Supreme Court (SC).

In an official statement issued today, PTI expressed grave concern over its founder’s health, saying his blood pressure had surged to 192. It demanded his immediate transfer to Shifa International Hospital for independent medical treatment under the supervision of his personal physicians.

PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram said repeated fluctuations in the ex-cricketer’s blood pressure were a matter of extreme concern, stressing that protecting his health was the responsibility of the state.

He accused the government of denying Imran adequate medical facilities, family access and treatment of his choice.

He demanded immediate implementation of the SC’s Aug 18 order directing Imran’s transfer to Shifa International Hospital, with treatment supervised by his personal and family-appointed doctors.

Imran’s eye ailment — right central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) — came to light in late January. While he has undergone eye procedures and check-ups at the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), his family demands that he be shifted to a hospital of his choice.

The government and the opposition have been engaged in a blame game , with the latter accusing the former of a lack of transparency on the matter, of not ensuring appropriate treatment for Imran, and of not allowing his personal physicians access to him.

The government denies these allegations, saying the required medical treatment is being ensured and ample facilities are being provided at the Adiala jail, including a healthy diet plan and exercise equipment.

Fazl’s PTI ties amid row with Centre

Wednesday’s gathering came a day after PTI said it would welcome support from Fazl in its struggle against the government, with Raja telling the media that the party would welcome anyone who stood by it and supported its struggle.

“It is possible that some may walk with us for one mile, some for 10 miles, and some may go with us till the end. But why should we reject them?” the PTI secretary general said.

Fazl has been critical of the federal government over the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He accused the Centre of reneging on its commitments amid his efforts to mediate between the federal and KP governments.

Since mid-October , the veteran politician and key federal ministers have also made harsh remarks against each other, after Fazl accused the Centre of depriving the provinces of their rights.

Last week, Fazl accused the government of misusing the Constitution and resorting to unconstitutional measures in imposing the emergency.

In September, TTAP and PTI leaders said they intended to hold consultations to call an MPC to discuss several issues, including the creation of new provinces, law and order, and the economy. This was prior to the government’s declaration of emergency and governor’s rule in KP on Oct 11.

In the days preceding the emergency, political tensions between the Centre and the opposition — including the PTI, which was in power in KP — had remained high since Imran’s party announced a protest march to Islamabad to demand his release.

World.title: Petrol price dropped by Rs7.06 per litre, high-speed diesel by Rs3.71
World.content:
The government on Wednesday cut the price of petrol by Rs7.06 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs3.71.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs362.00 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs387.81 on Nov 5 (Thursday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

Wednesday’s cut is the third consecutive reduction in fuel prices.

It came as international oil prices fell under $100 in volatile trade on Wednesday, with investors awaiting Washington’s next move in the US-Israeli war with Iran after President Donald Trump’s Republican Party lost control of Congress in midterm elections.

Brent futures were down $4.50, or 4.3 per cent, to $99.07 a barrel at 1619 GMT (9:19pm, PKT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures are down $4.13, or 4.3pc, to $92.02.

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

Under an arrangement announced on Monday for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end.

Addressing a press conference on Tuesday, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik said efforts were being made to introduce a similar system for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).

Meanwhile, the Jamaat-i-Islami and the government are set to follow up on their recent discussions on possible relief in petroleum prices and hold another round of talks on Thursday, the party said.

Rise in fuel prices

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months.

On Sept 13, PM Shehbaz also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices.

Previously, on July 17, the petroleum minister announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Additional input by Reuters

World.title: UN panel hails Pakistan’s marriage-age law, flags bonded labour
World.content:
• Experts seek details on child brides, rehabilitation of flood victims and reconstruction efforts

• Pakistani delegation says 600,000 destroyed homes rebuilt

ISLAMABAD: The United Nations Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights on Wednesday concluded its review of Pakistan’s second periodic report under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, welcoming the country’s 2025 legal amendment raising the minimum age of marriage to 18.

However, committee members raised questions about bonded labour and reconstruction efforts following the 2022 and 2025 floods, among other topics.

Committee expert and member of the task force for Pakistan, Michael Windfuhr, welcomed the 2025 amendment to the Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929, which raised the minimum age of marriage to 18 for both males and females.

However, he noted that the committee remained concerned about the high number of child brides and asked about the impact of measures taken to prevent child marriage.

Lazhari Bouzid, another committee expert and member of the task force for Pakistan, said bonded labour continued to be prevalent in agriculture and was also found in the informal sector, particularly brick making.

Construction companies and government agencies were reportedly complicit in the practice by purchasing bricks produced through debt bondage. He asked how Pakistan had responded to these reports.

Mr Windfuhr also asked how the country had coped with the impact of the devastating floods in 2022 and 2025. He inquired whether Pakistan could rebuild housing for affected people and restore their access to land or resources, and how many people remained displaced.

‘Range of measures’

Minister of State for Law and Justice and head of the delegation, Barrister Aqeel Malik, said in his opening remarks that Pakistan had taken a range of legislative, policy and institutional measures since 2017 for the progressive realisation of covenant rights.

He said child marriage restraint laws had set the minimum age of marriage at 18 for both boys and girls in Islamabad, Balochistan, Punjab and Sindh, and criminalised child, early and forced marriages.

During the ensuing dialogue, the delegation said Pakistan’s Constitution prohibited slavery and all forms of forced labour, while the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1992 had abolished the practice.

Punjab had documented more than 210,000 kiln workers, and district vigilance committees had been established in many districts. Labour inspectors had identified more than 2,900 victims of forced labour last year.

On flood recovery, the delegation said the government had established a national emergency operations centre focusing on high-risk areas and launched a national flood protection programme. The programme aimed to protect at-risk people, eight million acres of agricultural land and 2.2 million housing units.

Each province was also implementing flood protection measures. Of the 2.1 million homes destroyed in the 2022 floods, 600,000 had been rebuilt, while reconstruction of the remaining houses was under way.

In her concluding remarks, committee expert and task force leader for Pakistan, Julieta Rossi, said the delegation had outlined processes for implementing economic, social and cultural rights, as well as the significant challenges facing the country and gaps between legislative progress and implementation.

“This information would be reflected in the committee’s concluding observations, which the panel hoped that Pakistan would implement in good faith,” she added.

Mr Malik said in his concluding remarks that the delegation had outlined its efforts to bridge the gaps between constitutional guarantees and their realisation.

“The country’s trajectory was toward the progressive realisation of covenant rights,” he said, adding that despite constraints and challenges, Pakistan had made considerable progress since its first review.

“[Pakistan] hopes that the committee’s candour and rigour will help pave the way for the full realisation of economic, social and cultural rights for all,” he added.

Committee vice chair and acting chair of the dialogue, Asraf Ally Caunhye, thanked the delegation for its participation in the constructive dialogue and its expression of unwavering commitment to protecting the rights enshrined in the covenant.

The Pakistani delegation comprised representatives from the Ministry of Law and Justice, the Ministry of Human Rights and the Permanent Mission of Pakistan to the United Nations Office at Geneva.

Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

World.title: Foreign ministry told to tighten accounting rules
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: A parliamentary committee on Wednesday criticised the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for having no control over funds management and lax accounting procedures, instructing its new secretary Asim Iftikhar Ahmad to streamline and tighten accounting procedures and make rules and share them with the committee.

The directive came after the Public Accounts Committee, while discussing audit objections of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs 2024-25, observed that its staff posted in foreign missions was embezzling and mismanaging public funds without accountability.

One case in particular caused massive losses to the public exchequer, when an ex-accountant posted in the Pakistan embassy in Vienna, Austria, fraudulently drew 442,256 euros and $134,292 over a period of two years.

Officials from the office of Auditor General of Pakistan suspected that the former accountant was not alone in tampering and transferring the public money into his personal and wife’s bank accounts and that senior officials in the Pakistani Mission were also involved in the scam.

PAC told staff posted in foreign missions ‘embezzling funds’

The PAC expressed strong dissatisfaction with Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) for failing to recover the embezzled amount after a case was registered against the ex-accountant, Muhammad Sulaiman Qureshi, six years ago.

Members of the panel were more surprised upon learning that Muhammad Sulaiman Qureshi was in Pakistan and he has been out on bail.

The chairman of the committee, MNA Naveed Qamar, directed officials concerned to summon the FIA director general for a better response.

Similarly, another accountant, during posting in Pakistan emb­assy in Sofia, Bulgaria, also frau­dulently withdrew 56,499 Lev and $74,415 between 2018-23.

Audit officials expressed concern that the misappropriated public money had still not been recovered from the accountant. Furthermore, the accountant, after being dismissed from service, approached courts, which reinstated him in service.

In response to failure to recover the embezzled amount, the PAC chairman directed that officials investigating fraud should be exempted from travel bans introduced under austerity measures.

In another case pertaining to unjustified retention of heavy balance of Higher Education Commission (HEC) on account of overseas scholarship in the US, amounting to $4.5 million, the PAC expressed surprise why the funds had not been disbursed among needy students.

“The Pakistani mission did not have clear instructions from HEC on the matter,” said Asim Iftikhar Ahmad.

In response, Mr Qamar argued that HEC should be held accountable over this. Similarly, in another matter pertaining to unauthorised borrowing of loan from HEC’s account of 360,000 euros, Mr Ahmad said that his office was in process of returning funds to the commission.

In the case of unjustified blockage of government funds in an unauthorised suspense account in Dhaka, Bangladesh, a sum of $1.143m was parked idle. Audit officials observed that holding a huge amount in suspense account without approval of the finance division was a clear violation of rules, which required settlement of inevitable payment at the earliest.

They also observed that the Pakistani mission maintaining the US dollar account in the name of suspense account for payment of rent of chancery whose ownership issue was disputed, had not been resolved yet. The PAC referred the matter to departmental accounts committee.

Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

World.title: Swat basin faces over 5°C warming by century’s end
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: A glacier risk assessment of the Swat watershed has war­ned that the basin is expected to warm by more than 5°C by the end of the century, particularly bet­ween October and June.

Winter rainfall is expected to change little, but summer rainfall could more than double under some climate scenarios, according to the assessment carried out by the Green Climate Fund (GCF), with support from the Asian Development Bank (ADB).

The changes are likely to increase the risk of severe floods and erosion, cause a short-term rise in water availability due to glacier melt and runoff, and lead to long-term declines as glaciers continue to recede, according to the assessment made available on Wednesday.

The Swat basin, which has more than 10,000 glaciers, faces an increased risk of infrastructure failure and resulting floods. The assessment also warned of agricultural losses, erosion in valley areas, and a short-term water surplus followed by a long-term deficit.

The GCF has conducted glacier risk assessments for four representative wat­e­rsheds: Kura (Arme­nia, Azerbaijan and Georgia), Naryn (Kyrgyz Republic, with downstream links to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan), Pyanj (Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Afghanistan) and Swat (Hindu Kush-Karakoram-Himalaya).

The four pilot basins capture diverse glacier and hydrological conditions across Central and West Asia. Together, they illustrate how elevation, glacier mass and snow duration shape regional water supplies and risks.

These assessments serve as initial pilots under the ‘Glacier to Farms’ (G2F) programme and complement the existing ADB country-level climate risk assessments. Although only four basins were studied, they were strategically selected to represent the nine developing member countries covered by G2F and inform the programme’s future expansion to other transboundary watersheds and basins in the region.

The climate risk and capacity assessment of the four glacier-fed watersheds in Central and West Asia highlights accelerating glacier retreat, growing water security risks and priority actions to strengthen resilience, adaptation and regional cooperation.

The assessment analysed 40 years of weather records to identify spatial and temporal variations in temperature, rainfall and snowfall across mountain and lowland areas. Historical data were used to bias-correct global climate models to improve their local accuracy. Statistical clustering of multiple models produced basin-specific projections focused on glacier, snow and permafrost areas, providing a realistic basis for understanding future climate impacts across the G2F region.

It analysed long-term temperature, precipitation and cryosphere trends across the four watersheds to establish a regional baseline and develop future scenarios for 2035, 2055, 2085 and 2100. Using multi-model climate datasets validated against regional observations, the analysis identified key impact pathways, sectoral risks and opportunities to strengthen resilience in agriculture, energy and human settlements.

Across the G2F basins, temperatures are projected to rise by around 3°C to 5°C by the end of the century, accelerating the loss of glaciers, snow and permafrost. Seasonal water availability will shift, with earlier snowmelt and river flow peaks, while hotter summers will increase drought risks and water demand. Although some areas may receive more winter precipitation, overall water availability will decline as glacier-fed runoff diminishes.

The assessment examines how projected changes in temperature, precipitation and glacier mass will affect hazards, water resources and livelihoods across the G2F region. It highlights the main risks — glacier retreat, slope instability and shifting water availability — and explains how these processes interact to shape local and downstream impacts.

Risks associated with glacier melt and extreme events, such as glacial lake outburst floods (Glofs) and landslides, are already high across High Mountain Asia and are expected to intensify as the climate continues to warm. However, the assessment notes that appropriate resilience measures can reduce these risks to manageable levels.

As glaciers and permafrost melt, slopes and natural dams become unstable, increasing the likelihood of rockfalls, ice avalanches and Glofs. Such events can travel long distances, threatening homes, roads and other infrastructure in mountainous and downstream areas.

Heavier rain and snowfall, followed by rapid spring melting, are likely to trigger flash floods and debris flows. Inadequate watershed management will exacerbate these effects, accelerating soil erosion, degrading water quality and compromising the integrity of dams and irrigation systems.

Higher temperatures will increase water demand, particularly during summer. Glacier melt has historically provided a buffer against drought in the region, but this buffer will disappear as glaciers retreat and heatwaves intensify, reducing water supplies when they are most needed.

Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

World.title: US Vice President JD Vance says Iran war is 'the reason we lost' midterms
World.content:
US Vice President JD Vance said on Wednesday that the Iran war had doomed Republicans in the midterm elections, moving to distance himself from the unpopular conflict ahead of a possible 2028 White House run.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said in a lengthy post on X — apparently referring to President Donald Trump’s remarks that the Iran war was “part of it” but that it was still justified.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” added Vance.

“But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

The Democratic wave in Tuesday’s midterms has raised major questions over Vance’s previous status as the frontrunner for the Republican nomination in the 2028 presidential election. He has not yet formally declared that he will run.

Vance, a longtime vocal critic of US foreign interventionism, had reportedly been sceptical behind the scenes about the war on Iran that Trump and Israel launched in late February.

Vance also acknowledged that Republican voters who backed Trump and himself two years ago had switched sides due to the war and its effects on the US economy.

“The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026,” the vice president said.

He said a pollster that he respected showed that the Iran war and the economy were key factors in voters abandoning Republicans.

“In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats,” Vance wrote. “He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses, were:

End the war Focus on cost of living/inflation Put America First Change our relationship to Israel.”

Trump says war has been worth it despite election losses

Shortly after Vance made the post, Trump said it was “largely true” that the war caused his defeat.

“I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” said Trump, when asked about Vance’s comment while speaking to reporters at his White House ballroom construction site.

“But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again. Because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he insisted.

However, the US president ruled out firing Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, a staunch proponent of the war, saying: “I think he’s doing a very good job.”

Meanwhile, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said that the Iran war “must end” and suggested his party’s incoming majority in Congress could use their control over government funding to press for that goal.

“The American people don’t know what the heck we’re fighting for in Iran,” Schumer tells journalists, adding that Trump has never made it clear and “changes his mind day to day, minute to minute”.

“This war must end. It must end,” Schumer added.

He later noted that the “power of the purse” is “one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people”.

“Make no mistake: whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court and entangle him in legislative razor wire,” Schumer warns. “The days of Trump’s supplicant Senate are over.”

World.title: Govt says Islamabad's One Constitution Avenue to be turned into a five-star hotel
World.content:
The federal government on Wednesday said that a joint investigation team had revealed that Islamabad’s One Constitution Avenue was built on “irregularities and rigging” and announced that the residential building will soon be turned into a five-star hotel.

The building, a skyscraper in the federal capital that houses residential apartments, had its lease cancelled by the Capital Development Authority (CDA) due to the company behind the project defaulting on payments. The decision was upheld by the Islamabad High Court (IHC) in April.

The building was initially supposed to be a five-star hotel project; however, instead of functioning as a five-star hotel, it was converted into residential apartments and commercial areas. The IHC’s order led to the mass evictions of residents in May, following which Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif formed a joint investigation team (JIT) to probe the matter.

Addressing a press conference on Wednesday alongside Information Minister Attaullah Tarar and State Minister for Interior Tallal Chaudhry, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said the JIT presented its report to the federal cabinet today, noting that the project was fraudulent.

He said that the report had input from the National Accountability Bureau (NAB), the Federal Investigation Agency, the Federal Board of Revenue, the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan, the Intelligence Bureau and Inter-Services Intelligence.

“They carefully assessed this project and presented the report, and it was approved,” Iqbal said. “The JIT has clearly identified that the project was created based on irregularity and rigging and that the bidding process was manipulated.”

Iqbal added that, according to the report, rules were ignored to provide benefits and the company which was given the lease had no rightful claim.

“In this whole matter, the CDA was found complicit, and similarly, the conditions of the bank guarantee were removed to provide benefits to the developers,” he stated. “The work which was carried out was conducted in a very suspicious manner and the apartments were sold illegally.”

He noted that the project was initially approved as a five-star hotel two decades ago, but later it was turned into apartments.

“The JIT has identified Abdul Hafeez Sheikh, who has been called the mastermind and was found to be in connivance with CDA officials,” the planning minister added.

“CDA officers such as Kamran Lashari, who was chairman at the time, Dr Faisal Awan, Azhar Ali Chaudhry, Brigadier (retired) Nasrullah and Marhoom Rai Nawaz Kharal were found to be colluding in fraud,” he said.

Iqbal said that as a result of the scheme, the national exchequer suffered losses, while the aforementioned people “gained financially and defrauded the Pakistani people of their invested capital”.

“The JIT recommended that Sheikh and his company be blacklisted from future public projects and that proceedings be launched against him,” the minister added.

It was further recommended that the project be reviewed and work undertaken to achieve its original purpose as a hotel. Additionally, the report recommended that the project be started anew and auctioned in a transparent manner, he said.

“Security clearance and clearance from other institutions should also be sought so that future projects have a steady framework to prevent this type of fraud from happening again,” Iqbal said, adding that fire safety and other protocols must also be ensured.

He added that according to the JIT, the project should be renamed, as the name ‘One Constitution Avenue’ was the same address as the finance ministry.

“They used this address for marketing purposes only,” the minister asserted.

“There will be action taken against those found involved in fraud. The government has a responsibility to protect those who were robbed or swindled.”

Iqbal said it was decided that those defrauded would receive compensation, their principal investments would be refunded and payments would be adjusted against their Kibor interest “so they do not suffer losses”.

“It was also recommended that the CDA and its ordinance be overhauled and that an independent master plan commission be formed to shut the door on such fraud in the future,” he announced.

Iqbal added that all of the records must be digitised and officers should be rotated between the state planning, enforcement and building control departments every two years.

“People have held offices for 20 years and opened offices of fraud. With this constant rotation, it will close the door on these corrupt projects,” he explained.

“In the same way, pre-audit auctions and contracts from third parties will be consulted, and in light of this JIT report, NAB has been ordered to take action against anyone involved in this project, and those who facilitated it,” Iqbal said.

Meanwhile, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also addressed a press conference on Wednesday and said that the government had now regained possession of the skyscraper, vowing to turn the building into a five-star hotel within months.

“In official documents, we always had possession of this building, and after the cabinet’s approval, it is now legally in our possession,” Naqvi maintained.

He regretted that the government’s decision to regain control of the building earlier this year had been portrayed as a “crime”, decrying how Islamabad’s land had been infringed upon.

“We will try our best to convert this building into a five-star hotel in months,” the interior minister announced, reaffirming that this had been the project’s primary objective.

“There is a severe shortage of hotels in Islamabad. We will soon try to make an agreement with a large chain of hotels and convert this building into a five-star hotel,” he stated.

He commended the CDA chairman and legal team for pursuing this case; however, Naqvi also reproached the CDA for being at fault.

“NAB will tell who is responsible,” he said.

“As per JIT recommendations, we will try to make rightful payments to the occupants,” Naqvi said. “This is binding for us after the report.”

The interior minister said he was grateful to PM Shehbaz, recalling that the prime minister had assured him that the right decision would be taken.

Naqvi further said that a residents’ committee, which was overseeing the building’s affairs, had been abolished.

“A CDA member will look after the building’s matters from now on,” he said, reiterating that the hotel would be operational soon and be a “gift to the people of Islamabad”.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.
