World.title: Hong Kong helps mainland Chinese firms go global – but can they really win now?
World.content:
When Shenzhen-listed digital infrastructure provider Runjian Corporation expanded into the Middle East and Southeast Asia through Hong Kong, adapting meant more than translating software interfaces or navigating local data privacy laws.

It also meant changing the company’s working practices and abandoning the expectation, carried over from its domestic operations, that one mainland Chinese employee could match the output of three local hires.

“When expanding overseas, companies must do more than just take their products and technology abroad. We also need to respect local culture and truly integrate into the local market,” said Athena Zhao Hua, Runjian’s vice-president and president of its overseas business group. “When in Rome, you have to align with the local rhythm.”

World.title: Hong Kong’s No 2 official credits government for success in university rankings
World.content:
Hong Kong’s strong performance in a leading regional university league table – with five institutions among Asia’s top 10 – is the result of sustained government investment and clear policy direction, the city’s No 2 official has said, as a global alliance of 23 universities eyes the Northern Metropolis for collaboration opportunities.

Addressing leaders from more than 50 top universities across five continents at the World Class University Presidents Forum on Wednesday, Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki said the latest QS Asia University Rankings, announced a day earlier, showed that higher education had always been a vital pillar of Hong Kong’s success.

“This is not by chance. It is the result of sustained government investment, clear policy direction and the hard work of our universities. It reflects our commitment to excellence, openness, academic freedom and institutional autonomy,” Chan said.

World.title: Medical watchdog member quits to represent Tin-yu’s father at her death inquest
World.content:
A prominent patients’ rights advocate and lawyer has resigned from Hong Kong’s medical watchdog to represent the father of Chau Tin-yu at an inquest into her death, after she spent four years in a vegetative state following an alleged medical blunder.

Alex Lam Chi-yau, chairman of Hong Kong Patients’ Voices and a lay member of the Medical Council, submitted his resignation to council chairwoman Professor Grace Tang Wai-king on Wednesday amid concerns about a conflict of interest.

His resignation will take effect at 11.59pm on Thursday.

World.title: Education chief dismisses push for final-year university internships amid AI threat
World.content:
Hong Kong’s education minister has shot down a suggestion to turn the final stretch of undergraduate degree programmes into an internship period to boost employability, amid a fall in entry-level jobs due to the rise of artificial intelligence (AI).

Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin said on Wednesday that university courses should not be changed solely to meet manpower needs or be based on single indicators such as labour market supply and demand data.

She was responding to lawmaker Priscilla Leung Mei-fun’s question about whether authorities would reform four-year bachelor’s degree programmes by converting the final year into an internship year to let students enter the workforce earlier.

World.title: Roll-out of HK$5m anti-terrorism bollards in Causeway Bay draws mixed reactions
World.content:
The installation of anti-ram bollards costing HK$5 million (US$637,230) has begun at a busy crossing in Hong Kong’s Causeway Bay to prevent vehicles from mounting crowded pavements, sparking debate over whether the safety barriers justify the price tag.

By Wednesday afternoon, workers had installed four fixed bollards along the pavement outside the landmark Sogo department store, while construction continued on the ground behind temporary barriers.

Officials said the bollards and crash barriers were aimed at providing physical protection against vehicles deliberately mounting pedestrian areas, as vehicle-ramming attacks had been identified as a “long-standing risk” in Causeway Bay.

World.title: Hongkongers to draft end-of-life treatment refusals online from next year
World.content:
Hongkongers will be able to create advance medical directives electronically on the city’s eHealth record platform as early as next year, setting out which life-sustaining treatments they do not wish to receive when terminally ill, authorities have said.

In a written reply to lawmakers on Wednesday, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said the electronic service for advance medical directives, which currently exist in paper form only, would be rolled out “in phases”.

He said that after consulting government units including the Health Bureau, eHealth would serve as the designated electronic system for residents to make, store and revoke a directive.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.title: Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.content:
A Chinese app designed to report hotels that allegedly have bedbugs and other pests has been updated and re-released following controversy over the validity of the claims. The app attracted more than 300,000 users at its peak, flagging over 600 hotels nationwide, according to its creator.

In a Sunday post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, the creator of the app, a WeChat mini-program called “Bedbug Map,” announced that he alone would now review bedbug reports — previously, evidence was approved if a majority of users verified it. He also clarified that users are required to upload photographic evidence of bedbugs. The next day, he also posted a review of nearly 300 rejected bedbug reports, explaining why each had been declined.

Released Sept. 16, the mini-program lets users report hotels with bedbugs, cockroaches, or other pests, resulting in a bug or question mark icon over the hotel’s location. Tapping it reveals the number of user reports.

Controversy arose after reports that multiple hotels were asked by customers for refunds after they reported having found bedbugs via the app after their stay. One hotel was allegedly asked to refund 3,000 yuan ($450) in room charges after a report citing “two bumps” on a guest’s body was posted on the map and approved by users. According to the report, the hotel later asked a third party to inspect the premises, but found no traces of bedbugs.

The creator, a 26-year-old manufacturing industry worker who asked to remain anonymous, told Sixth Tone that in the past few days he had personally reviewed more than 700 pieces of photo evidence submitted over the previous two months.

A Wednesday check by Sixth Tone revealed that 232 hotels are now marked on the mini-program’s map, down from the more than 600 reported before Monday. The mini-program currently lists 36 hotels as having successfully appealed reports after submitting third-party evidence.

The app has also been taken down twice, most recently in late October, by WeChat parent company Tencent, citing its restrictions on applications run by and registered to individuals.

The creator told Sixth Tone that Bedbug Map was created with the help of AI in under two weeks. He said he got the idea after searching online for bedbug information after he and his girlfriend developed bites following a move, discovering most bedbug posts involved hotels.

On the day of its release, the mini-program attracted over 100,000 users, according to the creator. Under his release announcement on Xiaohongshu, many commented asking him to expand the function to public transportation, which he then added to the app. However, the function was removed in subsequent updates.

“I guess the reason the app was well-received is that it addresses a key pain point for the average traveler: the lack of cleanliness and the resurgence of bedbugs.”

The mini-program previously allowed users to submit reports without photo evidence. However, after users raised concerns about the potential for people to maliciously target hotels without evidence, the program was updated in late September to allow users to upload photographic evidence. Photos can be either uploaded or taken directly via the mini-program — in the latter case, the app automatically adds a watermark showing the time and location.

“I’m simply the initiator,” he said. “The goal is to get everyone involved in managing the mini-program’s data and reviews.”

Hotels can also appeal bedbug reports — indicated on the map by blue semicircular icons above such locations — as well as upload disinfection records, business licenses, and photos of pest-control operations.

The creator said he even recruited volunteers at one point to inspect the hygiene of hotels that filed appeals. However, the function was soon taken down because of concerns about volunteers’ safety, among other issues.

He said that managing the mini-program alone has “brought pressure and criticism,” adding that he hopes the government will “provide professional guidance to improve (the app’s) credibility.”

In an interview with domestic media, Lin Feiran, a lawyer at Beijing King & Capital Law Firm, suggested the company bring in professionals to identify insects reported at different locations.

State media outlet CNR News wrote in a Monday commentary that “a map pieced together by internet users being used to fill the gap in hygiene information shows that formal (reporting) channels are lacking,” encouraging hotel booking platforms to display bedbug records publicly.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Weibo and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.title: Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.content:
A few weeks ago, I served as a judge on a food program in China, where I met many chefs and got a close look at how they develop new dishes. I was particularly impressed by one dish: a steamed egg custard topped with a rich crab paste made from crab roe and fat. It was a combination I had never considered before. The crab paste had a delicate aroma and a rich, oily texture, while the steamed egg custard was soft and silky, perfectly balancing its richness.

I was struck by the dish’s ingenuity, but it also raised a question: Would people be willing to pay for the recipe and instructions on how to make it?

I put this question to one of the chefs on the program. He smiled at me as though I were a child and asked why anyone would pay for a recipe. He then let me in on an industry secret: When a restaurant discovers that a competitor has introduced a new dish, it will order it and have its own chefs taste it, analyze its ingredients, cooking techniques, and seasonings, and work out how it was made. In most cases, they can reproduce it. The chef told me he had recreated other people’s dishes and had his own copied by others.

It all sounded rather cutthroat. The person who bears the cost of innovation often reaps little of the reward.

In Chinese cuisine, creating a new dish is not nearly as simple as diners might imagine. Chefs must find the right ingredients, adjust proportions, experiment with different cooking temperatures, refine textures, and continually adjust based on customer feedback. Developing a successful dish can involve dozens or even hundreds of failed attempts before it is ready to serve.

The time, ingredients, and labor costs of this trial-and-error process are all borne by the original creator. Yet as soon as the dish reaches the table, anyone can observe, taste, analyze, and even reproduce it. For a competitor, learning most of the techniques needed to make a dish may cost little more than the price of a meal.

Even more frustrating, many of these innovators lack the resources to promote their creations. A small restaurant might be the first to develop a dish but lack the advertising budget, media exposure, or network of locations to popularize it. Meanwhile, a larger restaurant can simply copy the dish and quickly introduce it to a wider audience. Since more people encounter it there first, they may assume the larger restaurant came up with it.

This suggests that the first-mover advantage does not necessarily apply in the restaurant business. Being first matters only if consumers know who created the dish and the original creator has the resources and business acumen to turn that innovation into a brand and a source of revenue. Otherwise, the creator is essentially providing free research and development while introducing consumers to a dish that benefits the entire market.

The challenge of protecting intellectual property is not unique to Chinese cuisine. It affects chefs around the world. Business schools often hold up KFC’s fried chicken recipe as a classic example of a trade secret, but the company’s real competitive advantage lies in its supply chains, restaurant network, and brand value. The law does not prohibit you from reverse-engineering KFC’s fried chicken and making it yourself, or even selling it to your neighbors, provided you don’t market it as “KFC Original Recipe Chicken.” For smaller restaurants, therefore, protecting a recipe may matter less than building the brand and reputation that give it lasting commercial value.

The celebrated 18th-century Chinese food writer Yuan Mei associated dishes with particular names as a way of preserving their origins. For example, in his influential cookbook “Suiyuan Shidan” (“Recipes from the Garden of Contentment”), he included dishes called “Prefect Wang’s eight-treasure tofu” and “Governor Yang’s tofu.” In this way, no matter how often later generations copied these dishes, their names remained tied to their origins.

However, this naming convention has its limitations. Prefect Wang, Governor Yang, and the better-known Kung Pao (of Kung Pao chicken fame) all refer to the chefs’ employers rather than the people who actually did the cooking. Only in his “Biography of Chef Wang Xiaoyu” did Yuan Mei praise a chef, elevating an obscure kitchen worker to a culinary figure remembered by later generations.

Similarly, General Tso’s chicken is familiar to almost everyone in the United States, yet few know the name Peng Chang-kuei, the chef credited with creating the dish and introducing it to America. Diners know the name of General Tso, but not the person behind the dish.

One way to recognize innovative chefs would be to give them explicit credit for their creations. For example, instead of simply labeling a dish “Chef’s Recommendation,” menus could identify the chef or team of chefs who developed it, along with the restaurant and year it first appeared. This would acknowledge the contributions of both the creators and the restaurants that invested in their work.

Chefs could also license their original recipes to restaurants and large chains. Another possibility would be to establish an industry-wide registry of original dishes, where chefs and restaurants could record development dates, launch locations, photographs, and successive versions of their recipes. That way, even if other restaurants later copied a dish and achieved greater commercial success, its creator’s contribution would not simply be forgotten.

Of course, implementing such measures would not be easy. The greatest resistance might not even come from imitators, but from within the restaurants where new dishes are developed.

For restaurant owners, naming a dish after its creator also poses risks. Chefs tend to move between jobs, and when one leaves, dishes bearing their name could become an awkward legacy, potentially even requiring a restaurant to overhaul its menu. At the same time, chefs have traditionally enjoyed relatively low social status. Within restaurants, they often have little say in day-to-day operations and limited bargaining power to protect their own interests, making it difficult to secure adequate recognition for their contributions.

These two problems are closely related. When chefs receive little recognition for their work and feel little ownership over the dishes they create or the restaurants where they work, they may be more inclined to leave. This, in turn, gives restaurants even less incentive to credit individual chefs. It may help explain why, in the rare cases in which a dish bears its creator’s name — such as Fei Da Chu’s chili stir-fried pork, sold in cities across China — the chef behind it is also the restaurant’s owner.

Protecting and rewarding the creators of original dishes, whether through naming rights or other institutional and technological mechanisms, could help raise chefs’ social status, strengthen their bargaining power, and create a more equitable relationship between chefs and restaurant owners. Restaurants, in turn, could attract diners who appreciate the work of individual chefs and are willing to pay for originality. The result could be a positive cycle of culinary innovation, recognition, and consumption.

A dish may be replicated almost perfectly, but the experience, creativity, and reputation behind it cannot. The chef who conceived the idea, the sous chefs who tested the recipe, the team members who continually refined it, and the restaurant that provided the resources and space for experimentation all contributed to the story behind the dish. Recognizing their contributions is about more than giving credit where it is due. It is also about respecting the generations of chefs who have shaped Chinese cuisine and ensuring that their knowledge, skills, and traditions continue to be valued.

(Header image: The illustration in the center depicts Yuan Mei, a Qing Dynasty poet, scholar, and artist, in a 19th-century painting by Chinese artist Ye Yanlan. Images from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone.)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.title: China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
World.content:
China has approved its first domestically developed amino acid-based nutritional powder, designed to give patients with phenylketonuria (PKU) — a rare genetic disorder that affects metabolism of the amino acid phenylalanine — greater freedom in what they eat. Treatment of PKU requires lifelong dietary restrictions to prevent developmental disorders and brain damage.

The new formula officially entered the Chinese market on Oct. 30 and was jointly developed by Shanghai-based Xinhua Hospital, affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research, and dairy producer Bright Dairy.

PKU affects about one in every 11,000 newborns in China, with an estimated 120,000 to 150,000 registered patients nationwide.

Due to a genetic defect, people with PKU cannot break down phenylalanine, an amino acid found in protein-rich foods. The resulting buildup can damage brain cells, requiring patients to follow a low-phenylalanine diet by cutting out meat and eating low-protein grains, while relying on milk powder-like formulas to supplement the other amino acids they need.

Earlier formulas contained 30% to 60% amino acids, with the rest composed of fats, carbohydrates, and other nutrients.

“As patients grow older, they need more protein. That means consuming more of these formulas, which also means taking in more fats and carbohydrates, increasing the risk of obesity,” Cai Wei, director of the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research and leader of the research team, told domestic media.

In contrast, the new formula contains 95% amino acids, allowing patients to meet their amino acid needs without consuming as much fat or as many carbohydrates, and giving them more freedom to enjoy other normal low-protein foods.

Zhuang Yingying, a 33-year-old PKU patient, told domestic media that patients previously relied heavily on imported products, and overseas supply disruptions were common. Special low-protein foods such as rice and noodles cost five to 10 times as much as regular varieties.

The formula, designed for PKU patients aged 1 and older, could save some families more than 1,000 yuan ($140) a month, according to domestic media.

Domestic PKU formulas have existed for decades, but long faced hurdles in gaining regulatory approval in China, partly because of gaps in national standards for food-grade amino acids, according to a 2020 report by domestic media outlet China Times. High registration costs and the small patient population have also discouraged manufacturers from entering the market.

China approved its first PKU medical formula in 2018, an imported product, while the first domestically produced formula received regulatory approval in 2025.

Since 2018, some parts of China, including Shanghai and neighboring Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces, have introduced public health insurance coverage for foods formulated for PKU patients. In Shanghai, annual coverage ranges from 8,000 yuan for infants under 1 to 12,000 yuan for patients over 10.

Development of the new formula began in 2024 and received regulatory approval in September 2026. The research team has also worked with companies to develop everyday foods for PKU patients, including noodles, steamed buns, cookies, and mochi.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: From the Shanghai Morning Post)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019198/Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
World.title: Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019198/Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
World.content:
At her desk in a press-on nail workshop in Donghai, a county in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, Chai Fenfen has hung a large print of a 100-yuan banknote.

“I came here to make money,” she says. “That’s what keeps me motivated.”

After jobs selling insurance and real estate, Chai joined the workshop in 2024. Making nails offers steady earnings and the flexibility to take her children to and from school. Workers there are paid by the piece, typically earning 3,000 to 4,000 yuan a month ($450 to $600).

But for the businesses supplying that work, the early boom has given way to fierce competition over price.

Once known for its crystal trade, Donghai used its existing e-commerce networks to build an industry around press-on nails — ready-made artificial nails that customers attach themselves. By 2024, the county had nearly 25,000 businesses in the trade, according to its press-on nail industry association.

Chai’s employer, wholesaler Li Zhifu, entered the business in 2021, and now has around 2,000 workers across his production sites and more than 20 storefronts in the county.

In the beginning, Li says, almost anything sold, regardless of color or design. Competition has since squeezed profits. He estimates that six or seven out of every 10 people who entered the trade have gone out of business.

Some businesses are competing on design, selling elaborate, handmade sets for hundreds of yuan. Others are expanding overseas sales through TikTok Shop.

As overseas orders grow, Li is experimenting with machines to make nails his workers currently produce by hand.

“For large overseas orders, consistency is key. Everything, from colors and designs to rhinestone placement, has to match,” he says. He expects machine-made nails to eventually dominate that market.

(Header image: Craftswomen work in a press-on nail workshop in Donghai County, Jiangsu province, August 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.title: China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
World.content:
China’s latest viral reality show is about broken friendships — rather than failing romance — between celebrities.

“I Miss You” surpassed 100 million views within two days of its Oct. 22 debut, and topped the real-time TV popularity chart on Chinese review platform Douban since last Thursday. Topics related to the show have repeatedly trended on the microblogging platform Weibo since airing.

Produced by streaming platform Mango TV, the show brings together four pairs of celebrities who have reportedly fallen out for an 18-day trip through the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region.

The show is widely seen as a riff on China’s popular relationship reality shows and follows a similar format to “See You Again,” whose fifth season aired in late 2025, which takes celebrity couples in troubled marriages on an 18-day trip before they decide whether to divorce.

In “I Miss You,” guests discuss their former friendships as a group and one-on-one with their ex-friends, play games, and share their feelings with the production team. A panel of celebrities, a psychologist, and a journalist comment on their interactions.

The most discussed pair on “I Miss You” so far has been Xu Fei and Li Na, two contestants from the 2006 season of “Super Girl,” a popular televised singing competition regarded as a cornerstone of China’s fan culture.

The two were close friends during the competition 20 years ago, but their friendship later collapsed after Li came to believe that Xu had reported her to their management company for taking outside jobs in violation of her contract. Li said the company subsequently stopped arranging work for her, which she sees as having dealt a major blow to her career. Xu denied the accusation, instead blaming a third person.

As the two revisited their past on the show, their memories of their friendship moved many viewers, with one highly upvoted comment describing their relationship as “an epic saga of love and hate.”

Xu said in tears that she had loved “wasting time together,” and noted that her current preferred snacks are the “ones Li loved back then.” Li also recalled how, even when the two appeared to be bitter enemies, they would sometimes end up crying in each other’s arms after getting drunk at gatherings.

Yet the two remained at odds over the past accusation. During an interview with the production team, Li said she had hated Xu “for a long time,” at one point shouting, “What about the money I lost?”

The other three pairs of celebrities include an actor who cut ties with a longtime producer friend after feeling pressured to accept a role, an actress and a writer who fell out when the latter grew closer to a third person, and former professional esports teammates who fought over training strategies, eventually leading one to leave the team.

“‘I Miss You’ feels so much more pure than ‘See You Again,’” read a post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, that received almost 3,700 likes. “In a marriage, you have to argue about more than feelings. There’s property, children, parents, and so much else. With friendship, we can sit down and focus on just one thing: how we feel about each other.”

Fu, a 21-year-old viewer from the southern Guangdong province, told Sixth Tone that she found the show’s focus on friendship “refreshing” given how rarely such relationships take center stage on screen.

“We’re so used to understanding intimate relationships through the lens of romance, but rarely give serious thought to the love, possessiveness, jealousy, dependence, disappointment, and reconciliation that exist in friendships,” she said.

Another 21-year-old viewer based in Shanghai, surnamed You, added that the show’s appeal lies in friendship’s lack of definition.

“Friendship can be as intense and possessive as romance, full of love and resentment, or it can be something much more casual,” You said. “People can have very different ideas of what friendship means, and that alone can create tension.”

Contributions: Yang Yang; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for “I Miss You.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019200/Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
World.title: Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019200/Writing on the Wall? How AI Is Reinventing Chinese Typography
World.content:
Many assume the writing is on the wall for human typographers. For decades, the industry has been slowly decimated by the advance of digital publishing software. Now, artificial intelligence is here to finish off the job.

That view has only strengthened since the launch of OpenAI’s Image 2.0 earlier this year. Until then, type designers and typographers had clung to the hope that AI would never be able to replace them: AI-generated fonts and layouts had always looked clunky, inconsistent, error-ridden, or somehow just a bit off.

But Image 2.0’s capabilities took many by surprise: it was able to produce beautifully designed documents featuring long passages of text in multiple languages, while maintaining a high degree of accuracy. The work was not as good as that produced by professional type designers, but for a layperson looking to make a poster or a brochure, it was just fine.

Suddenly, typography — perhaps the last stronghold of graphic design still firmly controlled by professional designers — looked at risk of falling as well. If everyone can generate typefaces and layouts with a simple prompt, or even ask a frontier AI model to operate design software on its own — just as non-programmers can now “write code” through vibe coding — how many designers will lose their jobs?

In the English-speaking world, the AI revolution may indeed prove to be a hammer blow for the typography community. But things are likely to play out a little differently in China: the relationship between text and technology has always been more complex due to the nature of its writing system.

Most contemporary typographic practice derives from movable-type printing technology. Developed in medieval Germany, typography is closely tied to the inherent characteristics of the Latin alphabet: there are only a few dozen letters, and the same letters recur constantly throughout a printed text.

With these characteristics in mind, Johannes Gutenberg developed an entire technological process of carving, reproducing, retrieving, and repeatedly reusing individual letter forms. Once a complete set of letters had been produced, it could be used to print texts containing vast numbers of repetitions of exactly the same glyphs.

Gutenberg would later be credited as a pioneer of movable type printing, a technology whose logic has been carried intact from books to the screen you are now looking at. But applying this technique to Chinese characters is a huge challenge, as there is such a vast number of them. While function words such as de may appear repeatedly on a single page, most characters may occur only once or twice in a given text — or not at all.

Statistically, 3,500 characters is enough to cover most everyday text — studies have shown they account for 99.5% of character usage. But to avoid the awkward situation where a character outside the “common 3,500” can’t be rendered properly, the industry often sets 7,000 characters as the target size for a typeface. Some larger projects cover 27,000, or even 87,000 characters.

This means that Chinese typeface design has always been extremely labor-intensive. Designers have to invest huge resources in reproducing thousands of rare characters that are only used about 1% of the time. It’s one reason why Chinese printers — who actually invented movable type even earlier than Gutenberg — largely stuck with carving entire texts onto woodblocks to mass-print books for centuries. It saved producing and organizing thousands of characters that might never be used. Only gigantic projects, such as state-backed archives, would use movable-type printing.

But in the modern era, movable type-inspired workflows have come to dominate Chinese typeface design. As a result, advertisers who need to print a 20-character slogan may have to purchase the license for a typeface containing 7,000 characters. Understandably, many users are reluctant to pay type foundries, who also feel it’s an enormous burden to cover as many characters as possible.

This cost-efficiency problem is where AI can help. In fact, Chinese type foundries have been using internal AI tools to assist in typeface production for years.

Traditionally, when developing a new typeface, the lead designer will often create several hundred characters to establish the design direction, with the remaining thousands produced by a team along those lines. An AI model can also do this work with a little training: extracting patterns from those hundreds of directional characters, learning the typeface’s stylistic characteristics, and then applying them according to the structural features of different characters. The model doesn’t have to be advanced, and with human adjustment, it can deliver products with considerably increased productivity.

Since the early 2020s, open-source AI tools have also enabled independent designers to produce usable typefaces on their own. For example, designer Wang Tingrui has been using AI tools to develop typefaces reminiscent of classic lead-type printing. With the emergence of stronger models capable of generating high-quality glyph outlines, such work has become even easier.

These developments mark a new chapter for Chinese typeface design. Once a typeface’s design concept is established, whether by a lead designer or an independent practitioner, AI could be used to expand it across thousands of additional characters, making that long tail of less common characters far less of a burden.

AI may also unlock new possibilities for Chinese characters once incompatible with movable type or typefaces. The overwhelming majority of Chinese characters are created by flexibly combining different components. In theory, anyone can combine components to create a new Chinese character.

This happened in the 19th century, when Chinese chemists — tasked with translating the names of newly discovered elements into Chinese — created compound characters by combining a semantic component indicating the element type and a phonetic component based on the initial sound of its Western name. This system continues to this day, when scientists occasionally need to name new synthetic elements.

While inventing a new character is relatively simple, it used to be difficult to introduce them into everyday language because of the inherent barriers created by digital typefaces. Traditional typeface design is built around recording whole characters, not their components, so any new character would not appear in previously existing typefaces.

With AI, however, that could all change. The technology should allow users to render new characters in the style of an existing typeface, making it easier for them to gain traction.

Beyond this, AI is ushering in a fundamental shift in the nature of typography. While the modern typeface system uses the single character or letter as its basic unit, this is just one way to recreate text. In woodblock printing, for example, Chinese printers produced entire pages all at once.

Today’s leading AI models — including Qwen, Seedream, ChatGPT, and DALL-E — are moving towards a system that bypasses typefaces entirely. Text is generated directly onto posters, videos, and the cover images for posts on China’s version of TikTok, Douyin, in a particular visual style, according to a user’s preferences. Users specify the style they want using a prompt — or a handwritten demonstration — and the AI model simply creates a font, rather than using a commercial one.

This approach still has problems. One issue often raised is the inconsistency of AI-crafted characters, but this should be solvable as models become more advanced. There is also a debate over copyright, especially when generated text resembles existing typefaces. Yet these issues are unlikely to stop ordinary users from using AI to speed up their design work.

It is easy to imagine a not-so-distant future in which everyone can generate high-quality typefaces and typography through instructions, whether they are designing for an illustration, an , a poster, or even an entire book. For type foundries, AI is likely to be incorporated into their workflows, just like what has been happening in the “hybrid” mode of production in the film industry.

Then, what is left for professional type designers to do?

One thing is clear: they will no longer monopolize the creation of stylistic Chinese characters. Similar upheavals have happened in the past, when typewriters, computers, and smartphones granted more people the power to produce texts.

But professionals have a more important job: pushing the boundaries of design. In a world where the production of text becomes effortless and inexhaustible, designers’ role as the gatekeepers of taste and judgment only becomes more prominent.

We should keep experimenting to deliver high-quality work with novel and sophisticated aesthetics. The decades of training we have received won’t be wasted. Rather, it will continue to shape a philosophy that pioneers future designs, regardless of what technology is involved.

(Header image: Fu Xiaofan/Sixth Tone)

World.title: Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019197/Chinese Study: Depressed Moms’ Breast Milk May Change Babies’ Brains
World.content:
Breast milk from mothers with postpartum depression may negatively impact infants’ brain development, a Chinese study has found.

The study, published Oct. 27 in the top academic journal Cell Metabolism, was led by a team at Nanjing University, in the eastern Jiangsu province. Through a mouse model, it shows, for the first time, how depression-related changes in levels of microRNA, a type of gene-regulating molecule, contained in structures called extracellular vesicles in breast milk can affect offspring brains.

Between 10% and 20% of mothers worldwide experience postpartum depression. Children of affected mothers are more likely to face challenges in cognition, language, behavior, and school performance, and are at a higher risk of developing depression themselves.

Past research has implicated genetics and the way mothers with postpartum depression bond with, and care for, their infants as contributing to this phenomenon, but the broad and long-lasting effects of postpartum depression on child development remain unclear, according to the researchers.

Because breast milk is increasingly viewed as a “signaling system orchestrating infant development,” the researchers wrote, they looked at the relationship between milk-based microRNAs and extracellular vesicles, key parts of this signaling. Because babies’ blood-brain barrier is more permeable than adults’, these vesicles can enter the brain during nursing, making its development more sensitive to diet.

The researchers compared the breast milk of 40 human mothers clinically diagnosed with postpartum depression, and 51 without, finding that those with depression had elevated levels of three types of microRNA implicated in psychiatric illness. The same was true of the breast milk of depressed mice.

To test nursing’s role in brain development, swapping mouse pups between healthy and depressed mouse mothers. Pups born to healthy mice but nursed by their depressed counterparts showed worse cognitive and emotional behavior than pups born to depressed mothers but nursed by healthy ones.

They also found that neurons in pups nursed by depressed mothers had shorter dendrites and fewer branches in the hippocampal dentate gyrus, a part of the brain believed to play a role in memory development and depression. The problems arose mainly as the neurons matured, were detectable by day 21 after birth, and persisted into adulthood, suggesting that early nursing-environment effects can last into later development.

Giving milk from depressed mothers to healthy pups was also enough to cause cognitive impairment after weaning, while milk where the vesicles had been removed had no such effect, the researchers found.

When the team inhibited Rab27a, a protein and key factor in vesicle secretion, in the mammary glands of depressed mothers, vesicle secretion fell by 58%, and the cognitive and neurodevelopmental deficits in their pups improved significantly.

The researchers also found that microRNA in milk vesicles from depressed mothers blocks a “brake” receptor called mGluR8 in pups’ brains. Without this brake, brain regions can become overstimulated, impairing the development of neural connections. As a result, new brain cells are more active overall but respond more weakly to memory tasks, helping explain the cognitive problems seen in pups nursed by depressed mothers.

The study offers the key findings of both a new communication pathway and a microRNA-based mechanism of inheritance between mothers and babies, according to the researchers.

Breastfeeding is widely seen as good for babies’ brain development, but this study also suggests that breastfeeding by mothers with postpartum depression may have a “double-edged effect on offspring health,” the researchers wrote.

“Elucidating the molecular mechanisms linking maternal postnatal depression to offspring neurological outcomes therefore holds considerable public health value and underscores the urgent need for targeted maternal mental health interventions during lactation,” they added.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.title: 90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019191/90 Face Chinese Legal Action After $1 Billion Tax Fraud
World.content:
Chinese prosecutors have exposed an invoice-trading network that illegally traded special value-added tax (VAT) invoices totaling more than 7.4 billion yuan ($1.1 billion) over three years.

Under the guise of a Shanghai-based advertising business, the group profited by issuing and charging service fees for fake invoices from shell companies it registered to customers seeking to illegally claim tax deductions — which can be claimed for special tax invoices, but not ordinary tax invoices in China — domestic media reported Tuesday.

The case has exposed major weaknesses in business-registration oversight, tax monitoring, and financial regulators’ ability to detect suspicious fund flows between affiliated company accounts, according to experts.

From June 2025 to June 2026, more than 90 criminal suspects on the case were processed by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Procuratorate, some of whom were ordered to return their illegal gains. Processing of the case is ongoing.

The group’s ringleaders, surnamed Cui and Shen, first had employees register over 70 shell companies in their own names. Invoices were then handled via three steps: a sales team first connected with customers, who transferred money to the group in order to receive invoices; then a team obtained invoices from both the operation’s registered shell companies or legitimate businesses with unused invoicing quotas; before another team returned funds to customers following invoice-fee deductions. Customers were charged a service fee of between 7% and 13% of the invoice value.

Chinese tax law requires contracts, fund transfers, invoices, and movement of goods to align. Falsely issuing invoices can result in fines of up to 500,000 yuan, while tax dodgers may be fined up to five times the underpaid tax. Both carry risks of criminal prosecution.

To circumvent the law, customers transferred the full invoice amount to the group, which then transferred the remaining funds back to the customer through a separate, third account.

The group illegally traded over 7.4 billion yuan in VAT invoices, involving more than 420 million yuan in VAT. It also conducted illegal foreign-exchange transactions totaling 420 million yuan.

“The scale of the crimes, the degree of organization, and the length of time over which they were committed were all relatively unusual,” Li Huaisheng, a professor at the School of Criminal Justice at China University of Political Science and Law, told state media outlet CCTV.

Similar cases involving companies that obtained invoices through intermediaries have made national headlines in recent years. Last year, a group allegedly used 15 shell companies to falsely issue almost 3,500 special VAT invoices totaling 300 million yuan, domestic media reported. The defendant, surnamed Li, was sentenced to 13 years and six months in prison and fined 500,000 yuan.

According to the State Taxation Administration, such companies often disguise themselves as consulting, advertising, or other business services in industries with low fixed-asset requirements, long industrial chains, and large transaction values, such as recycling, road freight transport, and information technology consulting.

Li Huaisheng recommended that market regulatory authorities establish early-warning models to flag suspicious company registrations, and tax authorities improve big-data checks on invoices, capital, contracts, and goods.

In an interview with CCTV, Zhou Xianbao, a lawyer at BZW Law Firm in Beijing, also recommended establishing a system requiring real-name authorization for invoice issuance and formal tax-compliance commitments.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.title: El Niño now very strong, impacts to be felt until 2027
World.content:
PAGASA projections show the very strong El Niño or so-called Super El Niño may cause drought in virtually the entire country by March 2027

MANILA, Philippines – A very strong El Niño is now present in the tropical Pacific Ocean, the Philippine weather bureau announced in a statement posted on Thursday, November 5.

Also informally called Super El Niño, this current episode of the weather phenomenon might reach its peak by the end of 2026, but persist until the first half of 2027.

In the Philippines, El Niño leads to less rainfall, causing dry spells and drought.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) defines a dry spell as three straight months of below normal rainfall or two straight months of way below normal rainfall.

Drought, meanwhile, is experienced when there is three straight months of way below normal rainfall or five straight months of below normal rainfall.

Below normal refers to a 21% to 60% drop from the average rainfall volume in a particular area, while way below normal means a reduction of more than 60%.

PAGASA expects below normal to way below normal rainfall in most parts of the country in November. Temperatures are also likely to be higher than average, despite the presence of the northeast monsoon or amihan, which brings cool air.

By the end of November, the following areas may have drought, according to PAGASA forecasts:

Luzon – Albay, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Catanduanes

– Albay, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Catanduanes Visayas – Capiz, Leyte, Negros Oriental, Samar, Siquijor, Southern Leyte

– Capiz, Leyte, Negros Oriental, Samar, Siquijor, Southern Leyte Mindanao – Isabela City, Misamis Oriental

These areas could be experiencing dry spells by the end of the month:

Luzon – Abra, Apayao, Bataan, Batanes, Batangas, Benguet, Cagayan, Cavite, Ifugao, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Isabela, Palawan (Kalayaan), Kalinga, La Union, Marinduque, Masbate, Mountain Province, Metro Manila, Nueva Vizcaya, Occidental Mindoro, Oriental Mindoro, Palawan, Pangasinan, Quezon, Quirino, Romblon, Sorsogon, Zambales

– Abra, Apayao, Bataan, Batanes, Batangas, Benguet, Cagayan, Cavite, Ifugao, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Isabela, Palawan (Kalayaan), Kalinga, La Union, Marinduque, Masbate, Mountain Province, Metro Manila, Nueva Vizcaya, Occidental Mindoro, Oriental Mindoro, Palawan, Pangasinan, Quezon, Quirino, Romblon, Sorsogon, Zambales Visayas – Aklan, Antique, Biliran, Bohol, Cebu, Guimaras, Iloilo, Negros Occidental, Northern Samar

– Aklan, Antique, Biliran, Bohol, Cebu, Guimaras, Iloilo, Negros Occidental, Northern Samar Mindanao – Basilan, Camiguin, Cotabato, Davao del Sur, Davao Occidental, Dinagat Islands, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, Misamis Occidental, Sarangani, South Cotabato, Special Geographic Area, Sultan Kudarat, Sulu, Surigao del Norte, Tawi-Tawi, Zamboanga del Norte, Zamboanga del Sur, Zamboanga Sibugay

By March 2027, virtually the entire country may face drought, further affecting agriculture, water resources, energy, and public health.

“The public and all concerned agencies are strongly advised to implement appropriate sectoral interventions, conservation and mitigation measures, particularly water conservation and efficient management of water resources, to minimize the potential impacts of El Niño,” PAGASA Administrator Nathaniel Servando said in a statement.

El Niño has already caused massive damage and losses to agriculture this year. As of October 21, the Department of Agriculture (DA) pegged the cost of damage at P8.57 billion, with more than 288,000 farmers affected.

The DA said its assistance so far includes P10.81 billion worth of production support, such as seeds, fertilizers, and soil conditioner, as well as P569.95 million worth of Philippine Crop Insurance Corporation indemnification for 68,980 affected farmers.

In a worst-case scenario, according to the DA, the Super El Niño could affect around 4.6 million of the country’s 10.4 million farmers and fisherfolk.

El Niño is the warm phase of El Niño Southern Oscillation or ENSO, which the World Meteorological Organization defines as “a recurring natural phenomenon characterized by fluctuating ocean temperatures in the equatorial Pacific, coupled with changes in the atmosphere.” ENSO has two other phases: La Niña or the cool phase, and neutral.

El Niño does not mean complete absence of rainfall in the Philippines. Weather systems such as tropical cyclones, the northeast monsoon, the intertropical convergence zone, and the easterlies can still trigger rain in the coming months.

PAGASA said two to six tropical cyclones may develop within or enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility from November 2026 to April 2027. – Rappler.com

World.title: Why Ralph Sarmiento refused to testify at Sara Duterte’s trial
World.content:
RALPH SARMIENTO. The defense counsel of Vice President Sara Duterte had wanted law dean Ralph Sarmiento as their first witness but he declined.

The defense team had wanted the constitutional expert and former law dean to be their first witness in the Vice President's impeachment trial

MANILA, Philippines – The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte will have to find another first witness for her impeachment trial which resumes on Monday, November 9.

In a video message on Thursday, November 5, former law school dean Ralph Sarmiento said he had declined the defense team’s request for him to testify, saying he wanted to preserve the independence of his constitutional law scholarship and the impartiality of his legal views.

This came a day after the defense identified Sarmiento as its first witness, submitting a manifestation before the Senate impeachment court seeking the issuance of subpoenas ad testificandum (or a summon to appear before the court) and duces tecum (to compel him to bring relevant documents including a copy of his curriculum vitae).

“After careful consideration, I have decided to decline participation as a witness in the proceedings,” said Sarmiento.

“This is a personal decision to preserve the independence of my constitutional law scholarship and the impartiality of my legal views and opinions,” he added.

The defense team had wanted the law professor to testify on legal and constitutional principles relevant to the impeachment case, particularly Article II, which involves Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.

He said he had already communicated with the defense to withdraw its request for a subpoena compelling his appearance, or seek its recall if it had already been issued.

“I remain committed to contributing to public understanding of the Constitution through independent and balanced legal analysis,” Sarmiento added.

Michael Poa, spokesperson for Duterte’s defense team, said they respected Sarmiento’s decision.

“We respect Dean Sarmiento’s personal decision and appreciate his initial consideration of our invitation. We wish him well in his continued contributions to constitutional discourse,” said Poa.

Sarmiento was law school dean of the University of St. La Salle in Bacolod City until September 30, 2025, and has since been the university’s vice chancellor for administration.

He earned his Juris Doctor degree in the University of St. La Salle. He was admitted to the Bar in 1997, placing 10th in the Bar exam.

A lawyer with expertise in International Law, Sarmiento also served as a bar lecturer and reviewer, and has authored several books including International Law: Compendium and Bar Reviewer and Bar Exam Logic: Mastering Legal Reasoning for the Bar Exams and Law Practice.

He had earlier called for fairness after the prosecution dropped three of four articles of impeachment against Duterte, saying the defense “should be given even just a limited opportunity to present rebuttal evidence in the same Impeachment Court, under oath and subject to cross-examination.”

The impeachment trial was temporarily paused to give way to the Senate committee hearings on the proposed 2027 national budget. The trial will resume on November 9, when the defense will begin its presentation of evidence. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tencent rolls out AI model trained with limited cybersecurity data amid hacking fears
World.content:
TENCENT. The Tencent logo is seen in this illustration taken February 16, 2025.

Tencent said it restricted the Hy4 AI model's cybersecurity training to defensive uses, such as identifying software flaws and helping fix them

Chinese tech giant Tencent on Wednesday, November 4, released Hy4, a new AI model it said was designed with limits intended to reduce the risk that it could be used for cyberattacks or harmful biological research.

Tencent said it restricted the model’s cybersecurity training to defensive uses, such as identifying software flaws and helping fix them. It excluded material on building hacking tools, breaking into systems and testing systems for weaknesses.

The Shenzhen-based company and developer of WeChat, China’s most popular app with over ⁠1 billion monthly active users, said internal security specialists tested Hy4 and found no sign that it posed higher risks in helping users break into software or bypass security protections. Tencent also said its testing found that the model was not capable of meaningfully making harmful biological experiments easier to carry out.

The release comes at a time of surging global concern over AI-powered hacking and follows Tencent’s disclosure last month that AI agents it used to test third-party models displayed unintended web-browsing behavior. Researchers said agents linked to Tencent Cloud had sought information from Alibaba’s Amap service.

Tencent said the activity did not come from its Hunyuan models, and that its review found no evidence of deliberate targeting or coordination, while vowing to strengthen controls over agents’ internet access and monitoring.

Despite cutthroat domestic competition and an intensifying rivalry with the US, Chinese AI firms have in recent months shown signs of investing more in model safety. Beijing-based Moonshot AI last month limited its newest model’s cyber-offensive capabilities.

Tencent said it plans to release its model weights later along with a report describing its safety testing.

“We recognize the potential safety risks posed by advanced cyber and biological capabilities, and we are committed to a more responsible approach to model training, open-sourcing, and release,” Tencent said. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Good Business] Sari-sari stores: Kapwa at play amid economic crises
World.content:
Your childhood was incomplete had you not been asked to buy a thing or two from your local sari-sari (small neighborhood convenience) store. Be it as simple as patis (fish sauce) or toyo (soy sauce) to complete today’s ulam (viand), or even a sachet of detergent to finish one’s laundry, these tried and tested local stores have been a staple in the lives of Filipinos.

My exposure to the business model has been quite in-depth, at least for the past couple months, as a budding category manager for an FMCG (Fast-Moving Consumer Goods). Not often is it pointed out that 1.3 million of these shopping points are scattered across the archipelago–withstanding the aggressive expansion of giant hypermarket chains and an ever-evolving retail trade landscape.

There’s a Pinoy adage that goes “Huwag i-smallin” or not to belittle something and I would care to argue that it applies to how we see these stores each day. From a consumer goods perspective, one cannot hope to grow their business in the Philippines if they do not crack the route-to-market (RTM) recipe for sari-sari stores. These local shops help provide proximitized availability of the goods we so-carefully craft inside boardrooms to be within arms reach of the shoppers.

Setting aside FMCG nomenclature, one cannot help but see how innately Filipino this system translates into trade. Every now and then–and just so my manager reads it as firm proof of my diligence–I would go around our village, even outside to nearby neighborhoods checking on how our products fair in different channels. This practice of trade visits is a staple within the category development and sales industry in general as it allows us to see the realities, keeping our strategizing grounded especially in dire times such as now. It goes without saying that realizations also came into play as I went on these occasional rounds.

“Isang tawid lang kasi.” (It’s just a short distance to the store.) I recall a casual conversation with a more senior shopper in our village as she justified her preference of buying from their sari-sari store. Just when I thought her story was finished, she came closer, clutching her Good Morning towel and whispered “Tsaka puwede kang umutang.” (Plus, you can buy on credit.) It all seems stereotypical but the simple truth one can derive from this testament is the importance of credit in this business model.

Palista, utang muna, (List it, buying on credit) or whatever term may be affixed to this extension of credit is undoubtedly a crucial advantage of sari-sari stores among other channels. What’s striking, at the very least, is how both shoppers and shop owners see that these local credit lines allow a “lifeline” of sorts.

For shop owners, the act of pautang (lending) is a necessity. “Ito na rin pakikisama namin. Kapag hindi ka nagpautang, hindi na sila babalik.” (This is how we get along with others. If you don’t let them buy on credit, they won’t return.) A rather profound statement that proves how extending credit is a unique value proposition for sari-sari store owners in retaining shopper loyalty. Nonetheless, one can also interpret that this crucial tactic is not merely an “always on promo” but a compassionate gesture. Bullseye on the mention of the word pakikisama (getting along) as this solidifies that, at the onset, entrepreneurial thinking and humanistic insights go hand-in-hand. At the very least, we can surmise that kapwa (shared humanity) is not undermined by kita (profit) but is actually driven by the former.

On the other side of the coin, we look at how shoppers rely on the palista (credit list) system. Now, more than ever, when “isang kahig, isang tuka” (hand to mouth existence) is not just a dramatic line for jesting but a harsh truth lived by the majority of Filipinos is the importance of surviving everyday. By allowing shoppers to accrue their payables, sari-sari stores provide an extension for hardworking Pinoys to make ends meet until the next payday.

Harsh truths

Sure, boundaries are often set. More often than not do we hear horror stories of customers over-extending their credit yet the system of trust is undoubtedly integral to sustain this rather unique model. Pakikipagkapwa, as more formally referred to, banks heavily on the concept of seeing things in the perspective of others which conversely allows Filipinos to know their boundaries, albeit even in their sari-sari store transactions. Simply put, we know up to what extent we may lend a hand to our neighbors and we know our limits in accepting such help—hiya (shame) acting as a sort of internal moral compass.

Sari-sari stores are far from a perfect model but it is a lifeboat that the country relies on amid rising oil prices and political instability. Through each assortment offered in urban jungles to the most remote islands, essential goods are readily available while allowing tight-budgeted Filipinos an opportunity to survive an increasingly hard economy.

From time to time, we will see a “Bawal umutang” (No credit allowed) signage in all capital letters. Then again, an Aling Belen or Mang Tony would be amiable enough to have a handy list of their pautang (items on credit list)—allowing us to see good business in practice. It comes off as a two-way street if you ask me: retaining customers while also allowing a sense of ginhawa (relief) to an already struggling individual. Call it good karma, if you may, but this thinking perhaps actualizes the sustainability of the sari-sari store model.

Next time we pass by to get our fix of pancit canton or sitsirya (snack food), I openly welcome anyone to ask their sari-sari store owners how they are fairing these days. This gesture is not merely an intellectual exercise but a sort of pakikipagkapwa (solidarity)—allowing us to better understand their situation and support local businesses in a more sustainable way. – Rappler.com

Leon “Eo” Matawaran is a commercial development executive (category manager) from Nestle Philippines, Inc. handling NESTEA. Aside from being a category manager, he is a culture and inclusivity advocate that champions Filipino values in leadership—among other humanistic initiatives.

ALSO ON RAPPLER

World.title: Inflation surges to 7.8% in October 2026 as fuel prices, fares climb
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) This marks the second consecutive month of accelerating inflation and the highest rate since February 2023

MANILA, Philippines – Inflation sped up further for the second straight month as higher fuel, electricity, and transport prices squeezed households already struggling with the rising cost of living.

Inflation soared to 7.8% in October from 7.2% in September, the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) said on Thursday, November 5. It stood at just 1.7% in October 2025.

October 2026’s rate now marks the highest inflation rate since February 2023, when it reached 8.6% amid the lingering effects of Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which had disrupted global food and energy markets.

The latest inflation figure brought average inflation from January to October to 5.6%, well above the government’s target range of 2% to 4%.

OCTOBER INFLATION. The commodities above contributed the most to October’s overall inflation, but they are not necessarily the same ones that drove its acceleration, which measures what pushed inflation up compared with September. Image from Philippine Statistics Authority

Transport was the biggest driver of the rise in October inflation. As a whole commodity group, transport inflation surged to 20.1% from 14.6% as fare increases implemented in late September reflected fully in the data. Inflation for other passenger transport by road, including jeepneys and tricycles, reached 11.6%, its highest since June 2023. Bus fares recorded 10.2% inflation. Fuel prices added to the pressure, with gasoline inflation reaching 51.1% and diesel 62.4%.

The second biggest commodity group driver was housing, water, electricity, gas, and other fuels, which recorded 9.3% inflation. Liquefied petroleum gas or LPG inflation soared to 43.4%, while electricity and housing rents registered 14.5% and 4.2%, respectively.

Food inflation actually eased to 6.1% from 6.7% in September. However, rice inflation reached 20.7%, its highest since July 2024. Rice alone contributed 1.4 percentage points to October’s 7.8% headline inflation rate. National Statistician Dennis Mapa attributed this partly to a drop in palay production throughout the third quarter of 2026 and the effects of El Niño.

More worrying was the continued rise in core inflation, which excludes volatile components of the inflation basket, like food and energy. Even without those, the core inflation rate climbed to 5.4% in October 2026, its highest since September 2023, when it reached 5.9%.

The poorest Filipinos continue to be the hardest hit. Inflation among the bottom 30% income households reached 9.5%, up from 9% in September. Average inflation for the bottom 30% has now reached 6.8% for 2026.

The weakening peso has also made imported fuel and other goods more expensive, although Mapa said the PSA had yet to estimate the exact impact of the depreciation.

Asked by Rappler about the late September minimum wage hike, Mapa said higher labor costs could be feeding into prices of restaurant meals and labor-intensive services, but how much of those increases came from wages alone has yet to be established.

Looking ahead, Mapa warned that the effects of El Niño on agricultural production, continued increases in global energy prices, and transport fares could keep inflation elevated. Transport inflation, in particular, could be a repeated pressure point because fares are now being compared with lower levels a year ago, before the recent hikes.

Filipinos are already feeling financially stretched. An October study by Organic Intelligence found that 45% of urban Filipinos said inflation had drained their motivation to get ahead, while 42% had borrowed money for essentials such as food and transportation.

The persistent price pressures have also pushed the BSP to tighten monetary policy. The central bank hiked its benchmark interest rate by a “jumbo” 50 basis points to 5.50%, its fourth consecutive increase in 2026.

BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr. warned that inflation could accelerate further in the coming months due to oil prices, transport fares, and the potential effects of El Niño on food production.

The BSP forecasts inflation to average 6.1% in 2026 and 6% in 2027. – Rappler.com

World.title: Lawmakers who didn’t support Sara impeachment get scraps in proposed 2027 budget
World.content:
Tweny-eight of the 36 district lawmakers who are poised to get the smallest public works budgets for 2027 either objected to the impeachment of the Vice President or abstained from the vote

Ahead of the House vote on the second impeachment case of Sara Duterte earlier this year, the National Unity Party called on the House majority not to retaliate against lawmakers who will not support their battle against the Vice President.

That appeal appears to have fallen on deaf ears, going by the proposed 2027 national budget.

Rappler’s analysis of public works funding allocations for congressional districts, based on aggregated data from People’s Budget Coalition and BetterGov.PH, indicate that congressmen who didn’t take a stand against the Vice President tended to receive smaller budgets for the upcoming fiscal year.

Small slice of the pie

Our review found that 28 out of 36 district lawmakers who did not vote to impeach the veep are poised to receive no more than P300 million each in Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) project funding for 2027.

From this number, 13 cast a no vote on Duterte’s impeachment. They include father-and-son Paolo and Omar Duterte, Southern Leyte 1st District Representative and Duterte-era public works chief Roger Mercado, and a handful of Mindanaoan lawmakers, such as Dal Corvera of Agusan del Norte, Laarni Roque of Bukidnon, Isidro Ungab of Davao City, and Nelson Dayanghirang of Davao Oriental.

Two specifically voted to abstain, namely Steve Solon of Sarangani and Audrey Zubiri of Bukidnon. Zubiri is the wife of current Senate Majority Leader Miguel Zubiri, who is seen by analysts as likely to vote in favor of Duterte’s conviction at the Senate.

Another 13 lawmakers did not vote at all. In Congress, legislators caught between opposing camps during contentious proceedings sometimes skip plenary sessions altogether, allowing them to avoid taking a position that could alienate either side.

A trio of lawmakers from Rizal who were absent during the vote — Jose Arturo Garcia, Tom Hernandez, and Emigdio Tanjuatco — are set to receive only P163 million for their shared engineering office in the proposed 2027 budget.

Even Deputy Speaker Kristine Meehan-Singson, despite her leadership role, had to deal with a smaller budget for her district. The Ilocos Sur congresswoman also skipped the May vote on Duterte’s impeachment.

Chump change

At the bottom of the list is the engineering office that serves Davao City 2nd District Representative Omar Duterte, which received a measly P4.2 million in infrastructure funding for 2027.

The younger Duterte is the grandson of former president Rodrigo Duterte and son of incumbent Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte, whose engineering office received the third lowest public works budget at P5.2 million.

The two Dutertes are often either absent or non-participating members during key House deliberations, but took the time to cast their no vote to the impeachment of the Vice President.

It is important to note that the figures could be higher. The budget watchdogs’ computation is still conservative, taking into account only projects handled by district engineering offices.

In reality, the budget for some public works projects is sourced from the regional or central office of DPWH. Lawmakers do not necessarily have control over all of these projects.

House prosecutors’ share

Some engineering offices serving the districts of lawmakers tapped to prosecute the Vice President at her impeachment trial fared better in the 2027 budget.

Most notably, the district engineering office that lead prosecutor Jinky Luistro shares with another Batangas congresswoman is poised to receive at least P3.1 billion in public works funds for 2027, putting her in the top 20.

The engineering offices associated with the districts of prosecutors Joel Chua and Bel Zamora are also getting more than a billion pesos in funding each, while lawmakers Lorenz Defensor, Lordan Suan, and Kaka Bag-ao’s associated engineering offices are poised to receive more than half a billion pesos in infrastructure funds.

In Congress, where patronage politics runs deep, it is not unusual for allies of the administration to get a bigger slice of the pie. In fact, the top beneficiaries of public works funds in the 2027 budget, based on the watchdogs’ computation, include Sandro Marcos, Speaker Bojie Dy, and appropriations chair Mika Suansing.

But the House has attracted growing scrutiny over its supposed failure to make the budget process in the lower chamber transparent, and to properly explain billions of pesos in adjustments it made in the President’s National Expenditure Program through the House spending bill.

The finding also comes on the heels of the Vice President’s concerns that the 2027 budget could be weaponized to pressure senator-judges into voting a certain way in her trial. Senator-judges have already pushed back against the allegation. – Rappler.com

World.title: A nuclear Philippines in six years? OECD’s nuclear chief isn’t convinced.
World.content:
The head of the OECD's Nuclear Energy Agency casts doubt on the Philippines' 2032 nuclear target, saying that getting its first reactor operating will likely take longer than six years

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines is unlikely to have its first nuclear reactor operating by 2032, according to the head of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Nuclear Energy Agency (OECD-NEA), who warned that developing a nuclear power plant would take longer than six years.

“I don’t think you’re going to have the first reactor operating in six years. It simply takes longer than that. You might have a decision in six years,” OECD-NEA director-general William Magwood told reporters on Wednesday, November 4.

“There’s a lot of discussions that have to be had between governments, between the utility and vendors. These take years to go through,” he added. “And the regulator is still very nascent. It’s just getting started. So no, it won’t happen in five or six years. But it will certainly happen within the foreseeable future if things stay on track.”

The international nuclear expert’s assessment comes less than a month after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. confirmed that the government’s target of introducing 1,200 megawatts (MW) of nuclear capacity by 2032 was achievable.

That timeline is already being reconsidered by Energy Secretary Sharon Garin. In addition, the Department of Energy’s (DOE) draft nuclear power capacity tender guidelines is already framed more conservatively, with initial electricity deliveries in 2038, six years later than Marcos’ endorsed target. This timetable applies to projects under the proposed tender though, meaning earlier projects through other arrangements may also be possible.

TIMELINE. DOE’s timeline in its draft nuclear capacity tender as of September 2026 shows a first target delivery date of 2038.

“The draft nuclear energy tender does indicate already that delivery starts in 2038. And we’ve also gone on record in statements that we will stick to what’s in the plan,” DOE Director IV Patrick Aquino told reporters. “As you know, nuclear power projects takes a long time, takes a lot of push, so we are still not officially changing. We’re still hopeful on getting it done.”

With the ambitious goal, the DOE has been busy hosting forums and courting nuclear experts, suppliers, and developers. However, some early roadblocks have already appeared, with the Philippine Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (PhilATOM) still awaiting the appointment of its leadership and its unfinished implementing rules and regulation.

Beyond setting up the regulator, Aquino said the DOE was pursuing capacity-building initiatives, including human resource development and technical cooperation with countries that already operate nuclear facilities.

Magwood, however, warned that recruiting qualified personnel remains a “very big struggle” even in OECD countries, with nuclear regulators requiring specialists in engineering, science, geology, and other fields.

Public acceptance, nuclear waste

Then there is the issue of getting the public to accept nuclear energy, with its risks and long-lasting waste.

So far, DOE surveys have shown relatively strong nationwide support for nuclear energy, with approval rising from 79% in 2019 to 82% in 2024.

Aquino said acceptance in communities being considered for nuclear development has also been relatively high, ranging from 60% to 90% depending on the location. Potential sites assessed include Bataan, Palawan, Masbate, Pangasinan, and Camarines Norte, while another nationwide survey is being prepared.

Still, Magwood cautioned that support could vary between communities.

“People in Philippines seem to be ready to have this conversation and to see where it takes them,” he said. “There’s a lot of support in some parts of the country and in other parts, maybe not as much. That’s pretty typical.”

Among the concerns is nuclear waste, which can remain dangerously radioactive long after it is removed from a reactor.

Magwood said there already exists technology to safely store spent nuclear fuel in specialized containers for decades before eventual disposal in geological repositories. However, he acknowledged that despite the technological advances made, nuclear waste is still “a very emotional topic,” especially for host communities.

While expressing confidence that the Philippines could manage nuclear waste, Magwood acknowledged that the country has yet to determine its approach to final disposal.

“The cost comes at the final disposal. But the Philippines hasn’t decided on that yet so it’s hard to put a cost estimate to it,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Myanmar’s NUG Warns US Against Prioritizing Its Interests Over Peace
World.content:
In response to the new U.S. Mission Strategy for war-torn Myanmar, the parallel civilian National Unity Government (NUG) and observers urged Washington to help solve the country’s political crisis first instead of prioritizing its own security and economic interests.

Speaking with The Irrawaddy, NUG Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister David Gum Awng said that if the U.S. had a genuine desire to see sustainable peace and economic development in the country, the root cause of the political crisis must be solved first.

“An approach that sidelines the core principles such as democracy, human rights and establishment of a federal union in favor of prioritizing its [own] security and economic interests is not sufficient and lacks the comprehensive scope needed to solve the Myanmar crisis,” he added.

The U.S. State Department recently published its latest strategy for Myanmar, prioritizing the fight against online scam networks that target Americans, increasing U.S. investment, and access to rare earth minerals. Additional objectives include expanding U.S. regional influence and brokering a peace agreement by 2030.

Recently, U.S. officials held talks with junta leaders in Naypyitaw and Tokyo, increasing Washington’s engagement with the internationally isolated coup regime that ousted the democratically elected civilian government led by pro-democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021.

Washington said in its latest statement that facilitating dialogue and supporting multi-stakeholder engagement would help lay the groundwork for lasting peace and national reconciliation.

However, Gum Awng argued that peace cannot be achieved simply by forcing stakeholders to sit together at a negotiating table, noting that the primary challenge is whether the regime is genuinely willing to give up its dictatorship and accept real change.

“Without the definitive end of the military dictatorship, the emergence of an inclusive political process involving all stakeholders (including ethnic groups), and the establishment of robust monitoring mechanisms to guarantee agreements, any hastily brokered peace driven by a specific timeline will only temporarily de-escalate the conflict without solving the underlying root problem.”

Regarding the U.S. goal of building regional influence, the NUG minister said Myanmar cannot be viewed solely as a proxy battleground for U.S.-China influence, adding that the sovereignty and the right to self-determination of the nation’s people remain paramount.
