“If the U.S. wishes to build long-term, sustainable influence, engaging with the military council alone is insufficient. The U.S. must respect the democratic will of the Myanmar people, increase its engagement with federal democratic forces, and prove through practical actions that it is a reliable partner,” Gum Awng said.

“U.S. influence cannot be measured solely by its ability to counter China. It depends entirely on earning the trust of the Myanmar people and participating constructively in the building of a future federal democratic nation.”

Regarding U.S. efforts to gain access to rare earth minerals through its peace efforts, the NUG’s deputy foreign minister warned that the country’s resources cannot be treated merely as a component of a peace process or a political compromise, since they are directly tied to the long-term interests of the people, the rights of ethnic groups, and the resource management rights of the future federal union.

Regarding Washington’s move to boost engagement with the regime, Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative ASEAN Network on Burma, said a strategy based on appeasing the root cause of Myanmar’s notorious transnational crime hubs is doomed to fail. U.S. citizens, along with the people of Myanmar and the region, continue to suffer due to this irresponsible approach, she said.

“It is like engaging serial killers in order to persuade them to kill fewer people instead of acting to stop their crimes,” she said.

“It is both illogical and immoral to bribe [coup president] Min Aung Hlaing’s junta with trade and aid to secure rare earths while looking away from the security, economic and humanitarian crises he is intensifying every day.”

She also warned that the U.S. was in danger of falling into Min Aung Hlaing’s trap, in which he is able to pit Moscow, Beijing and Washington against each other to secure more weapons, more cash and more legitimacy without concrete solutions.

Regarding U.S. peace efforts, Myanmar political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye said, “I don’t think it [a U.S.-brokered peace plan] will work. Myanmar’s political situation and its underlying problem cannot be resolved easily or quickly. Its peace plan is likely either a strategic miscalculation or merely a gesture to show the U.S. is interested in it.”

World.title: Is Myanmar’s Regime Preparing Another ‘Summit Surprise’?
World.content:
As regional leaders finalize their itineraries for this month’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila, a grim and familiar pattern is playing out in Myanmar. For four years, the military junta has delivered a “summit surprise”: a sharp escalation in violence, usually deadly airstrikes on civilians, timed to coincide with high-level diplomatic gatherings.

Human rights organizations and UN bodies have documented this cycle extensively. Ahead of the May 2023 ASEAN Summit in Indonesia, the military bombed the village of Pazigyi, killing more than 160 people. Human Rights Watch cited the attack as evidence of the junta’s disregard for ASEAN’s peace plan for Myanmar, known as the Five-Point Consensus. Later that year, as leaders were still managing the diplomatic fallout, the military struck a displaced persons camp in Kachin State, killing 28 civilians, including children. Amnesty International described the attack as a likely war crime. The brazenness grew ahead of the October 2024 summits in Laos, when the military launched some of its heaviest aerial campaigns since the 2021 coup. In September 2024 alone, monitors recorded 153 airstrikes, which destroyed schools and hospitals among other civilian targets. A report by the OHCHR, the UN’s human rights body, confirmed that airstrike fatalities nearly doubled that year.

Shortly before his visit to Malaysia in October this year, Min Aung Hlaing’s regime intensified its bombardment of Rakhine State, where an airstrike on a crowded local market killed at least 50 people, including children. The attack was so bloody that UN human rights chief Volker Türk said, “This latest attack raises serious concerns about respect for international humanitarian law with respect to the conduct of hostilities.”

The gap between diplomatic theater and reality on the ground has rarely been wider. Last week, Philippine Foreign Secretary and ASEAN Special Envoy Maria Theresa Lazaro made a two-day visit to Myanmar, overseeing humanitarian aid in Shan State and discussing the restoration of Myanmar’s ASEAN status with regime officials. She left without meeting detained State Counselor Aung San Suu Kyi. Manila has repeatedly pressed for access to the 81-year-old Nobel peace laureate, but Lazaro reportedly did not even request a meeting this time, fearing the junta would cancel her trip.

The regime was quick to exploit the optics, projecting an image of cooperation through state media. It also continues to use Aung San Suu Kyi as a bargaining chip. Recent limited contact, including a brief consular phone call with her son and a package from Britain’s King Charles, appear aimed at softening its pariah status abroad while denying ASEAN any meaningful access. Soon after the envoy’s departure, the junta’s fighter jets were back over civilian areas.

This approach is now alienating even Naypyitaw’s most accommodating neighbors. In August, Thailand rolled out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing, the newly self-appointed president, in the hope of pragmatic dialogue. Many in Myanmar consider him a war criminal. Thailand is now facing the fallout of the regime’s violence. Its reckless operations along the frontier recently prompted the Thai military to summon Myanmar’s defense attaché to lodge a formal protest. The embarrassment has spilled into domestic politics, where the opposition has accused the Anutin government of being dangerously soft on Naypyitaw. Critics argue that accommodation not only undermines democratic values but also emboldens a junta willing to threaten Thai security and humiliate neighbors who extend a hand.

For the Philippines, this year’s ASEAN chair, the crisis has proven exhausting. Manila has tried to balance quiet diplomacy with firmer rhetoric, but the junta’s relentless violence has stalled any real progress. When the summit ends, Manila will likely be relieved to hand the “Myanmar headache” to incoming chair Singapore.

Singapore will inherit a deeply fractured regional approach to a crisis that continues to embarrass Southeast Asia. Though historically a champion of pragmatic diplomacy, it has grown more assertive as its chairmanship nears, and many hope it will take a firm stand against the regime. At an informal ASEAN foreign ministers’ meeting in Bangkok in July 2026, brokered by Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, Singapore’s Vivian Balakrishnan pressed Myanmar’s representatives directly to release political prisoners, naming Aung San Suu Kyi, and to allow safe, unimpeded delivery of humanitarian aid. Singapore has also shown a growing willingness to scrutinize financial flows and aviation fuel reaching the junta. Yet the fundamental equation remains unchanged: the regime has proven immune to standard diplomatic persuasion and incremental sanctions.

When the gavel falls in Manila this month, there will no doubt be renewed expressions of “deep concern” and calls for an end to hostilities. But as the smoke clears over Rakhine State and diplomatic protests are filed in Bangkok, the truer story emerges. For the people of Myanmar, ASEAN’s diplomatic milestones are no longer opportunities for a breakthrough. They are dark omens of the violence that follows.

World.title: Thailand’s New Deals with Myanmar and Washington’s Changing Priorities
World.content:
As we approach the end of October, it is worth revisiting Myanmar regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s official visit to Thailand in August, particularly in light of what has happened since. Within two months, Myanmar has concluded new technological cooperation arrangements with Thailand and Russia, while the United States has held two rounds of direct talks with the regime. These developments may look unrelated, but they point towards something considerably more interesting: the regime is expanding its international relationships, acquiring access to new technologies and developing opportunities for intelligence cooperation.

On August 6-7, Min Aung Hlaing visited Thailand, where the two governments exchanged four cooperation instruments. The most interesting, no doubt, was a Memorandum of Understanding between Thailand’s Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency (GISTDA) and the Myanmar Space Agency. The agreement concerns Earth-observation technology and satellite information, officially intended for natural-resource management, environmental monitoring and disaster response.

As I discussed in my previous article, Buying Gas or Buying Surveillance? Gas-Rich Myanmar’s Deal With Russia, Moscow is already providing Myanmar with access to satellite and communications technology. Thailand’s new agreement adds another dimension to Myanmar’s expanding international technological cooperation.

But Thailand’s agreement is particularly interesting because satellite technology is only one component of the cooperation it is offering Myanmar.

The joint statement issued during the August visit contains an important commitment: Thailand officially pledged to support Myanmar’s membership in the Egmont Group, an international network of financial intelligence units (FIUs) that facilitates financial intelligence sharing across jurisdictions.

Thailand has been an Egmont Group member since 2001. Its Anti-Money Laundering Office already participates in the international network, and Bangkok has now committed to strengthening cooperation with Myanmar’s anti-money-laundering authorities, including information sharing and capacity-building.

Through Egmont cooperation, financial intelligence units can exchange information concerning suspicious transactions, financial relationships and the movement of funds across jurisdictions. The information can also help establish connections between individuals, companies and organizations operating internationally.

And what transactions are considered suspicious? Pretty much all of them—unless the Myanmar regime has personally approved them.

For the regime, acquiring such capabilities would represent a significant institutional development, particularly when considered alongside its expanding access to satellite technology.

The official justification is combating transnational organized crime. Both governments agreed to intensify efforts against online scams, narcotics and criminal networks operating along their shared border, including disrupting illicit financial flows.

The United States is pursuing similar objectives.

In September and October, American officials held two rounds of discussions with representatives of Myanmar’s military-backed government.

Following the regime’s release of American businessman Adam Castillo in September 2026, Washington is believed to be seeking cooperation from Myanmar’s military authorities to shut down cybercrime operations targeting Americans. Same old story—we’ve heard it all before.

But the Trump administration has its own priorities. There is little reason to interpret these discussions through the political priorities of previous administrations. The United States has a different president, and his administration is pursuing different interests.

What deserves attention is the relationship between these developments. Russia is expanding cooperation on satellite technologies. Washington is engaging the regime on transnational crime. Thailand is explicitly identifying the disruption of criminal financial networks as a priority, promising to strengthen Myanmar’s financial intelligence capabilities.

On October 23, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow went further, welcoming the renewed American engagement with Myanmar. He explained that Thailand did not want Myanmar isolated or turned into an arena for geopolitical rivalry. Bangkok therefore welcomes U.S. involvement alongside its own bilateral cooperation.

The regime is developing relationships with governments whose interests are not identical but whose cooperation could nevertheless strengthen its technological and intelligence capabilities.

And that brings us to the possible consequences of combating transnational crime.

Cybercrime networks along the Thai-Myanmar border are obvious targets for financial investigations. But what begins as an international effort against scam centers could provide the infrastructure for a much wider witch-hunt.

The same mechanisms that trace financial transactions involving criminal networks can expose financial relationships involving independent media or NGOs. Banking information, company records, beneficial ownership structures and cross-border transactions can reveal how organizations are financed and who maintains commercial relationships with them.

The regime could therefore strengthen its ability to investigate financial flows involving ethnic armed organizations, political opposition groups and businesses across Myanmar, including those entirely unrelated to cybercrime.

Combined with improved satellite information, these capabilities could provide the regime with considerably greater visibility over both the physical infrastructure and financial relationships of organizations operating against it.

Officially, the objective is disrupting organized crime. But the regime has fought ethnic armed organizations for decades. It would be rather optimistic to assume that expanded financial surveillance capabilities will never be directed against political or military opponents.

There is another dimension to Thailand’s growing role in Myanmar, particularly concerning the United States.

U.S. legislative policy towards Thailand has changed considerably over the past three decades.

Remember the three Burma acts?

In 1995, the proposed Free Burma Act was rather uncompromising. Section 6 would have required the U.S. president to withhold assistance to Thailand until Bangkok fully cooperated in supporting Myanmar refugees and exiles. Section 7 demanded reports on Thailand’s treatment of refugees, students and exiles. Although the bill was never enacted, the message was clear: Thailand’s treatment of Myanmar nationals could come at a financial cost.

By 2003, Washington had apparently discovered the virtues of diplomacy. The Burmese Freedom and Democracy Act described Thailand as a close U.S. ally and called for Washington to work closely with Bangkok on human rights, political freedom and coordinated sanctions against Myanmar. The threat of withholding U.S. assistance had disappeared, replaced by considerably friendlier language about cooperation.

The BURMA Act of 2022 was even more accommodating. It supported humanitarian assistance and refugee protection involving Thailand and neighboring countries, without imposing comparable financial penalties on Bangkok over its treatment of Myanmar refugees. By this point, Washington was more interested in financing cooperation with Thailand than threatening to cut off assistance.

So, in 1995, U.S. legislators contemplated withholding assistance from Thailand over Myanmar refugees. By 2003, Thailand was being treated as a partner in implementing U.S. policy towards Myanmar. By 2022, cooperation with Thailand had become part of the broader framework for cross-border humanitarian assistance.

Now, in October 2026, Washington is conducting direct negotiations with the regime, and Thailand has publicly welcomed those discussions.

For organizations operating against the regime, these developments should be taken seriously.

The regime is establishing international relationships that can provide technological assistance, institutional development, financial intelligence cooperation and new channels of diplomatic engagement. These relationships do not depend on the regime resolving its conflicts with ethnic armed organizations or reaching an agreement with the National Unity Government (NUG).

If the NUG is underestimating the regime’s ability to develop such relationships, or underplaying the strategic importance of the capabilities being offered, that would be a serious mistake.

Military strength is not measured exclusively by the number of soldiers, weapons or territorial positions an organization controls. Access to information, institutional capacity and sustainable financing can be equally consequential.

The financial situation of Myanmar’s democracy movement is becoming increasingly difficult. For FY2024 and FY2025, Washington allocated $121 million annually to democracy, governance, human rights and humanitarian assistance programs concerning Myanmar. However, the Trump administration’s foreign aid cuts in 2025 affected several programs supporting pro-democracy organisations, including those operating in exile.

A November 2025 study by the Stimson Center interviewed 30 Myanmar civil society leaders, all of whom reported insufficient or short-term funding. Some organizations have already suspended activities, reduced staff or closed offices. International funding is also increasingly directed towards humanitarian assistance rather than political advocacy and institution-building.

A September 2026 study published in Civil Wars highlights the NUG’s financial difficulties, particularly its limited access to stable revenue sources due to its lack of control over substantial territory and economic resources.

Meanwhile, the regime is building international partnerships that could help it monitor its opponents and trace their finances. The NUG could find itself with fewer resources while the military acquires better tools to track and undermine it.

Ana Brown is a nuclear lawyer, academic and intelligence analyst specializing in defense economics, and an ALM candidate at Harvard University.

World.title: Top UN Court to Rule November 19 on Myanmar Rohingya Genocide Case
World.content:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands—The top UN court will on November 19 deliver a landmark ruling on whether Myanmar’s crackdown against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority constituted a genocide, officials said on Tuesday.

Judges at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) have for seven years been weighing accusations by Gambia that Myanmar’s brutal repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

While the ICJ has no means of enforcing its decisions, a ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would heap more international pressure on its military junta and be seen as justice for hundreds of thousands of Rohingya.

Legal experts are closely watching the verdict from the ICJ, which rules in disputes between countries, for clues as to how the court might rule in the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.

Myanmar has always denied carrying out a genocide against the Rohingya, arguing its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

The crackdown by the Myanmar military and Buddhist militias forced hundreds of thousands of Rohingya to flee to neighboring Bangladesh, bringing with them harrowing accounts of gang rape and mass executions.

More than 1 million Rohingya still live across the border in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement.

‘Collective conscience’

During hearings on the case in January, Gambian Justice Minister Dawda Jallow told the court the Rohingya had suffered “the most horrific violence and destruction one could imagine.”

“It is not about esoteric issues of international law. It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow.

“The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction,” added the minister.

Gambia brought the case to the ICJ under the terms of the UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to sound the alarm if it suspects genocide is being committed.

The alleged violations of the convention “are a stain on our collective conscience and it would be irresponsible to pretend that it is not our business,” Jallow said.

Myanmar retorted at the hearing that the allegations were “unsubstantiated.”

“Emotional language and blurry factual pictures are not a substitute for a rigorous presentation of facts,” said Ko Ko Hlaing, a minister in the President’s Office.

In a previous hearing in 2019, then-de facto civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi herself addressed the court, housed in the iconic Peace Palace in The Hague.

The Nobel peace laureate said the case risked reigniting the crisis that led to the Rohingyas’ expulsion and there was no “genocidal intent” behind the crackdown.

Aung San Suu Kyi, 81, will not be attending the verdict, however. She has been detained in Myanmar’s capital Naypyitaw since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.

The ICJ has already made one ruling in this case, ordering Myanmar in 2020 to “take all measures within its power to prevent the commission of all acts” described by the Genocide Convention.

These acts included “killing members of the group” and “deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part.”

ICJ judges also threw out a challenge to its jurisdiction by Myanmar, ruling that it did have the power to decide on the genocide question.

The ICJ is not the only court looking into possible crimes against the Rohingya.

In 2024, the chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, also based in The Hague, asked judges for an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s junta chief Min Aung Hlaing over alleged crimes against humanity.

A case is also underway in Argentina, under the principle of universal jurisdiction, the idea that some crimes are so heinous they can be heard in any court.

World.title: China’s Myanmar Policy at Crossroads After 5 Years of Failure
World.content:
China’s Myanmar policy rests on a central assumption: that the military remains the country’s decisive political and military force. That assumption may have been valid in previous eras, but Myanmar’s post-coup reality demonstrates Beijing has overestimated the military while underestimating the revolutionary movement that has emerged since 2021.

The revolutionary forces factor

Throughout Myanmar’s civil war since 1948, and again after the 1988 pro-democracy uprising, successive revolutionary movements have failed to establish dominance, leaving most of the country in control of the military. Beijing has shaped its Myanmar policy accordingly, viewing the military as the guarantor of stability in an otherwise fractured nation.

Yet Myanmar after the 2021 coup bears little resemblance to either of those earlier periods.

The political and military balance has shifted dramatically. The Kachin Independence Army (KIA), Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), Arakan Army (AA), Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), and Chin and Karenni resistance forces have emerged as formidable military actors capable of seizing and controlling large swaths of territory.

Even the Karen National Union (KNU), weakened by decades of internal splits and defections since the 1990s, has regained momentum, recapturing numerous military bases and inflicting significant losses on regime forces.

Meanwhile, armed resistance has spread into the Bamar-majority heartland, posing an unprecedented challenge to central rule.

The National Unity Government (NUG) and its People’s Defense Forces (PDFs) have emerged as a major parallel authority, reinforced by cooperation with ethnic armed organizations.

China’s Special Envoy for Asian Affairs Deng Xijun has reportedly warned the United Wa State Army (UWSA) that the NUG will never be a genuine rival to Myanmar’s military. That judgement has historical precedent. Revolutionary movements that emerged after 1948 ultimately failed because of military and political mistakes coupled with weapons and funding shortages. Likewise, the National Coalition Government of the Union of Burma (NCGUB) and the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front (ABSDF), which emerged after the 1988 uprising, never threatened military dominance.

Beijing has calculated that the NUG and PDFs will follow suit and collapse.

But today’s realities point in the opposite direction. Plagued by systemic corruption, declining battlefield effectiveness and shrinking troop numbers, the military has lost support among the Bamar majority amid growing public revulsion over its war crimes against civilians.

Resistance movement: Past and present

The post-1988 NCGUB enjoyed political leadership but little organizational structure on the ground. By contrast, NUG networks extend deep into local communities.

Meanwhile, the ABSDF lacked the strength to operate effectively in Myanmar’s heartland and depended on ethnic armed organizations for refuge. Today’s PDFs and Spring Revolution forces operate independently across Sagaing, Mandalay, Magwe, Bago and Tanintharyi regions, also pushing into Ayeyarwady Region and conducting urban guerrilla warfare in Yangon.

Their military expansion has been matched by broad support among rural Bamar communities. Ethnic armed organizations, meanwhile, increasingly credit PDFs and other Spring Revolution groups with contributing to their own battlefield successes. That combat strength is supported by a centralized command chain and disciplined organization. Battlefield setbacks and defections in 2025 barely dented the movement’s momentum and never matched the mass desertions seen within the Myanmar military in recent years.

While resistance forces still face constraints in weaponry and logistics, by historical standards they remain well equipped.

Also, while the NCGUB and ABSDF were bound by ideology, the link between the NUG and PDF is institutional and operational.

While the NCGUB and ABSDF subsided into political opposition groups within five years, the NUG and PDF remain a formidable military force — arguably the strongest and most expansive resistance movement in modern Myanmar history.

As such, China’s assessment that the NUG and its armed wing are not a serious rival to the military no longer reflects realities on the ground. In today’s Myanmar, it is impossible to understand the conflict without including the NUG and PDF in the equation.

Democracy and China’s concerns

If Beijing has underestimated the military significance of revolutionary forces, it also remains wary of their political agenda — particularly their commitment to democracy.

Yet democracy is hardly an alien concept in China. During its own revolutionary era, the Chinese Communist Party described its struggle as a “people’s democratic revolution” and promoted Mao Zedong’s concept of a “New Democracy.”

The fight against military dictatorship naturally carries democratic aspirations. But that does not mean importing a Western political model wholesale, nor would such a model be easily transplanted.

Myanmar’s revolutionary forces recognize the critical importance of relations with neighboring China. After all, long-term economic engagement with Beijing was also a cornerstone of National League for Democracy (NLD) government’s foreign policy.

New alliances

Chinese pressure has sidelined two major ethnic political and military alliances, namely the Federal Political Negotiation and Consultative Committee led by the UWSA and the tripartite Brotherhood Alliance. Yet new revolutionary coalitions have emerged.

One is the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF), which brings together the NUG and major armed organizations including Kachin, Chin, Karen and Karenni forces. Another is the Spring Revolution Alliance (SRA), which unites anti-regime forces that emerged after the coup. Both alliances pursue political and military objectives, and coordination between them appears to be steadily improving.

The Arakan Army — which controls most of Rakhine State and remains the biggest thorn in the regime’s side — is forging deepening ties with both groupings.

The trajectory of once-isolated resistance organizations is thus becoming increasingly interconnected, gradually evolving into a broader political and military bloc. These organizations are indispensable not only to achieving peace and nationwide stability, but also to safeguard long-term China-Myanmar relations and Chinese interests in the country.

Weaknesses of revolutionary forces

The resistance continues to suffer gaps in institutionalization, chain of command, logistics and weapons supply, and unification. Yet these are offset by substantial public support, a reputation largely unstained by atrocities, and high internal morale.

Most revolutionary groups also refrain from the systemic corruption that characterizes regime rule. Those who do profit from drug trafficking or online scam operations remain exceptions rather than the norm.

Close public scrutiny and critical supporters generally ensures that revolutionary misrule is generally harder to conceal and easier to correct. Myanmar’s military, by contrast, exhibits many of the opposite traits and has also repeatedly failed to unite the country’s ethnic communities or deliver lasting stability.

China’s Myanmar policy vs Myanmar’s reality

Taken together, these developments expose two fundamental errors in China’s reading of post-coup Myanmar.

While Beijing justifiably views the military as a key actor in Myanmar’s future, it overestimates its ability to achieve stability in the face of an increasingly entrenched and unified armed resistance. A military-centric policy no longer reflects a landscape transformed since the 2021 coup.

The second error lies in the timing of Beijing’s intervention. China moved to shore up the regime as Min Aung Hlaing faced mounting pressure from battlefield defeats, economic crisis and growing dissent within the military.

Had Beijing waited for his removal before backing the regime, more pragmatic figures may have taken the military helm.

Instead, China’s hasty support strengthened hardliners around Min Aung Hlaing while sidelining moderates and internal critics. In effect, Beijing’s scramble to preserve the military prolonged the rule of a failing strongman. Desperate to salvage his diminished authority and prestige, Min Aung Hlaing has vowed to reclaim all territory lost to revolutionary forces. As such, the civil war looks set to escalate rather than ease.

China’s policy has yielded gains for the regime, most notably by pressing ASEAN countries to reengage with Naypyitaw. But it has come at the cost of entrenching Naypyitaw’s hardliners, the root cause of instability.

The generals’ flawed policies and spiraling military spending have opened the door to economic collapse and poverty, while systematic corruption has fueled narcotics trafficking and online scam networks.

Despite China’s support, they have failed to achieve the military, political, and economic stability that Beijing craves.

Time for a policy shift?

Recent developments suggest Beijing may already be reassessing its Myanmar strategy. While China remains Myanmar’s largest foreign investor, new investment in fiscal 2025-26 fell to just US$ 158.2 million. Large-scale Chinese investment and lending failed to materialize even after the junta rebranded as a pseudo-civilian government in April.

Meanwhile, China’s Special Envoy Deng Xijun has broken off from frequent visits to Myanmar, where he has not been seen since March. Likewise, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia, who regularly met Min Aung Hlaing and senior regime officials after taking up her post in August 2024, last met the junta chief in Naypyitaw on April 6, 2026.

The Chinese Communist Party regularly evaluates its policy outcomes. As pragmatists, Chinese leaders place considerable emphasis on results.

In Myanmar’s case, Beijing’s objective remains unchanged: stability. Yet stability remains elusive even as China’s core interests — including Belt and Road development and multibillion-dollar border trade — continue to face severe disruption. Under such circumstances, Beijing cannot afford to proceed with the status quo. While China’s core aim in Myanmar is unlikely to change, its strategic assumptions and methods must adapt.

Thet Htar Maung is a political analyst.

World.title: Thai Military Chief Summons Myanmar Attaché Over Border Fighting
World.content:
Thailand’s Chief of Defense Forces General Ukrit Buntanont summoned Myanmar military attaché Brigadier General Win Thu Lin on Monday over fighting along the Thai-Myanmar border, warning the regime to exercise caution in its military operations.

The action was driven by rising concerns among Thai residents near the border, some of whom have staged protests calling for greater security after clashes and Myanmar regime airstrikes in Karen State injured a Thai person and damaged property on the Thai side.

During Monday’s meeting, the Thai defense chief emphasized the need to consider potential impacts on the safety of Thai citizens and their property, according to a statement from the Royal Thai Armed Forces Headquarters.

It stated that the discussion reflected a “shared commitment” to maintaining communication channels and promoting positive relations between the two militaries.

Thai officials also sent formal protest letters to Naypyitaw to prevent further escalation, Thai PBS reported on Tuesday, citing the chief of Thailand’s National Security Council.

Ongoing clashes between the Myanmar regime and the Karen National Union’s armed wings and its allies in Myawaddy, Karen State, have sent stray rounds into Thailand, while explosions have been felt across the border.

On October 22, a 40-mm mortar shell landed in Thailand and damaged two houses. On October 26, the Thai military deployed troops to reinforce security along the border and warned that it was ready to respond.

As fighting intensified in Min Let Pan Village in Myawaddy, spillover rounds injured a Thai citizen, prompting Thai forces to fire two warning smoke rounds back toward the Myanmar side on October 29.

Despite Thailand’s warning, Myanmar regime aircraft dropped two bombs on the KNU-controlled border checkpoint at Thaw Le Hta, opposite Mae Sam Laep pier in Mae Hong Son, Thailand, on October 31. The shockwaves shattered windows of buildings in Thailand, prompting the Thai Air Force to deploy two F-16 fighter jets to patrol the border.

Following the incident, a letter was leaked in which the Myanmar regime warned Thai businessmen to end contact with the KNU and to stop trading through Thaw Le Hta, which it described as a violation of Myanmar law.

Neither the Myanmar regime nor the KNU has yet released an official statement about the leaked letter.

World.title: America’s New Myanmar Strategy Puts a Price Tag on Peace
World.content:
For more than three decades, Washington’s Myanmar policy began with one question: how does the country get back to democracy? Under President Trump, that has changed.

The new “Integrated Country Strategy for Burma,” approved Aug. 31 and published recently, asks instead: what can Myanmar do for America? Its four goals are to stop scams and visa overstays, sell more American goods, broker peace by 2030, and push back against China.

That does not mean Washington has abandoned sanctions or opposition contacts. It means the embassy’s metrics of success have changed.

At times, the 11-page document reads like a scorecard: three commercial deals, triple Myanmar’s imports from the U.S., three peace forums, zero visa overstays. The embassy’s 2022 strategy prioritized restoring inclusive democracy. In the new one the word “democracy” does not even appear, nor do “political prisoners” or “airstrikes.” Human rights feature mostly as a benefit of stability.

Its most revealing line, on Page 9, says talks on “fiscal federalism and territorial demarcation…will create opportunities to access Burma’s bountiful rare earth resources and combat scam centers.”

There is nothing wrong with Washington pursuing its interests. But a country at war is not a market where one government can sign away the obstacles. In Myanmar, authority to sign agreements, control of territory and public consent rarely rest in the same hands, and this strategy confuses the first with the other two.

Assistant Secretary of State Michael Vance met Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw on Sept. 15-16, ostensibly to seek the release of American businessman Adam Castillo and discuss scam operations. Talks also took place in Tokyo in June and again in October. Some Myanmar-linked individuals have come off U.S. sanctions lists, though Min Aung Hlaing remains blacklisted. The generals have also made their case through a $3 million-a-year lobbying contract with DCI Group, later involving Trump ally Roger Stone.

No mineral deal can bypass China

Myanmar is a major source of heavy rare earths used in powerful magnets. In 2024, however, the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) took Pangwa and Chipwi, the heart of the border mining belt, from a military-aligned militia. Stimson Center researchers have documented mining expanding into other ethnic armed territories, including the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA)’s.

Even if they wanted to forge a new deal with the U.S., the generals cannot hand over land they do not hold, nor would getting ore out of Myanmar by itself create an American alternative to China. The trade depends on Chinese buyers, routes, chemicals and processing. Almost all of Myanmar’s heavy rare earths are transported overland to China. No deal signed in Naypyitaw can replace a whole supply chain.

Asking the arsonist to fight the fire

On scams, Washington has a strong national-security case: Americans have lost billions to Southeast Asian fraud operations, some staffed by trafficked people forced to commit crimes.

But look at who protects the compounds. The most notorious epicenters of scam operations, such as Shwe Kokko and KK Park, grew up along the Thai border under the protection of Naypyitaw-allied armed militias. In May 2025, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned the Karen National Army, formerly the Karen Border Guard Force, and commander Saw Chit Thu for enabling scams and trafficking. Treasury knew that the militia had profited from its military ties.

In an Oct. 30 assessment, the Financial Action Task Force kept Myanmar on its high-risk list, citing scam centers. A law-enforcement deal with Naypyitaw might help individual cases but will not dismantle networks whose protectors profit from them. Washington cannot suddenly expect verifiable action against their finances and operators from the generals.

The human reality behind overstay numbers

The repatriation goal carries another danger. It seeks to eliminate visa overstays, a popular policy objective for Trump, by fostering closer cooperation with “Burmese authorities.” Yet Washington’s own travel advisory warns of arbitrary detention, punishment for criticism and military conscription in Myanmar, and the strategy offers no specific safeguards for dissidents, journalists, defectors or draft-age people facing return. Are overstay statistics to replace individual assessments of protection claims against these dangers that the U.S. itself has flagged? People fleeing persecution must not become bargaining chips.

Selling soybeans in a warzone

The State Department wants three deals worth more than US$5 million each and a tripling of goods and agricultural exports to Myanmar by 2030. In 2025, U.S. exports to Myanmar totaled $78.7 million, compared with $762.3 million in imports. The strategy blames import licensing and currency controls, again proposing talks with “decision-makers in Naypyitaw.” But these are not merely paperwork problems. They come from a regime that is short of dollars, prints money to pay for a war, and runs a banking system on the global watchdog’s blacklist. This is no emerging market waiting for American soybeans. It is an economy ravaged by the war these decision-makers in Naypyitaw unleashed.

Peace is not a box to check

Most troubling is how peace fits into this commercial plan. Ethnic and religious minorities, displaced communities and residents of mining areas need a say, not a place as beneficiaries of someone else’s deal. Without a federal government, there is no one in Myanmar who can govern, collect revenue, protect minorities and answer when armed men abuse civilians. Any peace forum is only as credible as the voices it allows in.

The strategy’s goal of reaching 3 million vulnerable people with humanitarian assistance is welcome. But access also depends on local authorities and civil groups whose futures cannot be negotiated in Naypyitaw.

None of this means Washington should stop pursuing its interests or categorically reject engagement with the military. Some channels can still free detainees, fight crime, and deliver aid. But the U.S. should maintain targeted pressure on military finances, arms procurement and jet-fuel supplies while continuing to engage seriously with the National Unity Government (NUG), Myanmar’s parallel pro-democracy government formed after the 2021 coup, ethnic armed organizations and local administrations, recognizing their different roles and political interests. Treating the generals as the principal brokers of Myanmar’s future would be a fundamental mistake.

America need not choose between its strategic interests and Myanmar’s democratic future. An “America First” policy could serve both: durable trade, credible law enforcement and secure mineral supplies depend on accountable power. The Trump administration needs to recognize that America’s long-term interests would be better served by a democratic, federal Myanmar than by continued military rule.

Nyein Chan Aye is a Burmese journalist based in Washington, D.C., who previously worked for the BBC and Voice of America. He writes on Myanmar, U.S. policy, China and regional affairs.

World.title: China’s BRI Plans Take Shape in Myanmar’s Rebel-Held Borderlands
World.content:
China’s long-standing plans to expand border trade and infrastructure links with Myanmar have stalled amid border instability and shifting power dynamics. But even as Beijing struggles to reassert control, two ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) in northern Shan State are taking steps that could advance its economic ambitions.

Chinese business interests and mineral extraction have drawn attention in territories controlled by the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) in northern Shan State. But drawing less attention is the strategic importance of these areas to Beijing’s China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) — part of its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

In early October, the MNDAA opened a new border-trade gate in Chinshwehaw. Further east, the TNLA is upgrading the border crossing in Namkham Township. Both developments effectively connect EAO-controlled territories to China’s broader cross-border economic plans.

Chinshwehaw: A strategic gateway

The new Chinshwehaw gate plugs into China’s long-standing plan for the Chinshwehaw–Lincang Border Economic Cooperation Zone (CBECZ) under the CMEC. The proposed zone would connect Myanmar’s Laukkai in the Kokang Self-Administered Zone with Lincang in Yunnan Province.

The CMEC route runs west from Kunming through Kokang to Kyaukpyu Port on the Bay of Bengal and is designed to grant China access to the Indian Ocean and markets in South Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. The CBECZ envisages a 200-square-kilometer cross-border development zone, with a new gate —now opened by the MNDAA — serving container and truck traffic and the existing gate reserved for passenger buses and cars. The plan includes export and import zones in Laukkai and Kunlong townships, factories in Kunlong, a bridge over the Salween River, upgraded highways, and interconnected economic zones, including the 125 Economic Zone near Laukkai.

The wider plan features railway and highway links from Kunming through Chinshwehaw, Kunlong, and Lashio. On the Chinese side, Lincang’s development strategy centers on Mengding’s Qingshuihe river port, with industrial parks also earmarked for border towns Nansan and Yonghe under a “One Zone with Multiple Parks” model. The master plan sets ambitious targets for cross-border trade and regional economic growth, but implementation was stalled by security and bureaucratic barriers during the Thein Sein and National League for Democracy governments. After the 2021 coup, the military regime revived the plan through reconstituted border economic cooperation committees and inspections of the 125 Economic Zone.

The MNDAA’s new gate marks a significant shift: infrastructure originally negotiated between the two governments is now emerging in territory controlled by an ethnic armed group. Although no formal agreement between the MNDAA and Beijing has been confirmed, the development suggests that control of crucial nodes in China’s cross-border economic plan has shifted from the central military government to ethnic rebel groups.

Mong Ko and Namkham: More border infrastructure

The MNDAA’s infrastructure initiatives extend beyond Chinshwehaw to other border territory it controls. In Mong Ko, the group plans a six-month, 2.3-million-yuan project to build an international bridge linking to the Chinese border town of Manhai. Since capturing Mong Ko in November 2023, the MNDAA has overseen improvements to local roads and infrastructure. However, residents complain that an influx of Chinese businesses has deprived local communities of economic benefits.

Similar developments are taking shape in Namkham Township, a strategic border town under TNLA control. The group is set to replace the existing Nongdao boat crossing to China’s Yunnan Province with a two-lane bridge for vehicles up to 100 tonnes. Construction of the bridge and border gate is scheduled to begin in December.

Nongdao — part of the CMEC’s Muse (Hosan)–Ruili (Jiegao) Border Economic Cooperation Zone — is envisaged as an international port and bonded agricultural-livestock manufacturing hub. Additional trade crossings are planned for Kyukok–Wanding, Kyin San Kyawt–Maimeng, and Manhero–Jiexiang, supported by road upgrades and new routes.

The Muse–Ruili CBECZ aims to establish an industrial, logistics, and import-export processing hub serving China’s trade with Southeast and South Asia. The plan targets regional GDP of US$6–8 billion and annual trade of $35–45 billion by 2030, with added service-sector value of $1–1.5 billion.

The long-term plan is to link five pairs of China–Myanmar border towns to establish a cross-border free trade zone covering Mangshi, Ruili, and Longchuan by 2040.

However, infrastructure development planned since 2018 has been stymied by border disputes and local opposition. Now, with the TNLA controlling Namkham and upgrading the Nongdao crossing, another component of China’s proposed strategic corridor looks set to proceed under an ethnic armed group rather than Naypyitaw.

Trade restrictions and changing border dynamics

While pressing its infrastructure initiatives, China has also eased import restrictions in some areas of northern Shan State controlled by ethnic armed groups.

Beijing restricted imports after the ethnic Brotherhood Alliance seized large swathes of northern Shan during Operation 1027 in late 2023, threatening the regime’s grip on power. In mid-October it reopened the gate to Chinshwehaw, allowing through construction materials, electrical appliances, and telecoms products. There are also unverified reports that entry has been granted to explosives and chemicals used in Chinese-run gold and mineral mining operations.

Imports have also resumed through the 105-mile trade zone and the Kyinsankyawt crossing, both under Brotherhood Alliance control. Coupled with the groups’ infrastructure projects, the trade resumption points to changing patterns of cross-border economic activity beyond the Myanmar military’s control.

While the armed groups are seeking to consolidate their administration and secure revenue from trade, China wants to maintain border access, connectivity, and economic activity. Though lacking formal cross-border agreements, conditions are now ripe for China’s economic plans to proceed through cooperation with the armed groups. This development threatens Naypyitaw’s dominion over both border trade and multibillion-dollar infrastructure investments.

On Oct. 28, regime chief Min Aung Hlaing accused EAOs of using border trade revenue to bolster their military capabilities, undermining the peace process.

Implications for China’s Myanmar strategy

These developments suggest three broader implications for China’s engagement with Myanmar and the future of the CMEC.

First, China’s economic corridor plan may no longer depend entirely on agreements with Myanmar’s central government. The Chinshwehaw gate opening and planned Nongdao crossing upgrade suggest that components of the CMEC can advance under cooperation with ethnic armed organizations. While Beijing has neither abandoned Naypyitaw nor officially transferred responsibility for its projects to armed groups, practical opportunities for cooperation with local border authorities are now present.

Second, if ethnic armed organizations succeed in developing and managing border and trade infrastructure under China’s connectivity plans, Beijing’s engagement with Myanmar could diversify from its traditional focus on central government to EAOs and other actors who control strategic territory. While not necessarily accompanied by formal recognition, such a shift could mark a multi-layered approach to pursuing Beijing’s economic and security interests.

Third, such diversification could place Myanmar’s military regime under pressure on two fronts: the battlefield and China’s changing economic, security, and geopolitical calculations. The regime has repeatedly vowed to reclaim lost territories but has little to show for its efforts. If Beijing continues to facilitate border trade through EAO-controlled areas, revenues crucial to sustaining the regime’s military campaign against resistance forces will decline further.

Meanwhile, Naypyitaw’s bid to restore relations with the United States and Japan may also prompt China to rethink its regime-centric Myanmar policy.

Beijing also has a strong interest in preventing instability along its own border. Renewed fighting would disrupt trade routes and threaten Yunnan’s security and economy. China must balance engagement with groups controlling the border and maintaining relations with Naypyitaw.

Ultimately, the future of CMEC may depend as much on Myanmar’s shifting territorial realities as on agreements between Beijing and Naypyitaw. As long as the central government cannot exercise effective control over key border areas, Beijing will need to work with the authorities that govern them in practice.

Athena Awn Naw is an expert on ethnic conflict in Myanmar, focusing on China’s expanding influence across economic sectors.

World.title: Kazakhstan Calls for Stronger Implementation of Humanitarian Law at Geneva Dialogue
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has called for stronger national mechanisms to ensure compliance with international humanitarian law (IHL), stressing that efforts to protect civilians must begin long before armed conflicts break out.

The position was presented by Kazakhstan’s delegation at the Global Dialogue on International Humanitarian Law, held in Geneva and organized by the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), reported the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ press service.

The delegation was led by Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office and other international organizations in Geneva Erzhan Kazykhan.

The dialogue brought together representatives of more than 100 countries, international and humanitarian organizations, academic institutions and non-governmental organizations. It was held as part of the Global Initiative to Galvanize Political Commitment to International Humanitarian Law.

In its statement, the Kazakh delegation emphasized that respect for international humanitarian law should be promoted not only during armed conflicts but also in advance. This requires strengthening national mechanisms for implementing IHL, incorporating its rules into military training and instructions, and raising awareness among public authorities and military personnel.

Discussions focused on practical recommendations developed under the Global Initiative’s seven thematic workstreams to improve compliance with existing humanitarian law. Participants addressed the protection of civilians and critical infrastructure, as well as risks associated with the use of new technologies in armed conflicts.

The next major milestone will be the High-Level Conference on Humanity in War, scheduled for Dec. 7 in Amman, Jordan. The conference is expected to secure high-level political support for the understandings reached through the initiative and encourage concrete action by states to uphold international humanitarian law.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans National Laboratory for Critical Materials as Manufacturing Sector Expands
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to establish a National Laboratory for Critical Materials in Astana as part of efforts to develop its mineral resources, strengthen geological exploration and reduce reliance on imports, First Deputy Prime Minister Nurlan Nalybayev said at a Nov. 4 government press conference.

According to him, the laboratory will help identify priority areas for developing the country’s resource base and support Kazakhstan’s integration into global production chains.

The government’s strategy focuses on four production areas: materials for batteries, processing and production of materials for jet engine components, semiconductor manufacturing and the development of a complete production cycle for permanent magnets.

A portfolio of projects has been formed in these areas, including initiatives involving foreign investors. Kazakhstan is developing cooperation with Germany’s Bergbau AG, the Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources, Australia’s Lindian Resources and other international partners.

Manufacturing sector gains momentum

The initiative comes as Kazakhstan seeks to expand its manufacturing base and reduce the economy’s dependence on raw material exports.

Manufacturing output reached nearly 24.2 trillion tenge (US$53.3 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, increasing by 8.6% compared with the same period last year. The sector’s share of gross domestic product exceeded 14%, Nalybayev said.

Several industries recorded particularly strong growth. Machinery production increased by 22.8%, chemicals by 23.4%, food production by 13.8% and pharmaceuticals by 31%.

Kazakhstan plans to launch approximately 200 new industrial enterprises in 2026, with a combined investment of around 1.7 trillion tenge (US $3.7 billion).

“Our main priority for the sector is to rely on domestic production capabilities and reduce dependence on imports. State support will be provided to projects that deliver the greatest positive impact on the country’s economy,” Nalybayev said.

The government is also introducing a new approach to assessing industrial capacity. The Ministry of Industry and Construction has approved a methodology that will assess each proposed project against market demand, the capacity utilization of existing enterprises and the availability of resources.

The findings will be taken into account when granting incentives and refining government support measures.

A new industrial cluster model is also being introduced to strengthen cooperation between manufacturers, support the production of finished goods and bring small and medium-sized businesses into supply chains around major industrial enterprises.

New approaches to geological exploration

Kazakhstan is also introducing new technologies to improve geological exploration. For the first time, the country has launched state geological mapping at a scale of 1:50,000.

Over the next three years, the government plans to implement 20 projects covering approximately 100,000 square kilometers.

Alongside conventional exploration methods, specialists are using Ionic Leach technology to identify concealed mineral deposits, as well as artificial intelligence, satellite data and unmanned aerial vehicles.

Preliminary results have identified seven promising sites. Areas confirmed to have potential are expected to be prepared for auction next year, Nalybayev said.

The government is also integrating approximately 4.8 million records of primary geological information into the Unified Subsoil Use Platform. The integration is expected to improve access to existing geological data and support the search for new deposits.

By combining geological exploration with investment in domestic processing and manufacturing, Kazakhstan aims to strengthen its position in critical materials supply chains and develop industries that produce higher-value goods.

World.title: Tokayev Meets Network School Founder, Welcomes Launch of Kazakhstan Branch
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Balaji Srinivasan, founder of Network School, to discuss cooperation in technology, education and innovation, reported the presidential press service on Nov. 4.

Tokayev praised Network School’s contribution to the development of Kazakhstan’s technology ecosystem and expressed readiness to strengthen cooperation with the organization.

He said Kazakhstan is investing in education, science and digital skills to prepare a new generation of technology leaders.

In this context, Tokayev spoke about the People’s Construction initiative, announced in his recent address, saying it would help create a lasting legacy for future generations. The program envisages large-scale construction of social infrastructure, including schools, universities and healthcare facilities.

President Tokayev welcomed the launch of Network School Kazakhstan in Astana and the organization’s interest in expanding partnerships with Kazakh universities, startups and technology companies.

Tokayev also thanked Srinivasan for his investment support for the Astana AI Film Festival. In turn, Srinivasan highlighted Kazakhstan’s ability to combine advanced technological solutions with traditional sectors of the economy. He presented Network School Kazakhstan’s priorities, which include promoting digital solutions, developing human capital and creating an environment conducive to innovation.

World.title: Kazakhstan and China Build Digital Bridge for Data Economy
World.content:
Access to reliable data gives businesses a competitive advantage when they develop AI tools, build digital services or enter new markets. Kazakhstan and China are working to make that resource easier to use securely across borders.

China and Kazakhstan deepened their cooperation in the data economy at the Global Data Ecosystem Conference 2026 (GDEC 2026) in Shanghai on Oct. 30–31. Kazakhstan participated as the Special Invited International Partner, a sign of the growing importance of data cooperation in relations between the two countries. At the opening session, Kazakhstan’s Bureau of National Statistics outlined the country’s approach to building a data market. The Bureau is part of the Agency for Strategic Planning and Reforms, which oversees the development of the data economy.

On Oct. 31, Astana Data Exchange (ADX) and Shanghai Data Exchange (SDE) began to work on their first joint listing of data products so that data providers could offer them on both platforms. Industry associations, state-owned enterprises and private firms in finance and IT also joined a broader initiative on data markets, research on the digital economy and smart city projects.

The cooperation fits a broader agenda discussed by Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Xi Jinping in Shanghai in July, when digital technologies and AI were identified as areas for closer ties. At the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, Tokayev proposed the Kazakhstan–China Digital Bridge Initiative to expand digital trade and connect the two countries’ digital economies. For Kazakhstan, the proposal builds on its record as a digital state. The country is now turning to the economic use of the data its industries and public institutions generate.

If Kazakhstan and China connect their national data exchanges under rules both sides trust, other countries could use the same approach to share data securely and transparently.

From digital government to a data economy

This cooperation follows years of digitization in Kazakhstan, particularly in public services and banking. More than 90% of public services are available online, and the country ranked 24th among 193 countries in the 2024 UN E-Government Development Index. In 2025, 98.3% of personal payments and transfers were cashless.

The Digital Qazaqstan strategy builds on that experience and sets out how the country plans to develop its data economy through 2029. It calls for wider use of AI across industries and for government agencies to use data when making decisions. The Law on Artificial Intelligence establishes rules for developing and using AI systems.

Under Kazakhstan’s Digital Code, in force since July 2026, organizations can exchange data products through registered platforms. Providers set the terms of use, and the products must exclude personal data that could identify individuals.

As part of a broader effort to treat data as an economic asset, Kazakhstan has adopted a method for valuing data products held by public agencies and state-owned enterprises.

China took an early lead in building a market for such assets when it recognized data as a factor of production in 2019. It has since set rules for using data, built a network of exchanges and introduced a national system for registering data rights. Its National Data Administration supports the development of industry datasets for training AI models.

A digital bridge between these markets would give Kazakhstan and China a stronger basis for joint work on AI. With agreed rules for secure access, researchers and businesses could draw on data from both countries to train models and build digital services for a wider market.

A digital bridge in practice

One example of this digital bridge is the partnership between Astana Data Exchange and Shanghai Data Exchange. Their 2025 strategic cooperation agreement laid the groundwork for the joint listing. ADX, one of the platforms on Kazakhstan’s national register under the Digital Code, helps organizations list, find and exchange data products.

SDE is a leading hub for cross-border data exchange, connecting international providers with buyers in China and helping Chinese firms bring their data products to markets abroad. In 2026, it became one of three institutions designated to register data rights under China’s national system.

Eleven international providers, including KoDATA, are preparing to list products on ADX. Their products cover business information, finance, shipping and logistics, research and AI. The partnership could also help Kazakhstani providers offer data products and services in China, including market analysis based on aggregated, anonymized records. A data service could show a Chinese exporter where household appliances sell best in Kazakhstan without sharing individual sales receipts.

China’s experience with data assets suggests a next step for the partnership. The exchanges could agree on how to value data products and register rights in them. Banks could then assess whether those rights can serve as collateral. In shared data spaces, partners could agree on who may use sensitive records. Confidential computing could let them analyze those records together while keeping the underlying data private.

What this means for trade and investment

Secure data exchange could help Kazakhstan and China expand trade and investment. Bilateral trade reached $48.7 billion in 2025, according to Chinese customs figures. As their data markets develop, sharing verified records could help the two countries reach their $100 billion target by speeding up border checks and customs clearance.

An importer could verify a supplier’s registration, a shipment’s origin or a product certificate. A Chinese exporter could check a Kazakhstani distributor’s trading history before offering credit. A retailer choosing a site for a store in Almaty could use aggregated mobility data to compare foot traffic across neighborhoods.

A global network of data exchanges could widen access while leaving providers in control of who may use their data and for what purpose. If those terms are clear and enforceable across borders, more countries could use shared data to build their own AI tools and digital services and expand trade and investment.

Lu Yong is the Executive Director of Shanghai Data Service Provider Association and the Chief Expert of Shanghai Data Exchange. Sarsen Zhanabekov is CEO of Astana Data Exchange.

World.title: Kazakhstan Eyes 2035 Completion for First Two Nuclear Power Plants
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan expects its first two nuclear power plants to be completed by 2035, with construction of the Balkhash plant involving a Russian-led consortium headed by Rosatom and negotiations underway with China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) over the second plant, known as Moyinkum, Minister of Energy Erlan Akkenzhenov said at a Nov. 4 government briefing.

According to Akkenzhenov, discussions with CNNC are ongoing and cover the terms of the agreement, project parameters and construction timeline.

“The parameters of the project are currently being discussed, including the terms of the deal and the timeline. We believe that the projects should be completed by 2035,” he told journalists.

The minister said the Balkhash plant would be implemented with the participation of the Russian consortium, while cooperation with CNNC is being explored for the Moyinkum project.

Responsibility for nuclear energy projects was initially held by the Ministry of Energy but was later transferred to the newly established Agency for Atomic Energy. Akkenzhenov noted that the agency is now responsible for the projects.

Meanwhile, Kazakhstan plans to establish a strategic uranium reserve by the end of 2027, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin said on Nov. 3. The reserve is intended to supply three nuclear power plants planned in the country, involving Russia’s Rosatom and China’s CNNC.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Complete Construction of Three New Airports by End of 2026
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to complete construction of three new airports in Zaisan, Katon-Karagai and Kenderli by the end of 2026 as part of efforts to expand the country’s aviation infrastructure and strengthen its transit potential, First Deputy Prime Minister Nurlan Nalybayev said at a Nov. 4 government press conference.

Nalybayev also added that the government is also working to modernize existing airports and improve air navigation systems. Construction and modernization work is underway at Almaty and Urdzhar airports, while a second runway is being built in Shymkent. In August, Pavlodar Airport’s runway was reconstructed and Arkalyk Airport was restored.

Kazakhstan is also upgrading its air navigation system using international equipment and standards.

New routes and cargo capacity

The country is expanding its international air connections. The first flight on the Almaty-Tokyo route is scheduled for Nov. 30, while new routes to Vienna, New York, Milan and other cities are planned for 2027.

Kazakhstan is also developing a national cargo airline, Air Cargo, which is expected to operate a fleet of 10 aircraft.

The first aircraft is expected to arrive in November 2026, followed by a second in March 2027. The carrier will operate in the international air freight market as part of the government’s efforts to strengthen Kazakhstan’s position in global cargo transportation.

Fueling facilities and cargo terminals are also being modernized and connected to road and railway networks to support multimodal transportation.

The government is working to digitize the transport sector through the integration of information systems into the unified E-Kolik intelligent platform. The system is expected to enable fully paperless documentation, shorten the processing time for transport documents and improve transparency in cargo flows.

Kazakhstan’s transit ambitions

The airport projects form part of a broader effort to develop Kazakhstan’s transport and logistics infrastructure and improve connections between international markets. The government has identified several key transport hubs where free economic zone arrangements have been introduced. Modernization of fuel facilities and cargo terminals, alongside better road and railway connections, is expected to support the development of multimodal freight services.

The expansion of airport capacity, international routes and cargo operations is intended to strengthen Kazakhstan’s role as a regional aviation and logistics hub.

World.title: Tokayev’s ‘Build! Once Again – Build!’ Initiative Takes Shape Across Kazakhstan With $14.3 Billion Plan
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is preparing for a nationwide construction drive that will direct nearly 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) toward infrastructure development through 2029, as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev calls for a new phase of economic modernization built around tangible improvements in people’s lives.

The initiative, known as Khalyktyq Qurylys, or the People’s Construction program, will cover roads, airports, railway stations, power plants, hospitals, schools, rehabilitation centers, sports facilities and other public infrastructure across the country. Tokayev has designated 2027 as the Year of Nationwide Large-Scale Construction.

First Deputy Prime Minister Nurlan Nalybayev announced the funding plans at a Nov. 4 government press conference on the development of Kazakhstan’s real economy. He said the National Fund would provide resources for social, transport and engineering infrastructure projects across all regions by the end of 2029.

The initiative is already moving forward. According to Nalybayev, 262 projects worth a combined 1.5 trillion tenge (US$3.3 billion) have been approved through the Infrastructure Development Fund. A significant share of the funding is earmarked for social infrastructure.

Hospitals, schools and public facilities

The approved project pipeline covers several sectors, with healthcare, education, culture, sports and utilities among the priorities.

Healthcare projects account for 344 billion tenge (US$758 million) and include the construction of hospitals, outpatient clinics, perinatal centers and maternity hospitals. Another 266 billion tenge (US$586 million) is allocated to culture, tourism and sports, with 23 facilities planned, including sports complexes, cultural centers and theaters.

Education projects will receive 101 billion tenge (US$223 million) for the construction of 28 facilities, including schools and multifunctional complexes.

Transport infrastructure accounts for 369 billion tenge (US$813 million) across 48 projects, including road reconstruction and the construction of new roads and bridges. A further 284 billion tenge (US$626 million) is earmarked for 55 water supply and wastewater facilities, including main pipelines, treatment plants, protective dams and reservoirs. Another 136 billion tenge (US$300 million) will support 67 projects to develop heating and gas supply systems.

“This is not just plans on paper. A total of 497 billion tenge (US$1.1 billion) has already been allocated for the implementation of these 122 projects. I would particularly like to emphasize that all 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) allocated for infrastructure modernization will be under strict government oversight,” he said.

The government also plans to establish a state commission to oversee the People’s Construction program and ensure public monitoring of how the funds are spent. It will include representatives of government agencies, members of the Kurultai and the People’s Council, public figures, activists, volunteers and journalists.

Nalybayev also said the construction program would rely on domestic building materials and production capacity.

Investment and domestic industry

The infrastructure drive is also expected to create opportunities for Kazakh businesses and manufacturers.

At a separate meeting of the Board of Directors of Samruk Kazyna, chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov on Nov. 4, the fund reviewed progress on 69 major investment projects with a combined value of 43.8 trillion tenge (US$96.5 billion). The largest share of investment is directed toward the oil and gas industry, petrochemicals and conventional power generation, alongside gas transportation, energy infrastructure, transport and communications.

Construction and installation work is underway on 44 projects, while the remaining initiatives are at different stages of implementation.

The fund reported that purchases from Kazakh companies reached approximately 1.4 trillion tenge (US$3.1 billion) in the first nine months of the year, a 45% increase compared with the same period last year. Offtake contracts with domestic producers amounted to 73 billion tenge (US$161 million).

Among the projects launched in October was a 380-kilometer fiber-optic communication line connecting Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan. The link is expected to expand international data exchange and strengthen digital connectivity between the two countries.

Samruk Kazyna is also continuing construction of social facilities. Several major healthcare projects in Astana, Turkistan and Petropavlovsk are scheduled for completion in 2027 and 2028. Other initiatives cover inclusive sports, rehabilitation, education and culture.

Transport corridors and road modernization

Transport remains another major focus of the government’s infrastructure plans, as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its position as a transit and logistics hub in Eurasia.

Rail freight transit through Kazakhstan increased by 15% to 33.8 million tons, Nalybayev said. The government is also modernizing 37 automobile border crossing points, with completion scheduled by the end of 2027.

The Aral-Caspian highway, construction of which officially began in August 2026, is expected to reduce cargo delivery times to three days. The project is scheduled for completion by the end of 2028. Preparations are also underway to expand the Kokshetau-Petropavlovsk highway, with construction expected to begin in the first half of 2027.

The government is placing particular emphasis on road quality and accountability in the construction sector. A working group led by Nalybayev has been established to review international practices and develop proposals to improve road construction standards and strengthen the responsibility of all parties involved.

Along international road corridors, Kazakhstan currently has 1,465 roadside service facilities. A total of 221 facilities have been built over the past three years, including service complexes with fuel stations, hotels, shops and vehicle maintenance services.

Construction sector growth

The new program comes as Kazakhstan’s construction industry continues to expand. Construction work reached 7.8 trillion tenge (US$17.2 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, up 11.5% compared with the same period last year. More than 20 million square meters of housing are expected to be commissioned nationwide by the end of the year.

The broader economy has also recorded growth in infrastructure-related sectors. Kazakhstan’s gross domestic product grew by 6.5% in 2025, with construction expanding by 17.5% and transport and warehousing by 19.4%, according to the Bureau of National Statistics.

The government says the People’s Construction program is intended to turn this momentum into visible changes across the country. Over the next few years, the results will be measured not only by investment figures and completed projects, but also by the roads people travel, the schools and hospitals they use, and the utilities that serve their communities.

World.title: AI Bubble: Global Investors Seek AI’s Real Enterprise Value at Hong Kong’s Cyberport Forum
World.content:
HONG KONG — The term “bubble” was not a whispered fear but a baseline for discussion at the Nov. 4 Cyberport Venture and Capital Forum, where participants focused on winning the next competitive cycle in AI. As artificial intelligence valuations soar to unprecedented heights, venture capitalists are shifting their focus from the marketing noise of .ai domain names to the harder realities of monetization, scaling bottlenecks, and a shifting geopolitical landscape in which China and the United States (U.S.) are locked in a high-stakes race for dominance.

For Ganesh Rengaswamy, founding managing partner at Quona Capital, the current atmosphere feels hauntingly familiar, yet fundamentally different from the dot-com era.

“Yes, of course we are in a bubble, but great transformation also comes out of the bubble,” Rengaswamy noted.

He pointed out that while modern capital deployment features “a couple of more zeros,” the foundational stack of AI: compute, cloud, models, and tooling, remains in flux. Unlike the early internet, where protocols and browsers stabilized quickly, the AI industry is still searching for its definitive architecture.

“Human beings don’t like that change; we don’t like this rapid transformation. How do we break through that and find real value? It’s tough, and I think we’re all going through that experience,” Rengaswamy added.

AI bubble: are we living it?

The sheer volume of venture capital currently in the market is historically unprecedented. Christine Keung, an advisor at Capital6 and former Bridgewater associate, suggested that the market is in a state where it remains “unclear if the public markets can withstand” the massive private valuations assigned to “hot” companies like Anthropic.

Keung highlighted a growing divide: a “Cambrian explosion” of small businesses empowered by AI, contrasted against a shrinking pool of “venture-backable” companies capable of returning the massive funds now managed by institutional investors.

“Our funds are getting bigger, which means the hurdle in which we need to return those funds increases substantially. It is only a bubble if the markets can’t absorb it… right now the bubble actually hasn’t burst yet,” she said.

Jeremy Dalton, an advisor to FOV Ventures, issued a stern warning to founders: the era of AI as a mere marketing term is over.

“Stop buying .ai domain names,” Dalton said.

He cited a recent Deloitte report showing that only a quarter of business leaders have successfully pushed even 40% of their AI pilots into production. According to Dalton, the disconnect between “hype” and “utility” is the primary driver of current turbulence.

Michael Phillips, executive managing director at Alumni Ventures, echoed the need for resilience, emphasizing that “investing through the bubbles” is the only way to catch the next generation of breakout leaders.
