Why nobody talks about how many weapons we bought from Russia? Only Turkey. Because Turkey is now in the center of attack from unfortunately, different European politicians. There are attempts to demonize Turkey. There are attempts to blackmail Turkey, to press it. This is absolutely unacceptable. We buy, main of our weapons from Russia. We buy weapons from other countries. Only Turkey is here. So, this is first. Second, those who always keep saying that Turkey provides military support to us, why don’t they say that Russia provides military support to Armenia? A mediator, Minsk Group co-chair. We have proofs in our hands. We delivered this information to Russian officials. How much weapons were delivered to Armenia during this forty days? Why nobody talks about that? Let’s talk about that. Let’s be fair. Therefore, first, this is wrong. Second, we buy Turkish military equipment and we will continue to do it. And third, there should be no double standards about that. And those, by the way, who tell that Azerbaijan is militarily supported by Turkey, I think should refrain from these absurd accusations.

-Turkey obviously has interests in the region as has also Iran and Russia. Armenia has asked Russia for a possibility to guarantee its security. Do you fear an internationalization of the war?

-That is what Armenia wanted to do from the very beginning. And we were always against. I said many times to all the countries, ‘stay away from this conflict’. It is our business, it’s our battle for territorial integrity. And there should be no attempts to internationalize the conflict. But Armenia did everything to do it. And the letter which Armenian prime minister sent to Russian president, not only demonstrates that they already admit their defeat, that we beat them on the battlefield, it also shows that they want to internationalize the conflict. They want to drag Russia into a direct participation on the ground, which is absolutely unacceptable. As far as I know, it was rejected by Russia and Russian foreign minister issued a statement about that. That maybe I’m not precisely correct in my words, but the sense was that the fight is taking place on the territory of Azerbaijan. If Azerbaijan attacks, or if any country attacks Armenia, then Russia will have their obligations. But the battle is going on our soil. So, these attempts I think are absolutely useless. Russian position was articulated by the foreign minister. Iranian position was also articulated. Probably you heard about Iranian plan for the settlement, which provides territorial integrity of countries. And recently, the Iranian religious leader made a statement that Armenia should liberate internationally recognized territories of Azerbaijan. So, this is a reaction of two neighbors. Position of Turkey is well-known. It always stands for international law and UN Security Council resolutions. Georgia, on many occasions before, also supported Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity. This is a position of our neighbors. So, Armenia is in isolation. So, they want to internationalize the conflict. They want to exploit some fake news and some fake news from the history, in order to get support. But the best way for Armenia to act now is to admit their defeat, admit our victory and make a commitment that they will withdraw from the remaining part of the territories.

-If they recognize the independence of Nagorno-Karabakh what would your reaction be?

-You know, if they wanted to recognize, they would have recognized long time ago. Why didn’t they recognize it before? Because, they clearly understand that by this very irrational step, negotiations will stop. Absolutely. So, if they do it, there will be nothing to talk about. And then, no peaceful initiative, no basic principles, no future settlement, nothing will be on the table. So, I think that they understand it. They always wanted to use it as a kind of an instrument in order to frighten us, saying that if Azerbaijan does that we will recognize. I tell them many times during this days of war and I tell now, Armenian prime minister, recognize Nagorno-Karabakh today. Do it. Show your courage. Show that your words mean something. Recognize Nagorno-Karabakh today. Again, and you will see that they will not do it. Because they are cowards. They can fight only against peaceful civilians and when they see our strength and our unity they run away.

-Will you be willing to accept an autonomy of the region?

-This should be part of the future discussions, on the basic principles. Because the first part of the basic principles demanded the withdrawal from occupied territories. Five plus two in time-table, then, there were other elements of the basic principles, like security, peacekeeping operations, status of Nagorno-Karabakh and we always were very open to discuss it. We offered them many times different ways, but they rejected. We offered them autonomy inside Azerbaijan. We offered them cultural autonomy, we said that there are good examples in the world, in Europe, in Scandinavia this Aland Islands, in Italy this South Tyrol district, in many other. But they rejected everything. They demanded independence only. And they wanted us to recognize this independence. By doing that they actually knowing that we will never do it, they were doing everything to freeze the conflict. So, I don’t know, we need to first to end this hot stage of the conflict, come back to negotiation table. Armenia should make these commitments which I already said. And then we can talk about what will be happening in the future. I cannot say anything about that now.

-Thank you very much, Mr. President. I really appreciate your time.

-Thank you very much for your questions, for your interest in Azerbaijan.

World.title: Azerbaijan-Georgia trade turnover rises 42.3% to around $888M
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. Trade turnover between Azerbaijan and Georgia increased by 42.3% year-on-year to $887.95 million in January-September 2026, Trend's calculations, based on data from Azerbaijan's State Customs Committee, show.

In value terms, trade turnover between Azerbaijan and Georgia grew by $264 million compared to the same period in 2025.

During the reporting period, trade turnover with Georgia accounted for 2.39% of Azerbaijan's total trade turnover, placing Georgia 8th among Azerbaijan's largest trading partners.

From January through September 2026, Azerbaijan exported products worth $757.49 million to Georgia. This was an increase of $262 million, or approximately 52.9%, compared to the same period last year.

Non-oil products accounted for $443 million of export operations. Compared to the same period last year, the export of non-oil products from Azerbaijan to Georgia increased by $198.2 million, or 1.8 times.

During the reporting period, Azerbaijan imported goods worth nearly $130.46 million from Georgia, up $1.93 million, or 1.5%, compared to the same period in 2025.

Azerbaijan conducted trade operations with foreign countries worth a total of $37.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026. Azerbaijan’s foreign trade turnover rose by $1.8 billion, or 5.2%, compared with the same period last year.

Exports accounted for $23.8 billion of the foreign trade turnover, while imports totaled $13.34 billion. Thus, over the past year, exports increased by $5.25 billion, or 28.3%, while imports decreased by $3.423 billion, or 20.4%.

As a result, Azerbaijan recorded a positive foreign trade balance of $10.5 billion. This figure increased by $8.67 billion, or about 5.7-fold, year-on-year.

World.title: Uzbekistan’s microfinance assets reach $1.8B, sector remains concentrated
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. Microfinance organizations in Uzbekistan held total assets of 21.75 trillion soums (about $1.8 billion) as of October 1, 2026, with institutions whose assets exceeded 10 billion soums (around $832,160) accounting for nearly 99% of the sector’s total.

According to the Central Bank of Uzbekistan, a total of 142 microfinance organizations were operating in the country, including 86 with assets exceeding 10 billion soums (around $832,160). These larger institutions held 21.54 trillion soums (approx. $1.79 billion) in assets, while their net loan portfolios totaled 19.35 trillion soums (about $1.6 billion).

According to Trend’s calculations, organizations in this category represented approximately 60.6% of all microfinance institutions but controlled 99% of the sector’s assets. The remaining 56 organizations held a combined 210 billion soums (about $17.4 million) in assets, or less than 1% of the total.

Capital was similarly concentrated among larger institutions. Their combined capital amounted to 4.33 trillion soums (around $360.3 million), compared with total sector capital of 4.49 trillion soums (approx. $373.6 million). This means they accounted for approximately 96.4% of the sector’s capital. Their authorized capital stood at 2.03 trillion soums (about $168.9 million).

Liabilities showed an even higher concentration. The 86 organizations accounted for 17.2 trillion soums (around $1.43 billion) of the sector’s total liabilities of 17.27 trillion soums (approx. $1.43 billion), representing approximately 99.6%.

Loans, borrowings and lease financing obtained by these organizations totaled 13.67 trillion soums (about $1.14 billion). This was equivalent to approximately 79.5% of their combined liabilities.

The figures indicate that Uzbekistan’s microfinance sector is highly concentrated, with the overwhelming majority of assets, capital and liabilities held by organizations with assets exceeding 10 billion soums (around $832,160).

World.title: Azerbaijan's lending to real sector climbs to $21B
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. Banks and non-bank credit institutions (NBCIs) in Azerbaijan had a combined 35.7 billion manat ($21 billion) in loans outstanding to the real sector as of October 1 this year.

According to calculations by Trend based on data from the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA), this represents an increase of 4.7 billion manat ($2.76 billion), or 15.1%, compared with the same period last year. Loans to the real sector totaled 31 billion manat ($18.24 billion) as of October 1, 2025.

The reporting period also saw an increase in overdue loans. Their total volume reached 754 million manat ($443.5 million), up 226 million manat ($132.9 million), or 42.8%, year on year. For comparison, overdue loans stood at 528 million manat ($310.6 million) as of October 1, 2025. Their share of the overall loan portfolio rose from 1.7% to 2.1%.

A breakdown of lending by economic sector shows that households accounted for the largest share of the overall loan portfolio. Loans to households totalled 21.1 billion manat ($12.41 billion) during the reporting period, an increase of 2.6 billion manat ($1.53 billion), or 14.3%, compared with the same period last year. The figure stood at 18.5 billion manat ($10.88 billion) as of October 1, 2025.

Among other sectors, trade and services ranked second in terms of lending volume. Outstanding loans to this sector reached 4.6 billion manat ($2.71 billion), up 344 million manat ($202.4 million), or 8%, year on year. The corresponding figure for the same period last year was 4.3 billion manat ($2.53 billion).

Construction was another sector to record substantial growth in lending. Outstanding loans to the sector amounted to 2.8 billion manat ($1.65 billion) as of October 1, up 1 billion manat ($588.2 million), or 56.3%, compared with the same period last year. This made construction one of the sectors with the highest annual growth rates.

Loans to the transport and communications sector also increased, reaching 2.8 billion manat ($1.65 billion). This compares with 2.1 billion manat ($1.24 billion) in the corresponding period of 2025, representing an increase of 745 million manat ($438.2 million), or 35.6%.

Total lending to the industrial and manufacturing sector stood at 1.7 billion manat ($1 billion). The figure was also approximately 1.7 billion manat ($1 billion) in the same period last year. The annual increase amounted to just 2.5 million manat ($1.47 million), or 0.1%, indicating that lending to the sector remained virtually unchanged.

Meanwhile, lending declined in mining, electricity, gas, steam and water supply. Loans to these sectors totalled 552 million manat ($324.7 million) during the reporting period, down 158 million manat ($92.9 million), or 22.3%, from 710 million manat ($417.6 million) in the same period last year.

Agriculture, forestry and fishing also recorded a decline in lending. Loans to the sector amounted to 505 million manat ($297.1 million), compared with 563 million manat ($331.2 million) a year earlier, representing a decrease of 58 million manat ($34.1 million), or 10.4%.

Overall, households, trade and services, construction, and transport account for the largest shares of lending across economic sectors. The increase in both the volume of overdue loans and their share of the overall loan portfolio was another notable development during the reporting period.

World.title: Azerbaijan imports 544.89 tons of RON-98 gasoline from Romania in 8 months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. Azerbaijan imported 544.89 tons of RON-98 gasoline worth $694,610 from Romania in the first eight months of 2026, the largest share of total imports.

In the reporting period, Azerbaijan totally imported 1,422 tons of RON-98 gasoline worth $1.8 million from three countries - Romania, Russia, and Belarus.

According to Trend's calculations based on data from the Azerbaijani State Statistics Committee, RON-98 gasoline imports declined in both value and volume during the reporting period compared to the same period last year.

Specifically, compared to the first eight months of 2025, the value of imports decreased by $373,000, or 17.1%, while the physical volume fell by 355 tons, or 20%. Based on these figures, approximately 1,777 tons of RON-98 gasoline worth about $2.18 million were imported into Azerbaijan during the same period last year.

From which countries Azerbaijan imported RON-98 gasoline?

From January through August 2026, Azerbaijan mainly imported RON-98 gasoline from Romania, Russia and Belarus.

Romania ranked 1st, accounting for approximately 38.3% of total import volume and 38.5% of import value.

Russia ranked 2nd. During the reporting period, Azerbaijan imported 460.31 tons of RON-98 gasoline from this country. The total value of the product amounted to $564,340. Russia accounted for approximately 32.4% of total import volume and 31.2% of import value.

Belarus ranked 3rd, supplying 416.95 tons of gasoline. Imports from this country were valued at $546,870. Belarus accounted for approximately 29.3% of total import volume and 30.3% of import value.

Thus, during the reporting period, RON-98 gasoline imports were distributed relatively evenly among the three countries. Nevertheless, Romania remained Azerbaijan's largest supplier in terms of both physical volume and value.

Countries from which Azerbaijan imported RON-98 in the reporting period:

Countries Volume Value Belarus 416.95 tons $546,870 Russia 460.31 tons $564,340 Romania 544.89 tons $694,610

RON-98 gasoline is a type of motor fuel with a lead content not exceeding 0.013 grams per liter and an octane rating of 98 or higher.

World.title: Sabah suffers defeat to Viking in Champions League
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. Azerbaijani club Sabah suffered a heavy defeat in the fourth round of the UEFA Champions League league phase.

Valdas Dambrauskas' side lost 4-1 away to Norway's Viking.

The match was held at Lyse Arena in Stavanger.

As a result, Sabah have suffered their third defeat in four league-phase matches of the Champions League and remain on three points.

World.title: Android's market share in Azerbaijan falls to 54.9% in October
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. The Android operating system’s market share in Azerbaijan has declined.

According to Trend’s calculations based on data from the Global Stats analytics platform, as of the end of October 2026, Android’s share of the Azerbaijani market fell by 1.55 percentage points compared to the previous month, reaching 54.9%.

Nevertheless, Android retained its leading position among operating systems in Azerbaijan. Microsoft Windows took second place, with its market share declining by 0.16 percentage points over the month to 29.51%.

iOS ranked third with a market share of 11.71%. Compared to September, this figure increased by 1.23 percentage points.

According to data from Global Stats, as of the end of October 2026, Android also retained its leadership in the global operating system market. Microsoft Windows took second place, and iOS took third.

According to information published on Android's official website, Android 17 is the current major version of the operating system. Google continues to release updates for this version. On October 2, 2026, Android 17 QPR 3 Beta 1 was released, marking the latest quarterly update for supported devices.

"As we continue to build on the initial release of Android 17, we are updating the platform by addressing identified issues and implementing improvements that will subsequently become available on supported devices. These updates are released quarterly as part of the Quarterly Platform Releases (QPR) program and become available both in AOSP and on Google Pixel devices as part of Feature Drops.

Although these updates do not contain API changes that affect app functionality, we provide images of the latest QPR beta versions so that developers can test their apps on these builds if necessary. This is particularly relevant when planning to implement new features that could impact the user experience," the statement reads.

World.title: Tradies film, follow alleged drink driver as police urge against vigilantism
World.content:
Police have not ruled out charging two men who pursued an alleged drink driver on the northern Gold Coast who they filmed speeding through suburban roads and into oncoming traffic.

Police allege a 49-year-old man was drink driving when he crashed his ute into another ute on the Pacific Motorway at Helensvale yesterday afternoon.

It is alleged he fled the scene, before returning and crashing into the same ute a second time and again driving away.

Tradies Jack Stanley and Jordan Matterson witnessed parts of the incident and began following the man and filming his alleged escape.

Gold Coast Police District Superintendent Craig McGrath said the alleged drink driver was later arrested at his home and investigations were ongoing.

The Helensvale man has been charged with one count each of dangerous operation of a vehicle and adversely affected by an intoxicating substance, and failing to provide a specimen breath for analysis.

He is scheduled to appear before the Southport Magistrates Court on November 18.

Vigilance is not vigilantism, police say

While there were no serious injuries reported, Superintendent McGrath said the response of Mr Stanley and Mr Matterson was concerning.

Gold Coast Superintendent Craig McGrath says police investigations are continuing. (ABC Gold Coast: Gemma Sapwell)

He urged motorists not to engage with erratic drivers and to instead contact police.

"From what I've seen, the footage of both drivers is quite distressing.This could have had dire consequences," Superintendent McGrath said.

" Being vigilant is not the same thing as conducting yourself as a vigilante. "

He said while it could be frustrating for the community, it was important police were able to do their job.

"It's an important reminder, if someone sees someone commit an offence, not to take the law into their own hands … it can have dire consequences and they are not immune to the law," Superintendent McGrath said.

He said investigations would continue, and has not ruled out further charges against both drivers.

'He would have got away'

Mr Stanley and Mr Matterson, who gave the ABC permission to use their footage provided their business was mentioned, began filming the incident after noticing the driver's "erratic" behaviour.

"He was swerving at cars, I thought if the police aren't here and no-one else is alerting [motorists] this could end really bad," Mr Matterson said.

He had been driving the car following the 49-year-old man, while Mr Stanley was the passenger.

The pair said they were compelled to follow the car and that they used their hazard lights to notify other road users of the car.

"People like that don't need to be on the roads … it was peak-hour traffic, children leaving school," Mr Matterson said.

He said the alleged offender's car was significantly damaged, leaving debris on the road and billowing smoke that the pair were able to follow.

"We tracked him down to Helensvale, got his address and contacted police," Mr Matterson said.

Mr Matterson said he did not believe following the man antagonised him or worsened his driving.

The video, which was first uploaded to Matto's Mowing and Property Maintenance social media pages, shows the pair also mounted the kerb and drove on a footpath to continue following the driver.

"He was driving crazy anyway, we kept our distance and were sticking to the road rules," Mr Matterson said.

"I think what we did was best for the community, considering there was no police at the scene at the time, he would have got away."

World.title: US rejection of data centres is a warning for Australia — and maybe leverage
World.content:
It's hard to imagine that someone was a bigger loser than the Republican Party in yesterday's US midterm "blue wave".

But somehow, things went even worse for the data centre industry.

When data centres were on the ballot, they overwhelmingly lost. There were about 41 different proposals put to voters in ten states, and all but one are on track for a loss for data centres.

An upset in the Texas governor's race saw Democrat Gina Hinojosa sail to victory. This puts Hinojosa, who has called for a ban on data centre construction, in charge of a state that currently has the biggest pipeline for data centre construction. If the ban is carried out, this will likely put a big dent in national construction.

Less directly but perhaps more consequentially, it's also cemented data centres as a politically toxic issue.

Five per cent of all political ads on TV mentioned data centres, and the majority of them were negative. It was an even bigger proportion in states that have become hot spots for data centre construction — the topic was covered in as many as 14 per cent of all political ads in Wisconsin.

An exit poll of voters conducted by NBC News found that three-quarters of voters oppose the construction of data centres in their community. More than 50 per cent of them said it was a crucial issue or major issue in their vote.

The Raging Grannies protest data centres and power hikes in North Carolina, US. (ABC News: Bec Symons)

Admittedly, data centres weren't the biggest issue overall. Corruption, cost of living, immigration and the Iran War all rated higher. But to keep things in perspective, data centres were not a political issue just two years ago.

I mean this literally: I couldn't find an exit poll that even asked voters about data centres. Nor can I remember a time that a technology issue was so front and centre for voters. (It feels a bit like a cursed monkey's paw somewhere just put one, shrivelled finger down for those who were hoping more people would pay attention to AI.)

By the end of the 2026 midterm elections, data centres had become a bipartisan issue with candidates from both major parties opposing their construction.

(As always, US President Donald Trump was iconoclastic in his increasingly lonely but still vocal support for data centres and his rebranded "super intelligence".)

There will be a lot of ink spilled on what voters were actually rejecting in this data centre repudiation.

Was this motivated by environmental concerns? NIMBYism? The industry's significant contribution to inflation? Is the opposition to data centres a proxy for opposition to AI — obviously intrinsically intertwined as its physical manifest — or the impact of big tech itself?

More broadly, was this white collar voters experiencing a new type of economic anxiety because they fear their roles could be automated using data centres?

It's obviously some combination of the above, but the proportions will matter a lot.

What does this mean for Australia?

One group keenly watching this result is Australia's political class.

It's not surprising that people who walk the halls of parliament are political sickos like many of us, but they're also certainly taking note of the data centre issue with an eye to what it means for us, here.

We should heed a note of caution against trying to directly transplant the midterm results to our political environment.

Australia is not America in a lot of ways, including when it comes to data centres. We've definitely seen an explosion in construction and proposals for a new generation of bigger, hungrier data centres, but the scale of our build out pales in comparison to our American friends.

People power costs NEXTDC A neighbourhood dispute over power poles has wiped $3 billion from a listed company in a day and made the AI boom a little shakier.

The combined capacity of Australia's existing 163 data centres is about 1.6 gigawatts, according to Data Centres Australia. America has about 30 times that, at around 50 gigawatts of capacity, by one estimate.

Our biggest data centre, AirTrunk's MEL1 in western Melbourne, is ten times smaller than the known capacity of Elon Musk's monstrous Colossus 2 (which was reportedly powered for a while by gas turbines without environmental permits, thanks in part to the laxer rules in the land of the free — another difference between our contexts).

Nor is the opposition to data centres here quite at the level of the American backlash. Recent polling found that 44 per cent of Australians would oppose a data centre built near them — not a great number for the industry, but not quite like the 76 per cent of Americans in exit polls.

Another major difference? Australia has a bipartisan consensus from the two major parties on data centres, but in the opposite direction.

Just last month, the chairs of the parliament's joint inquiry into AI — Labor's Jo Briskey and the Liberal's deputy chair Jonathon Duniam — took the unusual step of sending a letter mid-way through the inquiry's investigation to give an "early indicator" of what they'd found.

Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam and Labor MP Jo Briskey are co-chairs the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

It outlined several things that would be required to get the top AI companies doing their "training" here — a goal that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has also explicitly stated is an objective of his government.

Translation: Australia wants AI companies to build big data centres here.

Could there be a silver lining for America's data centre blues?

Now, the Australian politicians, staffers and those in the data centre industry who I spoke to about the midterms aren't completely terrified by the result.

They're very aware of the existing political stigma around data centres. Many of them expect that this result, even though it's in a different context, will embolden anti-data centre organisers, who are already fresh off a few wins in the last few weeks.

But there is a sense that it's possible to avoid this kind of response if we can thread the needle of attracting AI investment — again, this means building data centres — if we do it on, in their words, "our terms".

This is the motivation behind the government's proposed new rules for data centres that are expected to be released by the end of the year.

There are proposals for data centres in many places across Australia. This artist's impression shows one proposed for near Wagga Wagga, NSW. (Supplied: CDC Data Centres )

There is one other interesting downstream impact of a cooling data centre industry in the US.

With an American data centre slowdown, the computing crunch on major AI companies who are already fighting amongst themselves for resources will get even worse. This means there's even more pressure to look outside of the US. And guess which country is high up on many of the top AI companies' wish lists?

Australia is in a small group of dream destinations for major AI companies, and our leverage just grew. This could mean we can negotiate more from a tech industry increasingly desperate for a new place to call home: more money, stricter rules, a greater say over how they run — it's all on the table.

That must be an enticing thought for politicians already banking on extract concessions from these companies to piggyback our own AI industry and to jump-start our economy.

But there's probably another question itching at the back of their minds: Is this febrile feeling by the electorate towards data centres a cautionary tale that we can avoid? Or if our government's goal to lure major AI companies down here comes true, is it our political destiny?

World.title: Big batteries ready to power one-third of ACT for hours if needed
World.content:
The largest battery energy storage system in Canberra's history is online, with the ACT government saying the batteries could power one-third of Canberra's electricity needs for two hours in times of peak demand.

The Williamsdale site, south of Tuggeranong, has 136 Tesla Megapack 2 batteries and connects to the electricity grid, absorbing excess energy in times of low demand, before returning it to the grid when demand is high.

The project is a partnership between the government and private company Eku Energy, which designed, built and owns the 250-megawatt capacity batteries.

The timeline to complete the project blew out twice after its delivery was projected to be in 2025, then later extended to early in 2026, which was also not realised.

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr (centre) says he believes the project will be cost-positive for the ACT government. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr said as part of the operating agreement, the government would pay Eku Energy a support charge of $368 million in instalments across 15 years.

The government is then entitled to 50 per cent of the battery's net revenue, which it earns when energy is sold back to the grid.

Mr Barr said he expected the project to become revenue-positive.

"So, the territory makes a contribution, then receives more in its share of the revenue," he said.

"We are building this technology for households, small business, for our hospitals, for our schools, for our universities, for all of the industrial output that occurs in Canberra ... data centres are part of that," Mr Barr said.

"That's why this is such a good project for the ACT."

How does it work?

The batteries are located in Williamsdale in the ACT's south. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

Eku Energy policy director Rachel Rundle explained that the battery system was connected to Evoenergy's infrastructure.

"Essentially they're plugged into the electricity network," she said.

"They are always on … [and] because they're always on, they soak up all of the excess energy that is in the network.

Eku Energy policy director Rachel Rundle said she expected the system would sell energy back to the grid each day. (Supplied)

"Lots of that excess energy comes from the great wind and solar resources that we have in Australia.

"It stores and holds onto that energy for a number of hours.

"And then when that demand picks up … say, on a hot evening night or when there's a lot of industrial processing, the battery discharges that energy back into the grid, helping meet that peak demand and reducing the strain on the network."

Ms Rundle said it could quickly store up to 500-megawatt hours and then discharge that amount each day.

Eku Energy chief operating officer Tom Best said there were no promises that the system would put downward pressure on Canberra household electricity bills.

World.title: Research could reverse peanut allergy diagnosis for some infants
World.content:
More than one third of babies thought to have a peanut allergy may actually be able to safely eat nuts, according to a new study.

Researchers say the study could change the way the healthcare system approaches infant food allergies and lead to many children having their allergy diagnosis removed.

The research was led by the Murdoch Children's Research Institute and the National Allergy Centre of Excellence (NACE) in partnership with 10 paediatric public hospitals across Australia.

Researchers found 35 per cent of infants with a previous reaction to peanut and a positive allergy test did not react to an oral food challenge.

Researchers say peanut allergies affect about one in 30 children in Australia. (Adobe Stock)

NACE Director Kirsten Perrett said the number of children who did not react to peanut during a supervised food challenge was "surprising".

"These were children that had had a history of reactions when they were introduced to peanuts and they'd had a positive test, be it a skin prick test or a blood test," Professor Perrett told ABC News Breakfast.

"Our results show that clinical history and allergy testing alone were not enough to accurately diagnose peanut allergy in many cases.

"A supervised oral food challenge should be routinely considered to confirm the diagnosis before an infant starts oral immunotherapy."

Kirsten Perrett leads the ADAPT program at Monash Children's Research Institute. (Supplied)

Melbourne School of Public Health biostatistics professor Lyle Gurrin, who was not involved in the research, said he was not surprised that the figure reported in the research was so high.

"A lot of people think their children are allergic when they're probably not, so I think this paper is good from that point of view that it's encouraging people to seek proper advice," he said.

"I'm not surprised that a large proportion of these infants didn't return a positive result in an oral food challenge."

The study involved 1,275 infants under 18 months of age at hospitals in Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia and Western Australia.

The findings emerged from the ADAPT Peanut Oral Immunotherapy Program hosted by the Murdoch Children's Research Institute, which required infants to undergo a food challenge before starting treatment.

The program exposed children to small, daily doses of peanut to build tolerance.

Hopes to expand study to cashews

Victorian couple Leah and Jake introduced their infant son Arthur to peanuts when he was five months old.

They said the reaction was instant, with his face turning red and hives appearing on his shoulders and under his nose.

Leah and Jake with baby Arthur who ws initially diagnosed with a peanut allergy. (Supplied)

The boy was referred to the ADAPT program but then tolerated the supervised oral food challenge and had his allergy diagnosis removed.

"It's a huge relief knowing Arthur can tolerate peanut and we can move forward without the uncertainty of managing a suspected allergy," Leah said.

" Having the opportunity to find out he could tolerate peanuts has made a real difference to our family. "

Arthur had a reaction to peanuts when he first tried them, leading to an allergy diagnosis. (Supplied)

Professor Perrett said it was hoped the research would make the process of identifying food allergies more accurate for parents like Leah and Jake.

"With peanut allergy one of the most common childhood food allergies, it's particularly important that we have an accurate diagnosis when a baby first shows signs of a possible peanut allergy," she said.

"We want to reduce the burden of food allergy for children and their families, and the ADAPT Program is a step in this direction."

Professor Gurrin said the research did not necessarily mean it would become easier for GPs to better diagnose a child with a peanut allergy.

He said oral food challenges still need to be carried out under appropriate conditions.

"You can't really do that in a GP surgery or a child maternal health clinic," he said.

"You need all the material and the broader understanding to be able to assist the child who is having a reaction, whether it be mild or right through to anaphylaxis."

Professor Perrett said NACE was hoping to expand the ADAPT program to cover cashew allergy, which was almost as prevalent as peanut allergy.

However, Professor Perrett advised parents not to conduct an oral food challenge at home, warning that 12 per cent of infants with a peanut allergy had a potentially-life threatening anaphylactic response.

World.title: Canadian police find remains of mother and daughter killed by grizzly bears
World.content:
Canadian authorities say more than one grizzly bear may have been involved in a deadly attack on a mother and daughter on the country's west coast.

Investigators discovered the remains of art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her daughter Selah Reed shortly after their family reported them missing from Bella Coola, British Columbia on Sunday, local time.

Jenny Balcarras and her daughter Selah Reed on a hike. (Supplied)

Jeff Tyre, an inspector at the province's Conservation Officer Service, said any bears captured would be assessed.

He advised hikers to stay away from the trail where the attack unfolded.

Mr Tyre said efforts to capture the bear or bears involved in the attack continued, and any animals captured by the service would be killed in accordance with provincial guidelines.

"It's not yet clear if more than one bear was involved," he said.

Canadian mum and baby killed by bear The mother and daughter went for a walk near Einarson Lake, where they were attacked by the same bear that the baby's father later fought and killed.

A fundraiser set up by relative Mary Melissa Smith said Ms Reed was 20 "with her whole life ahead of her".

The fundraiser has so far raised about 60 per cent of the $CAD70,000 ($71,500) target.

She said Ms Balcarras, a mother and grandmother, had recently moved to Bella Coola to pursue a new career.

Ms Balcarras is survived by a son, two daughters and a grandson who now are "faced with the devastating loss of their mother", Ms Smith said.

Jenny Balcarras recently moved to Bella Coola, where she worked as a school counsellor. (GoFundMe: Mary Melissa Smith)

The Central Coast Teachers' Association said on social media that Ms Balcarras joined their school community as a counsellor in August.

She devoted "countless hours to connecting with the students she served and worked closely with teachers and other staff supporting their wellbeing", the post read.

Jenny Balcarras with her family, including daughter Selah Reed. (Supplied)

The attack comes nearly a year after a grizzly bear attack on a group of 20 elementary school students and teachers in the same area, which left one adult and three children badly hurt.

The animal involved in that attack last November was never captured.

Bella Coola is well-known for its large population of grizzly and black bears.

Kim Titchener, founder of Bear Safety & More Inc based in Calgary, said bears were often spotted walking near residential areas in Bella Coola.

She said bears' loss of habitat, combined with food stress caused by an ongoing drought in the region, were setting off more conflicts with people.

AP

World.title: Our critics review the six books vying for the $95,000 Booker Prize
World.content:
For an author of literary fiction, having a novel shortlisted for the Booker Prize is career-changing.

The result is a frenzy of international attention, endless interview requests, invitations to writers' festivals the world over, and, crucially, a boost to book sales.

Last year, the award went to Hungarian-British author David Szalay for his novel Flesh, a darkly humorous story described by the judges as "hypnotically tense and compelling … an astonishingly moving portrait of a man's life".

In 2026, classicist Mary Beard leads a judging panel featuring poet Raymond Antrobus; musician Jarvis Cocker; editor and critic Rebecca Liu; and Booker Prize-shortlisted novelist and essayist Patricia Lockwood.

Listen to ABC RN's The Bookshelf The latest and best fiction reviewed by a team of dedicated bibliophiles.

After reading 163 books in seven months, the judges have settled on a shortlist of six novels.

This year's half dozen features books by two past winners: The Disappearers by Jamaican author Marlon James, whose A Brief History of Seven Killings won in 2015, and John of John by Scottish wordsmith Douglas Stuart, whose moving debut novel, Shuggie Bain, took out the prize in 2020.

Another strong contender is The Things We Never Say by literary powerhouse Elizabeth Strout, previously shortlisted in 2022 for Oh William! Strout won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for her novel Olive Kitteridge in 2009, before eligibility for the Booker Prize opened up to US authors in 2014.

Of the first-time nominees, two are poets: Luke Kennard, shortlisted for Black Bag, and Rebecca Perry, shortlisted for her debut novel, May We Feed the King.

An outside chance, but no less worthy for it, is The End of Everything by M John Harrison, a storied sci-fi and fantasy author representing genre fiction on the shortlist.

"I knew I wanted to write historical fiction somewhat outside of the genre," shortlisted author Rebecca Perry told The Booker Prizes. (Supplied: Robin Christian)

Cutting down a longlist of 13 titles to just six results in tough decisions.

Fans of Emma Cline's buzzy novel Switzy, about a man with dementia travelling to Zurich to access assisted dying, can feel justified in their disappointment at its omission from the list.

Many, too, were surprised to see Gwendoline Riley, a recipient of the Windham-Campbell Prize in 2026, miss out on a call-up for her novel The Palm House.

Together with the reading public, the authors of the six books to make this year's shortlist will find out who will take home the £50,000 ($95,000) prize in a ceremony in London on November 9 (November 10 in Australia).

To take a closer look at the list, we've enlisted a team of critics to review the six shortlisted titles.

The End of Everything by M John Harrison

Serpent's Tail

M John Harrison is known for his Viriconium series and the Kefahuchi Tract trilogy, which included the Arthur C Clarke Award-winning Nova Swing. (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)

Phillip Tennent is a beachcomber who makes his living picking scraps from the shoreline of the English Channel. One day, the sea coughs up an "artefact" that strikes him as valuable; his "ticket out" of this marginal existence.

He takes it — a baby-sized bundle, wrapped in rags — to his aunt Marnie's house in a once thriving arts community known as the Strip. Her house overlooks the wreckage of an airliner, from which she can see attack helicopters flying among plumes of smoke to the north.

South-eastern England has been occupied by the iGhetti, an amorphous enemy that seemed to descend upon, or erupt from, the Square Mile, London's financial centre. Decades on from the invasion, everything is degraded; the landscape strewn with litter and the government no longer functioning. Refugees queue at ports seeking escape by boat. With no notion of what might await them, it is a "passage to nowhere", but it's a risk they are willing to take.

Much in The End of Everything pushes the boundaries of comprehension. A grotesque act of violence early on, one of several similarly shocking episodes, signals that something is deeply awry in the world.

Unsettling imagery only entrenches the sense of unease. Children play in a snow flurry that turns out to be falling ash, "feathery as the waste from a chicken factory". But there are glimpses of beauty among the junk and debris in M John Harrison's arresting descriptions of the coastal terrain: the mudbanks, estuaries and chalky soil.

Meanwhile, the artefact, one of innumerable "biological gadgets" discarded by the iGhetti, becomes more humanoid as it hovers close to Phillip and Marnie like a faithful dog.

Surreal and satirical, The End of Everything reads like a hallucinatory elegy. As one character observes: "The world's over. But that doesn't matter. Because another one will be along soon enough."

— Nicola Heath

The Disappearers by Marlon James

Hamish Hamilton

The Disappearers is "a gasp-inducing work of fiction", Kate Evans told ABC Radio National's The Bookshelf. (Supplied: Penguin Books Australia)

Certain ways of writing about violence are described as unflinching: the crunch of bone and blood spattered across the page. But The Disappearers, Marlon James's sixth novel, is, instead, all about the flinch.

It takes aim at homophobia and Jamaica, and encompasses many other things too: the erotic, explicit, harsh, intimate and painful.

The Disappearers begins in 1988 in Kingston, as a group of gay men gather to rehearse a queer play. They argue and tell stories as they begin to know each other, always understanding what they're hoping to do is risky. Performing and appearing as gay men, telling gay stories, is in itself dangerous. Even so, they have no idea what's coming for them.

As the novel opens, the youngest of the group tells the story. But one day he skips a rehearsal — and misses something truly terrible.

A ravening mob attacks the men in homophobic glee. The violence is told from the perspective of the perpetrators, the Blackjacks, and while some of them are appalled at what they're a part of, none of them stop. One man is killed; what's done to the others is unspeakable, but James doesn't so much speak as yell it in a fury; others disappear.

The rest of this book is about the aftermath. Not just scars, but haunted stories and lives, and terrible silences. Some of the mob members were policemen; another was a well-known singer. The shape and quality of the cover-up, the blaming of the victims, goes on for years.

This is a powerful and difficult book, whose narrators and perspectives shift with bloody and bruised agility. It's poetry of the worst kind, for the worst reason. And because of that, you really can't look away.

— Kate Evans

Black Bag by Luke Kennard

John Murray

Luke Kennard is an award-winning poet who teaches creative writing at the University of Birmingham. (Supplied: Hachette Australia)

Imagine if Bridget Jones's Diary was narrated by a middle-aged male slob and you'd have something like Luke Kennard's second novel, Black Bag. Sure, Bridget Jones for men already exists — it's called Nick Hornby — but Kennard, whose poetry collections and 2017 debut novel established him as an author with a fondness for wry self-awareness, fashions satirical oddity from middle-class disaffection.

A 37-year-old mostly unemployed actor longs for Ibsen and Chekhov but resigns himself to dinner party murder mystery roles. One day, he gets the part he may have been born for: a black leather bag.

Our actor is enlisted by a local university professor to attend lectures encased head-to-groin in the bag. He is instructed to neither speak nor gesture during the lectures. The actor grows fond of his role, putting on the bag and going about daily life.

His rise-and-grind flatmate thinks it's time to monetise. BagFans? MyBag? Bagcoin?! Meanwhile, post-humanism professor Justine wants to sleep with him, but only while he is bagged up. (She imagines eros as a kind of erasure; goodbye gender binary, hello orgasm!)

Inspired partly by the real-life 60s experiments of Charles Goetzinger, themselves designed to explore how people adapt to change and relate to things through exposure — even the presence of a person draped head to toe in a bag — Black Bag recalls Japanese author Kobo Abe's 1973 novel Hako Otoko (literally, Box Man) in which a man decides to live every day with a box over his head in order to learn who he truly is (with squeamishly disastrous results).

Kennard's novel is more comic and less broodingly cerebral than Abe's, but it shares Abe's concern with the ultimate existential question: what actually makes you, you?

— Declan Fry

May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry

Granta

Rebecca Perry is the author of two poetry collections, Beauty/Beauty and Stone Fruit, and a non-fiction work, On Trampolining. (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)

In May We Feed the King, British poet Rebecca Perry's debut novel, a curator receives a commission to create an installation commemorating the 750-year anniversary of a former royal palace. The curator's job, as they see it, is to not only give the viewer a sense of what life was like in a period of history, but to communicate something specific about the person who once lived in the room.

In Part I, the curator documents the project as it unfolds, explaining the nature of the work, much of it related to replica food, and their process. The tone is matter of fact and attuned to detail; little is shared of the curator's personal life save for allusions to a traumatic relationship break-up.

On day five, a "scant entry" in the palace ledger captures the curator's interest: a single page dedicated to a king's reign. The record gives "no sense of the man" and in this absence of "colour or context" — or perhaps because of it — the curator becomes fixated with this shadowy figure, who they soon think of as "my King".

Part I ends as the curator enters the King's chambers "like thread through the eye of a needle". On the other side is Part II, a vivid and sympathetic re-imagining of the King's life as he resided in the palace. From a brief historical record blooms "a whole world" as Perry animates characters and scenes long lost to history in meticulous and poetic detail.

In Part III, set once again in the present, Perry considers the question of what we can know of history: what the records can tell us of the past and what is lost to time. "There are no answers," the curator says. As Perry so expertly shows, what brings history to life is imagination.

— Nicola Heath

The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout

Viking Fiction

Elizabeth Strout is known for writing books featuring recurring characters, including Olive Kitteridge and Lucy Barton. (Supplied: Penguin Books Australia)

If Elizabeth Strout's previous works sting like a paper cut, The Things We Never Say punctures like a hypodermic needle administered by an expert hand, a smooth glide of pain and remedy in one.

The story follows a well-intentioned but existentially angsty 57-year-old teacher, Artie Dam, living a comfortable life in coastal Massachusetts. Despite all the outward markers of middle-class status, Artie feels isolated from his wife and adult son, which may or may not be the result of a decade-old car accident.

On top of that, his best friend moved away, leaving him with plenty of time to spin out with rage and grief, fluctuating between memories of his traumatic childhood and the hostile realities of America under Trump.

In one way, The Things We Never Say feels essentially Strout, scratching at the psyches of repressed older white folks living in small towns. In another way, it feels like an instrument for railing against a world that's lost its way. Some scenes feel a little heavy-handed, but for the most part, it's a compelling rallying cry for decency.

A word of warning: The Things We Never Say is not a book to read if you're feeling tender. Or perhaps it's a wonderful book to read if you're feeling tender and want to stay submerged in that state.

— Bhakthi Puvanenthiran

John of John by Douglas Stuart

Picador

Douglas Stuart could become the fifth author to win the Booker twice, following in the footsteps of Peter Carey. (Supplied: Pan Macmillan Australia)

Scottish American author Douglas Stuart's third novel, John of John, is a book about fathers and sons, and the secrets they keep from each other and themselves.

As John of John opens, John-Calum, aka Cal, is a heavily indebted art school graduate, exploring his sexuality and couch-surfing in Edinburgh as the UK crawls out of recession in the 90s. He's called by his father, John, to return home to an isolated island in the Outer Hebrides, to care for his ailing maternal grandmother, Ella.

On the island, Cal is confronted by the life he left behind, the school friends struggling in jobs soon to be made obsolete by globalisation, on an island where everyone knows each other's business.

He's also met with his father's barely contained feelings of injustice and "quiet, loch-deep rage". John is pious and ruled by a sense of obligation to tradition, whether in religion or weaving, which drives him to repress his desire for his neighbour and best friend Innes.

He feels abandoned by Cal and resents the "life that he had tied himself to", living and working at his mother-in-law Ella's croft, even though Cal's mother, Grace, left when Cal was a boy. He takes it out on Ella by speaking Gaelic, a language he knows she doesn't understand.

Stuart's vivid and moving prose, laden with cultural references and wry humour, brings to life the brutality, and unexpected comforts, of the island and the people on it, as both Cal and John reckon with what has kept them stuck for so many years.

— Hannah Story

World.title: 'Combined failure' behind $116m for Queensland police building
World.content:
The decision by Queensland police to spend $116 million to lease a building it has never used was a "combined failure", with opportunities to stop it missed at every turn, the state's corruption watchdog has found.

The Crime and Corruption Commission (CCC) noted in its report the Queensland Police Service (QPS) did not consider buying the property in the inner Brisbane suburb of Stones Corner throughout the process, even though the lease over 15 years "far exceeded" the purchase price.

In its bid to consolidate its accommodation in Brisbane, the QPS entered into a conditional agreement to lease the property at about $500,000 a month, but it was later assessed as not being fit for purpose.

The matter was investigated by the CCC following a complaint by former police commissioner Steve Gollschewski in November 2024, over the procurement process and lack of due diligence before a contract was entered.

The investigation identified no dishonesty, improper relationship or personal gains, but the CCC found opportunities were missed at every stage to halt the transaction.

"The significance of the matter lies in the governance and control weaknesses that allowed a commitment of this size to be made and to become binding," the report states.

"Due diligence was undertaken and legal advice sought only after the commitment, and the QPS did not use available opportunities to reconsider before becoming bound."

The report found there was no competitive process or independent check to determine whether the terms were appropriate, reasonable, and represented value for money.

The CCC also found the QPS committed to spending beyond its budget without government approval, with its request for funding later denied.

"By committing before securing funding, it lost both the option to withdraw and its negotiating leverage," the report states.

The CCC has made nine recommendations to the QPS and has noted it has been working with senior officers since June to discuss the corruption risks it identified.

The recommendations include conducting reviews of leasing processes to examine compliance with proper policies and developing and implementing an action plan to address systemic organisational culture issues.

To address the broader risks to the public sector the CCC has recommended the Queensland Government review its whole-of-government accommodation policy to determine if additional advice or direction is required to ensure appropriate public sector representation in office accommodation matters, including clearer guidance on what constitutes an "operational workplace" and how to apply this definition.

The QPS has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Thriving koala population near major NSW city could be chlamydia-free
World.content:
For Daryn McKenny, the Sugarloaf-Stockrington State Conservation Area feels like his backyard.

It was seven years ago that he first spotted a koala in this protected bushland, just a 35-minute drive from Newcastle's CBD.

Daryn McKenny, Gamilaraay and Wiradjuri man, has been tracking koalas in the Sugarloaf-Stockrington Conservation area for over seven years. (Supplied: The University of Newcastle)

Since then, Mr McKenny has spent hundreds of hours observing and tracking koalas in the area using discreet, motion-activated trail cameras attached to trees.

The Gamilaraay and Wiradjuri man said walking on country was the key to spotting them.

"I've spent years looking for all the food trees out there, then looking at the messages they give through the tracks and scratchings on them," he said.

" It's about understanding the environment and the ecology from an Aboriginal lens. "

Daryn McKenny uses motion-activated trail cameras attached to trees to track koalas. (Supplied: The University of Newcastle)

A secret population of koalas

Mr McKenny's observations prompted Ryan Witt, a conservation scientist at the University of Newcastle, to study the area.

Since 2020, Dr Witt and his team, including Mr McKenny as Aboriginal lead, have spent more than 250 nights surveying koalas to monitor and track populations across 23,900 hectares.

Ryan Witt began studying koalas in the Sugarloaf-Stockrington Conservation area in 2022. (ABC Newcastle: Laurise Dickson)

"We fly thermal-imaging drones up and back, sort of like a lawnmower," Dr Witt said.

"We do this across consecutive nights to account for whether a koala is there on a particular night or not."

Ryan Witt (left) and Daryn McKenny. (Supplied: The University of Newcastle)

In late 2025, the research team confirmed 292 koalas in the Sugarloaf-Stockrington area; however, drone surveys and modelling conducted in 2026 have revealed a much larger population.

"We think we have around 2,300 potential koalas in this landscape," Dr Witt said.

" Given the fact that it is an urban population that has somehow survived on the edge of a major city, they seem to be thriving. "

Loading...

Koala population shows no evidence of chlamydia

After noticing an influx of koala joeys on footage throughout 2026, Dr Witt turned his focus to the reproductive health of the Sugarloaf-Stockrington population.

According to Wildlife Health Australia (2023), the number of koalas infected with chlamydia can vary widely between wild populations, from zero to nearly 90 per cent.

Researchers have used drone technology to track koalas across the conservation area. (Supplied: Daryn McKenny)

To test for the disease, University of Newcastle researchers used drones to locate koalas before collecting fresh scats.

The koala scat, or poo, was preserved on dry ice and transported to specialist laboratories at the University of the Sunshine Coast for genetic and disease testing.

"We found 27 wild koalas without any evidence of chlamydia at the time of testing," Dr Witt said.

" The disease is really prevalent in New South Wales populations, so it's pretty unusual. "

Daryn McKenny and Ryan Witt track and monitor koalas across the reserve. (Supplied: The University of Newcastle )

A review of wildlife rescue and clinical records from the Lower Hunter region between October 2022 and September 2026 also found no evidence of chlamydia among a further 27 koalas within 30 kilometres of the Sugarloaf-Stockrington State Conservation area.

Dr Witt said while his report's findings were encouraging, they also suggested low genetic diversity among the koalas.

"We think they've been isolated from other populations for some time, which could be why they don't appear to have any disease," he said.

" Monitoring a larger landscape will give us a better understanding of the genetics outside of the core group. "

Koala scats tested from the Sugarloaf-Stockrington State Conservation area are chlamydia-free. (Supplied: Daryn McKenny)

Mark Krockenberger, a specialist veterinary pathologist at the University of Sydney, has studied infectious diseases in koalas for 20 years.

He said only three koala populations in NSW appeared to be chlamydia-free.

"In three years of sampling in southern Sydney, Kanangra-Boyd National Park and Narrandera in the Riverina, no disease was detected," said Professor Krockenberger.

Mark Krokenberger has been testing and monitoring koalas for disease in NSW. (Supplied: University of Sydney)

" You can't have 100 per cent say that the pocket near Newcastle is disease-free, but the genetic testing looks promising. "

Professor Krockenberger says continued monitoring would give researchers a better picture of koala health in the Sugarloaf-Stockrington area.

"Evidence supports that they are pushing out west of the Pacific Highway, which puts them at risk of contacting other populations with disease," he said.

"This does make it an area worthy of further study and conservation of koalas."

Calls to protect chlamydia-free koala population

Dr Witt has submitted his research to the NSW government for consideration as part of the state's Draft Koala Conservation strategy, which sets out targeted actions to protect koalas and their habitat across the state.

He has recommended increased habitat protection in the Sugarloaf-Stockrington area, installing wildlife exclusion fencing and establishing ongoing, long-term monitoring of this koala population, including longitudinal disease screening.

Researchers from the University of Newcastle will continue to monitor the Sugarloaf-Stockrington State Conservation area for koalas. (Supplied: Daryn McKenny )

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has won her bid to mount a High Court challenge arguing that Section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act should be declared unconstitutional and torn up.

The Queensland senator applied for special leave to appear before the High Court after the Full Federal Court upheld findings that she had subjected Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi to racist hate speech with her “piss off back to Pakistan” tweet, sent in 2022.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson argues that Section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act is invalid. Alex Ellinghausen

The case is expected to test the limits of the implied freedom of political communication, a doctrine which the High Court has applied for decades but with an ongoing and at-times heated debate over its reach.

“Special leave to appeal is granted,” read the High Court’s single-line ruling, released on Thursday afternoon.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Alleged double murderer, former NSW Police officer enters witness box; recounts meeting Jesse Baird, experiencing homophobia as police officer in tearful testimony
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of former NSW police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial in the Supreme Court in Sydney.

Today marks the beginning of the defence case after more than six weeks of evidence from the Crown.

The accused killer and former NSW police officer will give evidence about what he says happened on the day Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies died of gunshot wounds from his police-issued Glock pistol.

Beau Lamarre-Condon (left) is accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, in Paddington on February 19, 2024. His case is that he acted in self-defence, the 15-person jury has been told.

He has also pleaded not guilty to an aggravated charge of breaking into Baird’s home six months earlier on August 17, 2023, and stealing his mobile phone and wallet.

The Crown alleges Lamarre-Condon developed an obsessive and jealous infatuation with Baird that escalated when Baird ended their casual romantic relationship in November 2023.

The prosecution case is that he planned to kill Baird and took a number of preparatory steps, including practising shooting his police weapon in a national park to experiment with the sound of gunshots and buying a surfboard bag to dispose of his body. The Crown alleges the accused killed Davies spontaneously to eliminate a witness to the crime.

The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon went to Baird’s home disguised as an Uber Eats delivery rider to collect some of his belongings and that his gun went off twice during a struggle with Baird, wounding him fatally, and that Davies shot himself during a second struggle.

There is no dispute that Lamarre-Condon cleaned Baird’s share house while his housemates were out and disposed of the men’s bodies.

Baird had been due to move out of the home that week, the court has heard. The Crown alleges he sent messages from Baird’s phone to the housemates’ group chat to give the impression he was still alive and in the process of packing.

As to the charge of aggravated break and enter, the defence says Lamarre-Condon used a key Baird had given him to enter his home at night.

Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, said in his opening address to the jury in September that Lamarre-Condon had “indicated that he pleaded not guilty to murder but guilty to manslaughter of Jesse Baird”.

“He’s entitled to enter a plea in those terms, but it’s not accepted by the Crown,” Hatfield said.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Vance believes America’s future is MAGA, and the future of MAGA is him
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaUS midterms Vance believes America’s future is MAGA, and the future of MAGA is him Michael Koziol November 5, 2026 — 2:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Follow along with our live coverage of the 2026 US midterms here. Washington: JD Vance blaming the Republicans’ midterm rout on the Iran war was surprising not because of the substance, but because we are so unfamiliar with anyone in this administration saying openly that Donald Trump got it wrong. That was effectively Vance’s message on Wednesday (Washington time). In a 600-word post on X, he did not just say the war had caused higher petrol prices, which Trump accepts, but that the war was not worth the electoral cost, on which Trump disagrees. Vice President JD Vance says the war is to blame for the Demcratic victory, but linked it to the US relationship with Israel. Tom Brenner/POOL Getty Images North America via AP He also identified four things that Trump/Vance voters wanted: end the war, focus on the cost of living and inflation, put America first and “change our relationship to Israel”.



Vance’s reaction to the midterm results was always going to be fascinating. As a potential 2028 presidential contender, he is possibly the biggest loser from a day on which Americans voiced their dissatisfaction with the mob that’s currently in charge. But it depends on how you parse the politics of what happened. Did Americans move away from Trumpism, populism and conservatism? Or did they determine that Trump and his Republicans failed to deliver on the populism, isolationism and “America First” doctrine they had promised? James Talarico became the first Democrat elected to the US Senate in Texas since 1988. AP Photo/Eric Gay Vance believes it’s the latter. And his election autopsy tried to position him as the movement’s future standard-bearer – one who would really put America first, rather than paying lip service to the idea. He hit upon the same themes that were discussed that morning by MAGA influencer Steve Bannon and long-time Trump adviser Jason Miller, who recently returned to the White House in a strategy role, on Bannon’s War Room TV show and podcast.



Bannon and Miller spoke of the need to end the Iran war, reject any Democratic push for amnesties for illegal immigrants, and rethink the US relationship with Israel – all things Vance highlighted. “The president said it last night – I’ve got to applaud him on this – Israel being a strong ally, they don’t need to get $US4 billion ($5.7 billion) a year or whatever it is the US is sending them,” Miller said on the show. “When we talk about America first, that means America first.” View post on X Alexander Gray, a Republican who was on the National Security Council during Trump 1.0, and is now chief executive of advisory firm American Global Strategies, supported Vance’s analysis. Some Republicans would predictably seek to parse the election results as “a repudiation of America First”, he wrote on X. But “the data makes clear that the message that won in 2024 hasn’t ceased being on the money; voters just didn’t perceive the Republicans to be standing for it this cycle”.



We know that Vance was never on board with the war started by Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. As a member of the executive, he was bound to publicly defend the president’s decision. Clearly, he believes the election loss now gives him more freedom. Related Article US midterms Lame-duck Trump swamped by a blue wave: What happens next? Vance has always been an opportunist: he was once sharply critical of Trump, even describing him as “America’s Hitler”, before changing his stance when it became politically expedient. On CNN, conservative writer Jonah Goldberg called Vance “exceedingly deceitful” amid Wednesday’s election fallout. But the vice president believes his path to the presidency, if he runs, depends on holding together Trump’s MAGA coalition. He sees the isolationist, Tucker Carlson-type part of their base – the so-called “new right” – as a key component. His problem with the Iran war was not just the price of fuel, but that it further aligned the United States with Israel and jettisoned America First. Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, said on i24 that it was “unfortunate” to bring Israel into the Republicans’ drubbing. “It’s very easy to always blame Israel for everything, but that is not the case.”



Things can and will change over the coming 18 months; some may work in Vance’s favour, others not. Some solution to the Iran war will probably be found; petrol prices will most likely come down. Netanyahu may no longer be Israel’s prime minister. Democrats might succeed in Congress, or they could overplay their hand. Related Article Live data

US midterms Live battleground tracker: The two races too close to call – and every seat the Democrats flipped Vance probably needs Trump’s endorsement to become the Republican nominee, which is why some people were surprised that he made the comments that he did on Wednesday. But Trump may well have licensed Vance’s strategy. He said he had spoken to Vance, and the vice president’s statement was “good”. Maybe he wouldn’t run, Trump said casually. “Maybe nobody’s going to run.” And Trump’s endorsement may also be a diminishing currency. His persistently low approval ratings are unlikely to change. It’s very difficult for the vice president of an unpopular president to succeed; we saw that with Kamala Harris after Joe Biden.

World.title: Gollan says import will go the distance in hunt for elusive Five Diamonds
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Gollan says import will go the distance in hunt for elusive Five Diamonds Craig Kerry November 5, 2026 — 2:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Tony Gollan has taken better horses than Brindavan to the $2 million Five Diamonds (1800m) over the past three years, but the premier Queensland trainer believes the improving import has the timing and profile to challenge for a breakthrough win. Gollan looked set for victory last year in the race for five-year-olds at Rosehill when group 1 winner and favourite Transatlantic hit the front late, only for Vivy Air to relegate him to second with a rails run. Tony Gollan-trained Brindavan. Racing Queensland/Michael McInally A year earlier, $15 shot Freedom Rally stormed down the outside to beat all but Pericles. In 2023, Antino, which went on to win two group 1s, finished 10th. Import Brindavan ($13 TAB) has earned a shot at the Five Diamonds with strong Saturday grade performances in Queensland.



Gollan and First Light Racing paid about $A515,000 (250,000 pounds) at the 2025 Goffs London Sale for Brindavan, which has two wins and two placings in each of his two Australian preparations. His latest victory was a two and a half-length domination in a 1600m open handicap at Eagle Farm on heavy 10 going, giving Gollan added confidence if rain comes on Saturday. “He’s a really nice horse, and a typical import,” Gollan said. “His first prep was OK, but certainly off a break, and this time around, he’s been a whole lot better again. He’s a totally different beast this preparation. You will get to see a really nice, furnished racehorse there on Saturday. “We’re really happy with him and he’s got a nice sense of timing about him.



Leading Queensland trainer Tony Gollan. Getty Images “It’s obviously a step up from the races he’s been … and if we’re lucky enough to get some rain on the day, even better, from what we saw the other day at Eagle Farm. “He’s a little bit different to what we’ve seen in previous years in the runners we’ve taken down there, but it’s certainly not an afterthought race. We’ve had this race in mind for some time.” He was also confident Brindavan would run the 1800m trip, which will be a test for many stepping up from the 1500m prelude won by Declichy Boulevard. The Chris Waller-trained mare was a $4 favourite for Saturday. “Transatlantic was coming off winning a group 1 in the Toorak and had that group 1 mile form,” he said.



“This horse has got good, solid city class mile form up here, but I think what’s not in the consideration here is the trip. “He will get the trip, and there’s probably a few in this race where there’s a question mark about running a strong 1800. Transatlantic last year, that was probably the query on him, but he ran awfully well. “We’ve come close in this race, so hopefully this is the year. Transatlantic cruises to victory in the Five Diamonds Prelude under Tommy Berry at Randwick last year. Getty Images “We’ve been thereabouts, anywhere between favourite and 20-1, like we sort of are on the weekend, but he’s the right profile of horse for this race and I wouldn’t be taking him if I didn’t think he had a chance. He profiles different to the others I’ve taken down, but, to me, he profiles like a horse who will run well.”



Ben Thompson rides Brindavan from gate eight. “He’s a lovely go-forward horse, he’ll lob anywhere I would imagine in the first three pairs,” Gollan said. “We saw him with a new string to his bow the other day, sitting outside leader and careering away, so he’s pretty versatile. “When we bought him, with his profile, we were thinking more winter carnival, but I think he’s developed really into a nice mile-2000m horse. “Whether we bring him back and we target some of the good mile races through the summer or we give him a break, depends on how he runs Saturday.”
