World.title: Alan Jones trial hears of ‘bizarre coincidence’ with complainant and Herald journalist
World.content:
NationalNSWAlan Jones trial Alan Jones trial hears of ‘bizarre coincidence’ with complainant and Herald journalist Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander November 5, 2026 — 2:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

An alleged victim of Alan Jones declared to his wife days after he received a gushing birthday message from the former broadcaster that if Sydney Morning Herald investigative reporter Kate McClymont ever called him, he would tell her “everything”, a court has heard. And the very next day, she did. Sydney Morning Herald journalist Kate McClymont, right, arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court for Alan Jones’ indecent assault and sexual touching trial. Sitthixay Ditthavong McClymont, whose reporting of the sexual assault allegations against Jones triggered a police investigation in 2024, described the coincidence during her third day in the witness box at his local court criminal trial. Jones, 85, is standing trial on 19 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent against five male complainants between 2003 and 2020. He has pleaded not guilty and denies that the alleged acts ever occurred.



McClymont was asked about a text message that complainant “C” told her he had received from Jones in 2023. It was the only text message he received from Jones that he showed to McClymont, who told the court on Wednesday that there was a reason for that. She explained on Thursday that the man had received the “very gushing” message from Jones on his birthday four days earlier. Alan Jones (centre) arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court for his indecent assault and sexual touching trial on Thursday. Sitthixay Ditthavong “He said to his wife, ‘If Kate McClymont ever rings I’m going to tell her everything’ and for some bizarre reason I ring the next day,” McClymont said. Four years earlier, “C” had alleged to Herald columnist Peter FitzSimons that Jones had kissed and touched him non-consensually, while he was working on the then-2GB host’s personal staff.



FitzSimons had planned to put him in touch with McClymont, the court has heard, but “C” panicked before that occurred, and the interview never went ahead. McClymont said she was never told “C”’s real name during his short period of contact with FitzSimons, and it was a “bizarre coincidence” that she happened to call him the day after he made the comment to his wife. She had reanimated her investigation into Jones after receiving new information and another source had suggested she contact “C”. Jones is charged with indecently assaulting “C” eight times over a five-month period by touching and kissing him without his consent. The court has heard McClymont spoke to three of the five complainants at the centre of Jones’ trial, dubbed “C”, “A” and “H” to protect their identities, before police laid charges. She published a series of stories on Jones in late 2023 and early 2024. She told the court she gave her own statement to police about Jones in June 2024 – five months before his arrest – and another statement in September 2025.



Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, has suggested that the allegations against Jones were the product of “rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more”. FitzSimons was introduced to C by Jones’ stablemate and rival Ray Hadley, who had signed a secret contract to take over Jones’ prestigious breakfast slot only to have the offer rescinded when the station changed hands. Earlier in the week, McClymont told the court her reporting on Jones was not driven by newspaper profits or online page views. ‘I just wanted to make sure it was accurate, he was happy with what had been said.’ Kate McClymont in court on Thursday. She denied to Bashir that a quote set out in an article she wrote about “C”’s allegations did not reflect “the way it transpired in the interview”. Under re-examination on Thursday, she said that a day or so before publication, she had sat down with “C” to allow him to review his quotes from the interview. “I just wanted to make sure it was accurate, he was happy with what had been said and if he was worried there was anything that might identify him,” she said.



“C” earlier told the court the former 2GB host bombarded him with “love-bombing” in texts in the lead up to the alleged incidents. He said Jones first kissed him in the lift of the broadcaster’s harbourside apartment, but the “extraordinary” power imbalance stopped him speaking out as the alleged assaults continued. He also testified that Jones touched him under the table on the penis over his clothing at a lunch in Sydney in front of other guests. “C” alleged Jones also touched him in the car while he was driving the broadcaster. During emotional testimony, “C” said that he felt regret every day that he “didn’t fight back or say ‘no’ louder, but you couldn’t”. “Alan was protected, he was the Golden Goose,” he told the court. “There was no way in the world I could have said anything to anyone.”



Related Article Graphic content

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones sent ‘love-bombing’ texts to staffer before indecent assaults, court told On Wednesday, the court was played part of a recorded interview between McClymont and the mother of another of Jones’ alleged victims, dubbed “A”. In the call, the journalist said it was “brilliant” that police were involved and it would be “the nail in the coffin”. McClymont denied Bashir’s suggestion that she was referring to “the nail in the coffin of Alan Jones”. Police had said around the time of the call that they had received no complaints about Jones and were not investigating him, McClymont said, and someone coming forward saying they went to police was a “significant event” for her reporting.



The court has heard that “A” and his mother connected with McClymont after reading a story she wrote about Jones in late 2023. “A” first spoke to police in 2018, the court has heard, but a formal investigation did not commence until years later. The trial continues. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: ‘Game, set and match’: LIV Golf on the brink as investor pulls out
World.content:
Updated SportGolfLIV Golf Series ‘Game, set and match’: LIV Golf on the brink as investor pulls out Reuters Updated November 5, 2026 — 2:18pm ,first published November 5, 2026 — 9:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia has all but given up on hosting the popular LIV Golf event in Adelaide, with a senior government official calling “game, set and match” for the embattled circuit following an exodus of players and reports of a key investor pulling its funding commitment. LIV filed for bankruptcy protection in September as part of a restructuring after Saudi Arabia’s Public ​Investment Fund announced it would end its financial backing after the 2026 season. Cameron Smith tees off in Adelaide for the popular LIV Golf event. Getty Images A raft of players, including former world No.1 Jon Rahm, have since left LIV, prompting private capital firm BC Partners to drop its bid to relaunch the breakaway circuit, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday. Backed by public funding in South Australia, Adelaide has hosted four annual LIV events at the Grange Golf Club and was scheduled to stage the next one at Kooyonga Golf Club in March.



South Australia Premier Peter Malinauskas said on Thursday he could not see the event going ahead and cast doubt on the future of the entire circuit. “It feels like it’s game, set and match as far as I can tell,” Malinauskas told radio station ABC Adelaide. “That’s because BC Partners, that is the funders of LIV 2.0, I guess, have arrived at the same conclusion that we were, like, if you don’t get the players to sign up, then it doesn’t go ahead. Loading “In terms of other arrangements, we’ll have to take advice on that ... but clearly the event as far as we can tell won’t be going ahead at Kooyonga next year.” Kooyonga Golf Club filed a motion in a US bankruptcy court in September that said LIV had failed to pay the first instalment of its venue fee, despite being granted an extension.



The club said in an emailed statement on Thursday that it was aware of reports regarding LIV’s financing but had not received any advice from LIV. “We are seeking clarification,” it said. In October, BC Partners made an initial investment in LIV and planned to provide up to $US300 million ($428 million) in financing to help the league emerge from restructuring and strengthen its finances ahead of the 2027 season. The sinking LIV Golf series has copped another financial blow. LIV and BC Partners did not provide comment when contacted. The disruption caused by the Saudi-backed league to global golf has drawn plenty of critics but Australia has been one of its most enthusiastic hosts.





Related Article LIV Golf Series ‘We need a few more answers’: Why Cameron Smith’s future on LIV tour is still uncertain LIV is expected to appear at a Thursday hearing in US bankruptcy court in Trenton, New Jersey, to discuss various contracts, leases and assets. It is unclear whether LIV’s fate may also be discussed. LIV Golf launched in 2022 with funding from Saudi Arabia and lured leading players from the PGA Tour including Phil Mickelson, Bryson DeChambeau, Brooks Koepka, Australian Cameron Smith and Dustin Johnson with lucrative contracts. Others have been critical of LIV Golf, with DP ‌World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings saying that LIV had sought to undermine the European circuit. Kinnings is having to weigh up regaining some star power with unhappiness among some of his members that LIV players are just walking back onto the tour having caused so much disruption.



In an interview with The Scotsman newspaper, Kinnings accepted there was a balance to strike in integrating the returning players. “But we also have to protect the tour against an entity who spent, so we are told, over $7 billion, with one of their aims being to ‘destroy the DP World Tour,’” Kinnings said. “I have heard that from so many different people they talked to, who I have known for over 30 years within the game and who I trust implicitly.” Rory McIlroy has been outspoken in his criticism of LIV Golf. Getty Images Six-time major champion Rory McIlroy, who has been outspoken against LIV Golf since its formation, backed up Kinnings’ comments. Speaking Wednesday at the Abu Dhabi Championship, McIlroy said: “I agree with everything that Guy said. They took players, they took sponsors, they turned professional golf into an arms race.



“They were going around Augusta saying they wanted to destroy the European tour.” Reuters, AP News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: Swans ‘bitterly disappointed’ as new details emerge in Papley’s case
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLAFL 2026 Swans ‘bitterly disappointed’ as new details emerge in Papley’s case Jake Niall and Christy Doran Updated November 5, 2026 — 2:18pm ,first published 1:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The AFL is not expected to take punitive action against Swans star Tom Papley for allegedly driving under the influence of an illicit drug until police confirm the second sample for presence of the drug. As Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich said the Swans were “bitterly disappointed”, sources familiar with the league’s position said that the AFL and the Swans intended to wait until the results of the secondary sample taken at the scene by police (often called the “B sample”) were determined. Tom Papley has failed a roadside drug test. AFL Photos Papley tested positive to methylamphetamine when he was pulled over by police for a roadside drug test, caused by the suspension of his licence for unpaid parking fines. While the Swans and the AFL await confirmation of the positive result, a source familiar with Papley’s explanation said he had paid the parking fines over the weekend, but that he had been pulled over by NSW Police because his licence was suspended on October 29 (last Thursday).



Papley had paid the fines shortly after returning from overseas, but he did not call Service NSW to register the payment, which was in the backlog of late payment fees. Consequently, his licence was cancelled one day before he was pulled over. The AFL is conscious that an NRL player, Josh Addo-Carr, had a false positive test for illicit drugs and does not intend to rush any potential sanction until police have completed their process and the secondary test finding has been made. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich. Sitthixay Ditthavong The standard punishment for a player whose alleged drug use enters the public domain is a two-match ban, as evident with Jack Ginnivan and Bailey Smith at their previous clubs and most recently with Carlton’s Lachie Cowan, who was taken to hospital by ambulance last month. The Papley incident has exasperated the Swans, given that it follows the Pullman Hotel scandal, in which five current players (Papley not being one of them) were present in the hotel room in an incident in which some of the women, exotic dancers, alleged inappropriate touching, prompting a police investigation that is ongoing.



Vice captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice were stood down from round 24 and the club’s two finals for what the Swans termed a “serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards”. Those AFL-endorsed club bans were separate from the ongoing police investigation. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Swans star Tom Papley returns a positive roadside drug test The players have denied wrongdoing from the incident, which is also subject to potential civil legal action by the women. All-Australian defender Blakey, who was unhappy with the club over the portrayal of his involvement in the Pullman scandal, has since been traded to North Melbourne and signed a contract worth close to $12 million over eight years. Speaking briefly to reporters on Thursday at the club’s Moore Park base, Pavlich issued an “unreserved apology” to members, fans and corporate partners for “letting them down again”.



“We’re obviously bitterly disappointed that we’re here talking about this today,” Pavlich said. “We’re really disappointed in Tom, himself – we voiced that pretty directly to him yesterday. “We apologise unreservedly to our members, fans and corporate partners – we’ve let them down again. We must be better. It’s a really disappointing time for the footy club. “But given this is a police matter we cannot make any further comment until such time that the secondary sample comes through, and that test is verified. We’ll work through that process over the next period, and we’ll update everyone after that.”



Asked whether the latest incident was further evidence of a cultural issue at the club, Pavlich acknowledged the club had to do better. “I think we’re looking at the right now,” he said. “We’ve been identifying that over the last eight weeks. We’ve started some deep work in that with our AFL men’s department, independent advisors helping us through that. But they’re the questions that we’re asking ourselves right now, and asking our players. “We’ll continue to update everyone about that, and probably later today. We need to be better. This is not something that anyone is stopping short of knowing that we’ve got a long way to go, and we’ve got some deep work to do to understand how we get better for the future.” The Swans’ latest scandal will further stretch the patience of the club’s sponsors, with Pavlich admitting they were “angry”. “We’ve spoken to a number of them across this last period. We’re staying connected to them. They’re disappointed, they’re angry, [but] they’re supportive. They know that over a long period of time that the club has upheld really high standards, and I can guarantee them and everyone we’ll continue to do that,” he said.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has won her bid to mount a High Court challenge arguing that Section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act should be declared unconstitutional and torn up.

The Queensland senator applied for special leave to appear before the High Court after the Full Federal Court upheld findings that she had subjected Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi to racist hate speech with her “piss off back to Pakistan” tweet, sent in 2022.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson argues that Section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act is invalid. Alex Ellinghausen

The case is expected to test the limits of the implied freedom of political communication, a doctrine which the High Court has applied for decades but with an ongoing and at-times heated debate over its reach.

“Special leave to appeal is granted,” read the High Court’s single-line ruling, released on Thursday afternoon.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Alleged double murderer, former NSW Police officer enters witness box; recounts meeting Jesse Baird, experiencing homophobia as police officer in tearful testimony
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of former NSW police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial in the Supreme Court in Sydney.

Today marks the beginning of the defence case after more than six weeks of evidence from the Crown.

The accused killer and former NSW police officer will give evidence about what he says happened on the day Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies died of gunshot wounds from his police-issued Glock pistol.

Beau Lamarre-Condon (left) is accused of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, in Paddington on February 19, 2024. His case is that he acted in self-defence, the 15-person jury has been told.

He has also pleaded not guilty to an aggravated charge of breaking into Baird’s home six months earlier on August 17, 2023, and stealing his mobile phone and wallet.

The Crown alleges Lamarre-Condon developed an obsessive and jealous infatuation with Baird that escalated when Baird ended their casual romantic relationship in November 2023.

The prosecution case is that he planned to kill Baird and took a number of preparatory steps, including practising shooting his police weapon in a national park to experiment with the sound of gunshots and buying a surfboard bag to dispose of his body. The Crown alleges the accused killed Davies spontaneously to eliminate a witness to the crime.

The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon went to Baird’s home disguised as an Uber Eats delivery rider to collect some of his belongings and that his gun went off twice during a struggle with Baird, wounding him fatally, and that Davies shot himself during a second struggle.

There is no dispute that Lamarre-Condon cleaned Baird’s share house while his housemates were out and disposed of the men’s bodies.

Baird had been due to move out of the home that week, the court has heard. The Crown alleges he sent messages from Baird’s phone to the housemates’ group chat to give the impression he was still alive and in the process of packing.

As to the charge of aggravated break and enter, the defence says Lamarre-Condon used a key Baird had given him to enter his home at night.

Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, said in his opening address to the jury in September that Lamarre-Condon had “indicated that he pleaded not guilty to murder but guilty to manslaughter of Jesse Baird”.

“He’s entitled to enter a plea in those terms, but it’s not accepted by the Crown,” Hatfield said.

World.title: Vance believes America’s future is MAGA, and the future of MAGA is him
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaUS midterms Vance believes America’s future is MAGA, and the future of MAGA is him Michael Koziol November 5, 2026 — 2:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Follow along with our live coverage of the 2026 US midterms here. Washington: JD Vance blaming the Republicans’ midterm rout on the Iran war was surprising not because of the substance, but because we are so unfamiliar with anyone in this administration saying openly that Donald Trump got it wrong. That was effectively Vance’s message on Wednesday (Washington time). In a 600-word post on X, he did not just say the war had caused higher petrol prices, which Trump accepts, but that the war was not worth the electoral cost, on which Trump disagrees. Vice President JD Vance says the war is to blame for the Demcratic victory, but linked it to the US relationship with Israel. Tom Brenner/POOL Getty Images North America via AP He also identified four things that Trump/Vance voters wanted: end the war, focus on the cost of living and inflation, put America first and “change our relationship to Israel”.



Vance’s reaction to the midterm results was always going to be fascinating. As a potential 2028 presidential contender, he is possibly the biggest loser from a day on which Americans voiced their dissatisfaction with the mob that’s currently in charge. But it depends on how you parse the politics of what happened. Did Americans move away from Trumpism, populism and conservatism? Or did they determine that Trump and his Republicans failed to deliver on the populism, isolationism and “America First” doctrine they had promised? James Talarico became the first Democrat elected to the US Senate in Texas since 1988. AP Photo/Eric Gay Vance believes it’s the latter. And his election autopsy tried to position him as the movement’s future standard-bearer – one who would really put America first, rather than paying lip service to the idea. He hit upon the same themes that were discussed that morning by MAGA influencer Steve Bannon and long-time Trump adviser Jason Miller, who recently returned to the White House in a strategy role, on Bannon’s War Room TV show and podcast.



Bannon and Miller spoke of the need to end the Iran war, reject any Democratic push for amnesties for illegal immigrants, and rethink the US relationship with Israel – all things Vance highlighted. “The president said it last night – I’ve got to applaud him on this – Israel being a strong ally, they don’t need to get $US4 billion ($5.7 billion) a year or whatever it is the US is sending them,” Miller said on the show. “When we talk about America first, that means America first.” View post on X Alexander Gray, a Republican who was on the National Security Council during Trump 1.0, and is now chief executive of advisory firm American Global Strategies, supported Vance’s analysis. Some Republicans would predictably seek to parse the election results as “a repudiation of America First”, he wrote on X. But “the data makes clear that the message that won in 2024 hasn’t ceased being on the money; voters just didn’t perceive the Republicans to be standing for it this cycle”.



We know that Vance was never on board with the war started by Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. As a member of the executive, he was bound to publicly defend the president’s decision. Clearly, he believes the election loss now gives him more freedom. Related Article US midterms Lame-duck Trump swamped by a blue wave: What happens next? Vance has always been an opportunist: he was once sharply critical of Trump, even describing him as “America’s Hitler”, before changing his stance when it became politically expedient. On CNN, conservative writer Jonah Goldberg called Vance “exceedingly deceitful” amid Wednesday’s election fallout. But the vice president believes his path to the presidency, if he runs, depends on holding together Trump’s MAGA coalition. He sees the isolationist, Tucker Carlson-type part of their base – the so-called “new right” – as a key component. His problem with the Iran war was not just the price of fuel, but that it further aligned the United States with Israel and jettisoned America First. Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, said on i24 that it was “unfortunate” to bring Israel into the Republicans’ drubbing. “It’s very easy to always blame Israel for everything, but that is not the case.”



Things can and will change over the coming 18 months; some may work in Vance’s favour, others not. Some solution to the Iran war will probably be found; petrol prices will most likely come down. Netanyahu may no longer be Israel’s prime minister. Democrats might succeed in Congress, or they could overplay their hand. Related Article Live data

US midterms Live battleground tracker: The two races too close to call – and every seat the Democrats flipped Vance probably needs Trump’s endorsement to become the Republican nominee, which is why some people were surprised that he made the comments that he did on Wednesday. But Trump may well have licensed Vance’s strategy. He said he had spoken to Vance, and the vice president’s statement was “good”. Maybe he wouldn’t run, Trump said casually. “Maybe nobody’s going to run.” And Trump’s endorsement may also be a diminishing currency. His persistently low approval ratings are unlikely to change. It’s very difficult for the vice president of an unpopular president to succeed; we saw that with Kamala Harris after Joe Biden.

World.title: Gollan says import will go the distance in hunt for elusive Five Diamonds
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Gollan says import will go the distance in hunt for elusive Five Diamonds Craig Kerry November 5, 2026 — 2:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Tony Gollan has taken better horses than Brindavan to the $2 million Five Diamonds (1800m) over the past three years, but the premier Queensland trainer believes the improving import has the timing and profile to challenge for a breakthrough win. Gollan looked set for victory last year in the race for five-year-olds at Rosehill when group 1 winner and favourite Transatlantic hit the front late, only for Vivy Air to relegate him to second with a rails run. Tony Gollan-trained Brindavan. Racing Queensland/Michael McInally A year earlier, $15 shot Freedom Rally stormed down the outside to beat all but Pericles. In 2023, Antino, which went on to win two group 1s, finished 10th. Import Brindavan ($13 TAB) has earned a shot at the Five Diamonds with strong Saturday grade performances in Queensland.



Gollan and First Light Racing paid about $A515,000 (250,000 pounds) at the 2025 Goffs London Sale for Brindavan, which has two wins and two placings in each of his two Australian preparations. His latest victory was a two and a half-length domination in a 1600m open handicap at Eagle Farm on heavy 10 going, giving Gollan added confidence if rain comes on Saturday. “He’s a really nice horse, and a typical import,” Gollan said. “His first prep was OK, but certainly off a break, and this time around, he’s been a whole lot better again. He’s a totally different beast this preparation. You will get to see a really nice, furnished racehorse there on Saturday. “We’re really happy with him and he’s got a nice sense of timing about him.



Leading Queensland trainer Tony Gollan. Getty Images “It’s obviously a step up from the races he’s been … and if we’re lucky enough to get some rain on the day, even better, from what we saw the other day at Eagle Farm. “He’s a little bit different to what we’ve seen in previous years in the runners we’ve taken down there, but it’s certainly not an afterthought race. We’ve had this race in mind for some time.” He was also confident Brindavan would run the 1800m trip, which will be a test for many stepping up from the 1500m prelude won by Declichy Boulevard. The Chris Waller-trained mare was a $4 favourite for Saturday. “Transatlantic was coming off winning a group 1 in the Toorak and had that group 1 mile form,” he said.



“This horse has got good, solid city class mile form up here, but I think what’s not in the consideration here is the trip. “He will get the trip, and there’s probably a few in this race where there’s a question mark about running a strong 1800. Transatlantic last year, that was probably the query on him, but he ran awfully well. “We’ve come close in this race, so hopefully this is the year. Transatlantic cruises to victory in the Five Diamonds Prelude under Tommy Berry at Randwick last year. Getty Images “We’ve been thereabouts, anywhere between favourite and 20-1, like we sort of are on the weekend, but he’s the right profile of horse for this race and I wouldn’t be taking him if I didn’t think he had a chance. He profiles different to the others I’ve taken down, but, to me, he profiles like a horse who will run well.”



Ben Thompson rides Brindavan from gate eight. “He’s a lovely go-forward horse, he’ll lob anywhere I would imagine in the first three pairs,” Gollan said. “We saw him with a new string to his bow the other day, sitting outside leader and careering away, so he’s pretty versatile. “When we bought him, with his profile, we were thinking more winter carnival, but I think he’s developed really into a nice mile-2000m horse. “Whether we bring him back and we target some of the good mile races through the summer or we give him a break, depends on how he runs Saturday.”

World.title: Alan Jones trial hears of ‘bizarre coincidence’ with complainant and Herald journalist
World.content:
NationalNSWAlan Jones trial Alan Jones trial hears of ‘bizarre coincidence’ with complainant and Herald journalist Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander November 5, 2026 — 2:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

An alleged victim of Alan Jones declared to his wife days after he received a gushing birthday message from the former broadcaster that if Sydney Morning Herald investigative reporter Kate McClymont ever called him, he would tell her “everything”, a court has heard. And the very next day, she did. Sydney Morning Herald journalist Kate McClymont, right, arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court for Alan Jones’ indecent assault and sexual touching trial. Sitthixay Ditthavong McClymont, whose reporting of the sexual assault allegations against Jones triggered a police investigation in 2024, described the coincidence during her third day in the witness box at his local court criminal trial. Jones, 85, is standing trial on 19 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent against five male complainants between 2003 and 2020. He has pleaded not guilty and denies that the alleged acts ever occurred.



McClymont was asked about a text message that complainant “C” told her he had received from Jones in 2023. It was the only text message he received from Jones that he showed to McClymont, who told the court on Wednesday that there was a reason for that. She explained on Thursday that the man had received the “very gushing” message from Jones on his birthday four days earlier. Alan Jones (centre) arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court for his indecent assault and sexual touching trial on Thursday. Sitthixay Ditthavong “He said to his wife, ‘If Kate McClymont ever rings I’m going to tell her everything’ and for some bizarre reason I ring the next day,” McClymont said. Four years earlier, “C” had alleged to Herald columnist Peter FitzSimons that Jones had kissed and touched him non-consensually, while he was working on the then-2GB host’s personal staff.



FitzSimons had planned to put him in touch with McClymont, the court has heard, but “C” panicked before that occurred, and the interview never went ahead. McClymont said she was never told “C”’s real name during his short period of contact with FitzSimons, and it was a “bizarre coincidence” that she happened to call him the day after he made the comment to his wife. She had reanimated her investigation into Jones after receiving new information and another source had suggested she contact “C”. Jones is charged with indecently assaulting “C” eight times over a five-month period by touching and kissing him without his consent. The court has heard McClymont spoke to three of the five complainants at the centre of Jones’ trial, dubbed “C”, “A” and “H” to protect their identities, before police laid charges. She published a series of stories on Jones in late 2023 and early 2024. She told the court she gave her own statement to police about Jones in June 2024 – five months before his arrest – and another statement in September 2025.



Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, has suggested that the allegations against Jones were the product of “rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more”. FitzSimons was introduced to C by Jones’ stablemate and rival Ray Hadley, who had signed a secret contract to take over Jones’ prestigious breakfast slot only to have the offer rescinded when the station changed hands. Earlier in the week, McClymont told the court her reporting on Jones was not driven by newspaper profits or online page views. ‘I just wanted to make sure it was accurate, he was happy with what had been said.’ Kate McClymont in court on Thursday. She denied to Bashir that a quote set out in an article she wrote about “C”’s allegations did not reflect “the way it transpired in the interview”. Under re-examination on Thursday, she said that a day or so before publication, she had sat down with “C” to allow him to review his quotes from the interview. “I just wanted to make sure it was accurate, he was happy with what had been said and if he was worried there was anything that might identify him,” she said.



“C” earlier told the court the former 2GB host bombarded him with “love-bombing” in texts in the lead up to the alleged incidents. He said Jones first kissed him in the lift of the broadcaster’s harbourside apartment, but the “extraordinary” power imbalance stopped him speaking out as the alleged assaults continued. He also testified that Jones touched him under the table on the penis over his clothing at a lunch in Sydney in front of other guests. “C” alleged Jones also touched him in the car while he was driving the broadcaster. During emotional testimony, “C” said that he felt regret every day that he “didn’t fight back or say ‘no’ louder, but you couldn’t”. “Alan was protected, he was the Golden Goose,” he told the court. “There was no way in the world I could have said anything to anyone.”



Related Article Graphic content

Alan Jones trial Alan Jones sent ‘love-bombing’ texts to staffer before indecent assaults, court told On Wednesday, the court was played part of a recorded interview between McClymont and the mother of another of Jones’ alleged victims, dubbed “A”. In the call, the journalist said it was “brilliant” that police were involved and it would be “the nail in the coffin”. McClymont denied Bashir’s suggestion that she was referring to “the nail in the coffin of Alan Jones”. Police had said around the time of the call that they had received no complaints about Jones and were not investigating him, McClymont said, and someone coming forward saying they went to police was a “significant event” for her reporting.



The court has heard that “A” and his mother connected with McClymont after reading a story she wrote about Jones in late 2023. “A” first spoke to police in 2018, the court has heard, but a formal investigation did not commence until years later. The trial continues. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: ‘Game, set and match’: LIV Golf on the brink as investor pulls out
World.content:
Updated SportGolfLIV Golf Series ‘Game, set and match’: LIV Golf on the brink as investor pulls out Reuters Updated November 5, 2026 — 2:18pm ,first published November 5, 2026 — 9:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia has all but given up on hosting the popular LIV Golf event in Adelaide, with a senior government official calling “game, set and match” for the embattled circuit following an exodus of players and reports of a key investor pulling its funding commitment. LIV filed for bankruptcy protection in September as part of a restructuring after Saudi Arabia’s Public ​Investment Fund announced it would end its financial backing after the 2026 season. Cameron Smith tees off in Adelaide for the popular LIV Golf event. Getty Images A raft of players, including former world No.1 Jon Rahm, have since left LIV, prompting private capital firm BC Partners to drop its bid to relaunch the breakaway circuit, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday. Backed by public funding in South Australia, Adelaide has hosted four annual LIV events at the Grange Golf Club and was scheduled to stage the next one at Kooyonga Golf Club in March.



South Australia Premier Peter Malinauskas said on Thursday he could not see the event going ahead and cast doubt on the future of the entire circuit. “It feels like it’s game, set and match as far as I can tell,” Malinauskas told radio station ABC Adelaide. “That’s because BC Partners, that is the funders of LIV 2.0, I guess, have arrived at the same conclusion that we were, like, if you don’t get the players to sign up, then it doesn’t go ahead. Loading “In terms of other arrangements, we’ll have to take advice on that ... but clearly the event as far as we can tell won’t be going ahead at Kooyonga next year.” Kooyonga Golf Club filed a motion in a US bankruptcy court in September that said LIV had failed to pay the first instalment of its venue fee, despite being granted an extension.



The club said in an emailed statement on Thursday that it was aware of reports regarding LIV’s financing but had not received any advice from LIV. “We are seeking clarification,” it said. In October, BC Partners made an initial investment in LIV and planned to provide up to $US300 million ($428 million) in financing to help the league emerge from restructuring and strengthen its finances ahead of the 2027 season. The sinking LIV Golf series has copped another financial blow. LIV and BC Partners did not provide comment when contacted. The disruption caused by the Saudi-backed league to global golf has drawn plenty of critics but Australia has been one of its most enthusiastic hosts.





Related Article LIV Golf Series ‘We need a few more answers’: Why Cameron Smith’s future on LIV tour is still uncertain LIV is expected to appear at a Thursday hearing in US bankruptcy court in Trenton, New Jersey, to discuss various contracts, leases and assets. It is unclear whether LIV’s fate may also be discussed. LIV Golf launched in 2022 with funding from Saudi Arabia and lured leading players from the PGA Tour including Phil Mickelson, Bryson DeChambeau, Brooks Koepka, Australian Cameron Smith and Dustin Johnson with lucrative contracts. Others have been critical of LIV Golf, with DP ‌World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings saying that LIV had sought to undermine the European circuit. Kinnings is having to weigh up regaining some star power with unhappiness among some of his members that LIV players are just walking back onto the tour having caused so much disruption.



In an interview with The Scotsman newspaper, Kinnings accepted there was a balance to strike in integrating the returning players. “But we also have to protect the tour against an entity who spent, so we are told, over $7 billion, with one of their aims being to ‘destroy the DP World Tour,’” Kinnings said. “I have heard that from so many different people they talked to, who I have known for over 30 years within the game and who I trust implicitly.” Rory McIlroy has been outspoken in his criticism of LIV Golf. Getty Images Six-time major champion Rory McIlroy, who has been outspoken against LIV Golf since its formation, backed up Kinnings’ comments. Speaking Wednesday at the Abu Dhabi Championship, McIlroy said: “I agree with everything that Guy said. They took players, they took sponsors, they turned professional golf into an arms race.



“They were going around Augusta saying they wanted to destroy the European tour.” Reuters, AP News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: Swans ‘bitterly disappointed’ as new details emerge in Papley’s case
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLAFL 2026 Swans ‘bitterly disappointed’ as new details emerge in Papley’s case Jake Niall and Christy Doran Updated November 5, 2026 — 2:18pm ,first published 1:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The AFL is not expected to take punitive action against Swans star Tom Papley for allegedly driving under the influence of an illicit drug until police confirm the second sample for presence of the drug. As Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich said the Swans were “bitterly disappointed”, sources familiar with the league’s position said that the AFL and the Swans intended to wait until the results of the secondary sample taken at the scene by police (often called the “B sample”) were determined. Tom Papley has failed a roadside drug test. AFL Photos Papley tested positive to methylamphetamine when he was pulled over by police for a roadside drug test, caused by the suspension of his licence for unpaid parking fines. While the Swans and the AFL await confirmation of the positive result, a source familiar with Papley’s explanation said he had paid the parking fines over the weekend, but that he had been pulled over by NSW Police because his licence was suspended on October 29 (last Thursday).



Papley had paid the fines shortly after returning from overseas, but he did not call Service NSW to register the payment, which was in the backlog of late payment fees. Consequently, his licence was cancelled one day before he was pulled over. The AFL is conscious that an NRL player, Josh Addo-Carr, had a false positive test for illicit drugs and does not intend to rush any potential sanction until police have completed their process and the secondary test finding has been made. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich. Sitthixay Ditthavong The standard punishment for a player whose alleged drug use enters the public domain is a two-match ban, as evident with Jack Ginnivan and Bailey Smith at their previous clubs and most recently with Carlton’s Lachie Cowan, who was taken to hospital by ambulance last month. The Papley incident has exasperated the Swans, given that it follows the Pullman Hotel scandal, in which five current players (Papley not being one of them) were present in the hotel room in an incident in which some of the women, exotic dancers, alleged inappropriate touching, prompting a police investigation that is ongoing.



Vice captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice were stood down from round 24 and the club’s two finals for what the Swans termed a “serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards”. Those AFL-endorsed club bans were separate from the ongoing police investigation. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Swans star Tom Papley returns a positive roadside drug test The players have denied wrongdoing from the incident, which is also subject to potential civil legal action by the women. All-Australian defender Blakey, who was unhappy with the club over the portrayal of his involvement in the Pullman scandal, has since been traded to North Melbourne and signed a contract worth close to $12 million over eight years. Speaking briefly to reporters on Thursday at the club’s Moore Park base, Pavlich issued an “unreserved apology” to members, fans and corporate partners for “letting them down again”.



“We’re obviously bitterly disappointed that we’re here talking about this today,” Pavlich said. “We’re really disappointed in Tom, himself – we voiced that pretty directly to him yesterday. “We apologise unreservedly to our members, fans and corporate partners – we’ve let them down again. We must be better. It’s a really disappointing time for the footy club. “But given this is a police matter we cannot make any further comment until such time that the secondary sample comes through, and that test is verified. We’ll work through that process over the next period, and we’ll update everyone after that.”



Asked whether the latest incident was further evidence of a cultural issue at the club, Pavlich acknowledged the club had to do better. “I think we’re looking at the right now,” he said. “We’ve been identifying that over the last eight weeks. We’ve started some deep work in that with our AFL men’s department, independent advisors helping us through that. But they’re the questions that we’re asking ourselves right now, and asking our players. “We’ll continue to update everyone about that, and probably later today. We need to be better. This is not something that anyone is stopping short of knowing that we’ve got a long way to go, and we’ve got some deep work to do to understand how we get better for the future.” The Swans’ latest scandal will further stretch the patience of the club’s sponsors, with Pavlich admitting they were “angry”. “We’ve spoken to a number of them across this last period. We’re staying connected to them. They’re disappointed, they’re angry, [but] they’re supportive. They know that over a long period of time that the club has upheld really high standards, and I can guarantee them and everyone we’ll continue to do that,” he said.

World.title: Psychiatrist recalls Sockburn killer Zakariye Mohamed Hussein's 'dark and menacing' anger
World.content:
A psychiatrist who treated a mental health patient who murdered a Christchurch woman in the street says the man had spells of "dark and menacing" anger, an inquest has heard.

Laisa Waka Tunidau was stabbed to death by Zakariye Mohamed Hussein outside her Sockburn home on 25 June 2022, while Hussein was on unescorted leave from Hillmorton Hospital. Hussein was jailed for life with a 13-year non-parole period in November that year, and had previously been jailed for more than six years for kidnapping, stabbing and intimidating people across Christchurch in March 2012.

Hillmorton's risk assessment procedures were examined at the inquest in Christchurch on Thursday, with further testimony from Hussein's treating clinician, whose identity is suppressed.

Further questions about Hussein's psychological profile were raised in light of several threatening letters he wrote in September 2021, some of which targeted then-Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern. The letters also referenced conspiracy theories and multiple terror attacks staged in New Zealand and Australia. The clinician referred Hussein to New Zealand's Fixated Threat Assessment Centre (FTAC) as a result.

Waka Tunidau family lawyer Nikki Pender asked the clinician about Hussein's written comments two weeks after a mass stabbing at a Countdown supermarket in the West Auckland suburb of New Lynn in September 2021. The attacker, Ahamed Samsudeen, was being followed by police officers, who intervened during the attack, shooting and killing him after he charged at them.

"He referred to the recent stabbing at a supermarket in Auckland about this person [who] should have been deported and that if he himself was not deported, then he would also end up going on a killing spree," Pender said.

The clinician did not believe the attack was a catalyst for Hussein's threatening behaviour but said it was a period when he entered "quite a psychotic presentation". Pender later asked whether Hussein's recognition of a link to Samsudeen should have warranted a deeper risk analysis. The clinician said there was a lot of "odd content" and threats against both them and the prime minister at the time.

Coroner Alexandra Cunninghame asked the clinician about comments by another psychiatrist involved in the FTAC referral that Hussein was occasionally incorporating "Islamic violent extremism themes".

"I guess that in those moments when he's very psychotic, that he sort of became very dark and menacing and that was one of the themes that could be there," they said.

The clinician recalled a "flare-up" in 2015.

"He looked like a different human being. His look and his intensity, it was incredibly scary," they said.

"I remember an incident when he had ended up with a tennis racket on the lawn and we'd been watching him get unwell.

"When he was profoundly paranoid and psychotic, it wasn't something that came and went. It was something that was there, ever present and incredibly menacing, incredibly risky."

Pender also pressed the clinician on how Hussein's file was managed and documented after police laid charges for an assault against a nurse in December 2021. The clinician said communication lines between police and mental health services weren't always the best.

"We'd always really wanted more contact and engagement with the police," they said.

"I remember past cases where there hadn't been an indication that charges would be laid and that I'd made contacts without luck, but it hadn't been something that had happened in the past."

"We'd often wait for the process to happen and then hear what the police were doing and what the plan was, what the charge was, those sorts of things."

World.title: Fire breaks out near Auckland electricity substation
World.content:
A thick black plume of smoke is dominating the skyline in the Auckland suburb of Penrose as a fire breaks out near an electricity substation.

Fire crews from Ellerslie, Onehunga, Otahuhu, Remuera, Auckland City and Mt Wellington are at the scene.

Follow our blog for latest updates:

Vector has sent customers a text message saying there are power outages in Penrose, Mount Wellington, Ellerslie and Panmure.

Auckland City Fire and Emergency posted a message on their Facebook page saying the fire on McNab Street in Penrose was creating a lot of smoke.

World.title: Serious crash on State Highway 1 in Otago
World.content:
Firefighters are working to free two people trapped after a car and van collided on State Highway 1 near Waihola in Otago.

Emergency services were called to the crash near the township shortly before 3pm on Thursday.

The New Zealand Transport Agency said SH1 was closed between Surrey Bay Road and Lake Road, near Waihola.

Fire and Emergency said it appeared to be a head-on collision and crews were working to free those trapped.

World.title: Reports of triple assault at Auckland’s Alfriston College
World.content:
Alfriston College in South Auckland has come out of lockdown following a reported assault.

Police confirmed three people reported being assaulted around 1.19pm, though none are seriously injured.

The school placed itself into a precautionary lockdown. It lifted before 3pm.

Police stopped a vehicle in the nearby area and are speaking with its occupants in relation to the incident.

World.title: Graduate takes fight to be lawyer all the way to Supreme Court
World.content:
A law graduate who failed the Law Society's good character test has appealed the decision all the way to the Supreme Court where a judge has now decided his case is "weak but not wholly devoid of merit".

The man, referred to by the court as Mr Gold, was refused a certificate of good character on grounds the Law Society said included a Family Court case where a judge made previously reported findings of physical and psychological abuse of his wife.

While he denied the allegations, he completed a stopping violence programme required by the court. The Law Society said there were other aspects of his character indicating he was unfit, and his character references were "insubstantial".

The beneficiary's bid to practise the law then became a matter for the courts as he challenged the decision.

Years on, it has now arrived at the country's highest court where Justice Campbell overturned a decision on a fee waiver.

It meant Gold could now apply for permission to challenge an earlier lower court ruling - that he was out of time for further appeals - without paying the filing fee of about $1500.

The Law Society was approached by RNZ, and declined to comment on the judgment made publicly available last week.

An appeals journey begins

The Law Society's refusal to grant Gold a certificate of character - necessary for admission to the bar - prompted his application to the High Court, challenging the decision.

But in a February 2025 High Court ruling, Justice O'Gorman upheld the society's decision.

She said she was not satisfied that Gold was "a fit and proper person", claiming "a defect in character reflected in disproportionate and misguided aggravation against persons he perceives to have wrongly challenged him, coupled with the tendency to blame others".

She declined to admit him as a barrister and solicitor. Gold was also ordered to pay court costs.

Gold then tried to appeal the judgments but didn't do so within the required timeframe, and the Court of Appeal declined to extend the timeframe.

Gold sought leave to appeal that decision not to give an extension in the Supreme Court, where he also asked for the $1500 filing fee to be waived on the basis that he was on the benefit and couldn't afford it.

In his judgment published last week, Campbell said the deputy registrar had to weigh whether waiving the fee would promote access to justice.

He said the deputy registrar accepted that Gold was unable to pay, but declined the waiver, considering the proposed appeal was "wholly devoid of merit, was vexatious and would not be pursued by a reasonable and solvent litigant".

It appeared to be a further manifestation of what the High Court characterised as a "tendency to make personalised attacks and retaliate by inappropriate use of legal processes", Campbell said.

"The vast majority of the submissions were not relevant to an appeal against the Court of Appeal decision and instead were devoted to alleging misconduct by the NZLS [Law Society], officers of the court and the judiciary."

Gold asked for the deputy registrar's decision to be reviewed alongside his revised submissions supporting his application for leave to appeal.

In assessing both, Campbell said the merits of Gold's application were "weak, but not wholly devoid of merit".

"His underlying claim is not frivolous. While he has pursued the proceeding with much vigour, he has not crossed the border into vexatiousness.

"I therefore do not consider that the high threshold for declining to waive the filing fee has been met," Campbell said.

"The filing fee payable for the application for leave to appeal is waived."

World.title: Police seek driver, victim in Whangārei hit-and-run incident
World.content:
Northland police are appealing for information about a mysterious hit-and-run in Whangārei on Wednesday night.

Police say a car was seen hitting a pedestrian on the footpath of Ōtaika Road, one of the city's busiest roads, about 10.45pm.

Both the pedestrian and the driver left the scene before police arrived, but the car was left behind.

Detective Senior Sergeant Shane Pilmer said police wanted to speak with the pedestrian to ensure they were OK and they wanted the driver to come forward to assist enquiries.

The car involved was a grey Mitsubishi Outlander, registration HDG380. It was not being driven by its registered owner at the time.

The vehicle was now undergoing a forensic examination.

Pilmer wanted to hear from anyone who saw the Outlander in the Ōtaika Road area before the incident or anyone with relevant dashcam footage from about that time.

Information could be passed to police at www.police.govt.nz/use-105 or by calling 105, quoting file number 261105/1328.

World.title: Watch: 'It's horrible': Fears over fate of dozens of pilot whales stranded in Wairarapa
World.content:
Some readers may find the video in this story upsetting.

Whale medics are mobilising in response to a mass stranding of pilot whales on the south coast of Wairarapa.

Ngawi locals say they've counted about 50 pilot whales trapped in the rocks along the rugged coastline.

Rob Bargh said it was tragic sight, with few of the animals still alive.

"It's horrible. The ones that are alive are on their last breaths."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407929786112

Fisherman Andrew Sim said he'd witnessed whale strandings before, but had never seen pilot whales come ashore in his more than four decades on the coast.

He said there was a group of people trying to keep the handful of pilot whales still alive wet and cool, but believed most of the pod had succumbed to their injuries.

Rob Bargh

"Nobody's happy about it. Very sad," he said.

"It's most strange that they've come in here, there's just no reason for it to be honest. Just bad luck, I don't know.

"It obviously happened in the middle of the night."

Project Jonah says at least 20 pilot whales have stranded. Andrew Sim

In a post online, whale rescue group Project Jonah said at least 20 had stranded. Four pilot whales were currently alive and health assessments were underway, it said.

"Preparations are being made for a refloat on this afternoon's high tide if appropriate.

"Project Jonah medics have been mobilised and we are working with Department of Conservation [DOC] staff and local iwi."

It said no further help was needed at this stage.

World.title: David Jones to continue trading under control of receiver while business reviewed
World.content:
The future of retailer David Jones's Auckland shop is up in the air after it was placed in administration and receivership.

However, the store will remain open for now.

The iconic department chain, which has dozens of stores across Australia and one in New Zealand, has according to the ABC had a breakdown in negotiations with its landlord over rent.

Receivers FTI Consulting and voluntary administrators McGrathNicol said in a statement today that David Jones's physical and online stores are continuing to trade under the control of the receivers, while they review the current operations.

David Jones chief executive Erica Berchtold said they have a well-developed plan on how to reset the business and will be working with the administrators, the receivers and our secured lender to pursue that.

"David Jones is an iconic company and so many Australians have stories and memories of visiting DJ's stores, and I thank customers, our team members and our partners for their continued support for David Jones through this period."

For the New Zealand arm of the business, David McGrath and Joseph Hansell of FTI Consulting have been appointed receivers of David Jones (NZ) Pty Limited, while Andrew Grenfell and Kare Johnstone of McGrathNicol have been appointed voluntary administrators.

Christopher Hill from FTI Consulting acknowledged the difficult trading environment for David Jones.

"We understand the current retail trading environment, rising costs, a significant and outdated retail footprint, and supply chain challenges have led to this point."

He said voluntary administration and receivership provide breathing space and an opportunity to restructure the business.

World.title: Australian racing icon and F1 world champion Alan Jones dies
World.content:
Alan Jones, the 1980 Formula 1 world champion, has died aged 80.

He won 12 grands prix during his F1 career and joined Sir Jack Brabham as the only Australian to be crowned world champion.

Jones turned 80 on Monday.

A statement released on behalf of Jones's wife, Amanda Butler-Davis, said the legendary racer died following a short illness.

"We are extremely saddened to announce the passing of our beloved Alan, who passed away on 5 November following a short illness," Butler-Davis said.

"He will be dearly missed and fondly remembered by those closest to him, as well as the many fans whose support he was always grateful for.

"Alan dedicated his life to motorsport, building a legacy that will live on through the countless people he touched along the way.

"Through his achievements, passion and unmistakable character, both on and off the track, Alan left an enduring mark on the sport both nationally and across the globe.

"As a family, we would like to take this opportunity to thank everyone who was part of Alan's journey for the many years of friendship, love and support. He was incredibly fortunate to have so many wonderful people around him."

Alan Jones won five races in the 1980 Formula 1 world championship race. (Getty Images: Rainer Schlegelmilch)

Jones was born in Melbourne on November 2, 1946.

His father, Stan, was a racing driver who won the 1959 Australian Grand Prix.

Jones wanted to follow in his father's footsteps and left for Europe in the late 60s, but could not afford to kick-start his racing career overseas.

He returned to Australia, but determined not to give up his dream, Jones moved to London in 1970.

He got his break in 1973 when he got a sponsored Formula 3 gig with GRD. He took his first win at Silverstone that year and went on to finish second in the British F3 championship.

He made his F1 debut in 1975 for Hesketh at the Spanish Grand Prix, a race remembered in infamy for a crash that caused the death of five spectators.

The team went out of business before the season finished, but Jones moved to Graham Hill's team, where a fifth-place finish at the Nürburgring was the highlight.

An ill-fated season with Surtees in 1976 left his F1 career in limbo, before the tragic death of driver Tom Pryce at the 1977 South African Grand Prix led to Jones being signed by the Shadow team.

Jones claimed his maiden win in Austria, which led to Ferrari offering and then reneging on a deal for the Australian.

Ferrari instead signed Gilles Villeneuve, while Jones ultimately signed for Williams.

Alan Jones drove his Williams to victory in the 1980 British Grand Prix. (Getty Images: LAT Images)

Jones won five grands prix in 1980 — Argentina, France, Britain, Canada and the USA — to claim the world title and become just the second Australian to achieve that honour.

He first retired from F1 at the end of the 1981 season, after winning the season finale at Caesars Palace.

He made a few brief returns before his final grand prix in 1986.

Jones continued racing internationally for many years, while also entering media. He was a commentator with Channel Nine as part of the F1 coverage in Australia from 1987 to 2002, and was also on Network 10 when it had the F1 races in the early 2010s.

He is survived by his wife and his six children, Christian, Amber, Zara, Jack, Camilla and Emma.

World.title: Brazil soccer match sets world record for most red cards after mass brawl
World.content:
An under-20s soccer match in Brazil is making headlines for all the wrong reasons, with more than 50 red cards handed out after a mass brawl.

The match happened on Sunday between Uberlândia and Mamoré in the first leg of their Minas Gerais Under-20 Championship semifinal.

As reported by the BBC, a brawl broke out when one of the Mamoré players taunted the opposition bench after his side took a 3-1 lead.

The mass brawl resulted in 40 players and eight staff members being dismissed.

Three players had earlier been shown red cards, as well as two Uberlândia board members afterwards, according to ESPN, taking the total to 53.

The damage to the Estádio Parque do Sabiá led to the military police being called, according to Brazilian news outlet O Tempo.

Uberlândia released a statement announcing it was withdrawing from the competition in a "gesture of fair play", allowing Mamoré to advance to the final.

The previous record for most red cards in a match was 36. That happened in an Argentinian fifth-division game between Atlético Claypole and Victoriano Arenas in 2011.

World.title: Rugby league great Paul Langmack dies aged 61
World.content:
Canterbury-Bankstown triple premiership winner Paul Langmack has died aged 61 after suffering a heart attack.

The club confirmed the death of the former Bulldogs, Western Suburbs and Sydney player, who represented New South Wales in four State of Origin matches.

After his playing career, at the end of the 1999 season, Langmack became an assistant coach at Wests Tigers, then head coach of South Sydney in 2003 and 2004.

"I am devastated to learn of Paul's sudden passing this morning," rugby league great Phil Gould said.

"He was a larger-than-life character. Paul was energetic, bubbly and enthusiastic.

"He loved his rugby league. He was so loyal to his many teammates and ex-coaches over the years. He loved them all.

"Paul also started many mental health support programs to help young kids, plus both current and former players.

"He was always thinking of other people. This is a significant loss to so many."

Phil Gould (left) and Paul Langmack (right) celebrate Canterbury-Bankstown's 1988 NSWRL grand final win over Balmain. (NRL.com)

Langmack's 174-game stint at the Bulldogs during the 80s was headlined by premiership wins in 1984, 1985 and 1988.

In total, he played 314 first grade matches in Australia, as well as 19 for Halifax in England.

Langmack was part of Australia's 1986 tour of Great Britain and France, playing 10 tour matches, but no Tests.

Benny Elias played alongside Langmack for NSW and on the 1986 Kangaroos's tour, as well as against him in the 1988 grand final.

Speaking to ABC Sport, Elias said the rugby league community will be saddened by the loss of a man who gave so much on and off the field.

"His name in rugby league will be forever remembered and always respected and regarded" Elias said.

"He was a champion of a player, champion of a man, and to see someone die so young is very sad."

Langmack had previously had cancer, and was an active member of the community.

He was passionate about mental health, working on programs with the NSW Rugby League.

"The greatest thing is philanthropy, and when you give your time back to people, and you help other people in society, in the community, it's certainly a real big tick," Elias said.

"That's what Paul did."

World.title: LIV Golf future in doubt as premier says Australia event likely cancelled
World.content:
The future of LIV Golf appears to be in serious doubt after reports that BC Partners, which provides financing to middle-market companies, is dropping its bid to relaunch the league.

The Financial Times reported that the private capital firm withdrew its support due to a failure to secure sufficient player commitments.

LIV Golf files for bankruptcy LIV Golf files for bankruptcy, flagging a restructure with a massive loan from the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia.

The professional men's golf league, a competitor to the PGA Tour, filed for bankruptcy protection in New Jersey in September as part of a restructuring after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), which has invested more than $US5 ⁠billion ($7 billion) in LIV since its launch in 2022, announced it was ending its financial backing after the 2026 season.

BC Partners's decision came as a deadline loomed to show there was enough player support to hold a tournament series in 2027, the FT said, citing people directly familiar with the matter.

The firm and LIV Golf did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

LIV has held four annual tournaments in Adelaide, starting in 2023, and was supposed to host an event next March at the Kooyonga Golf Club.

However, South Australia Premier Peter Malinauskas told 891 ABC Adelaide this morning that media reports suggest LIV's future, in his state at least, is over.

"I haven't had any official confirmation from LIV themselves, but I saw a report this morning, and it feels like it's game, set and match as far as I can tell," he said.

LIV Golf has died on a flawed premise and a broken promise While Adelaide showed just how good LIV Golf could be, the flawed premise of the breakaway tournament always spelled trouble.

"That's because BC Partners, that is the funders of LIV 2.0, I guess, have arrived at the same conclusion that we were, like, if you don't get the players to sign up, then it doesn't go ahead.

"As the state government, we've made clear to LIV that we're not going to be paying for an event that doesn't represent the calibre of what we've had in the past, and if the players aren't up for it, then it doesn't go ahead, and it looks like that's been the case with BC Capital Partners as well.

"The contractual arrangements between the state and LIV don't come into effect because we only pay them when we put on an event, so we don't pay for anything we don't get.

"In terms of other arrangements, we'll have to take advice on that in regard to others, but clearly the event as far as we can tell won't be going ahead at Kooyonga next year."

Former world number one Jon Rahm is among a wave of high-profile golfers who have left LIV Golf since it filed for bankruptcy protection.

LIV is expected to appear at a hearing on Thursday, local time, in US bankruptcy court in Trenton, New Jersey, to discuss various contracts, leases and assets. It is unclear whether LIV's ultimate fate may also be discussed.

In October, BC Partners made an initial investment in LIV Golf, providing up to $300 million in financing to help the league emerge from restructuring and strengthen its finances ahead of the 2027 season.

LIV Golf lured leading players from the PGA Tour, including Phil Mickelson, Bryson DeChambeau, Brooks Koepka and Dustin Johnson, with lucrative contracts.

DeChambeau, one of the biggest names on LIV's player roster, recently said the league's business model for the proposed 2.0 era "makes a lot of sense" and that he hoped that it would last "forever".

Others have been critical of LIV Golf, with DP ‌World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings saying LIV sought to undermine the European circuit.

"They took players; they took sponsors; they turned professional golf into an arms race," Rory McIlroy told reporters earlier on Wednesday ahead of the Abu Dhabi Championship.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Rarely used rule sees Renegades claim final ball win in WBBL thriller
World.content:
One of cricket's rarely needed rules has cost the Hobart Hurricanes in a four-wicket WBBL loss to the Melbourne Renegades.

With one ball remaining in the Renegades' run chase, scores were locked at 154 runs apiece in a Wednesday night thriller in Hobart.

Renegades batter Deandra Dottin missed the final delivery, which was taken by wicketkeeper Lizelle Lee standing up to the stumps.

But as players readied for a super over finish, replays showed Lee had taken the ball just in front of the stumps, leading to a no-ball — and a Renegades victory.

The Hurricanes, with captain Nicola Carey top-scoring with 62 from 43 balls, posted 7-154 despite Renegades skipper Sophie Molineux capturing 4-22.

The Renegades, powered by opener Hayley Matthews (59 from 44 balls), were cruising at 1-101 in the 13th over.

But the visitors stumbled, losing 5-37 to set up a bizarre finish that also featured a fielding restriction penalty against Hobart.

The Hurricanes remain winless on the bottom of the ladder after three games amid injury concern over West Indian ace Chinelle Henry.

Henry smacked 36 from 18 balls in Hobart's innings but, after bowling just one over costing 14 runs, hobbled from the field with a suspected hip injury.

Henry's departure came as her compatriot Matthews dominated Hobart's bowlers with a classy knock laced with eight boundaries.

Matthews and Courtney Webb (29 from 25) advanced the Renegades to 1-101 before late twists.

Webb's dismissal was rapidly followed by Molineux (six) falling to a spectacular caught-and-bowled by Molly Strano, who leapt high to complete a one-hander.

In the next over, the dangerous Matthews was bowled by Graham as the visitors slipped from 1-101 in the 13th over to a precarious 4-108 in a 12-ball span.

With 33 runs required from the last four overs, the Renegades took the power surge and soon whittled down their target to five runs from three balls.

Then, a fielding restriction penalty was imposed on the Hurricanes for not bowling their 20 overs in the specified time: they were only allowed two fielders outside the circle.

After a dot ball, Dottin edged the penultimate ball to the deep third man boundary, where a fielder likely would have been stationed.

With scores tied, Dottin couldn't make contact with the last ball and players converged, expecting a super over.

As they huddled, replays showed the gloves of Hurricanes keeper Lee taking the ball in front of the stumps and the umpires called a no ball, giving the Renegades the winning run and their first win of the tournament.

AAP

World.title: Keeper breaks silence after collision that led to Spanish player's death
World.content:
Warning: the video in this article may cause distress for some readers

Jesus Owono says he is going through the most difficult days of his life following the death of Tenerife forward Jesus De Miguel.

Owono and De Miguel were involved in a collision during a match between Andorra and Tenerife on Monday, after which the striker was taken into intensive care. De Miguel died on Tuesday morning.

"These are the most difficult days of my life," Owono said in a statement released by his club FC Andorra on Wednesday, local time.

Footballer dies after on-field collision Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel dies after a horrific clash with an opposition goalkeeper that has sparked an investigation by Spanish police.

"I struggle to find the words, and I find it very hard to process what has happened. I know there will be many questions to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect.

"But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are experiencing. Rest in peace, Jesus."

Owono deactivated his Instagram account on Tuesday after receiving abuse online, with some users commenting 'murderer' on his posts. Andorra said that they were offering psychological support to anyone at the club who needed it following De Miguel's death.

Andorra centre back Lautaro Spatz defended his teammate Owono on Tuesday evening.

"I also want to say a few words about my teammate, goalkeeper and friend, who is deeply affected by what has happened," Spatz said on social media.

"Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment, and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone."

"In football, unfortunate incidents can happen, but no one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences," continued Spatz, also sending his condolences to De Miguel's family and Tenerife.

The Equatoguinean Football Federation expressed support for Owono in a statement on Tuesday, adding that the 25-year-old was going through profound sorrow and grief.

Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.

Can Vidalet goalkeeper Michel Owono said on social media that he was receiving racist abuse, with people confusing him with the Andorra player.

Spanish national police have opened a routine investigation into De Miguel's death.

Reuters

World.title: Opetaia moves up to heavyweight to fight former world champ Wilder
World.content:
Jai Opetaia has been handed the fight of his life as he gambles on moving up to heavyweight to take on thunder-hitting former world champion Deontay Wilder.

Australia's unbeaten cruiserweight maestro, a contender for the sport's best pound-for-pound fighter, will venture into uncharted waters by tackling the explosive American veteran on the undercard of the blockbuster Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua show at Principality Stadium in Cardiff on December 11.

Wilder is now 41 and perhaps not the destructive force of old, but taking on one of the biggest hitters the sport has witnessed still represents a daring gamble for Opetaia, who is 10 years his junior, as the world-beating Gold Coast-based southpaw and The Ring Magazine champion protects his perfect 31-fight record.

It is the first major fight above the 200-pound division for Opetaia, with his promoter Dana White admitting: "It's a very dangerous fight for him considering where he sits in his division right now.

"But he's a fighter; he'll fight anybody, even at heavyweight with a guy who hits as hard as Wilder does."

It looks poised to be a one-off, with Opetaia likely returning to cruiserweight afterwards to chase a showdown with American David Benavidez, the division's other major unbeaten force.

Last time out in Nevada in September, Opetaia stopped Noel Mikaelian in the ninth round and called out ringside observer Benavidez, whose heritage has earned him the nickname the "Mexican Monster", with the request: "Respectfully, let's get it on.

"That's the fight Jai really wants, so we've got to figure that one out," White said.

"He wants to stay active, he wants to fight, and he doesn't care if it's at heavyweight or wherever. He's ready to go."

Wilder, though, is by far the biggest name Opetaia will have faced, a champion who held the WBC belt for five years between 2015 and 2020 and who had an epic trilogy of fights with Briton Fury, coming off worse twice after an extraordinary draw in their first bout.

But he has lost four of his last seven contests and, in his last outing, had to battle to earn a scruffy points win over British contender Derek Chisora in London in April, leaving his career record at 45 wins, four losses and a draw.

The all-British bill-topper between Fury ​and Joshua is being sold as the biggest night of boxing ever witnessed in the UK, with tickets in Cardiff going within an hour of going on sale and the bill being screened globally on Netflix.

AAP

World.title: Aussie stuns Djokovic to end tennis legend's ATP Finals chances
World.content:
